body.text: Until 2020, getting a computer to do something new meant writing code. After GPT-3, for a startling range of tasks, it meant writing a paragraph. The paragraph was called a prompt, and it turned out that the difference between a paragraph that worked and one that did not was — like the difference between a good brief and a bad one — a matter of clarity, context, and the right examples. Prompting is a writing skill. The best prompt engineers of 2026 tend to be former product managers, lawyers, technical editors, and teachers.

body.alt: Schematic of a feedforward neural network.
body.caption: What the model is, underneath: a very large feedforward network that has read more text than any human ever has. Every token you give it conditions every token it produces.

body.text: A language model is an extremely literal reader

Modern large language models read what you wrote, not what you meant. Ambiguity in the prompt becomes ambiguity in the output. If you ask for a summary without saying for whom, at what length, and in what tone, you will get an average of all the summaries the model saw in training — which is almost never what you wanted. The first discipline is saying what you want out loud, in ordinary English, the way you would brief a new colleague on their first day.

The way to test this is to read your prompt back to yourself as if you had never heard of the project. Is the task obvious? Is the audience clear? Is the shape of the expected output described? If any of those are vague, the model will average you into a blur. Writers get very good at this very quickly; engineers tend to resist it for about a year and then capitulate.
Clarity, context, constraints

Most working prompts share three moves. Clarity: state the task in one sentence at the top. Context: give the model the material it needs — the source document, the audience, the brand voice, the examples of good work. Constraints: name the format, the length, the register, the things to avoid. The Anthropic docs call these "successive clarifications," and the best practitioners iterate on them the way a copy editor iterates on a lede.

body.caption: Andrej Karpathy, "Intro to Large Language Models" — a one-hour survey of what you are actually talking to.

body.text: Examples beat adjectives

Asking for "a professional tone" gives you a model's average notion of professional. Pasting two short emails in the voice you actually want, then asking for a third in the same style, gives you something usable. This is called few-shot prompting and, for most creative or judgment-heavy work, it is the single biggest lever. Humans operate the same way — we are all taught to write by being shown writing that works.

The corollary: the examples you pick are louder than the instructions you give. A model will imitate patterns in the examples that you did not mean to teach it — a weird date format, a particular cadence, a use of em-dashes. If you want a specific behaviour, show it three times. If you want to avoid one, do not put it in even once, not even as a "do not do this."
The most overlooked move in prompting is the second draft. Read the model's output, notice where it missed, and add one sentence to the prompt addressing that specific miss. Repeat.
You cannot prompt-engineer what you cannot evaluate

A good prompt is the end of a loop, not the start of one. Before you tune, write down what "good" looks like: a handful of inputs, the outputs you would accept, and the ones you would reject. Run a draft prompt on the set. Look at where it fails. Adjust. The people who ship the best AI features in 2026 are the ones who treat evaluation like a first-class artifact and prompting like an implementation detail.
When to use a system prompt

The system prompt is the persistent instruction that rides along with every turn of a conversation. Put there: the identity of the assistant ("You are a careful editor for a law firm"), the non-negotiable constraints ("Never mention a specific dollar figure"), the output format, and the tone. Put there, not in every user message: policies, brand voice, format rules. The distinction is not technical — many APIs treat it the same as a user message — but it is architectural, and it keeps the running conversation clean.

body.label: Chain-of-thought, still useful
body.text: Adding "think step by step" to a prompt genuinely improves reasoning on hard tasks. The 2022 paper by Wei and colleagues showed this for a family of math problems; the technique has since become standard. With modern models, you often get the benefit automatically — they produce reasoning without being asked — but it is worth knowing the lever exists for the cases where they do not.
The 2026 working kit

The core skills worth developing in 2026: how to write a system prompt; how to assemble few-shot examples; how to write an eval set of ten inputs; how to compare two prompts on the set in a spreadsheet; how to use tool-calling so the model does not have to guess; how to use retrieval to ground a model in documents it did not memorize. None of these are mysterious. All of them reward about thirty hours of practice. The people who invest those thirty hours visibly outperform the people who do not.

body.text: A large language model is, in the most boring technical sense, a statistical completion engine trained on an enormous pile of text. Everything it is good at — writing, summarizing, reasoning in plausible-looking steps — falls out of that. So does everything it is bad at. The failures are not mysterious; they are what you would expect from a system that has never had a body, never been wrong out loud, and never known the difference between a document it memorized and one it is making up.
Confabulation, not lying

The industry calls it hallucination; a better word is confabulation. The model fills gaps with plausible-sounding material because that is what it was trained to do. It does not know it is doing this and cannot, by looking inward, tell a memorized fact from an invented one. A 2021 paper by Bender, Gebru, McMillan-Major, and Shmitchell — the "stochastic parrots" paper — was the first widely-cited warning that fluent text is not evidence of understanding. Five years and many capability jumps later, the warning is still live: the better a model gets at sounding right, the more expensive it is for a reader to notice when it is wrong.

body.caption: Computerphile on why ChatGPT lies — a plain-spoken explanation of confabulation.

body.text: The model inherits the shape of its data

A language model knows what its training corpus covered. The English-language internet over-represents some perspectives and under-represents others; so does the model. If the corpus thinks nurses are mostly women and CEOs are mostly men, so, by default, does the model. Post-training work — reinforcement learning from human feedback, constitutional methods, red-teaming — pushes back on some of this, but it is a correction, not a cure. Anything the model confidently says about the fringes of its data should be treated as a hypothesis.

The shape of the corpus also shows up in less obvious ways. Models over-format when the training corpus was formatted, over-use em-dashes when their RLHF examples used em-dashes, prefer certain structures when the fine-tuning set preferred them. Every model has a detectable house style. In 2024 several tools appeared that could distinguish GPT-4 output from human text with 80%+ accuracy on long samples, not because the text was bad but because it was suspiciously uniform.
Overconfidence is the common mode of failure

A well-calibrated system would say "I am not sure" when it is not sure. Modern LLMs are, by default, badly calibrated: they produce the same fluent prose whether the answer is in their training or not. Asking the model to show its work — chain-of-thought prompting — helps for reasoning tasks, but the deeper remedy is grounding: retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, citations. If the model says "according to this document" and the document is attached, you can check. If the model says "according to my training" you probably cannot.
The practical rule: the more confidently a model states a fact you cannot immediately verify, the more you should worry. Fluency is not evidence.
Jailbreaks and prompt injection

Because the model cannot reliably tell user instructions from content it has been given to process, a malicious input embedded in a document, a web page, or a tool response can override the system prompt. This is prompt injection, first systematically documented in 2022, and it is the AI-native security problem. Treat any text a model is about to read as potentially adversarial the same way you treat HTTP input in a web app. Defense is still an open research area; the production best practices in 2026 involve isolation (separate models for different trust levels), validation, and keeping high-authority actions behind human confirmation.

The 2024 Simon Willison classification is still the clearest map of the threat: direct injection (a user tries to override the system prompt), indirect injection (content the model retrieves tries to), and data exfiltration (the injection tricks the model into leaking something it was told not to). Of the three, indirect is the one most teams underestimate and the one most likely to produce a real incident.
What the agentic era changes

When a model is only answering questions, a wrong answer is embarrassing. When a model is using tools — sending emails, writing files, calling APIs, browsing the web — a wrong answer can do real harm. The move, well underway through 2025, toward agents has made every limitation above more consequential and added several new ones: tool-choice errors, planning failures, reward-hacking on long-horizon tasks, and attacks in which the tool itself is the injection vector. If you are shipping an agent in 2026, read the model's tool-call trace the way a surgeon reads a chart.

body.label: The good news
body.text: Every one of these failures has motivated a subfield. Evaluations have matured (HELM, MMLU, SWE-bench). Interpretability is producing real results. Red-teaming is now a profession. The gap between the frontier and the next failure mode has been closing, not widening. But it is closing by working on it, not by default.
What to do with all of this

Treat models like junior colleagues with patchy expertise, lightning reflexes, and a tendency to make things up under pressure. Verify. Ground them in your data. Give them tools. Keep the high-stakes decisions human. Write evals. Run red teams. Read Anthropic and DeepMind safety work; read the arXiv papers that arrived last Thursday. The field is young, the failure surface is large, and the best working attitude is to assume the next surprise is real and then go looking for it.

Rule of thumb for 2026: if a model's output would cause harm, spend money, or embarrass a human when wrong, a human should read it before it ships. The marginal cost of verification is almost always less than the expected cost of the error.

body.text: In 1886, a German-Jewish geographer named Franz Boas stepped off a ship on the north coast of British Columbia and began asking questions he was not yet sure how to answer. He spent the next fifty years in American anthropology and did two important things. He ran the field's first serious doctoral program at Columbia, training Margaret Mead, Ruth Benedict, and Zora Neale Hurston, and he used his data to dismantle the scientific racism that still dominated his discipline.

body.caption: Franz Boas (1858–1942), the founder of American anthropology. His students at Columbia — Margaret Mead, Ruth Benedict, Zora Neale Hurston, Ashley Montagu — shaped the discipline's twentieth-century direction.

body.text: Fieldwork, not library

The founding technique of modern cultural anthropology is participant observation — the researcher lives with the community studied for a year or more, learns the language, and makes a patient record of daily life. Bronislaw Malinowski, working in the Trobriand Islands during World War I (he was stranded there), wrote the first modern ethnography, Argonauts of the Western Pacific, as a study of a ceremonial trade network called the kula ring. The method he described is still, with modifications, what most working anthropologists do.

What makes a good ethnography is not the remoteness of the people studied but the quality of attention. Erving Goffman's Asylums (1961) did participant observation at St. Elizabeths psychiatric hospital in Washington, D.C. Philippe Bourgois's In Search of Respect (1995) lived for four years among crack dealers in East Harlem. Setha Low's work has been in gated suburban communities. The method travels; only the terrain changes.
Culture as the working lens

The central commitment of the field is methodological: that every human group has to be understood on its own terms before it is compared with any other. The anthropologist's problem is not that some practices look strange, but that one's own practices no longer do. A wedding, a war memorial, a sales meeting, a Little League game, a software team retrospective — each is a cultural performance, and a trained observer can describe any of them as an ethnographer from Mars would.
Mauss and the gift

Marcel Mauss's 1925 essay The Gift argued that in premodern societies, the giving of objects was never free: it obligated the recipient, bound communities, and structured rivalry. What looks like generosity, he showed, is often an assertion of honor and a downpayment on reciprocity. Mauss's framework illuminated the Kwakiutl potlatch, the kula ring, and — as later scholars (Marshall Sahlins, David Graeber) argued — the "reciprocity" of our own holiday gift-giving and of political favor-trading. Gift theory is one of the field's most portable exports.
The reflexive turn

In the 1970s and 1980s, cultural anthropology turned on itself. The discipline had been born in the shadow of empire; the ethnographer's authority had always been partly an artifact of unequal power. Writing Culture (1986), edited by James Clifford and George Marcus, argued for a more honest accounting of the encounter — whose voice is in the book, whose is absent, what the ethnographer is doing rhetorically. The field has not fully recovered from that critique, and probably should not.

Contemporary anthropology has largely metabolized the critique. Much current work is collaborative, with research designed and co-written with the communities studied. Indigenous anthropologists have become the leading voices in many subfields. The old model — a white researcher from a Western university descending on a non-Western community — is now the exception rather than the default. Whether this represents the subject's decline or its maturation depends on the commentator.
Why it still matters

A careful anthropology sits in the way of several bad habits: that the reader's own culture is the default, that other ways of living are charming but wrong, that a snapshot from one visit can stand in for a people's history. It is the social science most interested in listening before theorizing. The discipline's current reputation is uneven, but at its best it is still doing the hardest work in the social sciences.

Zora Neale Hurston, trained under Boas at Columbia, was both a distinguished ethnographer and a major novelist. Her 1935 collection Mules and Men — folklore collected in Florida and Louisiana — is anthropology as American literature. Their Eyes Were Watching God came out two years later.
Learn it: doing a two-hour mini-ethnography

Pick a semi-public setting you can sit in for two hours without attracting attention — a coffee shop, a laundromat, a subway platform. Take a notebook. For the first 20 minutes, record only physical description: what's there, who's there, what they look like, how loud it is, what it smells like. For the next 40 minutes, record behavior: what individuals do, in what order, for how long. For the final hour, record interactions: who speaks to whom, in what register (formal, joking, hostile), what the opening and closing rituals of each encounter look like. Do not talk to anyone. When you leave, take another thirty minutes to write a "thick" account — what the behaviors probably mean to the participants, what kind of norms they imply, what would look like a breach if someone did the wrong thing. Compare your notes to Whyte's Street Corner Society or Liebow's Tally's Corner; you will have reproduced, in miniature, the founding method of the discipline.
Worked example: the kula ring

Malinowski spent three years in the Trobriand Islands (1914–1918, partly because war had stranded him there as an Austro-Hungarian subject in British territory). He observed a ceremonial exchange system. Red shell necklaces (soulava) traveled clockwise around a ring of islands; white shell armbands (mwali) traveled counterclockwise. No one owned them permanently; each exchange partner held a valuable briefly, then passed it on. A Western economist would call this irrational — you gave up a valuable for another valuable with no net accumulation. Malinowski's insight was that the kula was not about accumulation; it was about social bonds, prestige, and the maintenance of peaceful relations across a dangerous sea. The "gift" bound giver and receiver in a way a market transaction could not. Every later anthropology of economic life — Polanyi's substantivism, Sahlins on stone-age affluence, Graeber on debt — argues with or against the kula. Read the first and last chapters of Argonauts; you will see the method being invented.
Practice problems

Problem 1. You are observing a small office. Every day, the person who arrives first makes coffee for everyone; the person who arrives second refills the water cooler; the person who arrives third empties the dishwasher. No one has assigned these tasks. How would you write this up as cultural practice rather than individual choice? What would a breach look like?

Answer: This is an informal reciprocity system — a gift-exchange ring in miniature. The unwritten rule is "each arrival contributes to the collective"; the currency is labor. A breach (someone arrives and does nothing) would produce the same kind of subtle sanction Goffman describes: a glance, a silence, a complaint to a coworker later. Describing it as "individual helpfulness" would miss the structural character. An ethnographer notices that the system is regular, that everyone understands it, and that failures are policed socially, not formally. This is how a small office is a tiny moral economy.

Problem 2. A graduate student travels to do fieldwork in a village where women do not speak to unrelated men. She is an unmarried woman. What methodological and ethical problems does this raise? What would a reflexive anthropologist put in the ethnography itself?

Answer: Access problems: she cannot interview men directly, but she gains access to women's lives an older male ethnographer could not. Ethical: she must be candid about the asymmetry. A reflexive ethnography names the researcher's position — age, sex, nationality, religion — and acknowledges how these shape what data is available. Margaret Mead in Samoa and Annette Weiner's return to the Trobriands (1976) both wrote about how different researchers saw different parts of the same community. The ethnography should not pretend to a view from nowhere.

Problem 3. An anthropologist returns from a year in a community. One village elder has shared a sacred story on condition it not be published. The story is central to the argument of the book. What should the anthropologist do?

Answer: The honest anthropologist keeps the promise. The book must be written around the absence, or the argument reshaped. This is not hypothetical — American Anthropological Association ethics guidelines (2012 revision) make informed consent non-negotiable. Some books never get written. The AAA's principles trace back to the horror of the Human Terrain System (2007–2014), in which the U.S. military used anthropologists in Iraq and Afghanistan; the profession's repudiation of that program is the context for current ethics rules.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What is participant observation and how does it differ from survey research? (2) What does Geertz mean by "thick description"? (3) State the emic/etic distinction with an example. (4) Who were Malinowski's kula ring partners, and what did they exchange? (5) What is the reflexive turn, and what book name-checked it? (6) What is the AAA code of ethics, and why does it exist? (7) Explain Mauss's claim that a gift obligates.
The learning progression

Brand new? Watch Wade Davis's TED talk and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's "single story." Read Geertz's "Deep Play" (about 30 pages). Spend two hours in a semi-public setting with a notebook. Once you've got the basics? Read Malinowski's Argonauts, Mauss's The Gift, and Levi-Strauss's Tristes Tropiques. Take an introductory cultural anthropology course (the University of Michigan offers a free online version). To go further? Take a graduate ethnographic methods seminar. Read Clifford and Marcus's Writing Culture, George Marcus on multi-sited ethnography, and at least one serious recent ethnography (Matthew Desmond's Evicted, Alice Goffman's On the Run, or Didier Fassin's At the Heart of the State). Then spend a semester actually doing fieldwork — there is no substitute.

body.text: In 1959, Mary Leakey was walking a gully in Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, when she noticed a tooth sticking out of the rock. It belonged to a hominin skull that turned out to be 1.75 million years old — older than anything yet found. Her husband Louis had been looking for such a thing for thirty years. She had gone for a walk because he had a bad cold. That is how archaeology actually proceeds: decades of patient fieldwork, punctuated by a morning with a good eye.

body.caption: Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania. The thirty-mile canyon through the Serengeti plains has produced hominin fossils spanning nearly two million years of the human story.
body.credit: Noel Feans, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: What archaeology is not

Archaeology is not treasure hunting. It is not Indiana Jones; it is not lost-civilization theorizing; it is not metal detection. Modern archaeology is a slow, regulated, quantitative discipline, governed by permits and destroying — irreversibly — anything it digs. The ethical core of the field is that the earth is a finite archive and any excavation is a one-time reading. Much of contemporary archaeology now tries to answer questions without digging at all: LiDAR, ground-penetrating radar, geophysics, legacy-collection reanalysis, isotope studies of already-excavated bones.
Stratigraphy and the law of superposition

The foundational principle, inherited from geology, is that in an undisturbed deposit, lower layers are older than upper ones. On that simple observation rests almost the entire discipline. A careful archaeologist records everything in three dimensions, maps every find to its context, and treats the spatial relationships as more important than the objects themselves. An unprovenanced pot is almost worthless; a potsherd in its exact context is gold.

Modern excavation records every find in x, y, and z coordinates within a site grid, photographs every layer, and draws section profiles at every wall. The paperwork is enormous. Digital tools (GIS, 3D photogrammetry, iPad-based recording forms) have sped up the bookkeeping without changing the principle. The gold standard is that a future archaeologist should be able to reconstruct the excavation from the records alone, even if the site itself is long since built over.
Dating

Radiocarbon dating, developed by Willard Libby in 1949 (Nobel, 1960), gave archaeology a clock for the last 50,000 years. Dendrochronology, based on tree rings, gave a finer scale for the last ten thousand. Luminescence dating reaches further back; electron-spin resonance further still. Argon-argon dating extends to millions of years, and was critical to dating the Olduvai hominins. Each technique has systematic errors, and the modern archaeologist treats dates as probabilities with calibration curves, not certainties. The precision of the best current chronologies is remarkable.
Why the story keeps being rewritten

Every decade the headlines re-break: Göbekli Tepe pushes monumental architecture back thousands of years; ancient DNA rewrites the populating of Europe; underwater surveys reveal flooded Paleolithic coastlines; LiDAR in the Mayan lowlands reveals tens of thousands of previously unmapped structures. Archaeology's picture of the human past is less settled than the textbook suggests, because the sampling is biased (toward what preserves, toward what has been dug, toward Europe) and the best new techniques keep reopening old questions.
Ethics and repatriation

The nineteenth and twentieth centuries filled Western museums with objects taken, often by force or under duress, from colonized people. The current century is in the middle of returning them. The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA, 1990) transformed American practice; the Benin Bronzes, the Elgin Marbles, and countless other contested holdings are being negotiated between museums and source communities. Working archaeologists now take community consent and co-authorship as seriously as stratigraphy, and the field's journals have rewritten their submission guidelines accordingly.

The Rosetta Stone, found near Rosetta, Egypt in 1799 by Napoleon's army, made the decipherment of hieroglyphs possible. It has been in the British Museum since 1802. Egypt has formally requested its return repeatedly; the question of where it should live in the twenty-first century is one of the current flashpoints in museum ethics.
Learn it: read a stratigraphic section

Imagine a trench wall two meters deep. From top to bottom you see: 10 cm of topsoil with modern trash; 30 cm of compact dark soil with 19th-century glass; 20 cm of clay with Roman pottery and a coin dated AD 135; 40 cm of sandy layer with no artifacts; 30 cm of black ashy soil with Iron Age pottery and charred wood; 70 cm of undisturbed sterile subsoil below. Read the column. Each layer is older than the one above (law of superposition). The coin gives you an absolute date for the Roman layer (terminus post quem = "after AD 135"). The Iron Age layer is older than the Roman. The sterile layer below is the original ground surface before human occupation. You can write the site's sequence: Iron Age occupation → abandonment (sterile sand blow-in) → Roman occupation → abandonment → 19th-century dump → modern. This is how a site's story gets built. Every well-kept dig diary contains a column like this for every excavation unit.
Worked example: dating a layer

A 2019 dig at a riverside site in Portugal finds charred seeds in a buried hearth. Labs return three radiocarbon dates: 4,230 ± 30 BP, 4,190 ± 25 BP, 4,260 ± 35 BP (BP = "before present," calibrated to 1950). The three dates cluster tightly around 4,220 BP. Calibrated to the calendar — because atmospheric 14C has fluctuated — this corresponds to about 2,880 to 2,780 BCE, with highest probability around 2,820 BCE. The archaeologist does not write "dated to 2,820 BCE"; she writes "late Chalcolithic, most probable calendar age 2,880–2,780 BCE (95% confidence)." Modern archaeology treats dates as probability distributions, not point estimates. Bayesian modeling (software: OxCal) combines multiple dates with stratigraphic constraints to produce tighter chronologies. The field has been quietly transformed by these statistical tools in the last two decades.
Practice problems

Problem 1. You find a potsherd on the surface of a field. A colleague says "Great — can you date it?" What do you say? Why is an unprovenanced sherd nearly worthless for dating even if the style is well-known?

Answer: A surface find has no stratigraphic context. You can stylistically date the sherd itself — say, "mid-third-millennium BCE red-polished ware" — but you cannot say what *context* produced it. It could have been dropped last year by a hiker; it could have been turned up by a plow in the 19th century; it could be erosion from a site kilometers upriver. Context — the three-dimensional relationship to other finds — is what makes a sherd a piece of evidence. This is why modern ethics forbid buying unprovenanced antiquities: each purchase rewards the destruction of context and funds looters.

Problem 2. Radiocarbon dating is reliable for organic material back to about 50,000 years. What techniques would you use to date (a) a 100,000-year-old stone tool found buried in volcanic ash; (b) a wooden beam from an ancient Pueblo structure; (c) a 2-million-year-old hominin tooth in a Tanzanian gorge?

Answer: (a) Argon-argon dating of the volcanic ash gives an age for the ash layer, and the tool is bracketed by the layers above and below. (b) Dendrochronology — tree-ring matching — can date the beam to the year, if the species has a reliable master chronology for the region (most southwestern U.S. woods do). (c) Potassium-argon or argon-argon on the surrounding volcanic tuff. The hominin tooth itself cannot be dated directly at that age, but its stratigraphic context can. This is how the Leakeys dated Olduvai.

Problem 3. A museum holds a set of human remains acquired from an archaeological expedition in 1910, in what was then a colonial territory. A modern Indigenous community claims descent and requests repatriation. What is the applicable U.S. legal framework? What questions would the museum need to answer?

Answer: NAGPRA (1990) in the U.S. governs human remains, funerary objects, sacred objects, and "objects of cultural patrimony" held by federally funded institutions. The museum must consult with lineal descendants or culturally affiliated tribes; if affiliation is established, the remains must be returned on request. Key questions: Can cultural affiliation be demonstrated to the required legal standard (continuity of a shared group identity)? Are there earlier competing claims? Is the material properly documented? Repatriation is now routine; in 2024, museums repatriated more human remains than in any previous year since NAGPRA's passage.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) State the law of superposition and one case where it fails. (2) Distinguish terminus post quem from terminus ante quem. (3) What can radiocarbon date, and what can't it? (4) Name three non-invasive archaeological techniques. (5) What is NAGPRA, and what does it require? (6) Why is "unprovenanced" a curse word in archaeology?
The learning progression

Brand new? Watch Stefan Milo or Sarah Parcak for two hours. Visit the AMNH's Hall of Human Origins or the Metropolitan Museum's Egyptian wing and read the provenience labels carefully. Read 1491 by Charles Mann. Once you've got the basics? Read Renfrew and Bahn's Archaeology: Theories, Methods and Practice cover to cover. Volunteer on a real dig — field schools are open to non-students. To go further? Take a master's degree, or focus: read Colin Renfrew on prehistoric Europe, Kent Flannery on Mesoamerica, Brian Fagan on the Ice Age, or Elizabeth Stone on ancient Mesopotamia. Current frontiers: ancient DNA (David Reich's lab), satellite archaeology (Sarah Parcak), and African pre-industrial urbanism (Akinwumi Ogundiran).

dek: The study of human societies through what they left behind — from Olduvai hand-axes to last year's landfill.
name: Archaeology

body.text: Around six or seven million years ago, somewhere in the forested margins of East Africa, a lineage of small apes split off from the line that would lead to modern chimpanzees. One branch stayed in the trees. The other became gradually, awkwardly, bipedal. The long argument about why — about whether upright walking came before or after the emergence of tool use, about whether it was provoked by a drying climate or by something else — is the central puzzle of paleoanthropology.

body.caption: "Lucy" — Australopithecus afarensis specimen AL 288-1, discovered at Hadar, Ethiopia, in 1974 by Donald Johanson and Tom Gray. 3.2 million years old; 40% of a skeleton; the fossil that reshaped public understanding of human origins.

body.text: Upright, then everything else

"Ardi," a 4.4-million-year-old partial skeleton from Ethiopia, walked on two legs while still climbing trees. Australopithecus afarensis (most famously "Lucy," 3.2 million years ago) had a small brain but a pelvis and foot structure much like ours. For most of the seven-million-year arc, our ancestors' brains were not much larger than a chimp's. The big-brain period is the last two million years only — a late and recent feature of the lineage, not the first move.

The bipedal package — double-arched foot, short pelvis, repositioned foramen magnum — is ancient. The tool-making hand that can oppose thumb and forefinger is not much newer. Brain expansion comes last. The sequence matters because it undercuts the old "the brain made us human" story: we were upright, tool-using creatures for millions of years before we were clever ones.
Homo erectus, the first great traveler

About 1.9 million years ago, Homo erectus appeared in Africa and, fairly quickly by geological standards, spread across Asia as far as Java and China. It made standardized stone tools (the Acheulean hand-axe), almost certainly used fire, and lasted — in some populations — until only a few hundred thousand years ago. Everything modern humans do is built on what Homo erectus already had the body and the skill to do.
Out of Africa, with company

Anatomically modern humans (Homo sapiens) emerged in Africa roughly 300,000 years ago — the Jebel Irhoud finds in Morocco, published in 2017, pushed the date back a hundred thousand years from the previous consensus. Modern humans began spreading out of Africa some 70,000 years ago. They were not alone when they arrived in Eurasia. Neanderthals and Denisovans were already there, and modern humans interbred with both. The descendants of that mixing are still walking around: non-African humans carry one to four percent Neanderthal DNA; many East and Southeast Asians carry Denisovan DNA; some Melanesians carry several percent. The story is messier and more interesting than it looked twenty years ago.
Ancient DNA

Ancient-DNA sequencing, developed largely by Svante Pääbo's group at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig (Nobel, 2022), has rewritten the textbook twice in the last fifteen years. Neanderthal, Denisovan, and a growing roster of other archaic human genomes are now published; they have shown that prehistoric Eurasia was more genetically diverse than the fossils alone suggested. The 2010 sequencing of the first Denisovan finger bone — from a few grams of material, identifying a previously unknown human species by DNA alone — is one of the great recent scientific achievements.

David Reich's 2018 book Who We Are and How We Got Here is the general-reader summary of the current picture. The headline: population movements and mixing have been the rule, not the exception, throughout human history. Any story that treats a modern "people" as the unbroken descendants of a single ancient one is almost always wrong in detail.
New hominins, new questions

New hominin species — Homo naledi in South Africa (2013), Homo floresiensis in Indonesia (2004), Homo luzonensis in the Philippines (2019), the Denisovans — have appeared faster than undergraduates can keep up. A reader who wants to understand the subject should get comfortable with a field whose headline facts revise on a decadal basis. The public image of a single linear progression from ape to man has been dead for a century; the actual shape is a tangled bush with many branches, most of them extinct.

body.cite: Common paraphrase of the modern cladistic view (see Jonathan Marks, Tales of the Ex-Apes, 2015)
body.text: We are not descended from monkeys. We are monkeys.

In 2022, Svante Pääbo won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for sequencing the Neanderthal and Denisovan genomes. Pääbo's father, Sune Bergström, had won the same Nobel forty years earlier — an unusual father-son repeat in the prize's history.
Learn it: place ten hominin species on a timeline

Draw a horizontal line from 7 million years ago to the present. Mark the following in roughly the right spot: Sahelanthropus (7 Ma), Ardipithecus (4.4 Ma), Australopithecus afarensis (3.2 Ma), Paranthropus boisei (2.3 Ma), Homo habilis (2.1 Ma), Homo erectus (1.9 Ma–700 Ka), Homo heidelbergensis (700 Ka–300 Ka), Homo neanderthalensis (400 Ka–40 Ka), Homo floresiensis (100 Ka–50 Ka), Homo sapiens (300 Ka–present). Notice three things: (1) bipedalism is ancient (7 million years), big brains are recent (last 2 million); (2) multiple hominin species coexisted for most of the record; (3) "human" in the sense of Homo is only about 2 million years old — a geological blink. The common image of linear progress from ape to man is wrong: the hominin family tree is a bush with many branches, and only one twig (Homo sapiens) survived.
Worked example: what Lucy tells us

Donald Johanson's team found Lucy in 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia — about 40% of a skeleton of Australopithecus afarensis, 3.2 million years old. What do we infer? (1) She was bipedal — her pelvis was bowl-shaped (human-like), her femur angled inward toward the knee, her foramen magnum centered on her skull (all adaptations for upright walking). (2) She was small — about 1.1 meters tall, 29 kg. (3) Her brain was chimp-sized — about 400–500 cc, a third of modern. (4) She still had curved fingers suggesting she climbed trees too. Lucy falsifies the hypothesis that big brains drove bipedalism — her brain is ape-sized, her gait is essentially human. The sequence was: upright first, then brain. Subsequent finds (Ardi, Sahelanthropus) have reinforced this. Every paleoanthropology textbook written since 1980 is, in some sense, a footnote to Lucy.
Practice problems

Problem 1. A new hominin fossil is discovered in Spain, dated to 430,000 years ago. The skull has a large brain, heavy brow ridges, a robust build. Ancient DNA later links it to Neanderthals. Was this population on the Neanderthal line, the modern-human line, or both? What can you infer about the Neanderthal-sapiens split?

Answer: This is the Sima de los Huesos material from Atapuerca. Its morphology pushed paleoanthropologists to classify it as an early Neanderthal or Neanderthal ancestor; 2013 ancient-mitochondrial-DNA analysis (Meyer et al.) linked it more closely to Denisovans — confusing things further — and 2016 nuclear DNA linked it primarily to Neanderthals. The lesson: hominin populations were not neatly separable lineages. The Neanderthal-sapiens split likely occurred between 500,000 and 700,000 years ago, and there was ongoing interbreeding between hominin populations well before modern humans left Africa.
Problem 2. A modern European has 2% Neanderthal DNA. A West African has 0%. Why? What does this tell you about when and where interbreeding occurred?

Answer: Neanderthal-modern-human interbreeding happened after modern humans left Africa, roughly 50,000–60,000 years ago, in Eurasia. West Africans descend from populations that stayed in Africa (or that arrived there only recently from Eurasian back-migrations), and therefore have little Neanderthal ancestry. Non-Africans carry 1–4% Neanderthal DNA; East and Southeast Asians additionally carry small amounts of Denisovan DNA from a separate hybridization event in Asia. Modern human genetic diversity is still higher in Africa than in all other continents combined.

Problem 3. Homo naledi was discovered in 2013 in a nearly inaccessible South African cave. It has some primitive and some modern-looking features, and was dated in 2017 to about 250,000 years ago. What questions does this pose for the human family tree?

Answer: The species is a puzzle: it looks archaic in its small brain and curved fingers, but it lived recently enough to overlap with anatomically modern humans in Africa. It suggests that multiple hominin lineages — some very archaic — persisted in sub-Saharan Africa well into the modern period. Whether it can be shown to have interbred with or been contemporaneous with early sapiens is unsettled. Lee Berger's team has argued the remains were deliberately placed in the cave, implying mortuary behavior in a small-brained hominin — a claim that has not been universally accepted. Naledi is a reminder that the fossil record still has gaps, and that every new find can overturn conclusions that seemed settled.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What came first in the hominin lineage, bipedalism or big brains? (2) Who was Lucy, and what species? (3) What tool industry is associated with Homo erectus? (4) How much Neanderthal DNA do modern non-Africans carry? (5) What was the Denisovan finger bone, and why is it historically important? (6) Name three hominin species discovered in the last 25 years. (7) Approximately when did modern humans leave Africa? When did they reach Australia?
The learning progression

Brand new? Watch Stefan Milo's playlist on human origins and Svante Pääbo's TED talk. Read Sapiens' first 80 pages. Visit a natural-history museum's human-evolution gallery with a printed timeline. Once you've got the basics? Read Kindred (Wragg Sykes) for Neanderthals, and Who We Are and How We Got Here (Reich) for the genetics. Subscribe to the Leakey Foundation's podcast. To go further? Take a biological-anthropology course, or read the primary literature in Nature, Science, and Cell — the field moves in monthly-paper-sized increments. Learn to read cladograms. The current frontiers are ancient DNA on African specimens (where the record is thinnest) and the interpretation of Middle Stone Age symbolic behavior (Blombos, Diepkloof).

dek: The seven-million-year story of how a small, tool-using, upright African ape became the species that is currently reading this sentence.
name: Human Evolution
sections: Homo erectus and the first great migration

body.text: Around 2550 BCE, along the west bank of the Nile, a pharaoh named Khufu commissioned a tomb in the shape of a pyramid. It took about two decades, a workforce of tens of thousands, and the displacement of roughly six million tons of limestone. For almost four thousand years, the Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest structure on Earth. Almost every later chapter of architectural history is a conversation with monuments like that one: how to make a building stand, how to make it say something, how to do both at once.
The classical orders

The Greeks, inheriting the Egyptian pyramid and the Mesopotamian ziggurat, did something different: they organized their columns into three orders — Doric, Ionic, Corinthian — each with its own proportions, capitals, and moods. The Parthenon on the Athenian Acropolis, built in the 430s BCE, is the canonical example. The Romans added engineering — concrete, the arch, the barrel vault, the dome — which let them build structures of a scale Greek post-and-lintel construction could not reach. The Pantheon's concrete dome, built around 128 CE, remained the largest unreinforced dome in the world for nearly two thousand years.
Gothic, the pointed arch, and the structural leap

Between about 1140 and 1500, in northern France and then across Europe, cathedral-builders worked out a new structural system: the pointed arch (which directs loads more vertically than the round arch), the ribbed vault (which concentrates loads onto columns rather than walls), and the flying buttress (which resists the outward thrust from outside). Together these three made possible walls of glass — the great stained-glass windows at Chartres (c. 1220), Notre-Dame (c. 1200), and Beauvais (c. 1272, partially collapsed). The Gothic was, in its day, a piece of high technology.
The Renaissance return

Filippo Brunelleschi, working in Florence in the 1420s, solved a problem that had stumped the city for a century: how to put a dome on the unfinished cathedral without the scaffolding that was available. His double-shell dome, rising 114 meters above the city, reopened a conversation with Roman architecture that Alberti, Palladio, and Michelangelo would continue for the next two centuries. Palladio's Four Books of Architecture, published in 1570, became the textbook of Renaissance architectural theory and, through Thomas Jefferson and the English country house, of American government buildings.
Modernism, postmodernism, and now

Steel, reinforced concrete, the elevator, and electric light — all arrived in the late nineteenth century, and together they rewrote the grammar. Louis Sullivan's tall buildings in Chicago, the Bauhaus in Weimar and Dessau, Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye (1931), Mies van der Rohe's Farnsworth House (1951), Frank Lloyd Wright's Fallingwater (1937) — the modernist canon still shapes how any architect thinks about space, surface, and structure. Since the 1970s the field has splintered: postmodernism, deconstructivism, sustainable design, parametric computation. The through-line is still Vitruvius's old three-part test: firmness, commodity, delight.
Architecture is frozen music.

dek: Five thousand years of humans sheltering and showing off — from pyramid to dome to glass wall.
name: History of Architecture

body.text: Every building, from a Sumerian hut to the Burj Khalifa, is a negotiation with gravity. The weight of the roof has to get to the ground. The wind on the facade has to get to the ground. The live load of the people on the fifth floor has to get to the ground. Structural engineering — which is what architecture is, under the dress — is the art of making those forces travel a clear path.
The four forces

Structural elements carry four kinds of force. Compression squeezes a member end to end: a stone column is in compression. Tension stretches a member: a steel cable is in tension. Bending combines the two unequally across a beam's cross-section: the top is in compression, the bottom in tension. Shear is the sliding of one plane past another. Every material has characteristic strengths: stone is strong in compression, weak in tension; steel is strong in both; concrete is strong in compression, which is why reinforced concrete embeds steel bars in its tension zones.
Post and lintel — the oldest system

Two vertical columns (posts) carry a horizontal beam (lintel). Stonehenge does this. The Parthenon does this. A framed house does this. The limitation is that stone cannot span very far in bending — its tension side fails — so post-and-lintel buildings in stone have small openings and thick walls. Greek temples look the way they do partly for reasons of beauty and partly because the architrave stones would have snapped if the columns had stood further apart.
The arch and its children

The Romans made an engineering leap: the arch. A semicircular arch carries its load along a curved line of compression, so it needs no material in tension. Arches can span further than beams. An arch extruded becomes a vault; a vault rotated becomes a dome. The Pantheon's dome, built around 128 CE, is still a standard item in every engineering curriculum. The Gothic pointed arch carries loads more vertically than the Roman round one, allowing thinner walls and taller cathedrals. Every great nineteenth-century railway viaduct is, in essence, a run of Roman arches.
Steel, cables, shells

Nineteenth-century iron and, after 1860, Bessemer steel transformed structure. Steel is strong in both compression and tension, so it can make beams that bend without breaking and cables that can carry huge loads in pure tension. The Brooklyn Bridge (1883), the Eiffel Tower (1889), and the first Chicago skyscrapers belong to this generation. In the twentieth century, thin concrete shells (Candela), cable-stayed domes (Buckminster Fuller), and tensile fabric roofs (Frei Otto) showed that structure could be pushed to astonishingly light forms. The best contemporary architecture often hides its structural logic, but the logic is always there.

A useful habit: when you walk past a building, ask how it is standing up. Where are the columns? Where are the beams? What is in compression, what is in tension? The answers are almost always legible, once you start looking.

dek: The physics of keeping buildings up — compression, tension, span, and the elegant economy of load paths.
name: Structural Thinking

body.text: In 1811, a commission appointed by the New York state legislature laid a plan across the empty upper half of Manhattan: 155 east-west streets crossing twelve north-south avenues, in an uncompromising grid that ran from Houston Street to 155th. There were no parks — Central Park would not be designed for another fifty years — and the plan was openly hostile to anything other than rectangular commercial lots. Almost everything any New Yorker has ever loved or complained about in their city was shaped by that plan. Urban design is what happens when someone decides at the scale of a city.
What a city is for

A city is an answer to the problem of too many strangers living too close together, and the answer gets different in each generation. Classical cities were organized around religious and civic centers. Roman cities were organized around the forum and the grid imposed on top of conquered land. Medieval European cities were organized around the cathedral, the market, and the walls. Nineteenth-century industrial cities were organized around the railway station and the factory. The contemporary city is organized, disagreeably, around the car — a decision that has aged worse than any other major twentieth-century design choice.
Jacobs versus Moses

The great American urbanist argument of the twentieth century was between Robert Moses, who built hundreds of miles of expressways through and around New York between the 1930s and the 1960s, and Jane Jacobs, whose 1961 book The Death and Life of Great American Cities defended the dense, mixed-use, walkable block against the towers-in-a-park logic of Le Corbusier and the highway logic of Moses. Jacobs won the argument intellectually and eventually on several key projects (her campaign stopped the Lower Manhattan Expressway). Moses won, for a long time, on the ground. The argument is still shaping every planning decision in every city.
The things a good urbanist pays attention to

Density — how many people live per acre. Walkability — can daily errands be done on foot. Transit — is there a functioning alternative to the car. Block size — small blocks create options, large blocks create barriers. Building frontage — blank walls kill a street. Mixed use — a neighborhood with only housing, or only offices, or only shops, is dead half the day. Public space — parks, plazas, benches, wide sidewalks. Great cities score well on all of these, mostly because of decisions made a hundred years ago.
The contemporary problem

Cities now house more than half of humanity, and climate change has raised the stakes for how we build them. The global housing crisis and the global climate crisis are the same crisis, and most of the workable answers look the same: build more housing, build it closer together, build transit that can move people without burning carbon, stop subsidizing single-family sprawl. Whether any country's political system can make those changes on the required timescale is a question neither architects nor urbanists can answer alone.

body.cite: Jane Jacobs, The Death and Life of Great American Cities
body.text: Cities have the capability of providing something for everybody, only because, and only when, they are created by everybody.

dek: The design of cities as wholes — the argument between grid and organic growth, highway and sidewalk, density and sprawl.
name: Urban Design

body.text: In a limestone cave in southern France, about 36,000 years ago, somebody ground charcoal into a paste and drew a running horse on the wall. The Chauvet paintings — rediscovered in 1994, and the subject of Werner Herzog's Cave of Forgotten Dreams — are not charming primitives. They are fully formed works of observation by someone who had spent a lifetime looking at animals. The history of Western art begins there, not at the Parthenon.
Paleolithic and Neolithic image-making

The cave painters of Chauvet, Lascaux, and Altamira worked with a tight palette (charcoal, ochre, manganese) and a genuine sense of animal anatomy. They painted by torchlight, often far inside caves, and their images appear to have had ritual rather than decorative purposes. With the Neolithic came pottery, figurines, and eventually monumental architecture — Stonehenge, Malta's megaliths, Göbekli Tepe in Turkey. The separation of "art" from "craft" is a modern invention; for most of human history the two were the same thing.
Egypt, Greece, Rome

Egyptian art, remarkably stable for three thousand years, is ruled by conventions of proportion — the human figure drawn with shoulders facing forward and face in profile, the figure's size indicating its social rank. Greek art, starting around 700 BCE, began to pursue naturalism and — by the fifth century, in Polykleitos and Phidias — reached a canonical rendering of the idealized human body that became the template for Western art for twenty-five centuries. Roman art inherited the Greek vocabulary and added something Greece had been reluctant about: individual portraiture, often with merciless realism. Read a Roman gravestone and you see the face of a bookkeeper dead two thousand years.
Byzantium and the medieval West

After Rome, the Eastern Roman Empire — Byzantium — developed a visual language organized around icons: images of Christ, the Mother of God, and the saints, rendered in a deliberately non-naturalistic flat style that emphasized spiritual presence over physical likeness. Western medieval art absorbed the icon and then diverged, through Romanesque and then Gothic, into the great programs of stained glass and stone sculpture at Chartres, Notre-Dame, and Amiens. For most of the Middle Ages, art was made for the Church and read by the Church-going public as theology.
Giotto and the opening

In the Arena Chapel at Padua, around 1305, a Tuscan painter named Giotto di Bondone did something nobody in Europe had done for centuries: he painted people as if they had weight, shadow, and psychology. Faces showed grief. Bodies had volume. Clothes draped over flesh. The frescoes are the single most important inflection point between the medieval and the Renaissance; every Italian painter for the next two hundred years worked in the shadow of what Giotto had opened.

body.cite: paraphrased from Cennino Cennini, Il libro dell'arte, c. 1400
body.text: All that philosophers had said of God was ineffable, and all that poets had sung of him, and yet Giotto painted him.

dek: Thirty-five thousand years of image-making — from Chauvet's bulls to Giotto's frescoes — sketched in a single arc.
name: Cave to Cathedral

body.text: Sometime around 1415, Filippo Brunelleschi stood in the main doorway of Florence's cathedral and held up a small painted panel with a hole drilled through the center. He asked a bystander to look through the hole at a mirror held out in front, which reflected the painted panel. The reflected image showed the Baptistery across the piazza — in one-point perspective, mathematically exact. In a single demonstration, Brunelleschi had reinvented a visual science that had been lost since Rome.
Linear perspective, the Florentine discovery

Brunelleschi's method was codified in 1435 by Leon Battista Alberti's treatise On Painting, which gave artists an exact geometric procedure: choose a horizon line, place a vanishing point, and draw orthogonals converging to it. Masaccio's fresco The Tribute Money, painted in the Brancacci Chapel around 1427, is usually cited as the first great painting to use the new system. Within a generation, every Italian painter who mattered was working in perspective. The flat gold-ground altarpieces of the medieval world gave way to paintings that looked like windows onto rooms.
Anatomy and the body

Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and a handful of their contemporaries were the first European artists in a thousand years to dissect cadavers systematically. Leonardo's anatomical drawings — now in Windsor Castle — are accurate in a way no Western drawings had been since Greek sculpture. Michelangelo painted the muscles on the Sistine ceiling as a man who had held the bones in his hands. This anatomical realism was coupled with a return to the classical idealization of the human body; the result was the High Renaissance figure, which every academic curriculum in Europe would teach for four hundred years.
The Northern alternative

Meanwhile, in Flanders, a different Renaissance was happening. Jan van Eyck in Bruges, working in oil on panel around the 1430s, achieved a level of observational precision — the stubble on a chin, the weave of a carpet, the reflection in an eye — that the Italians could not match, because they were still working in fresco and egg tempera. The Northern Renaissance (van Eyck, Rogier van der Weyden, Hieronymus Bosch, Pieter Bruegel the Elder, Albrecht Dürer) absorbed Italian perspective and added its own close observation of light, material, and the peasant world.
The longer meaning of "Renaissance"

The works we group under "Renaissance art" span about two centuries and several countries, and the things they have in common — realism, observation, the return to classical models, the emergence of the independent artist as a creative personality — mark a break in how Europe would make images for the next five hundred years. Leonardo kept notebooks. Dürer signed his prints. Titian negotiated his fees. The modern idea of the artist as genius was born here.

Giorgio Vasari's Lives of the Most Eminent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects (1550, revised 1568) is the founding book of art history, and also why the Italian Renaissance story has historically been told as primarily Florentine. Read him against the Northern sources.

dek: Two centuries in Italy, the Netherlands, and Germany when painters solved perspective, anatomy, and light — and made human beings look human.
name: Renaissance Art

body.text: In May 1863, the Salon des Refusés opened in Paris, showing works that had been rejected by the official Salon. One painting drew crowds and laughter and outrage: Édouard Manet's Déjeuner sur l'herbe, which showed two clothed men picnicking in a forest with a naked woman looking straight at the viewer. The scandal was not the nudity — the Salon was full of mythological nudes — but the directness of the gaze and the flatness of the paint. Most histories of modern art begin with that canvas.
Manet and the break

What made Manet a threshold figure was not his subject matter but his handling. He flattened shadows. He painted surfaces without modeling. He let the canvas show through. His Olympia, shown at the 1865 Salon, is a courtesan on a bed looking straight at you, painted in blocks of tone that refuse the conventional illusion of three-dimensional flesh. The painting is still at the Musée d'Orsay; it still makes visitors uncomfortable, which is approximately what Manet wanted.
Impressionism and post-impressionism

Monet, Renoir, Pissarro, Morisot, and Degas followed Manet's lead and worked outside — painting landscapes in broken color and shifting light, painting dancers and bathers and commuters. The 1874 group show that gave the movement its name was a commercial failure and a critical one; forty years later, Monet's Water Lilies were being painted at scale for museums. After Impressionism came Cézanne, who argued that painting was about structure and geometry; Van Gogh, who argued that it was about feeling; Gauguin, who argued that it was about symbol and decoration. All three had died by 1906; their arguments shaped the next half-century.
The twentieth-century explosions

In the decade before the First World War, Picasso and Braque invented Cubism — fractured surfaces, multiple viewpoints, collage. The Italian Futurists celebrated machines; the German Expressionists (Kirchner, Kandinsky, the Blue Rider group) pursued emotional intensity through color. The Russian Constructivists made art serve revolution. The Dadaists mocked everything. The Surrealists — Dalí, Magritte, de Chirico, Max Ernst — painted dreams with oil-painting craftsmanship. Each movement was, in effect, a hypothesis about what painting was still for now that photography had taken its old job of recording appearances.
After 1945: New York takes over

The Second World War pushed the center of Western art from Paris to New York. Jackson Pollock's drip paintings, Willem de Kooning's women, Mark Rothko's color-fields, Barnett Newman's zips — the Abstract Expressionists argued that a painting could dispense with subject matter entirely and still function as a serious object. Pop Art (Warhol, Lichtenstein) swung back to images from consumer culture. Minimalism (Donald Judd, Agnes Martin) reduced the object to its essentials. By the 1980s, "postmodern" painting was absorbing every prior movement at once. The twenty-first-century picture is more plural and more international than any prior moment in the history of art.

body.cite: Jackson Pollock, interview with William Wright, 1950
body.text: Every good painter paints what he is.

dek: From Manet's 1863 scandal to Pollock's drip paintings — a hundred years of painters asking what a painting could still do.
name: Modern Art

body.text: In a Florentine workshop in the 1470s, an apprentice named Leonardo da Vinci was given the usual beginner's task: copy the master's drawings. Leonardo took it further. He drew animals, machines, currents of water, the muscles of the shoulder, the wings of birds. His notebooks, running to some 7,000 surviving pages, are the single greatest argument ever made that to look hard is a thinking skill, not only an aesthetic one. Drawing, five hundred years after Leonardo, is still the quickest way to train a pair of eyes.
Why you should learn to draw even if you do not want to be an artist

Drawing is the act of paying close attention with your hand. It forces you to see things you have been looking past — the exact angle of a nose, the way a shadow falls across a chin, the real shape of a shoulder. Doctors in the early twentieth century were often taught anatomical drawing for this reason; so were architects, botanists, field biologists. The skill is not decorative. It is a form of noticing, and the noticing transfers to other domains.
Contour and gesture, the two drawings

The two foundational exercises in any beginning drawing class are contour and gesture. A contour drawing is a slow, continuous line that traces the edge of an object; a blind contour drawing (not looking at the paper) is a useful exercise in paying attention to the object rather than to the drawing. A gesture drawing is its opposite — ten to sixty seconds to capture the overall energy, weight, and motion of a figure or pose. Master those two, and the rest of drawing is an extension of them.
Value, light, and shadow

After line comes value — the gradations of light and dark. The Renaissance term is chiaroscuro, the play of light and shadow that gives a drawing the illusion of volume. Training the eye to see value means squinting at a subject until the color drops out and only the lightness-darkness remains; a beginner drawer is almost always getting colors right and values wrong. Most of the difference between a drawing that works and one that does not is in the values.
The habit more than the talent

People talk about drawing as if it were a gift. It is overwhelmingly a practice. A sketchbook, twenty minutes a day, for a year, will take almost anyone from "I cannot draw" to "I am, in fact, drawing." The test is not whether your drawings look like the object; the test is whether you have learned to look at the object. Kimon Nicolaides, an American drawing teacher, wrote that drawing does not make the hand skilled — it makes the eye honest. That is exactly right.

dek: The most basic visual art there is — a line, a surface, and a pair of eyes learning to agree.
name: Drawing

body.text: In 1666, a twenty-three-year-old Isaac Newton, sitting out the plague in his mother's farmhouse, held a glass prism up to a beam of sunlight and watched the white light split into a spectrum of colors on the wall. He repeated the experiment with a second prism, which combined the spectrum back into white. The argument this settled — that color is not a property of objects but of light — founded the physics of color. A hundred and forty years later, Goethe would spend most of his intellectual life trying to prove Newton wrong. He was wrong to do so, but he was productively wrong.
Newton and the physics of color

Newton identified seven colors in the spectrum — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet — and organized them on a color wheel, with red and violet meeting. (The number seven was partly a numerological choice; the physics does not care about it.) Color, in the Newtonian account, is a property of wavelengths of light. The color of an object depends on which wavelengths it reflects. This is the account physics and optics still teach.
Goethe's counter-argument

Goethe's Theory of Colours (1810) spent twenty years trying to reinterpret Newton's prism experiments as evidence that color emerges at the boundary between light and darkness, not from white light's internal structure. As physics he was wrong. As phenomenology he was onto something: he studied afterimages, color constancy, the way that a shadow cast in yellow lamplight can appear blue. Goethe's color wheel — organized by perceptual harmony rather than spectral position — became the one artists actually used.
How a working painter uses a color wheel

The painter's color wheel organizes colors around primaries (red, yellow, blue) and their mixtures (orange, green, violet, the secondaries), with tertiaries between them. Opposites on the wheel — red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet — are complementary; placed next to each other they intensify, and mixed together they mute toward grey. The rules of thumb are more useful than their theoretical justification: place warms against cools to make things advance; lower saturation to create distance; limit your palette to three colors plus white and you will almost always get a better painting than from a full paintbox.
The practical vocabulary

Hue is the name of the color — red, blue, chartreuse. Value is how light or dark it is. Chroma (or saturation) is how intense or muted it is. Most beginner mistakes are value mistakes; most intermediate mistakes are chroma mistakes. Joseph Albers's Interaction of Color (1963) — a book that consists mostly of colored paper squares with careful captions — is the single best training for an eye that wants to see these three variables separately.

dek: The science and practice of how colors behave next to each other — Newton, Goethe, and the artists who had to paint the consequences.
name: Color Theory

body.text: In the Louvre, hanging in the Denon wing, is a painting by Poussin called The Rape of the Sabine Women. Beneath the mythological subject is a ruthlessly organized grid of diagonals, verticals, and horizontal bands. Every figure is placed for a reason. No horse is looking in the wrong direction. Poussin was famous for laying out wax figures on a miniature stage to plan his compositions before he touched a brush. Composition is what every picture has, whether the painter admits to it or not.
What the word covers

Composition is the arrangement of the visual elements within the frame — shapes, masses, lines of force, areas of light and dark, focal points. It is not the same as subject matter. Two paintings of the same bowl of fruit can have opposite compositions. It is also not the same as style. A Pollock and a Raphael are both compositions, built on different principles. Composition is the answer to the question: where does the eye go, in what order, and why?
The classical devices

Renaissance and Baroque painters worked with a handful of reliable armatures. The rule of thirds — placing key elements along imaginary lines that divide the frame into nine equal rectangles. The golden ratio — a more exotic version of the same idea, based on a specific proportion repeatedly used in classical architecture. The Rembrandt triangle — the pyramidal group in which heavier elements anchor the bottom and lighter elements rise. The serpentine (figura serpentinata) — a twisting S-curve for single figures. These are not laws, but they are so regularly effective that every painter should know when they are using them and when they are not.
Value is composition's quietest tool

If you convert any great painting to greyscale, you see its underlying structure more clearly. A Caravaggio becomes three black shapes and two white ones. A Vermeer becomes a subtle gradient from a shadowed left side to a lit right. A successful composition is almost always a strong pattern of values — the colors come second. An old studio trick: squint at your own work in progress until the colors fade, and look at the values that remain.
The twentieth century's rebellion

Modernism generally, and abstract art specifically, rewrote the rules. Mondrian composed with perpendicular lines and three primary colors. Rothko composed with large stacked rectangles of fog-edged color. Pollock composed by pouring paint and stopping. The classical devices are still there in most of them — Mondrian worked out his grids with painstaking care — but the vocabulary has widened. A contemporary painter chooses from a much larger menu of compositional possibilities than a Renaissance painter did, and every choice still counts.

A useful exercise: take a painting you like, and make a small thumbnail of it in five gray values (white, light gray, mid gray, dark gray, black). You will see the composition's armature in two minutes. Do this for twenty paintings and you will start to see your own.

dek: The arrangement of shapes, values, and lines that decides whether the eye reads a picture at all.
name: Composition

body.text: In 1908, the Austrian architect Adolf Loos published an essay called "Ornament and Crime" in which he argued, in the then-new rhetoric of modernism, that decoration on a useful object was a cultural failing. The argument was a caricature, but it set the terms for the twentieth century: design, at its modernist best, was about clarity, function, and the removal of inessentials. That aesthetic argument is also, almost accidentally, a set of practical design principles — and those principles are older than the argument.
Design is not the same as decoration

Design is the discipline of making a thing — a typeface, a chair, a website, a salt shaker, a subway map — so that it works well, is understood, and can be made. Ornament is a subset of design, and usually a small one. A beautifully designed chair does not need carved legs to be beautifully designed. When design is done well, it gets out of the way: the viewer pays attention to the subject, the reader understands the text, the sitter sits comfortably.
Four principles everyone should learn

Contrast: make different things look different. If two elements are not the same, make them clearly not the same — in size, weight, color, or shape. Alignment: every element should have a visual relationship with another element on the page. Nothing floats at random. Proximity: group related items close together, and move unrelated items apart. Repetition: reuse elements — colors, shapes, spacing — to create rhythm and unity. Robin Williams's Non-Designer's Design Book, published in 1994, turned these four principles into an entire design education; she called them CRAP, which every design student has since memorized under duress.
Hierarchy and flow

Good design controls where the eye goes first, second, and third. Hierarchy is the deliberate arrangement of importance through size, weight, color, and spacing. A magazine article has a title that is larger than its author name that is larger than its body text; a subway map has thicker lines for the main trains than the branch lines; a website has a primary call-to-action that reads before the secondary one. The test is simple: look at the layout for one second, then look away. What do you remember? That is what you have emphasized — whether you meant to or not.
Form, function, and the quiet argument

The American architect Louis Sullivan wrote in 1896 that "form ever follows function," and the phrase became the rallying cry of modernist design. It is mostly true and occasionally glib. A purely functional chair is not always a good chair; a purely functional website is not always a good website. The discipline matures when it recognizes that function is plural — a chair needs to be sittable and also desirable and also manufacturable and also recognizable — and that good design is the art of balancing those functions in a single object.
Good design is as little design as possible.

dek: The discipline of making things that work, using tools — contrast, alignment, proximity, rhythm, hierarchy — old enough to be almost invisible.
name: Design Principles

body.text: Roughly four and a half billion years ago, a cloud of hydrogen and heavier debris began to collapse under its own gravity somewhere in the outer third of the Milky Way. The center condensed and ignited into a star. Around it, the remaining material flattened into a spinning disk and sorted itself — by temperature and gravity — into rocky worlds close in and gas giants further out. The story of how we know this is one of the great achievements of modern science.
Inner and outer

The inner solar system — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — is made of rock and metal, in shells of mantle and crust. The outer worlds — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — are enormous envelopes of hydrogen and helium around dense cores. Between them is the asteroid belt. Beyond Neptune is the Kuiper belt, and beyond that the Oort cloud, a vast and tenuous spherical shell of comets extending perhaps a light-year out. The Voyager probes, launched in 1977, are only just leaving its inner edge.
The Sun

The Sun is an average star — neither enormous, nor tiny, nor particularly hot or cool for its kind. It fuses hydrogen into helium in its core at a rate of roughly six hundred million tons a second, and has been doing so for five billion years. It has another five billion to go before it swells into a red giant and, in a series of relatively calm expansions, swallows the inner planets. The Sun is 99.86 percent of all the mass in the solar system.
Small bodies

Between the planets sit more than a million known asteroids, thousands of comets, and hundreds of moons. Some of these are worlds in their own right: Jupiter's Ganymede is larger than Mercury; Saturn's Titan has a dense atmosphere and liquid hydrocarbon lakes. Pluto, demoted from planet status in 2006, is one of a growing catalog of dwarf worlds in the outer reaches. Every decade we discover an object or two that forces us to revise the rough sketch.
Exoplanets — the solar system, elsewhere

Until the mid-1990s, no one had directly observed a planet around another star. Today, thanks to the Kepler, TESS, and James Webb missions, we know of more than 5,500 confirmed exoplanets. They range from Jupiter-sized gas giants in tight orbits (so-called "hot Jupiters") to rocky worlds in the habitable zones of red dwarfs. A significant fraction of Sun-like stars, we now believe, host at least one Earth-sized planet in the liquid-water zone. Whether any of them host life is the biggest question in the field.
What we are still learning

The Parker Solar Probe, launched in 2018, has dipped inside the Sun's corona. The James Webb Space Telescope is mapping the atmospheres of distant exoplanets. NASA's Europa Clipper, launched 2024, will probe the ice-covered ocean on Jupiter's Europa for signs of life. A thousand years from now it is not the planets themselves that will have changed — it is our map of them.
Voyager 1, now in interstellar space, remains our most distant working spacecraft. Its radio signal takes more than twenty-two hours to reach Earth.

dek: The Sun, eight planets, a few dwarf planets, and a few trillion smaller objects — the neighborhood, properly described.
name: Solar System

body.text: In the first years of the twentieth century, a Danish chemist named Ejnar Hertzsprung and a Princeton astronomer named Henry Norris Russell, working independently, each plotted stars on a graph: brightness against temperature. The plot was not the featureless scatter they expected. It was a narrow diagonal line, with a cluster of stars above it and a small population below. They had drawn, accidentally, the first map of stellar evolution.
Main sequence

The diagonal line on the HR diagram is called the main sequence. A main-sequence star is one that is fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, and almost every visible star is on it. The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star, a quiet worker in the middle of the diagram. More massive stars burn hotter and faster and die young — a star ten times the mass of the Sun may live only ten million years. Less massive stars fuse at a lazy pace and endure for a hundred billion.
The end of the middle age

When a star exhausts the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a red giant. The outer layers cool; the core contracts and begins to fuse helium into carbon. Sun-like stars go through this phase, shed their outer envelopes as a planetary nebula, and leave behind a dense, Earth-sized ember called a white dwarf. A white dwarf is the last page of the book for stars under about eight solar masses.
Supernova

Massive stars take a different road. In their cores, fusion proceeds through heavier and heavier elements — carbon, oxygen, neon, silicon — stopping only at iron, which costs more energy to fuse than it releases. At that point the core collapses in a fraction of a second and the outer layers explode. A supernova briefly outshines a galaxy and seeds space with the heavier elements. Almost all the iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones was forged in one of these explosions, a long time before the Earth existed.
Neutron stars and black holes

What's left after a supernova depends on how much mass survives. Below a few solar masses, you get a neutron star — the densest object in the universe short of a black hole, a sun's mass packed into a city. Pulsars, discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell in 1967, are rotating neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth on a predictable clock. Above that, you get a black hole. The end of a massive star is not a fizzle; it is a full punctuation.
We are made of star-stuff.

dek: From the collapse of a gas cloud to a white dwarf, a neutron star, or a black hole — the biography of a star.
name: Stars & Stellar Evolution
sections: The end of the middle age

body.text: For most of recorded history, the faint smudge in Andromeda was assumed to be a cloud of gas inside our own Milky Way. In 1923, Edwin Hubble photographed it with the hundred-inch telescope at Mount Wilson and identified a Cepheid variable star — a kind of star whose brightness reveals its distance. The number he got back made Andromeda a galaxy unto itself, two and a half million light-years away. The universe, overnight, became enormous.
