body.text: In 2016, a thirty-six-year-old American climber named Brad Gobright fell sixteen hundred feet to his death off a route in Mexico. His partner had weighted the rappel incorrectly and the rope ran through the anchor rather than through the rappel device. Gobright was one of the best free soloists alive. He had climbed El Capitan without ropes. He died on a casual, easy rappel because a system failed. The lesson of climbing safety is not that the sport is dangerous for extreme projects. It is that the sport kills people on the small things — the moments when attention lapsed, when a system went unchecked, when a partner was trusted without a second check. Climb long enough and you will find yourself in the casual moments. Safety is the discipline of staying alert during them.
Why safety matters more than skill

Climbing is an inherently risky sport. Every year a handful of experienced climbers die because a system failed, not because the climb was too hard. Lynn Hill, the first person ever to free-climb the Nose on El Capitan, has written that "a partner check takes ten seconds and might save your life." That is not rhetoric. It is numerical truth: most climbing accidents in the American Alpine Club's Accidents in North American Climbing would have been prevented by a partner check. Skill without safety systems just means climbing higher and harder before a system fails. Safety first means the margin for error is always wider than the climbing.
The knots that actually matter

A working climber needs four knots reliably: the figure-eight follow-through (for tying into the harness), the clove hitch (for anchor building), the Munter hitch (a backup belay when a device is lost), and the prusik or friction hitch (for ascending a rope or backing up a rappel). A good climbing gym teaches all four in the first week of a top-rope course. A climbing partner who cannot tie a figure-eight reliably in any light, in any weather, with any rope, should not be your rope partner. Knots are drilled the way a pilot drills checklists. They are tied the same way every single time. Variations are the opening of accidents.
Belaying, the partner's job

A belayer is the person at the other end of the rope. Their job is to catch a fall. Modern tube-style devices — the Black Diamond ATC and its cousins — require constant attention from the belayer; a lapse of a second at the wrong moment can kill a climber. Assisted-braking devices like the Petzl Grigri add a mechanical backup but do not eliminate the need for attention. Every gym teaches the PBUS technique (pull, brake, under, slide) because it keeps a hand on the brake strand at all times. A belayer who takes their brake hand off the rope to check their phone is committing the most common mistake in modern climbing. The phone can wait. The climber cannot.
Anchors and trust

In outdoor climbing, the anchor is the point at the top of a pitch where the rope is secured to the rock. A good anchor is redundant, equalized, and non-extending — the SERENE principle (or its various mnemonics). Redundant means at least two independent attachment points to the rock; if one fails, the other holds. Equalized means the load is shared between them. Non-extending means that if one fails, the other does not shock-load the system by allowing the anchor to fall several inches. Building anchors is the first skill an outdoor climber learns after belaying, and every single anchor is checked by both partners before any weight goes on it. There are no second chances on anchors.
Accidents happen in the casual moments

The American Alpine Club's annual Accidents in North American Climbing reports the same pattern over and over. Most climbing accidents happen to experienced climbers on routes that were not at their limit, in the transition moments — rappelling off the top, cleaning an anchor, lowering a partner, switching devices. The lapse is almost never on the hard move. It is in the moment when the climber's brain relaxes because the hard part is over. This is the real lesson of climbing safety. Stay alert in the casual moments. Check your knot before every climb. Check your partner's belay device before every climb. Check the rope threads through both loops of the harness. Every time. No exceptions.

Before every climb, perform the partner check. Harness buckled (doubled back). Figure-eight knot tied correctly through both loops. Belay device oriented correctly with the rope. Locking carabiner locked. Helmet on. Ask your partner: "On belay?" Wait for: "Belay on." This ritual takes ten seconds. Skipping it has killed hundreds of climbers.

A note on safety: climbing outside carries risks that climbing in the gym largely does not — objective hazards like rockfall, weather, and remote terrain. A climber who moves from the gym to the outdoors should take a single-pitch instructor course or climb with an experienced mentor for at least their first ten outdoor climbing days. There is no substitute for supervised in-person instruction when lives are on the rope.

dek: Knots, belays, anchors — the mechanical systems that hold human beings off the ground.
name: Safety Systems
sections: Why safety matters more than skill
Accidents happen in the casual moments

body.text: In May 1862, a bartender named Jerry Thomas published the first drinks book in America, titled plainly How to Mix Drinks, or, the Bon-Vivant's Companion. Thomas had traveled by steamer and stage up and down the East Coast working behind bars in New York, New Orleans, San Francisco, and Charleston, and his book was the first anyone had written down the recipes he had been mixing. A line in the introduction defined the word cocktail as a "bittered sling" — spirit, sugar, water, bitters. That four-ingredient formula is still, more than a century and a half later, the genetic code of most cocktails in a good bar.
Three, the perfect cocktail number

The great classic recipes are, almost without exception, three-ingredient drinks. Spirit plus modifier plus accent. An Old Fashioned: whiskey, sugar, bitters. A Daiquiri: rum, lime, sugar. A Martini: gin, vermouth, bitters. A Manhattan: whiskey, vermouth, bitters. David Embury, a New York attorney who wrote the 1948 reference The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, argued that a good cocktail needed one source of strength, one of softness, and one of seasoning. Every modern cocktail manual teaches the same rule. There are four- and five-ingredient drinks that work; there are very few that work better than their three-ingredient cousins.
The Old Fashioned

The Old Fashioned is the drink Jerry Thomas would recognize unchanged. Two ounces of bourbon or rye, a teaspoon of sugar (or a barspoon of simple syrup), two dashes of Angostura bitters, stirred over ice, served with a twist of orange peel. The drink is called Old Fashioned because, by the 1880s, it was — new bartenders were layering complication onto their cocktails, and drinkers asked for the old-fashioned way. A well-made Old Fashioned is the cleanest demonstration of whiskey's character. It is also the most-sold classic cocktail in the world, as of the 2020s, six years running.
The Martini

The Martini is the drink that argues with itself. Originally a 2:1 gin-to-vermouth stirred drink with orange bitters, the classic mid-century ratio moved to 5:1 and then, through the 1950s drift toward drier versions, to 7:1 or "breathe the vermouth over the gin." Vodka martinis displaced gin for a generation; the craft-cocktail revival pulled the ratio back to something the drink's nineteenth-century inventors would recognize. A modern bar's Martini is gin, a proper dry vermouth (Dolin or Noilly Prat), and a dash of bitters — stirred until the glass frosts, strained, garnished with a twist or an olive.
The Negroni and the Manhattan

The Negroni — equal parts gin, sweet vermouth, Campari — was reportedly first mixed for Count Camillo Negroni in Florence in 1919 when he asked his barman to strengthen his Americano. The proportion is iconic: a one-to-one-to-one ratio is not a common cocktail structure, and the bitterness of Campari is what pulls the drink together. The Manhattan — rye or bourbon, sweet vermouth, bitters — is New York's signature, attributed to the Manhattan Club in the 1870s and canonical since. Both age beautifully. Both can be made in a home kitchen with three bottles.
Why the classics stayed

A classic cocktail earns its staying power by being indestructible. The Old Fashioned survives bad whiskey and good, careful bartending and rushed. The Martini survives changes in ratio and changes in garnish. The Daiquiri survives cheap lime. The classics are robust because they were refined, over decades, into drinks that forgive everything but outright neglect. A modern craft bar's invention menu is a showcase of a particular bartender's style. The back of the classic list is the discipline. Every serious program keeps both open.

A great cocktail is mostly ice. Ice manages dilution — too little and the drink is hot and harsh; too much and it is watery. Stirred drinks are diluted about twenty percent; shaken drinks, thirty. The ice is not garnish. It is an ingredient.

dek: A dozen recipes that have not been improved in a hundred years — and a history that ties them to the dark-wood bar where each was born.
name: The Classics

body.text: In 1948, David Embury, a New York lawyer who took his cocktails more seriously than his legal practice, published a book whose opening chapters laid out an argument: a well-made cocktail was not a matter of creativity but of technique. He listed the mistakes — warm ice, bruised citrus, wrong strain — and then, methodically, the cures. The book was dismissed by some bartenders of the era as armchair theory. Every serious cocktail book written since has agreed with Embury. A bartender at the World Class bartending championships in 2025 will explain dilution curves in the same terms Embury did seventy years before.
The first rule: spirit-only stirs, citrus-containing shakes

The simplest rule in the craft: if a drink contains only spirits, bitters, and sugar — Martini, Manhattan, Old Fashioned, Negroni — stir it. If a drink contains citrus, dairy, or egg — Daiquiri, Whiskey Sour, Gimlet, Ramos Gin Fizz — shake it. The reason is aesthetic and physical: stirring produces a silky, clear drink; shaking produces a textured, aerated one. A stirred sour is dull; a shaken Manhattan is cloudy. The ingredients tell you which verb applies.
Stirring

A mixing glass filled two-thirds with ice, the ingredients poured in on top, a long barspoon worked smoothly around the inside of the glass. The motion is a quiet whirlpool — the ice circulates, the liquid chills, a small amount of water dilutes in. Thirty seconds is a rough target for a standard spec, though counting is a less reliable guide than a tasting spoon. The drink is ready when it tastes cold, diluted enough to round off the alcohol but still plainly strong. Strain into a chilled glass.
Shaking

A Boston shaker — two tins seated together — is the professional tool. A Cobbler shaker (the three-piece with a built-in strainer) is a serviceable home alternative. Fill with ice about two-thirds, add the ingredients, seat the tins firmly, and shake hard for twelve to fifteen seconds. The goal is chill, dilution, and aeration — the froth on a Daiquiri or the white cap on a sour is protein and air, not marketing. Double-strain through a fine mesh if the drink is egg-white or has small citrus fibers. A hard shake looks violent. It is supposed to.
Build and muddle

A built drink is made in its serving glass — a Mojito built over crushed ice, a Gin and Tonic built in a highball. Fewer dishes, simpler to execute, fewer places for things to go wrong. A muddled drink bruises a solid ingredient — usually herbs, fruit, or sugar — to release its oils. A Caipirinha starts muddled, with lime and sugar crushed under a wooden muddler before the cachaça is added. The key to muddling is firmness, not force. Pressing a mint leaf is right; pulverizing it releases chlorophyll and bitterness.
Ice and dilution, the hidden craft

Dilution is not a bug. A three-ounce stirred cocktail served straight up has dissolved roughly half an ounce of water on its way to the glass. That water is the reason the drink tastes round instead of hot. Shaken drinks dilute faster — twenty-five to thirty percent by volume. Big, dense ice dilutes more slowly than small, cloudy ice, which is why a single large cube in an Old Fashioned lasts half an hour while the bar next door's crushed-ice version is watery in five minutes. The ice is half the recipe.

A chilled glass matters more than most home bartenders believe. A cold martini poured into a warm glass is a warm martini within ninety seconds. Keep glasses in the freezer. Pull them out as you start the stir.

dek: Stir, shake, build, muddle — four verbs, each with a rule about when it applies and why the answer is almost never "whatever".
name: Technique
sections: The first rule: spirit-only stirs, citrus-containing shakes
Ice and dilution, the hidden craft

body.text: A shepherd named Kaldi, somewhere in the Ethiopian highlands around the ninth century, noticed his goats dancing after chewing on the red berries of a particular shrub. He tried the berries, stayed up all night, and — the story goes — showed them to a local monk. The monk's order, suspicious of a fruit that suppressed sleep, threw the berries onto a fire, smelled what was rising from them, and pulled the roasted beans back out of the coals. The whole of modern coffee begins with a smell. It begins, that is, with roasting.
The seed of a red fruit

Coffee is not a bean. It is a seed — in fact, the two seeds nested inside a small red fruit called a coffee cherry. The tree that produces them, Coffea, grows only in a narrow belt of tropical highlands. Picked ripe, the cherry is peeled, the fruit's sweet mucilage is washed or fermented off the seed, the seed is dried, and the green bean that remains is what gets shipped to roasters. Before it is roasted, it looks like a pale green pistachio. The color of coffee is an invention of the fire.
Arabica, Robusta, and the battle of species

Of the hundred-plus species in the Coffea genus, two matter commercially. Coffea arabica, the older and more delicate, accounts for about sixty percent of world production; it grows slowly at high altitude, needs cooler temperatures, and produces a more aromatic cup. Coffea canephora — commonly called Robusta — is a tougher lowland plant with about twice the caffeine, a more bitter profile, and a much higher disease tolerance. Most supermarket blends are mixed. Most specialty coffee is pure arabica. Climate change is quietly reshuffling this map: arabica's altitude requirement is being squeezed upward as growing regions warm.
The coffee belt

The tropical band where coffee grows, between roughly 23 degrees north and 23 degrees south, runs through Ethiopia and Kenya, across into Yemen, over to Colombia and Brazil, and through Indonesia and Vietnam. Each region has a signature: Ethiopian coffees tend toward floral jasmine and berry; Kenyan toward black-currant acidity; Colombian toward chocolate and red fruit; Ethiopian Yirgacheffes toward bright citrus; Sumatran toward earthy, low-acidity depth. Terroir, the same concept that governs wine, governs coffee, and the best third-wave roasters label the farm, the altitude, and the processing method of every lot.
Processing, the hidden variable

After picking, the cherry must be separated from the seed. Washed processing (wet-processing) removes the fruit quickly with water; the resulting coffee tastes cleaner, brighter, and more recognizably of origin. Natural processing (dry-processing) lets the cherry dry on the seed in the sun; the coffee tastes fruitier, heavier, sweeter. Honey processing is a middle path, keeping some of the mucilage during drying. Two beans from the same farm, processed differently, taste like different coffees. A bag that tells you the process is a bag from a roaster who cares.
Why a bag of beans is dated

Freshly roasted coffee off-gasses CO₂ and loses volatile aromatics over weeks. A roaster who stamps a roast date on the bag — not a best-by date — is selling you the information you need. Drink between seven and twenty-one days off-roast for the best cup. A bag stamped two months ago is still fine. A bag with no roast date is almost certainly already stale, regardless of what the packaging says.

The most instructive three dollars a coffee drinker can spend is on a small bag of a single-origin Ethiopian, drunk alongside a single-origin Colombian and a single-origin Sumatran — all brewed identically. The differences are a better education than any book.

dek: Every cup starts with a seed from a mountain shrub — and where that shrub grew explains almost everything that follows.
name: Beans & Origins
sections: The seed of a red fruit
Arabica, Robusta, and the battle of species
Why a bag of beans is dated

body.text: In 1864, a Cincinnati grocer named Jabez Burns patented a drum roaster that turned itself with a crank and ejected the beans through a side door at the moment the operator decided they were done. Before Burns, coffee was roasted at home over a fire, one pan at a time, and the variance was extraordinary. After Burns, coffee could be roasted in commercial quantities at a consistent level by a person with a watch. Every modern commercial roaster, from a one-kilo sample roaster to a two-hundred-kilo industrial drum, is descended from his basic design. The chemistry is the same as it ever was; the control has gotten better.
From pale green to aromatic brown

A green coffee bean is dense, flavorless, and smells vaguely grassy. Heat it past about 160°C in a drum and it loses water, turns yellow, then tan. Push past 200°C and the Maillard reaction accelerates, sugars caramelize, and the bean darkens to brown. The complexity is extraordinary: roasted coffee contains more than eight hundred identified aromatic compounds, many of which form in a specific thirty-second window of the roast and disappear if the window is missed. Coffee roasting is a chemistry problem, and roasters who understand that chemistry produce better coffee.
First crack, second crack

Somewhere around 196°C, the water vapor inside each bean builds enough pressure to crack the cellular structure audibly. A sample drum full of beans sounds like popcorn — this is first crack. It marks the beginning of what anyone can taste as coffee. The roaster can stop shortly after (a light roast), ride the long plateau between cracks (a medium), or push on until the bean cracks again at roughly 224°C — second crack — which is the marker of a dark roast. The two cracks are the roaster's map.
Light, medium, dark — and why

A light roast preserves the origin — the Ethiopian floral, the Kenyan blackcurrant, the Colombian caramel. The trade is that light roasts are more acidic and the flavor vocabulary is less familiar to American palates trained on darker coffee. A medium roast balances origin with the familiar caramel-chocolate-toast register. A dark roast tastes mostly like roasting itself; the origin is almost gone, replaced by carbon-forward, oily, smoky notes. French, Italian, and Starbucks roasts live here. There is no right answer. There is only what the roaster wants and what you do.
The roast curve

A modern sample roast records temperature and time continuously, producing a curve from charge to drop. A well-shaped curve rises through the drying phase, flattens through the Maillard phase, and shows a tight, measured development phase from first crack to drop. Scott Rao, the American roasting consultant, argues that a declining rate of rise past first crack is the signature of a clean roast. Read his books and you will never look at a curve the same way. Read his books and you may also decide you never want to roast a bean yourself.
Why roast date beats roast level

A fresh medium-roasted bean from a specialty roaster will, almost always, taste better than an expensive dark-roasted bean that has sat on a shelf for three months. Coffee loses aroma faster than almost any pantry item in your kitchen — within weeks, not months. The single biggest upgrade a drinker can make, before buying a new grinder or a better kettle, is to move from a supermarket bag to a local roaster's bag stamped with a roast date.

Oil on the surface of a bean is a sign of a dark roast — and of staling once the bag is open. Lightly roasted beans stay dry and retain their aromatics longer. A visibly oily bean is a bean past its best week.

dek: A green bean meets a drum at 200°C and, in about twelve minutes, becomes everything we think coffee is.
name: Roasting
sections: From pale green to aromatic brown
Why roast date beats roast level

body.text: In 1908, a Dresden housewife named Melitta Bentz got tired of bitter coffee. She punched holes in a brass cup, blotted a piece of her son's school paper across the holes, dumped ground coffee on top, and poured hot water through. The filter caught the grounds; the paper trapped the oils; the coffee tasted cleaner than anything her neighbors were drinking. Bentz patented the design in June of 1908. The Melitta filter is still, with small modifications, the pour-over cone everyone uses today. All the modern specialty brewers — the V60, the Kalita Wave, the Chemex — are variations on Bentz's insight.
What extraction really is

Brewing is chemistry. Hot water dissolves the soluble compounds inside a ground coffee particle — acids first (bright), then sugars (sweet), then bitter compounds (harsh). If you stop too early, the coffee is sour and thin. If you go too long, it is bitter and flat. The sweet spot, measured, is an extraction yield between 18 and 22 percent of the ground coffee's mass, with the resulting brew at around 1.3 to 1.5 percent dissolved solids. A refractometer reads these numbers. A tongue, with practice, does the same.
The four variables

Ratio (grams of coffee to grams of water), grind (coarseness), time (how long water and coffee are in contact), and temperature. That is the whole brew recipe. A French press wants coarse grind, long time, water off the boil. An espresso wants very fine grind, thirty seconds, and nine bars of pressure. A pour-over wants medium grind, three-and-a-half minutes, and a careful pour. Everything else is refinement.
Pour-over, French press, espresso

Pour-over — Hario V60, Kalita Wave, Chemex — passes water through the grounds into a cup. The result is bright, clean, origin-forward. French press immerses the grounds in water for four minutes and filters through a metal mesh; the result is heavier, with more suspended oils and fines. Espresso forces water at nine bars through a tightly packed puck in under thirty seconds, producing a concentrated shot with a layer of emulsified oils on top called crema. A drinker who learns the three has a working model of every major café drink on earth.
The grinder is the ingredient

The most common advice in modern coffee is also the most often ignored: buy a better grinder before you buy anything else. A burr grinder produces particles of consistent size. A blade grinder produces everything from dust to gravel, which extracts unevenly and tastes harsh. The quality of the particles — and especially the uniformity of the particle size — is the ceiling on every other decision. A cheap grinder on a good bean is worse than a good grinder on a decent bean.
A weekday cup, done right

A home drinker aiming for one excellent cup in under five minutes: fifteen grams of medium-ground specialty beans, stamped with a roast date in the past three weeks; 250 grams of water at 96°C; a pour-over cone; four minutes total contact time with a thirty-second bloom first. A kitchen scale, a gooseneck kettle, and a gram of attention. The difference between this cup and the drip machine on the counter is not small. It is not subtle. It is the difference between remembering the coffee and reaching for sugar to cover it.

Water matters more than home brewers suspect. Hard water pulls more body and bitterness; soft water pulls more acidity and clarity. Many specialty roasters sell water recipes (Third Wave Water, Lotus) that transform the cup for two dollars a month.

dek: Hot water through ground coffee, yes — but the ratio, the grind, and the time are where the whole craft lives.
name: Brewing Methods

body.text: In 1924 the British agronomist Sir Albert Howard, working in Indore in central India, watched local farmers build long, layered piles of crop residue and animal manure that became fragrant black humus in months instead of years. He called it the Indore method, and it became the foundation of the modern organic-farming movement. The method depends on one observation: a managed pile of organic matter, kept warm and moist and turned, will heat itself from inside, and the heat itself does most of the work.
What heat does

The microbial communities that decompose organic matter generate heat as a byproduct of metabolism. Pile a few cubic feet of the right mixture and the inside of the pile rises within days to 130 to 160 degrees Fahrenheit. At those temperatures, weed seeds die, plant pathogens die, and a different community of thermophilic microbes takes over and accelerates decomposition. The pile finishes faster, smells better, and produces a more uniform compost than the slow cold version that just sits in a corner.
The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio

Compost gardeners speak of "browns" and "greens." Browns are carbon-rich materials — dry leaves, straw, shredded cardboard, wood chips. Greens are nitrogen-rich — grass clippings, kitchen scraps, fresh manure, coffee grounds. The microbial chemistry wants roughly twenty-five to thirty parts carbon to one part nitrogen. By volume, the rough rule is two-to-one or three-to-one browns to greens. Too many greens and the pile turns slimy and smells of ammonia; too many browns and it does not heat at all and decomposes slowly.
Building a hot pile

A pile that will heat needs roughly a cubic yard of material — about three feet on each side. Smaller and the heat dissipates; larger and the inside goes anaerobic. Layer browns and greens like a lasagna, water as you build (the pile should feel like a wrung-out sponge), and turn it every four or five days for the first few weeks. Each turn introduces oxygen and exposes the cooler outer layers to the hot center. After a month it should be unrecognizable as its components; after three months you have finished compost — dark, crumbly, smelling of forest floor.
Reading the temperature

A long-stem compost thermometer, twenty dollars from any garden store, is the single most useful piece of compost equipment. A pile that climbs to 140 degrees in three days, holds for a week, then drops as you turn it, is doing what it should. A pile that never climbs needs more nitrogen, more moisture, or more mass. A pile that smells of ammonia needs more browns. A pile that smells like a swamp needs to be turned to introduce oxygen. Almost every compost problem is diagnosable from temperature and smell.

Two things to keep out of a home compost pile: meat or dairy (the wrong microbes; attracts vermin) and pet feces (pathogens that survive even hot composting). Everything else from a kitchen — including bones, in a working hot pile — eventually becomes soil.

dek: A managed pile reaches 130°F or more, kills weed seeds and pathogens, and turns kitchen scraps into garden gold in three months.
name: Hot Composting

body.text: Mary Appelhof was a Michigan biology teacher who, in the 1970s, became frustrated that her household kitchen scraps had nowhere useful to go in a Northern winter. She started keeping a wooden box of red wiggler worms under the sink. The book she wrote about it, Worms Eat My Garbage, came out in 1982 and has now introduced four decades of households to vermicomposting — the surprisingly elegant system in which earthworms, not heat, do the work.
Why worms

Vermicompost — the dark, granular castings that earthworms produce — is by every measure the most concentrated and biologically active compost a home gardener can make. Studies at Cornell and Ohio State have shown that small amounts of worm castings outperform much larger volumes of conventional compost in plant trials, with effects on plant growth that exceed what the simple nutrient analysis predicts. The microbial diversity of worm castings, and the trace plant hormones that pass through the worm gut, do more than feed plants — they prime them.
The right worm and the right bin

The worm to use is Eisenia fetida, the red wiggler — a small, tolerant, surface-dwelling species that thrives in shallow bins of decomposing organic matter. The earthworms in your garden are different species (mostly Lumbricus terrestris) and will not survive in a bin. The bin itself is simple: a shallow plastic tote with air holes, a layer of moist shredded cardboard or newspaper for bedding, a pound or two of red wigglers from a worm farm or local seller. Keep it between fifty-five and seventy-five degrees, in shade, indoors or in a garage. A good bin has no smell.
Feeding and harvesting

Red wigglers will eat about half their weight in kitchen scraps per day in optimal conditions. Bury small amounts in different corners of the bin so they have time to break down. Avoid meat, dairy, oil, citrus in quantity, and onions in quantity. The worms multiply to match the food supply, which is also their cap — they will not overrun a bin in normal household use. Harvesting after a few months is a matter of pushing the finished castings to one side, adding fresh bedding and food to the other, and waiting a couple of weeks for the worms to migrate.
Worm castings as fertilizer

A handful of worm castings worked into a planting hole, or a tablespoon brewed into a quart of water as a tea, will visibly accelerate seedlings and houseplants. Unlike strong synthetic fertilizers, worm castings cannot burn roots or leaves; the nutrients are released slowly as soil microbes process them. Many serious vegetable gardeners run a worm bin in parallel with a hot compost pile precisely because the two products do different things — bulk soil amendment from the pile, microbial inoculant from the worms.

A worm bin is the only food-scrap solution that works in an apartment with no yard. A small bin under the sink processes the daily output of one or two people, costs almost nothing to run, and produces, twice a year, the finest fertilizer available for houseplants and balcony pots.

dek: A bin of red wigglers under the sink turns kitchen scraps into the most valuable compost there is — and asks for almost nothing in return.
name: Vermicomposting
sections: The right worm and the right bin

body.text: In a Tokyo workshop lit by fluorescent tubes, a blacksmith named Masamoto folds carbon steel against iron at 1,200 degrees Celsius, hammers it out, folds it again, and grinds an edge so fine it splits a hair lengthwise. The knife he makes is not a tool. It is a bargain between the steel and the hand: if you learn to use it properly, it will last a lifetime, and you will be faster and safer than any cook with a dull blade.
The grip that professionals use

The pinch grip — thumb and forefinger on the blade just above the bolster, three remaining fingers wrapped around the handle — is the grip every culinary school teaches on the first day. It puts the hand close enough to the edge that the knife pivots on the cutting board like a seesaw, the wrist locked, the elbow doing most of the work. Beginners hold the handle like a tennis racket, which is why their wrists hurt after ten minutes and their cuts drift off line.
The claw that keeps your fingertips

The guiding hand curls into a claw: fingertips tucked under knuckles, the flat of the middle phalanges pressed against the blade's side. The blade rides up and down the knuckles; the fingertips are never in the path. Every professional cook has scars on their thumbs from learning this the wrong way first, which is why the advice from culinary school instructors is almost religious in its repetition: watch your fingertips, watch your fingertips, watch your fingertips.
Three cuts worth mastering

The rock chop, pivoting the tip on the board while the heel rises and falls, is for onions and herbs — anything you want fine and fast. The push cut, driving the blade forward and down in a single motion, is for firm vegetables and most meat. The slice, drawing the blade through delicate proteins without pressing, is for fish, tomatoes, and the soft summer fruit that a dull knife will crush. Learn these three and you have ninety percent of what a kitchen asks of you.
A sharp knife is a safe knife

The single most common kitchen injury — a deep slice across the top of a finger — is almost always caused by a dull knife slipping off a tomato's skin or a squash's rind. A sharp blade bites instantly and goes where you point it. A dull blade requires force, and force without control is how hospital visits begin. A cheap whetstone and five minutes a week are enough to keep a home knife sharper than most restaurant kitchens manage.
The long apprenticeship

In a Japanese professional kitchen, the new cook is handed an onion and a board, and told to keep cutting until told to stop. Nobody teaches them. They watch, they imitate, and they improve by the thousand repetitions the first year asks of them. A home cook does not need the same discipline, but the principle is the same: knife skills get better only with bored, repetitive practice, and they plateau the moment you stop practicing.

The damp kitchen towel under the cutting board is not superstition. It keeps the board from sliding, which keeps the knife from jumping, which keeps your fingers attached. Every serious kitchen does it and no one writes it down.

dek: The first technique and the one every other depends on — a sharp edge, two hands, and the patience to go slow.
name: Knife Skills
sections: A sharp knife is a safe knife

body.text: In 1912, a young French chemist named Louis Camille Maillard noticed that when he warmed a solution of amino acids and sugar, it turned brown and started to smell like toast. He was trying to understand protein synthesis. He stumbled, instead, onto the reaction responsible for the flavor of a roast chicken, a coffee bean, a seared steak, and the crust of every loaf of bread ever baked. A hundred years later, nobody has written down all the molecules the reaction can produce. There are thousands.
Four modes, one stove

Heat moves by conduction (touch), convection (a moving fluid), radiation (photons, mostly infrared), and evaporation (which removes heat, so it is cooling rather than heating). A covered pot of soup uses all four at once: the burner radiates to the pan, the pan conducts to the broth, the broth convects the heat through itself, and steam evaporates from the surface carrying heat out of the pot. A good cook thinks in these four modes without naming them.
The dry heat of a sear

A steak on a dry cast-iron skillet at 230°C browns through the Maillard reaction, which requires temperatures above 140°C and an absence of liquid water. Water, at sea level, cannot rise above 100°C — it boils off first. This is why a damp pan will not sear: the meat's surface cools the iron below browning temperature until the water has evaporated, and by the time the pan recovers, the meat is gray and overcooked. Dry the meat first. Let the pan get hot. Do not crowd it.
Water's ceiling and the 100°C problem

Any wet cooking — boiling, poaching, steaming, braising — is capped at water's boiling point. You cannot brown a thing underwater. This is why every braise begins with a sear: the flavor of the finished dish depends on the brown crust you build before the liquid goes in. A stew that skips this step tastes like boiled meat. Which is what it is.
Why fat is a better conductor than air

A film of oil in the pan does more than keep the food from sticking. It fills the microscopic valleys between the food and the metal, giving heat a direct path. Oil conducts heat about fifteen times faster than air, which is why food cooked in a dry pan browns unevenly and food cooked in a thin layer of oil browns across its entire surface. The same logic governs deep frying: the oil is a thermal coupling medium, and its temperature sets the cooking rate.
The carry-over cook

A roast chicken taken from a 220°C oven at an internal temperature of 70°C will continue to rise for another ten minutes — the outer layers are hotter than the inside, and their heat conducts inward as the bird rests. A cook who ignores carry-over overcooks everything they roast. A cook who learns to pull things ten degrees early, and lets the rest finish off the heat, never overcooks anything again.

A digital probe thermometer costs about fifteen dollars and replaces a lifetime of guessing. The food's internal temperature is the only number that matters; the oven's set point is mostly a suggestion.

dek: Everything that happens to food in a hot pan is one of four things — and knowing which is which is what separates a cook from an assembler.
name: Heat Transfer
sections: The dry heat of a sear
Why fat is a better conductor than air

body.text: In the 1960s, a New York food writer named James Beard watched a French chef season a chicken in his restaurant kitchen. The chef took a pinch of salt, held it a foot above the bird, and let it fall. Beard thought it was showmanship. It was not. The height let the salt distribute evenly across the skin, rather than piling up where the fingers opened. Decades later, when Samin Nosrat wrote a book arguing that salt was the first and most important pillar of good cooking, chefs recognized the argument as obvious and home cooks as a revelation.
What salt actually does

Salt does three things. It seasons, meaning it wakes up flavors you already have. It draws water out of cells through osmosis, which is how a dry brine works on a turkey. And it unfolds proteins, which is why a salted steak, left overnight, develops a tacky skin that browns beautifully in a pan. All three effects depend on time. A pinch at the table seasons. A tablespoon the day before seasons, brines, and transforms.
The timing question

Salt meat early — an hour before for thin cuts, a day before for thick ones — and the surface is dry when it hits the pan, which is what browning needs. Salt meat at the moment it meets the heat, and the salt will sit on top, bead out water, and steam rather than sear. Salt greens early and they weep; salt them late and they stay crisp. Every cooking mistake that tastes "under-seasoned" is often, in fact, under-timed.
Acid, fat, and the other pillars

Nosrat's argument in Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat is that four elements explain almost every dish that works: enough salt, the right fat, the right acid to cut the fat, and the right kind of heat. A vinaigrette is oil plus vinegar plus salt. A braise is fat plus acid plus salt plus low heat. The grammar of cooking, once you see it, is small.
Why a kitchen needs four salts

Diamond Crystal kosher, for almost everything — its flakes stick to food, dissolve quickly, and a tablespoon weighs about half what a tablespoon of Morton's does, which matters more in a recipe than anyone admits. Fine sea salt for baking, where gram weights matter. Maldon or a similar flake for the finish, when a salty crunch at the last second is the point. Fleur de sel for the occasional special thing. Four salts, one shelf, and everything a home kitchen needs.
The last ten percent

A dish seasoned exactly enough is a dish you do not think about seasoning. You taste it and reach for the next bite. A dish under-seasoned is a dish you reach for the salt shaker on, because your tongue is telling you something is missing. The fastest way to close the last ten percent of a recipe is to taste, add a quarter teaspoon, taste again, and stop when you stop thinking about it.

body.cite: Samin Nosrat, Salt Fat Acid Heat
body.text: Salt has a greater impact on flavor than any other ingredient.

dek: Seasoning is less about courage than timing — the difference between a good cook and a great one is usually when the salt went on.
name: Salt & Seasoning
sections: Acid, fat, and the other pillars
Why a kitchen needs four salts

body.text: Auguste Escoffier arrived at the Savoy Hotel in London in 1890 at the invitation of César Ritz, and spent the next decade rewriting how Western restaurants worked. He broke the kitchen into stations with a single chef in charge of each, a system called the brigade. He wrote Le Guide Culinaire, a five-thousand-recipe reference that doubled as a curriculum. And he declared — though really he inherited the claim from Marie-Antoine Carême — that every serious French sauce is a variation on one of five. A hundred and twenty years later, every culinary student in the world learns these five in their first month.
What a stock really is

Stock is water that has spent six to twelve hours with bones, mirepoix, and patience. Collagen in the bones dissolves into gelatin, which gives the liquid body. The vegetables — traditionally a two-to-one-to-one mix of onion, carrot, and celery — add sweetness and backbone. A proper stock, cooled, should wobble on a spoon like loose gelatin dessert. That wobble is the proof that it will thicken a sauce without any help from flour.
The five mother sauces

Béchamel is milk thickened with a white roux. Velouté is a light stock — chicken, fish, or veal — thickened the same way. Espagnole is a brown stock thickened with a brown roux and deepened with tomato. Tomato sauce is, canonically, a tomato sauce. Hollandaise is an emulsion of clarified butter into egg yolks, held together by lecithin. Escoffier codified the first four; the modern list of five replaces mayonnaise with hollandaise and has stayed put since roughly 1907.
The brown-versus-white fork in the road

A white stock starts with raw bones and clear vegetables; the liquid stays pale and the flavor stays clean. A brown stock starts with roasted bones and caramelized mirepoix; the Maillard reaction in the roasting pan gives the finished stock its color and a deeper, meatier dimension. White for lighter sauces, cream soups, and poultry velouté. Brown for beef sauces, demi-glace, and the long game.
The small-sauce tree

From béchamel: mornay (add cheese), soubise (onion), nantua (crayfish butter). From velouté: suprême (cream), allemande (egg yolks), bercy (shallots and wine). From espagnole: demi-glace (reduced by half), bordelaise (red wine and marrow), robert (mustard and onion). The pattern is the same everywhere: a mother sauce is a platform; a small sauce is what you build on it for this plate. The system is elegant the first time you see it.
A gallon on the back burner

A home cook does not need five mother sauces. A home cook needs one good stock, made on a Sunday, cooled overnight, and frozen in pint containers. Chicken is the best default — it builds anything, it stores well, and it makes the worst weeknight soup into a competent one. Save the bones from every roast bird. Save the vegetable ends. Simmer, strain, cool, freeze. The home version of Escoffier's system is two hours of work a month and a freezer that transforms every meal after.
Never boil a stock. A rolling boil emulsifies the fat back into the liquid and produces a cloudy, greasy result. Barely-moving surface ripples are the sign the pot has been set right.

dek: Every serious kitchen in the Western tradition rests on a short pantry of sauces, and all five of them rest on a good stock.
name: Stocks & Sauces
sections: The brown-versus-white fork in the road
A gallon on the back burner

body.text: In 1843 Ada Lovelace annotated an Italian paper on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and, in what she called Note G, described a procedure for computing Bernoulli numbers. The machine was never built. The procedure is the first thing most historians are willing to call a program. Programming began, in other words, as an act of careful writing — and in most of the important ways it still is.

body.alt: Ada Lovelace, daguerreotype by Antoine Claudet, 1843.
body.caption: Ada Lovelace, photographed by Antoine Claudet the same year she published her annotated translation of Menabrea's memoir on the Analytical Engine.
body.credit: Science Museum Group / Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

body.text: A program is a piece of writing

Source code is text. You write it in a file, save the file, and hand it to a compiler or an interpreter, which turns it into something a processor can run. The text has to be exact in a way that English does not — a misplaced bracket can stop the whole thing — but the craft is recognizably literary. You write, read back what you wrote, notice it does not say what you meant, and fix it. That loop, repeated for years, is what programmers do.

What makes the craft strange to outsiders is that every sentence is executable. You cannot bluff, cannot wave your hands, cannot write a paragraph that sounds good but does not cash. The machine will try, and either succeed or crash. That constraint — the total absence of charity from your reader — is why programming is easier to learn on a computer than from a book. The book will forgive you. The computer will not.
Three things every language gives you

Variables name values; functions name procedures; control flow — if, while, for — picks between procedures. With these three ideas you can, in principle, compute anything a modern computer can compute. Alan Turing showed this in 1936 before a single stored-program machine existed. The languages you will meet — Python, JavaScript, C, Rust — differ mostly in what they make easy and what they make hard, not in what they make possible.

Python makes beginners cry the least. JavaScript runs in every browser on earth. C is how the operating system under your feet is actually written. Rust is the new C, with the rough edges filed off. There is no right answer to "which one first." Start with whichever one is closest to the thing you want to build; the second language will take a fraction of the time of the first.
Ada Lovelace's Note G was published in 1843. Konrad Zuse's Z3, the first working programmable computer, ran its first program in 1941. The theory was a century ahead of the hardware.

body.caption: Professor David Brailsford, "What Is Programming?" on Computerphile — the cleanest ten-minute answer on the internet.

body.text: The underrated skill is reading

Beginners worry about writing code; professionals spend most of their time reading it. The code you work on was written by people who are not you, under deadlines you did not share, and your job is to understand it well enough to change one thing without breaking another. A good programmer reads more than they write, and argues less with the machine than with themselves.

The best way to get better at reading code is to read a lot of it. Open-source repositories on GitHub — CPython, SQLite, Redis, Lua — were written by some of the most careful engineers in the world and are meant to be read. Pick one you use daily and look at how the first ten pages of its source handle some concrete case. You will learn more from an hour of that than from a month of tutorials.

body.label: The first bug
body.text: On September 9, 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II found a moth stuck in one of the relays. Grace Hopper taped the moth into the log book with the note, "First actual case of bug being found." The word "bug" for machine malfunction was older than that — Thomas Edison used it in 1878 — but Hopper's moth is the reason every programmer alive has said "there's a bug" today.
Why it takes longer than you expect

The famous sentence — from Fred Brooks' The Mythical Man-Month — is that adding programmers to a late project makes it later. Software is hard because it composes, and composition is where surprise lives. A function that works and a function that works will, combined, sometimes do something neither of them does alone. Learning to anticipate that, to design programs whose pieces do not surprise each other, is what separates the first year of the craft from the tenth.

The good news is that the improvement is visible from the inside. The code you wrote a year ago will make you wince, reliably, forever. That is not a flaw in the craft; it is the craft. If you look at something you wrote in 2024 and do not wince, you have stopped learning.
Where to start

Pick a language. Pick a small project — not a calculator, something you actually want: a script that renames your photos by date, a tiny website that shows you the weather, a bot that posts to a family group chat. Finish it. It will be worse than you wanted. Ship it anyway. Then build the next one. The professional move is never the first project; it is the fortieth. Everything short of that is warm-up.

body.cite: Silvanus P. Thompson, Calculus Made Easy (1910)
body.text: What one fool can do, another can.

dek: Writing down, with uncomfortable precision, what you want a machine to do.
name: Programming Basics

body.text: The word algorithm is a corruption of the Latinized name of Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, the ninth-century scholar whose Baghdad arithmetic treatise taught Europe how to add and subtract in the Hindu–Arabic positional system. For a long time an algorithm just meant a procedure for doing decimal arithmetic. The modern sense — a finite, unambiguous procedure for solving a class of problems — is a twentieth-century generalization, made sharp by Turing and Church in 1936.
Counting steps instead of seconds

Two algorithms that solve the same problem can differ wildly in how long they take on a large input. Sorting a million numbers with bubble sort takes a trillion operations; sorting the same numbers with mergesort takes twenty million. The study of algorithms asks how the step count grows as the input grows — the famous big-O notation — rather than how many milliseconds it takes on a particular machine. Hardware gets faster; asymptotics do not change.

body.alt: Animated demonstration of merge sort on an array of bars.
body.caption: Merge sort, animated. Each pass doubles the size of the sorted regions until the whole array is in order. The cost is O(n log n), and has been since John von Neumann sketched it out in 1945.
body.credit: Animation by Swfung8, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

body.text: A small set of paradigms goes far

Divide and conquer (mergesort, quicksort, FFT) splits a problem in half and glues the results. Dynamic programming (shortest path, sequence alignment) remembers subproblems instead of recomputing them. Greedy methods (Huffman coding, minimum spanning tree) take the locally best step and hope it stays globally good — sometimes provably so. Graph search (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra) walks a network and learns its shape. A surprisingly large share of the problems industry actually cares about is one of these in disguise.

Once you can recognize the paradigm, most interview questions collapse. "Given a list of meetings, schedule as many as possible": greedy. "Shortest sequence of edits to turn one string into another": dynamic programming. "Does this network of friendships have a cycle": depth-first search. The patterns are older than the questions.

body.caption: Quicksort, visualized as a dance — a 2013 folk performance by students of Sapientia University, Romania.

body.text: Correctness, not just speed

A fast algorithm that produces the wrong answer is worse than a slow one that is right. Much of the discipline, from the 1960s on, has been about proving correctness — showing that a procedure does what it claims on every input, not just the ones you tested. Invariants, induction, and the occasional long paper are the tools. The craft is closer to mathematics than most of the rest of software is.
The first published algorithm was Euclid's — a method for finding the greatest common divisor of two numbers, written down around 300 BCE in Book VII of the Elements. It still works, unchanged.
The open question at the center

Some problems are easy to check but seem hard to solve: given a Sudoku puzzle, you can verify a solution in seconds, but finding one might take the age of the universe. Whether every problem whose answers can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly is the P versus NP question, unresolved since Cook and Levin posed it in 1971. A proof either way would restructure cryptography, logistics, and protein folding, among other things.

Most of the things that look hard — the travelling salesman, 3-SAT, vertex cover, graph colouring — are known to be NP-complete, meaning a polynomial-time algorithm for any one of them is a polynomial-time algorithm for all of them. No one in 55 years has found one, and most theorists suspect none exists. The Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a million dollars for a proof either way since 2000. It remains unclaimed.

body.label: A millennium of notation
body.text: The big-O notation that organizes modern algorithm analysis was invented by Paul Bachmann in 1894, long before computers. Knuth popularized it for algorithms in 1976. Before that, authors wrote prose: "the time grows as the square of the input." Big-O is what turned those prose estimates into a calculus.
Sorting, as a worked example

Sorting is the cleanest case of what algorithms study. Bubble sort, taught in every first course, compares adjacent elements and swaps them until nothing is out of place; its cost is proportional to the square of the input size. Mergesort splits the input in half, sorts each half, and merges them; its cost grows as n log n. For a thousand elements, the difference is a factor of a hundred. For a million, a factor of fifty thousand. In 1959, the US Census would have taken decades to run on the wrong sort. Choosing the right one is the whole subject in miniature.
An algorithm must be seen to be believed.

dek: A recipe precise enough for a machine — and a theory of how long the recipe takes.
name: Algorithms
sections: What P vs NP is really about

body.text: Computer memory, underneath everything, is a long hallway of numbered rooms. The only fast things a processor can do are fetch from a room, put something into a room, and move to a nearby room. Every data structure ever invented — arrays, lists, trees, hash tables, graphs — is a way to arrange rooms so that the operations a particular program needs stay cheap.
Arrays and linked lists

An array puts elements in contiguous rooms. Finding the thousandth element is instant; inserting one in the middle is ruinous, because everything after it has to shuffle down. A linked list puts elements anywhere and chains them with pointers. Inserting in the middle is free once you are there; finding the thousandth element takes a thousand steps. Pick the one whose cheap operation matches the one you will do often. That sentence, repeated in various costumes, is most of the subject.

The deeper, modern lesson is that on a real CPU, with caches and prefetching, arrays almost always win. Your intuition from a textbook — "linked lists are faster for inserts" — is wrong on current hardware by about a factor of ten, because a linked list walks random memory and an array marches linearly. Chandler Carruth's 2014 talk "Efficiency with Algorithms, Performance with Data Structures" is the standard reference.
Trees, when you need order and speed

body.alt: A binary search tree with the value 8 at the root.
body.caption: A binary search tree of depth 3. The "search" property — left children smaller, right children larger — means lookup takes time proportional to the depth, not the size.

body.text: A balanced binary tree — AVL, red-black, B-tree — lets you search, insert, and delete in time proportional to the logarithm of the size. A million-element tree takes twenty steps to search, not a million. B-trees, a disk-friendly variant invented at Boeing in 1971, are why your database can answer a query over a billion rows in a few milliseconds. Every serious database and filesystem uses one.
Hashing, the near-magic

A hash table turns a key into a small integer with a hash function and uses that integer as a room number. On average it searches, inserts, and deletes in constant time — faster than trees, fast enough to feel unreal. The catch is the average: a pathological input, or a malicious one, can collapse a hash table into a linked list. Much of the security literature on denial-of-service in the 2000s was about exactly this collapse.

Every Python dict, every JavaScript object, every Go map, every Ruby Hash is a hash table. When you write a[b] = c in any of these languages, you are running the same algorithm Hans Peter Luhn sketched at IBM in 1953.
Graphs, because the world is not a list

Roads, friendships, web pages, neurons, proteins, supply chains — none of them are naturally lists. A graph is a set of nodes and a set of edges, and most of what we call applied computing is really graph computing in disguise. Breadth-first search, depth-first search, Dijkstra's algorithm, and PageRank all start from the same data structure and do very different things with it.

The Google founders' 1998 paper on PageRank is, underneath the famous branding, a linear-algebra trick over a graph: the stationary distribution of a random walk on the web's link structure. The web is the largest sparse graph anyone has ever indexed, and the tools for handling it came, startlingly, from earlier work on social-network citations by the sociologist Eugene Garfield in the 1950s.

body.label: Why the interview obsession makes sense
body.text: Software interviews' algorithm-and-data-structure obsession is sometimes dismissed as a hazing ritual, but there is a grain of truth to it: if a candidate cannot choose between an array, a set, a hash map, and a heap for a concrete problem, they will write code that is fifty times slower than the right version — and the debugger will not save them.
What to reach for, when

Need a fast lookup by key: hash table. Need the smallest-so-far at every step: heap. Need range queries on sorted data: balanced tree or sorted array. Need "has this come up before" on a stream: Bloom filter. Need to store a million integers compactly: bitmap. Need to find the shortest path in a network: graph plus Dijkstra. Need an undo history: stack. Need a task queue: actually-usually-a-heap, not a literal queue. The professional skill is matching the shape of the data to the shape of the questions you will ask it.

dek: The shapes a program puts its data into — and the operations each shape makes cheap.
name: Data Structures
sections: Trees, when you need order and speed
Graphs, because the world is not a list

body.text: When you run a program on a laptop, the program believes it has the whole machine to itself — all the memory, all the CPU, its own private disk. None of that is true. Dozens of other programs are running at the same time, each told the same comforting lie. The piece of software that maintains this elaborate fiction, and does so fairly, safely, and fast, is the operating system.
Three illusions, maintained at speed

The operating systems textbook by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces — organizes the whole field around three big lies the kernel tells. Virtualization of the CPU makes every process feel like it owns the processor. Virtualization of memory makes every process feel like it has its own address space. Persistence — the filesystem — lets processes pretend the disk is reliable storage that survives crashes. Every other topic (scheduling, paging, concurrency, journaling) is a detail of one of these.

body.alt: Tux, the Linux kernel mascot.
body.caption: Tux — the Linux penguin, drawn by Larry Ewing in 1996. The mascot of the kernel now running on most servers on Earth, under every Android phone, and inside most network equipment.

body.text: Processes and context switches

A process is a running program plus everything it needs — registers, stack, heap, open files, memory map. The kernel switches between processes hundreds of times a second, saving each one's state and restoring another's. The switch takes microseconds; the illusion of parallelism on a single core is entirely built on doing it fast enough that you do not notice.

The scheduler that decides who runs next is one of the oldest and most-argued-over pieces of software in computing. Linux has been through five major schedulers since 1991. The current one, the Completely Fair Scheduler, was written by Ingo Molnár in 2007 and has been refined ever since; macOS uses a different one; Windows a different one still. All of them aim at roughly the same thing: let every process feel responsive without starving any of them.
Virtual memory, the hardware's accomplice

Modern CPUs ship with a memory-management unit that translates each address a program uses into a physical address in RAM on the fly. The mapping is maintained by the kernel in page tables. This lets the kernel give every process a clean, zero-based address space; swap rarely-used pages to disk; share read-only code among processes; and trap on illegal accesses. Without virtual memory, a single buggy program could corrupt any other. Unix's reputation for stability begins here.

Every segfault you have ever seen is a page-fault handler doing its job. The crash is the kernel refusing to give your program access to memory it did not own. The alternative — silent corruption — is much worse.
Concurrency is harder than it looks

As soon as two processes share anything — a counter, a file, a socket — you can get races. Edsger Dijkstra worked out the first careful solutions in the 1960s (semaphores, the dining philosophers problem), and operating systems have been paying interest on the resulting complexity ever since. The canonical warning is the 1999 Mars Polar Lander loss — a priority-inversion bug in a real-time scheduler, detectable only because the spacecraft kept rebooting. Much of modern language design — Rust's ownership model, Go's channels — is an effort to make these bugs harder to write in the first place.
The Unix family

Most of the kernels running on Earth in 2026 — Linux, Android, macOS, iOS, BSD — are descendants of Unix, which Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie wrote at Bell Labs in 1969. The ideas (everything is a file, small tools composed with pipes, a simple hierarchical filesystem, a shell that is itself a program) turned out to be more durable than any specific code. Thompson later told an interviewer he had not realized, when he wrote it, that he was designing for the next fifty years.

The modern Linux kernel — the one under most servers, every Android phone, and a lot of appliances — is 30+ million lines of C and is maintained by thousands of contributors through Linus Torvalds. It is the largest collaborative software project in history and, by any honest measure, the most important.

body.label: xv6
body.text: If the Linux kernel is overwhelming, the MIT teaching kernel xv6 is a gift. It is a small reimplementation of Unix Sixth Edition, under 10,000 lines of C, specifically designed to be read end to end. Pair it with the Three Easy Pieces textbook and you will come out understanding operating systems.
Why modern kernels look the way they do

Every OS is a compromise between safety and speed. Microkernels (Minix, QNX, the research systems at CMU) push most functionality out of the kernel into separate server processes — safer, slower. Monolithic kernels (Linux, BSD, Windows NT in practice) keep almost everything in-kernel — faster, riskier. The Tanenbaum–Torvalds debate of 1992 — the public argument about which approach is right — is still the best window into the trade-offs. Both men were right, about different things.
The purpose of an operating system is to make the hardware useful.

dek: The software that lies to every program about what it really has — memory, CPU, disk, the other programs.
name: Operating Systems

Why modern kernels look the way they do

body.text: At 10:30 p.m. on October 29, 1969, a student at UCLA named Charley Kline typed the letter L into a teletype. A machine at Stanford printed an L. He typed O. Stanford printed O. He typed G, and the system crashed. It took another hour to bring it back up. That two-character exchange, a glitch and all, is usually counted as the birth of the Internet.

body.alt: A hand-drawn map of ARPANET as of March 1977.
body.caption: ARPANET, March 1977 — the network that became the Internet. Roughly fifty nodes, most of them at universities and defence labs.
body.credit: US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

body.text: Layers, because nobody can design all of it

No single team can design something as complicated as a global network, so the field long ago agreed to layer it. Electrical signals at the bottom. Then frames, then packets, then reliable streams, then application protocols on top. Each layer talks only to the one above and the one below, and worries only about its own job. The OSI model has seven layers; the TCP/IP stack, which actually runs the Internet, has four or five depending on how you count. The idea is older than either — it goes back to Louis Pouzin's CYCLADES network in France in 1971 — and it is what lets your browser and an Ethernet cable cooperate without knowing about each other.

body.alt: Diagram of the OSI seven-layer model showing data traversing layers between two hosts.
body.caption: The OSI seven-layer model. In practice the Internet collapses these into four or five, but the intuition is the same: each layer depends only on its neighbours.

body.text: IP and the end-to-end principle

The Internet Protocol says: put a destination address on a packet and hand it to the network; the network will try its best, but does not promise anything. No delivery guarantees, no ordering, no timing. Reliability, if you need it, is the sender's and receiver's job. This end-to-end argument, spelled out by Saltzer, Reed, and Clark in 1981, is why the Internet could scale: the middle of the network stays dumb and fast, and smart behaviour lives at the edges.
TCP, which pretends packets are streams

Almost nothing you do online uses raw IP. Above it sits TCP, which turns an unreliable packet service into the illusion of a reliable byte stream: acknowledgments, retransmissions, flow control, congestion control. Van Jacobson's 1988 algorithms for congestion control — slow start, AIMD — rescued the Internet from collapse that year and are still in use. UDP, the other transport, skips all that and is what video calls and DNS use when latency matters more than correctness.
The 1969 ARPANET had four nodes: UCLA, Stanford, UCSB, Utah. The first message was LO. It was supposed to be LOGIN.
Names over numbers

Computers need numeric addresses; humans need names. The Domain Name System, designed by Paul Mockapetris in 1983, is a distributed database that translates one into the other — a hierarchy of servers in which no single one knows every answer but any one of them knows whom to ask. DNS is the quiet plumbing of the modern web, and almost every public Internet outage in the last decade has been a DNS outage in disguise.

body.caption: DNS, walked through at a whiteboard — Computerphile.

body.text: The 2020s shifts

The big protocol movements in the last few years: HTTP/3 migrating the web from TCP to QUIC for faster page loads on lossy mobile networks; the continued, slow rollout of IPv6, now past a quarter of global traffic; TLS 1.3 becoming universal; and DNS increasingly happening over HTTPS (DoH) for privacy. None of these are visible to a user directly, but together they make the Internet of 2026 noticeably snappier and more private than the Internet of 2020.

body.label: Why the cables matter
body.text: Most of the Internet's inter-continental traffic still crosses undersea cables — several hundred of them, owned by consortia of carriers, laid by specialized ships. Nicole Starosielski's book The Undersea Network is the best reminder that the "cloud" has physical geography, politics, and a few dozen chokepoints.

body.cite: Senator Ted Stevens (2006) — wrong in spirit, accidentally right about the cables
body.text: The Internet is not a truck. It's a series of tubes.

dek: How packets make it from a machine in Brooklyn to a machine in Tokyo in sixty milliseconds, give or take a cable.

body.text: In June 1970, an IBM researcher named Edgar F. Codd published a short paper titled A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks. Until then, databases were hierarchies or networks of pointers, and programs were tightly bound to the physical layout of storage. Codd's idea was to describe data as sets of relations — tables, to you and me — and let a query engine figure out the mechanics. His own employer spent a decade resisting the shift. The rest of the industry, including eventually IBM, agreed it was the right answer.
Tables, keys, and queries

A relational database is a set of tables; each row is a fact, each column a field, and a primary key identifies the row. Relationships between tables are expressed by foreign keys. SQL, standardized in 1986 and descended from Codd's ideas by way of IBM's System R, is how you ask questions. The important move is declarative: you say what you want, not how to get it, and the optimizer decides whether to scan, seek, or join.
The four letters that made databases trustworthy

Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability — ACID, coined by Jim Gray and Andreas Reuter in 1983 — describe what a transaction must guarantee. Either the whole thing happens or none of it. The database ends in a valid state. Concurrent transactions do not step on each other. Once committed, the change survives a crash. Implementing those four properties efficiently, on commodity hardware, is most of what a database engine does. Write-ahead logs, multi-version concurrency control, and two-phase commit are all in service of them.
Indexes, the hidden miracle

Without an index, every query scans the whole table. With a B-tree index on the right column, a query that touches a single row in a billion completes in a handful of disk seeks. The art of database tuning is mostly about choosing which indexes to build — too few and queries are slow, too many and inserts crawl. The inventor of the B-tree, Rudolf Bayer at Boeing in 1971, did not live to see his data structure indexing every email on Earth; but it does.
If a query is slow, look at the index first. Nine times out of ten, the query planner is forced into a full scan because the column you filter on is not indexed. EXPLAIN is your friend.
NoSQL was really a scale story

In the mid-2000s Google, Amazon, and Facebook hit limits with traditional relational databases and built document, key-value, and wide-column stores (Bigtable, Dynamo, Cassandra) that gave up some of SQL's guarantees to gain horizontal scale. Eric Brewer's CAP theorem — you can have at most two of consistency, availability, and partition-tolerance — was the theoretical frame for the trade. The industry learned a harder lesson: most applications do not need Google-scale, most developers want SQL, and by the late 2020s PostgreSQL and MySQL have absorbed most of the useful NoSQL ideas while remaining relational.

body.caption: Andy Pavlo, opening lecture of CMU 15-445 — the best database course on the internet.

body.text: Where the frontier is in 2026

The interesting work now is in analytical systems — columnar stores, DuckDB, ClickHouse, Snowflake — that separate compute from storage and query terabytes of data interactively. Vector search, for retrieval-augmented AI, is the other growing edge. Both are, underneath, applications of very old ideas: good indexing, good storage layout, and a query planner smart enough to stay out of the way.

body.label: On the word "database"
body.text: The word "database" entered English in 1962, in a military report on "flattened data bases." "Relational database" is a 1970 coinage of Codd's. "NoSQL" was coined in 1998 as the name of a specific product, then retroactively redefined in 2009 to mean "anything that is not relational." The field is much better at systems than at names.

dek: The long struggle to store, find, and update data without losing any of it.
