body.text: In 1936, in the teeth of the Great Depression, John Maynard Keynes published a book whose opening sentence was a quiet piece of academic cheek: "I shall argue that the postulates of the classical theory are applicable to a special case only." The classical theory said economies return to full employment on their own. Cambridge and Washington had been watching this fail for seven years. The General Theory invented macroeconomics so that what was happening could be talked about at all.

body.caption: John Maynard Keynes (1883–1946), photographed in 1933. His 1936 General Theory created macroeconomics as a separate discipline and gave the mid-twentieth-century state its economic toolkit.

body.text: The three numbers every economy reports

Macroeconomics organizes itself around three headline statistics. GDP — gross domestic product — measures the total market value of goods and services produced in a year. Unemployment measures the share of the labor force actively seeking work but not finding it. Inflation measures the rate at which the general level of prices is rising. Almost every policy argument in the news is ultimately about the trade-offs between these three.

Each number is a compromise. GDP misses the unpaid work that keeps households running (Marilyn Waring made the feminist case in the 1980s); it does not distinguish between productive and destructive output (a pipeline and a hurricane cleanup both count as growth); it does not capture distribution. But it is the best we have for a single-number summary of an economy's size, and its movements, watched quarterly, are genuinely informative.
The central-bank toolkit

A central bank sets short-term interest rates and manages the money supply; through those two levers, it tries to keep inflation near a target (usually two percent) and unemployment as low as it can without setting inflation off. The Federal Reserve has been doing this since 1913, the Bank of England since 1694. The techniques have changed — open-market operations, quantitative easing, forward guidance, standing repo — but the basic job has not.

Since 2008, central banks have operated in increasingly exotic territory: zero and even negative interest rates, direct asset purchases in the trillions, coordinated interventions across currencies. The 2020s inflation, the biggest in forty years in most advanced economies, has pushed the same banks back toward the orthodoxy of the 1980s. The vocabulary of modern macro — "hiking cycle," "landing zone," "neutral rate" — is borrowed from aviation on purpose.
The long argument between the schools

Macroeconomics is the branch of the field where the disagreements are loudest. Keynesians see a role for active fiscal and monetary policy; monetarists, following Milton Friedman, distrust fiscal intervention and watch the money supply; new classical and real-business-cycle economists treat recessions as optimal responses to real shocks; behavioral and heterodox economists challenge assumptions of rationality from several directions. A careful reader learns to notice which school an argument comes from without being told.

The Phillips curve — the empirical trade-off between unemployment and inflation — is the best example of the arguing. Discovered by the New Zealand economist A. W. Phillips in 1958, it suggested that policymakers could pick a point on the curve. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued in the 1960s that the curve was vertical in the long run: trying to buy lower unemployment with higher inflation would eventually give you both. The subsequent fifty years have produced a dozen "the Phillips curve is dead" and "the Phillips curve is back" op-eds. Both claims have been right at different times, which is the shape of the underlying argument.
Growth, which eventually dominates

Over a five-year horizon, unemployment and inflation are the stories that matter. Over a fifty-year horizon, growth dwarfs them. A one-percentage-point difference in annual growth, compounded for a century, is the difference between a poor country and a rich one. Understanding what drives growth — capital, labor, technology, institutions, geography, human capital — is the quiet, slow-moving heart of the subject. Robert Solow's 1956 model, for which he won the 1987 Nobel, gave the field its workhorse framework; modern work by Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson on institutions extends it in consequential directions.
The open economy

No modern country is a closed economy. Exchange rates, trade balances, capital flows, remittances, and foreign direct investment are all part of the macro picture. Robert Mundell's 1963 "impossible trinity" — a country cannot simultaneously fix its exchange rate, allow free capital movement, and run an independent monetary policy — is one of the cleanest and most durable results in the field. The euro crisis of the 2010s was, at root, a slow collision with that result.

The Federal Reserve's congressional mandate, set in 1977, is a "dual mandate": maximum employment and stable prices. Most other central banks (the ECB, the Bank of England) are mandated on inflation alone. Which mandate a central bank operates under is not just legal trivia — it changes what the bank will do in a crisis.

body.cite: John Maynard Keynes, The General Theory (1936)
body.text: The ideas of economists and political philosophers, both when they are right and when they are wrong, are more powerful than is commonly understood.
Learn it: computing GDP three ways

A small economy produces two goods this year: 100 loaves of bread at $3 each, and 50 chairs at $40 each. What is GDP? Work through all three methods. Production (value-added) approach: 100·3 + 50·40 = 300 + 2,000 = $2,300. Expenditure approach: if all of it is bought by households (C), GDP = $2,300. Income approach: the same $2,300 is paid out as wages, rents, interest, and profit. All three methods give the same number by construction; that is the central accounting identity of macro, GDP = C + I + G + NX = total income.

Now distinguish nominal from real. Next year, the same economy produces 100 loaves at $4 and 50 chairs at $42. Nominal GDP = 400 + 2,100 = $2,500. Real GDP (using year-one prices as base) = 100·3 + 50·40 = $2,300 — unchanged. The GDP deflator = nominal/real = 2,500/2,300 ≈ 1.087, implying 8.7% inflation. Growth in real terms is 0%. When news headlines say "GDP rose 5%," always ask: real or nominal? What base year? What deflator?
Practice problems

Problem 1. An economy has 1,000 working-age adults. 600 are employed, 60 are unemployed (looking for work), 340 are not in the labor force (retired, students, caregivers). What are the labor-force participation rate and the unemployment rate?

Answer: Labor force = employed + unemployed = 660. Participation = 660/1,000 = 66%. Unemployment rate = 60/660 ≈ 9.1%. Crucial note: unemployment is measured against the labor force, not the population. A country can have falling unemployment and falling participation at the same time, which is why economists watch both numbers.

Problem 2. A central bank raises its policy interest rate from 2% to 4%. Trace through the likely effects on (a) borrowing cost for businesses, (b) the currency's exchange rate, (c) the stock market, (d) inflation, and (e) unemployment, assuming a 6-to-18-month lag.

Answer: (a) higher — corporate bonds and loans reprice; (b) the currency usually appreciates as higher yields attract foreign capital; (c) stocks typically fall in the short run (higher discount rate on future earnings, weaker outlook); (d) inflation should fall with a lag as demand cools; (e) unemployment typically rises, often peaking 12–18 months after the tightening cycle ends. This is the classic monetary-transmission sequence; 2022–2024 is a textbook case study.

Problem 3. In 1923 Germany, prices doubled roughly every 3.7 days at the peak of the hyperinflation. What is the implied annual inflation rate, and what does this tell you about the relationship between the money supply and prices?

Answer: Doubling every 3.7 days = about 98 doublings per year = 2^98, which is an annual inflation rate in the trillions of percent. This is what Milton Friedman meant when he said "inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon" — at the extremes, the relationship is mechanical. At normal low inflation rates, the relationship is much looser; the monetarist story is best at explaining catastrophes, not everyday price drift.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What is the accounting identity GDP = C + I + G + NX actually saying? (2) Why does the Federal Reserve try to move unemployment and inflation in opposite directions? (3) What is the difference between monetary and fiscal policy? (4) Name two things that are produced but not counted in GDP. (5) Draw a Phillips curve. What did Friedman and Phelps claim about its long-run shape? (6) In the Solow model, what happens to growth as an economy approaches its steady state?
The learning progression

Brand new? Watch MRU's macro first-unit videos and one FOMC press conference in full. Read one Fed statement and Jerome Powell's opening remarks, then read one piece of news commentary on the same statement. When you can tell which school a commentator is drawing on, you've learned the vocabulary. Once you've got the basics? Read the first two chapters of Mankiw's Macroeconomics and the first two of Keynes's General Theory, back-to-back. Work through the Solow growth model on paper with sample numbers. To go further? Take Harvard's free Big Data course (Chetty), read Reinhart and Rogoff, and — if you're serious — sit in on David Romer's Berkeley Macro course. The advanced path is Sargent and Ljungqvist or Romer's Advanced Macroeconomics.

dek: The economics of whole economies — unemployment, inflation, growth, and the arguments over what a government should do about them.
name: Macroeconomics

body.text: In the early 1970s, two Israeli psychologists — Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky — began a collaboration in a small office in Jerusalem that would eventually win one of them a Nobel Prize in economics. They did not set out to found a subfield. They were trying to explain why experienced statisticians, shown certain kinds of problems, reliably got them wrong.

body.caption: Daniel Kahneman (1934–2024), who shared the 2002 Nobel in economics. His collaborator Amos Tversky had died in 1996; the prize is not awarded posthumously.
body.credit: nrkbeta, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: The systematic errors

Classical economics assumed people were rational: given full information, they would choose what maximized their expected utility. Kahneman and Tversky showed, experiment after experiment, that people are not rational in this sense, and — more importantly — that they are irrational in predictable ways. Anchoring, availability, loss aversion, framing: each is a named, measurable, reproducible deviation from the textbook.

Anchoring: show someone a random number before asking them to estimate a quantity, and their estimate shifts toward the number. Availability: ask someone the probability of an event, and they substitute how easily examples come to mind. Loss aversion: people feel the pain of losing $100 roughly twice as intensely as the pleasure of gaining $100. These are not quirks; they are almost universal, and they rewrite a surprising amount of what economics thought it knew.
Two systems

Kahneman's 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow organizes the findings around a metaphor: we have a fast, intuitive, pattern-matching "System 1" and a slow, deliberate, effortful "System 2." Most of our waking decisions run on System 1, which is usually right and occasionally spectacularly wrong. The distinction is more rhetorical than neurological, but it organizes a sprawling literature.
Prospect theory

Prospect theory, Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 paper, is the canonical formalization. It replaces expected-utility theory with a value function that is concave for gains, convex for losses, and steeper for losses than for gains. That asymmetry — the kink at zero — explains why people are simultaneously risk-averse over gains and risk-seeking over losses, a pattern classical theory could not account for. It is, in citations, one of the most influential economics papers of the late twentieth century.
Nudges, and the debate over them

Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein's 2008 book Nudge argued that small changes in how a choice is presented — the default option in a retirement plan, the position of the salad bar — can change behavior without restricting freedom. Governments in the UK, the US, and dozens of other countries now employ "behavioral insights" teams. The British example, the Behavioural Insights Team (founded 2010, spun out of the Cabinet Office in 2014), is the best-documented.

Critics on the left call nudges a band-aid that lets politicians avoid structural reform. Critics on the right call them paternalism in polite clothing. The debate is ongoing and worth paying attention to. The practical track record is mixed: some nudges (organ-donor defaults, retirement auto-enrollment) show large and durable effects; others (most text-message interventions) show small and decaying ones.
The replication reckoning

Behavioral economics shared the replication crisis that hit social psychology in the 2010s. Some of its famous findings — ego depletion, social priming, power posing — did not replicate at all. Others — loss aversion, anchoring, the endowment effect — have held up robustly across decades and cultures. A careful reader now treats the field the way one would treat any young science: fascinated, curious, and slow to believe the next headline. A living spreadsheet of replication outcomes for behavioral findings is maintained by researchers at Berkeley.
The limits of the program

Behavioral economics is strong on diagnosis and uneven on prescription. It has documented dozens of ways humans depart from the rational actor model; it has had a harder time saying what institutions should be redesigned to accommodate the departures. The field has also been criticized, including by Kahneman himself, for focusing on individuals when many of the decisions that matter are made by firms, bureaucracies, and political coalitions. A full sociology of the subject is arguably still to be written.

In 2002, Daniel Kahneman shared the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. Amos Tversky had died in 1996; the Nobel is not awarded posthumously. Kahneman spent a large part of his acceptance lecture talking about him.
Learn it: five biases you can catch yourself committing today

Anchoring. Think of the last two digits of your phone number. Now, without looking anything up, guess how many countries are in Africa. Write down both numbers. If you are like most subjects in Tversky and Kahneman's classic study, your guess correlates with the arbitrary anchor. (The answer is 54.) The moment the brain is given a number — any number — it uses it as a starting point, and every subsequent adjustment is insufficient.

Availability. Which word occurs more often in English text: words starting with "r", or words with "r" as the third letter? Most people say the first, because initial-letter words are easier to recall. The correct answer is the second, by a wide margin. The mind substitutes "how easily can I think of examples?" for "how frequent are the examples?"

Loss aversion. Flip a coin: heads you win $150, tails you lose $100. The expected value is positive, and a risk-neutral decision-maker would take the bet every time. Most people refuse. Prospect theory quantifies why: the pain of losing $100 is about twice the pleasure of winning $100. To make the bet attractive on average, the upside typically has to be twice the downside, not equal.

Framing. "95% of patients survive this surgery" vs. "5% of patients die from this surgery." Identical information; very different clinical decisions. Surgeons and patients both shift, and the effect survives training.

Endowment. Give half a class a mug; give the other half a chance to buy a mug. Let them trade. Classical theory predicts half the mugs change hands. In the actual experiment (Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler, 1990), almost none do — sellers want roughly twice what buyers will pay. People value things more once they own them.
Practice problems

Problem 1. A retirement plan has two possible default options: (A) employees are automatically enrolled at 6% of salary unless they opt out; (B) employees are not enrolled unless they opt in. Classical economics predicts the same participation rate under both. What does behavioral economics predict, and what has the empirical evidence shown? What is the policy name for this intervention?

Answer: Classical theory says rational workers know what they want and pick accordingly; defaults should not matter. Behavioral theory predicts massively higher participation under (A) because defaults exploit status-quo bias. The empirical evidence (Madrian and Shea, 2001, and many successors) shows participation roughly doubles. This is the canonical Thaler-Sunstein "nudge." Most U.S. 401(k) plans now use some form of auto-enrollment.

Problem 2. You own a stock bought at $50. It is now trading at $30. A similar stock you don't own is trading at $30. A rational investor should treat both the same. Most investors, however, refuse to sell at a loss. What bias is at work? Is the sunk cost really "sunk"?

Answer: Loss aversion — the disposition effect in finance. Selling at a loss makes the loss psychologically real; holding lets one keep hoping. The sunk cost is genuinely sunk — past prices should not affect forward decisions. Brokers who understand this phenomenon build it into their coaching. The empirical evidence (Shefrin and Statman, 1985) is robust across markets and decades.

Problem 3. A cafeteria wants students to eat more fruit. It puts the fruit at eye level at the front of the line, leaves desserts at the back in plainer containers. Consumption of fruit rises 25%. Dessert consumption falls. Is this paternalism? Is it manipulation? Is it ethically distinguishable from a junk-food tax?

Answer: There is no single right answer — this is the heart of the Thaler-Sunstein debate. A libertarian-paternalist argues this is acceptable because no option is removed; a harder-line libertarian says shaping defaults is still interference; a critic from the left says real change requires structural reform, not shelf-placement. The question is ethical, not empirical, and you should be able to articulate your own view in plain words.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What is the difference between a heuristic and a bias? (2) Why is loss aversion not the same as risk aversion? (3) What does "System 1 vs System 2" claim, and what is one criticism of the distinction? (4) Name three behavioral findings that have held up under replication, and one that has not. (5) Give a nudge and an equivalent mandate; which would you prefer, and why? (6) What does Kahneman mean by "noise" (as opposed to "bias") in his 2021 book?
The learning progression

Brand new? Watch Kahneman's TED talk and read the first three chapters of Thinking, Fast and Slow. Keep a "bias journal" for a week: every time you catch yourself in one, write down the bias, the context, and how you would have decided differently. This is the single most useful exercise in the field. Once you've got the basics? Read Nudge cover to cover, and the 1979 Prospect Theory paper (freely available through many university libraries). Work through the MIT 14.13 problem sets. To go further? Take a behavioral-economics graduate seminar, or pick one bias and read the last ten years of replication literature on it. The current frontier is heterogeneity — why the same nudge works on some people and not others — and you can read straight into it.

dek: The branch of economics that takes psychology seriously — and admits the "rational actor" of the textbook is a convenient fiction.
name: Behavioral Economics

body.text: In 1827, a German high-school teacher named Georg Ohm published a pamphlet in which he argued that the current through a wire was directly proportional to the voltage across it. The Prussian academic establishment called the work a fabric of naked fancies; he lost his teaching job. Thirty years later the same relationship was the foundation of every electrical engineering curriculum in the world. Every working electrician uses it, often without naming it, every time she picks the right wire for the right breaker.

body.caption: The circuit that defines Ohm's law: source, resistance, current.

body.text: The whole idea

Electricity in a house is water in a pipe. Voltage is the pressure, current is the flow, resistance is the narrowness. Multiply current by voltage and you get power. Pick a wire too small for the current and it gets hot. Pick a breaker too large for the wire and the wire burns before the breaker trips. That single sentence is the entire theory behind every residential circuit.
Before you start
Tools

A digital multimeter ($40 for a Fluke entry model), a non-contact voltage tester ($15), wire strippers, linesman's pliers, a tick tracer, insulated screwdrivers. For hands-on lab work: a bench power supply and a handful of resistors (1 kΩ, 10 kΩ, 100 kΩ) from any electronics hobby shop.
Safety

Never assume a circuit is dead. Test with a non-contact tester before touching any wire. Then test your tester on a known live circuit, then test your wire, then test your tester again. The one-hand rule: keep one hand in your pocket when working near live voltage, so current cannot cross your chest.
Words to know

Voltage (V) — potential difference, in volts. Current (I) — flow, in amps. Resistance (R) — opposition to flow, in ohms (Ω). Power (P) — work per second, in watts. Conductor — wire. Insulator — the plastic sheath. AC — alternating current (wall outlet). DC — direct current (battery). Hot — the energized conductor. Neutral — the return to source. Ground — safety path to earth.
The three quantities

Voltage is the pressure pushing electrons through a wire. Current is the flow itself — electrons passing a point per second. Resistance is how hard the wire or load pushes back. A higher voltage pushes more current through the same resistance. A higher resistance reduces current at the same voltage. The three are always related, always at the same instant.
Ohm's Law
V = I × R. Rearranged: I = V/R, R = V/I. Every troubleshooter in the trade uses this on the back of a receipt. Know two of the three, solve for the third.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: A 120 V circuit drives a 12 Ω heating element. Current: I = V/R = 120/12 = 10 amps. If the element is wired with 14-gauge wire (rated for 15 amps), you are within limits. If it were wired with 16-gauge (rated 13 amps at residential use), you are over — the wire will heat, the insulation will degrade, and eventually the wire will fail.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Forgetting that household resistors — filaments, heaters, motors — are not constant. A light bulb's resistance triples when hot vs cold; motors draw inrush current at startup that can be 6× running current. Sizing breakers for inrush is why you see "time-delay" fuses and magnetic-hydraulic breakers on motor circuits.
Power and why wires get hot

Power is voltage times current: P = V × I. A 1,500-watt hair dryer on 120 V draws 12.5 amps. Push that through an undersized wire and the wire's own resistance turns current into heat — enough to start a fire. That is the whole reason the American Wire Gauge scale and the breaker system exist.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: Power formulas combined: P = V × I = I² × R. For the 10-amp heating circuit above, P = 120 × 10 = 1,200 watts. Equivalently, I² × R = 100 × 12 = 1,200 watts. Same answer, different path.
AC versus DC

Direct current flows one way — battery, phone charger output. Alternating current reverses direction 60 times a second in North America, 50 in most of the world. The US grid settled on AC because high-voltage AC travels long distances efficiently and can be stepped down by transformers. The wall outlet in your kitchen carries single-phase 120 V AC; the service entrance brings split-phase 240/120 V from the utility.
Wire sizing — the practical consequence

The American Wire Gauge (AWG) scale runs inverted: smaller numbers are thicker wires that carry more current. For residential branch circuits: 14 AWG for 15 amps, 12 AWG for 20 amps, 10 AWG for 30 amps, 8 AWG for 40–50 amps (electric ranges, dryers), 6 AWG for 60 amps, 4 AWG for 100 amps. The NEC table 310.16 is where this lives; Ugly's Electrical References has it on a pocket-sized page.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: A 20-amp kitchen outlet circuit feeding a microwave (1,100 W) and a toaster (1,500 W) simultaneously: total 2,600 W / 120 V = 21.7 amps. The 20-amp breaker trips. Code requires at least two 20-amp small-appliance circuits in a kitchen for exactly this reason.
Troubleshooting

A breaker trips on a specific appliance. The load is drawing more than the breaker rating — possibly a motor with stuck bearings. An outlet is warm to the touch. Loose connection at the terminal; the heat is being generated by high resistance in a bad contact. Replace. A circuit works sometimes but not always. Intermittent bad connection inside a box or at a wire nut; pull and redo. All tests read near-zero. The circuit is de-energized; check the breaker and the upstream terminal.
Going deeper

Beyond Ohm's law, the next concepts are reactance (AC circuits with capacitors or inductors), power factor (the phase lag between voltage and current in motor loads), and three-phase power (the commercial service). MIT OCW 6.002 is the free undergraduate-level deep dive; Ugly's is the pocket reference.

body.label: Practice this week
body.text: With a multimeter, measure the voltage at three wall outlets in your house. Then, with the circuit breaker off, measure the resistance across the outlet slots (should be nearly infinite, since no load is connected). Turn the breaker back on and measure again with a known load (a lamp) plugged in. You will see every Ohm's-law quantity on a cheap meter.

body.label: Self-check
body.text: What is the current through a 240-ohm resistor at 120 V? (0.5 A.) What gauge wire is required for a 30-amp circuit? (10 AWG.) Why does a bulb filament have higher resistance cold? (No, it has lower resistance cold — resistance rises with temperature.) If any stumps you, watch Khan Academy's "Intro to circuits and Ohm's law."
First project: buy a $15 multimeter and measure voltage, current, and resistance on three household appliances. You will internalize the units and the relationships faster than a week of reading.

dek: V equals I times R — three letters that run every circuit in your house.
name: Ohm's Law & Basics

body.text: A single-family American house is typically fed by the utility with 200 amps of split-phase 240-volt service, entering through a meter, passing into a main panel, and branching into twenty or thirty circuits that feed outlets, lights, appliances, and the heat. The entire system is designed so that, in a failure, the smallest and cheapest component — the breaker in the panel — is the one that gives way, long before the wire gets hot enough to ignite the wood around it. Residential wiring is not complicated once you have seen it done ten times. It is disciplined.

body.caption: A residential receptacle terminated with hot, neutral, ground.

body.text: The whole idea

Every circuit is a complete loop from the breaker, through the load, back to the neutral bar. Every branch circuit has three conductors — hot, neutral, and ground — running in sheathed cable through the walls to outlets, switches, and lights. Every splice happens inside a junction box. Every device is screwed to a stud or joist, then screwed to the cable going in and out of it. That structure repeats, on every circuit, in every house.
Before you start
Tools

Wire strippers with marked gauges. Linesman's pliers. A 4-in-1 screwdriver. A non-contact voltage tester. A multimeter. A drywall saw. A drill with 1/2" auger bit for boring through studs. Staples and a staple gun for fastening cable. Wire nuts.
Safety

Turn off the circuit at the breaker. Test with a non-contact tester. Test your tester on a known live circuit. Then test your wire. Then test your tester again. Every electrical fatality in American houses is a story about someone who skipped that sequence. Never work on a live panel; call a licensed electrician for service-side work.
Words to know

Service entrance — the utility's connection to the house. Main breaker — the top-of-panel switch that disconnects the whole house. Branch circuit — a single breaker feeding one or more outlets/lights/loads. NM cable — non-metallic sheathed cable (Romex). Junction box — the metal or plastic enclosure containing a splice. Device — an outlet, switch, or light fixture. Pigtail — a short wire spliced to two others so only one wire lands on a screw. Bond — the intentional connection between metal parts to ground.
The service and the panel

Two hot conductors and one neutral enter the main panel at 240/120 V split-phase. The main breaker disconnects the whole house. Two hot bus bars carry 240 V across the panel; the neutral bar and ground bar run beside them. Each 120-V branch circuit takes one hot from a single-pole breaker, one neutral from the neutral bar, and one ground. A 240-V appliance circuit takes both hots via a two-pole breaker.
NM cable and boxes

Romex (trade name for non-metallic sheathed cable) carries the conductors through walls. 14/2 NM cable contains two 14 AWG insulated conductors plus a bare ground, sheathed in plastic. 14/3 adds a third insulated conductor (red, for three-way switches). Every connection happens inside a code-approved box with room for the splices according to "box fill" rules.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: Running a circuit: staple cable to every framing member within 8 inches of a box, then every 4½ feet through the field. Drill holes in studs at least 1¼ inches from the face (or add metal nail plates), run the cable through, secure into the box with a cable connector, strip 6 inches of sheath, trim 3/4" of insulation off each conductor before landing on terminals.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Running cable against the face of a stud too close to the drywall. Code requires cable to be at least 1¼" from the nearest face, or protected by a steel nail plate. An un-protected cable against the face will eventually catch a drywall screw, and the short-circuit shows up later as a mystery breaker trip.
Outlets

A duplex receptacle has hot (brass) screws, neutral (silver) screws, a ground (green) screw, and a break-off tab that lets you split the top half from the bottom. Most common wiring: pigtail the hots together with a short "pigtail" to the brass screw; same for neutrals; ground to the green. That way the circuit continues even if the receptacle is replaced.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: A mid-run outlet on a 15-amp circuit: two 14/2 cables enter the box (one "in", one "out"). Strip both. Twist the two blacks (hots) and a 6" pigtail together with a wire nut; the pigtail lands on the brass screw. Twist whites the same way to silver. Grounds: twist all three with a green pigtail to the green screw. Fold the conductors into the box, screw the receptacle on.
Switches

A single-pole switch interrupts the hot between the panel and a light. Two screws (brass), one for line in, one for load out, and a ground. A three-way switch is two switches on a pair of "travelers" that allow either to toggle the light from opposite ends of a hallway or stairway. A four-way goes in the middle of two three-ways for control from three or more locations.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Wiring a three-way by trial and error. The common terminal (darker or marked COM) is different on each brand. Identify the common terminal first; the two travelers can go on either of the remaining terminals, but the common must be the hot-feed wire on one switch and the load-out on the other.
GFCI and AFCI

The ground-fault circuit interrupter compares current leaving (hot) with current returning (neutral). If they differ by more than 5 mA — the current that will stop a heart — the GFCI trips in a thirtieth of a second. Required within six feet of water, at bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, unfinished basements. The arc-fault circuit interrupter listens for the electrical signature of a low-current arc (like a damaged lamp cord inside a pinched rug) and trips before the arc ignites the material around it. Required on most bedroom and living-area circuits since 1999.
Troubleshooting

The outlet is dead, breaker isn't tripped. Check GFCI upstream — many outlets are protected by a GFCI on the same circuit. The breaker won't reset. Something on the circuit has a dead short; unplug every load, reset, then add back one at a time. The light flickers. Loose neutral at a box somewhere on the circuit; pull and redo. The outlet is hot. Loose connection at a terminal; turn off, replace.
Going deeper

Once you can wire a receptacle, a switch, and a three-way, the next step is installing a 240-V appliance circuit, adding a subpanel, or running EV-charger wiring. The IBEW/NECA Electrical Training Alliance apprenticeship is the gold-standard training; Mike Holt's "Understanding the NEC" is the self-study text.

body.label: Practice this week
body.text: Replace a wall outlet in your house. Turn off the breaker. Verify dead with a non-contact tester. Remove the plate and receptacle. Note which wire went where. Connect to the new receptacle in the same pattern. Turn on. One receptacle, one screwdriver, thirty minutes — and you will understand the wiring in the walls of every house you ever own.

body.label: Self-check
body.text: What color is the hot conductor screw? (Brass.) What is a pigtail for? (To splice so the circuit continues even if the device is removed.) When does a GFCI trip? (At 5 mA imbalance between hot and neutral.) If any stumps you, watch Electrician U's "How to Wire an Outlet" series.
First project: replace a standard receptacle with a GFCI in a bathroom. One hour, $20 in parts. You will learn line-vs-load GFCI wiring and the correct protection of a downstream receptacle.

dek: Outlets, switches, panels — the day-to-day craft of running current safely through a house.
name: Residential Wiring

body.text: Between 1871 and 1897, twenty percent of all American homes that were destroyed by fire were lost to bad electrical wiring. In 1881, a committee of electrical engineers met in New York to begin writing a voluntary code; by 1897, five separate regional codes had merged into the first National Electrical Code, under the auspices of what would become the National Fire Protection Association. The NEC is now 1,100 pages long, updated every three years, and adopted as law in nearly every American jurisdiction. It is not a document about how to make things work. It is a document about how not to burn down a city.

body.caption: The current edition of NFPA 70.

body.text: The whole idea

The NEC tells you what must be in an electrical installation so that it does not start a fire, electrocute the occupants, or fail in a predictable way. It does not tell you how many outlets to put in a living room (a minimum, yes; a maximum, no), which brand to use, or whether the breaker should be on the left or the right of the panel. Its whole business is the failure case.
Before you start
Tools
A current copy of the NEC (or a Code Check Electrical flipchart, which covers the residential subset). A pen and the phone number of your local inspector. Ugly's Electrical References in the truck.
Mindset

Every NEC rule is written to prevent a specific past failure. Read the rules slowly; they are dense, and the exceptions usually matter. When in doubt, call the AHJ — they would rather answer the phone than fail an inspection.
Words to know

AHJ — Authority Having Jurisdiction, the inspector. Article — a numbered chapter of the NEC. Section — a subdivision of an article. Listed — approved by a nationally recognized testing laboratory (UL is the common one). Identified — the conductor is marked for a specific purpose. Raceway — any channel that encloses conductors. Overcurrent protection — a fuse or breaker.
Where the code comes from

The National Fire Protection Association publishes the NEC as NFPA 70. Twenty code-making panels, staffed by electricians, engineers, inspectors, and manufacturers, review every proposed change through a public comment process. The ICC, AHJs, NEMA, UL — the alphabet of standards bodies that orbit the code — all feed in. What emerges is a consensus document that states and cities then adopt, often with local amendments. The NEC itself is not federal law; it becomes law when your town council votes to adopt it.
Structure of the NEC

Chapter 1 (Articles 100–110) defines terms and general requirements. Chapters 2–4 (200–490) cover wiring and protection, wiring methods, equipment for general use. Chapter 5 covers special occupancies (hospitals, hazardous locations). Chapter 6 special equipment. Chapter 7 special conditions. Chapter 8 communications systems. Chapter 9 tables (ampacity, conduit fill, and the tables every electrician uses most). Annexes provide informative material.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: You need to know the ampacity of a 12 AWG copper conductor in a residential installation. Open NEC Table 310.16 (in Chapter 3, but the tables live at 310). Find 12 AWG, copper, 60°C column (residential default): 25 amps. Note the overcurrent-protection rule in 240.4(D): the breaker cannot exceed 20 amps on 12 AWG anyway. The two rules combine to give you 20A / 12 AWG as the standard residential pairing.
Key articles to know

Article 210: branch circuits — where outlets must be, how circuits are sized. Article 220: load calculation — how to size the service. Article 240: overcurrent protection. Article 250: grounding and bonding (the article where most mistakes happen). Article 310: conductor ampacity (the tables). Article 314: boxes and box fill. Article 406: receptacles. Article 408: panels. A residential electrician spends 90% of her code lookups in these articles.
Permits and inspection

A permit is pulled before the work begins — typically by the homeowner for minor work, the electrician for everything else. Rough inspection happens before the drywall goes up: the inspector verifies cable routing, box fill, staple spacing, box-to-box clearances. Final inspection happens before the service is energized: devices installed, panels labeled, GFCI/AFCI working. A good inspector has seen every mistake in the book and is looking for the one you made.
Troubleshooting code violations

The inspector red-tagged the rough. Read the violation code section; fix exactly that. Do not guess. Box fill is over. Deepen the box, or split the splices across two boxes. The staple spacing is wrong. Re-staple. The receptacle spacing is too far. Add one. The GFCI is in the wrong place. Move it to the first receptacle on the circuit, where it protects downstream.
Going deeper

After the residential side, the next code territory is commercial (Article 250 grounding gets hairy fast), industrial (hazardous locations, Articles 500–510), and specialty equipment (EV charging, PV solar, Article 690). Mike Holt's Understanding the NEC is the trade's reading of record.

body.label: Practice this week
body.text: Read Article 210 of the current NEC (available free online at nfpa.org with a free account). Note every residential requirement. Compare against the wiring in your own house. You will find at least one thing that is not to current code — and that is normal, since codes are not retroactive.

body.label: Self-check
body.text: What is an AHJ? (Authority Having Jurisdiction — the inspector.) Which article covers grounding and bonding? (250.) What is the most common 12 AWG residential breaker size? (20 A.) If any stumps you, read Mike Holt's Understanding the NEC Volume 1.

First project: pull a permit for a small electrical job (adding a single outlet, for example). The permit office will give you a booklet explaining local amendments. You will learn what an inspector actually checks — and your wiring will be correct for the rest of your life.

dek: The thousand-page rulebook written in the ashes of a hundred fires.
name: Electrical Code

body.text: In 1530, Erasmus of Rotterdam — who was at that point the most famous intellectual in Europe — wrote a small Latin book for children called De civilitate morum puerilium, "On civility in children." It told them not to spit on the floor at dinner, not to lick the common serving spoon, and not to blow their noses in the tablecloth. The book was one of the bestsellers of the sixteenth century, and it is a useful reminder that table manners are not snobbery. They are a thousand-year thread of agreements about how to sit down with other people and share food without making any of them unhappy.
The rulebook, such as it is

Emily Post published her first Etiquette in 1922, and her great-great-granddaughter Lizzie Post published the Centennial Edition a century later, in 2022. The book is five hundred pages and still organized around three principles: consideration, respect, and honesty. Almost every specific rule — outside-in with the silverware, napkin in the lap within a minute of sitting, soup spoon moves away from you — is a working specification of those three. When the rule and the principle conflict (the host is eating with her fingers because the meal requires it), go with the principle.
The three rules most people miss

One: wait until everyone is served before picking up a fork, unless the host invites you otherwise. In small groups, wait for the host to lift a fork first. Two: the knife and fork are held in opposite hands — American style switches between bites, European style keeps them in the original hands. Either is correct; picking one and being consistent is better than waffling. Three: phone face-down on the table, or off it entirely. The single rule that has done the most to erode modern meals is the tolerance of the unsilenced phone, and the single best correction is a host who says, quietly, "phones away, please" the moment the first person is seated.
The silverware has a map

At a formal table, the silverware is arranged in the order the courses will be eaten, from the outside in. The salad fork on the far left goes with the salad that will arrive first; the entree fork nearer the plate goes with the main course; the dessert spoon and fork above the plate go with dessert. Bread-and-butter plate on the upper left, water glass on the upper right, wine glasses (if any) to the right of the water. There is an old mnemonic — BMW, for bread-meal-water, left to right — that has taught a million people whose bread plate is whose. The diagrams on emilypost.com are the most useful single page on the internet the first time you have to set a formal table.
Conversation is the real meal

The food is an occasion for the talk. A good guest turns toward the less-included person, asks a real question, listens to the answer, and follows up. She does not monopolize. She does not lecture. She does not deliver an opinion uninvited, and she recognizes that politics, religion, and money — the three old forbidden topics — are forbidden not because they are unimportant but because they tend to produce monologues and ill feeling in almost every group where not everyone agrees on them already. Anna Post, the Centennial Edition's co-author, states the rule more generously: "steer toward what the room can share in."

Leave the phone in your pocket. A single glance at a screen during dinner is the clearest signal you can send that the person across from you is less interesting than whatever is not in the room. Do not send it, even inadvertently.
Host and guest

A host's job is to make the evening possible for the guests. This means the planning — the cooking, the serving, the timing — but also the gentle structural work of introductions, of moving the conversation when a corner of the table has gone quiet, of rescuing the person who has mentioned her divorce by accident. A guest's job is to be on time, bring something if asked, eat what is offered, talk with the stranger on her left, and write a thank-you note the next day. The two roles are older than dinner parties. Homer's Odyssey calls the guest-host relationship xenia and makes it the central moral principle of the whole poem.
Why manners are still worth learning

A hundred years after Emily Post's first book, manners are no longer a class marker the way they were, and the old performative rituals — the place cards, the finger bowls, the right address for the dowager countess — have been quietly retired. What remains is the working core: be considerate, be respectful, be honest. The specific rules about the fork exist to spare the person beside you from having to watch you use it awkwardly. That is the only reason any of them have ever existed.

dek: The silent language every adult is supposed to know — with the small kindnesses that keep a dinner from becoming a performance.
