body.text: In 1775, during the long winter of the Continental Army's occupation of Cambridge, Abigail Adams wrote a letter to her husband John that began "I wish you would ever write me a Letter half as long as I write you." Between 1762 and her death in 1818, Abigail wrote more than a thousand surviving letters — to her husband, her children, her sister, her confidantes — and they are now among the most important documents in the American archival record. Nothing she wrote was designed to last. Letters last anyway, in a way that email does not, and one reason an Emily Post Institute in Vermont still teaches the handwritten note is that the medium itself does work.
Why the handwritten note still matters

A handwritten note takes five minutes to write, costs less than a dollar, and produces an effect on the recipient wildly out of proportion to the labor. It signals, with no other information necessary, that you thought enough of the person or event to stop what you were doing and make something physical. Emails, texts, and DMs are all read inside a stream. A card is read standing alone at a mailbox, often twice. This is the whole secret of the form: the medium itself, before anything you say in it, is the message.
The four-line thank-you

A thank-you note does not have to be long. Four short lines is plenty. Greeting; the gift or occasion named specifically; one sentence of genuine response; close. "Dear Aunt Dorothy — Thank you so much for the copy of Turn Left at Orion. I used the finder charts to find the Andromeda Galaxy on Tuesday night; it was the first time I had ever seen it. Love, Nina." Forty-five seconds to write, fifteen seconds to read, and Aunt Dorothy will remember it for a year. The only absolute rule of the thank-you note is that it be written within a week of the gift or event; past a month it slightly insults the giver by suggesting she did not matter.
The structure of a letter

A letter has a salutation, a body, a closing, and a signature. "Dear" is the default salutation in English — there is no warmer or more formal word for the first position — and it can be followed by a first name (close), a full name (professional), or a title and surname (formal). The body is whatever you have to say. The close — "Sincerely," "With love," "Yours," "Best," "Warmly" — signals the temperature of the relationship. "Sincerely" and "Best" are the safe defaults; "Love" is reserved for family and close friends; "Yours" has a faintly British, vaguely literary warmth. The signature is always by hand, even if the letter is typed.
Condolence, congratulation, and apology

The three letters most adults will ever write are the letter of condolence, the letter of congratulation, and the letter of apology. Each has a rule. The condolence letter names the person who has died, says one specific thing the writer remembers about her, and offers no advice. The congratulation letter names the achievement specifically and does not compare the recipient to anyone else. The apology letter admits the fault in plain language ("I was wrong to have done that"), does not explain or defend, and proposes a concrete correction. All three should be handwritten, all three should be short, and all three should be sent the week the event occurs. Sending any of them late is worse than sending a brief version on time.

An apology that uses the word "if" — "I'm sorry if I upset you" — is not an apology. It is an evaluation of the recipient's reaction. The word to use is "that": "I'm sorry that I upset you." One letter changes the sentence from a defense into an admission.
Email is a letter, too

Almost everything above applies to email. A salutation, an informative body, a closing with your actual name — these are still the marks of a letter, regardless of the medium. Professional email should have a subject line that actually describes the subject ("Tuesday meeting confirmation" rather than "hi"). The reply-all button is an etiquette hazard. The phone is not always better than an email; an email is not always better than a letter; and the true skill is knowing which medium this message belongs in, then honoring what that medium asks.
Paper, pen, and the small habit

Buy a box of plain stationery — Crane's, Smythson's, or anything you like — keep it in a drawer, keep stamps with it, and keep a working pen nearby. The habit a lifetime of handwritten letters requires is roughly two minutes a week of actual writing and zero minutes of extra planning, because the supplies are in one place. Most people who abandon the habit do so because they ran out of stamps and never replaced them. The small boring infrastructure is the whole barrier, and it takes an afternoon to set up.

dek: Thank-you notes still work — and the short handwritten note is the single most underused tool in modern life.
name: Correspondence
sections: Why the handwritten note still matters
Paper, pen, and the small habit

body.text: In 219 BCE, the engineer building the Great Wall of China provisioned his laborers with a fermented cabbage pickled in rice wine. Two thousand years later, Captain Cook sailed to the Pacific with 60 barrels of sauerkraut on the Resolution and lost no sailor to scurvy. The same bacteria were doing the same job in both cases. Lacto-fermentation is the most widespread preservation technique in human history: found in almost every cuisine, developed independently on every inhabited continent, and still, in a refrigerated world, the technique that makes the most flavorful vegetables on a home shelf.
Salt, water, and a jar

The recipe, in its simplest form, is two percent salt by weight. Chop vegetables, salt them, pack them under their own liquid in a jar, and wait. Three to seven days at room temperature is enough for most things. The salt draws water out of the vegetables through osmosis and suppresses the bacteria that would rot them, while tolerating the ones that will preserve them. The Latin name is lactobacillus, which is also the bacterium at the bottom of every yogurt and sourdough starter. It arrives from the vegetables themselves and the air. You do not add it; you let it come.
The bacteria that show up

A ferment goes through three phases. Leuconostoc mesenteroides starts the work, producing carbon dioxide and mild acid. Lactobacillus plantarum takes over once the pH drops below 4.4, driving the acid production further and producing the tangy flavor that defines a finished ferment. Lactobacillus brevis finishes the job, if you let it, and produces the deeper flavor of a long-fermented kraut. A two-day ferment is spritely; a three-week ferment is serious. The same cabbage tastes different at every stage.
Sauerkraut, kimchi, and a world of cognates

Sauerkraut is cabbage, salt, and time. Kimchi is cabbage, salt, chiles, garlic, ginger, scallion, fish sauce, and time. Sauerkraut is the German cognate; kimchi the Korean; tsukemono the Japanese; choucroute the Alsatian; curtido the Salvadoran. The grammar is the same. The punctuation is the spice. Every traditional cuisine that faced winter without refrigeration invented some version of this preservation. Most of those versions are still being made.
Why it keeps

A finished lacto-ferment has a pH between 3.2 and 3.8 — sharply acidic. Very few spoilage bacteria can live at that acidity, which is why a properly fermented vegetable, refrigerated, keeps for months and often years. The same acidity makes the ferment hostile to botulism, which cannot grow below pH 4.6. Home fermentation, contrary to the worry most beginners arrive with, is the safest form of home food preservation, because the biology guards against failure. An obviously spoiled ferment smells wrong immediately; you will know.
A home ferment, safely

A half-gallon mason jar, two pounds of shredded green cabbage, twenty grams of kosher salt, a cabbage leaf to weigh the rest down, and a loose lid to let the gas escape. Pack, weigh down, cover, and leave on the counter at room temperature. Taste at day three; taste at day seven. When it tastes the way you want, move it to the fridge. That is the whole technique. A first ferment teaches you to trust the biology. The tenth teaches you to improvise.

Anything below the brine is safe; anything above it can mold. A weight — a plate, a glass lid, a fermentation-specific disk — that keeps the vegetables submerged is the single most important piece of equipment. The rest is optional.

body.cite: Sandor Katz, The Art of Fermentation
body.text: Fermentation is an act of co-creation, a collaboration with invisible workers who have been transforming food for as long as there has been food.

dek: The simplest preservation technique humans ever invented — salt, vegetables, time, and a family of bacteria that does the work for free.
name: Lacto-Fermentation

body.text: The French word vinaigre means, literally, sour wine — vin aigre. The product is older than its name: Babylonian cuneiform tablets from around 3000 BCE record vinegar as both a condiment and a cleaning agent. In 1863 Louis Pasteur, investigating why the vinegar production in the region of Orléans produced better and more reliable product than competitors', isolated the specific bacterium responsible: Acetobacter aceti. The same organism, then as now, converts ethanol to acetic acid. What Pasteur discovered was that vinegar is a two-step fermentation. First you make alcohol; then you wait.
From wine to vinegar

Any beverage that contains between five and twelve percent alcohol can become vinegar. Wine becomes wine vinegar. Cider becomes cider vinegar. Sake becomes rice vinegar. Beer becomes malt vinegar. The alcohol is the food; Acetobacter bacteria, which live on skins of grapes and apples and drift through any kitchen's air, eat the ethanol and excrete acetic acid. The process requires oxygen, so the liquid must be exposed to air. It takes from three weeks to three months, depending on the temperature and the strength of the starting alcohol.
The mother

On the surface of a vinegar in progress, the Acetobacter colony forms a gelatinous biofilm called the mother of vinegar. Translucent, beige, the texture of a soft rubber pancake. In a working vinegar culture, the mother sinks and rises as generations live and die. A commercial bottle of unpasteurized vinegar often contains a small piece of mother at the bottom, which will start a new ferment if given an appropriate alcohol to eat. It is the starter of the vinegar world.
The Orléans method and the factory shortcut

Traditional wine vinegar is made in wooden barrels, slowly, with the mother floating on a large surface of wine. The result is complex, aromatic, and expensive. Industrial vinegar is made in a submerged tank with forced oxygenation — the Frings process — which finishes in twenty-four hours. The fast method produces a vinegar that is acidic but thin. The slow method produces a vinegar that tastes like something. The single biggest upgrade a home cook can make is switching from supermarket white vinegar to an actual wine vinegar.
Kinds, and why each exists

White wine vinegar is for salads and pickles, where the wine flavor would overwhelm. Red wine vinegar is for heartier vinaigrettes and stews. Cider vinegar is for everything from the American South and most baking. Rice vinegar is for Japanese and Chinese kitchens, lower acid and gentler. Balsamic vinegar, real balsamic from Modena, is a concentrated grape must aged in wood for at least twelve years — a condiment rather than a vinegar, the way cognac is a brandy. The supermarket impostors aged four months in industrial tanks are not the same thing.
A vinegar on the counter

A half-gallon jar, two bottles of inexpensive red wine, a third of a cup of unpasteurized vinegar with its mother, a breathable cloth over the top. Sit it on a counter out of direct sunlight, stir once a week, and taste at six weeks. When the alcohol is gone and the vinegar smells sharp, strain and bottle. A kitchen producing its own vinegar smells faintly sour in a way that a lot of older European kitchens would have, year-round. Which is also to say that the smell is old, familiar, and correct.

Real balsamic, the DOP product of Modena and Reggio Emilia, is sold in fifty-milliliter bottles for twenty to two hundred dollars and drizzled at the table. The eight-dollar supermarket version is a different product — colored wine vinegar with caramel. It is useful. It is not balsamic.

dek: The second fermentation — what happens to alcohol when you let the right bacteria have a turn at it.
name: Vinegar
sections: The Orléans method and the factory shortcut

body.text: In 1903, Edwin S. Porter cut from a wide shot of a train robbery to a medium shot of a man firing a pistol straight at the audience, and the twelve-minute film that followed taught the world that a movie was not a play photographed from the front row. It was a sequence of frames, each with its own distance from the action, that a director chose in order. From that single cut forward — The Great Train Robbery, 1903 — film has had a grammar. Shot types are that grammar's basic nouns.
A grammar older than sound

The shot vocabulary — wide, medium, close — is older than color, older than talkies, older than montage theory. D. W. Griffith in the 1910s and Sergei Eisenstein in the 1920s formalized what Porter had stumbled onto: that an audience reads a cut from wide to close as "here is the world, now look at this face in it," and reads a cut from close to wide as "now see the face in context." The unspoken contract between filmmaker and viewer — that a new shot means a new amount of information — is what distinguishes cinema from every other narrative medium.
The shot scale

The standard scale runs from extreme wide to extreme close. The extreme wide — a landscape, a city, a crowd — establishes location and scale. The wide (or "full") shows the whole body. The medium, waist-up, is the conversation shot. The medium close, chest-up, is the television drama's workhorse. The close-up, from shoulders to head, brings the audience into an emotional intimacy. The extreme close-up — an eye, a mouth, a hand — lets the director point a finger at exactly the thing they want noticed. Every director has their preferred range. Sergio Leone built whole Westerns out of extreme close-ups. Yasujiro Ozu worked almost entirely in the medium.
Angle, framing, and the space around the subject

Shot type is not only distance. The angle — high, low, eye-level, overhead, Dutch tilt — changes the emotional reading of the same subject. A low-angle shot of a villain makes him imposing; the same villain in high angle looks cornered. "Headroom" is the space above the subject's head; "looking room" or "nose room" is the space they look into. A face framed tight to one edge of the frame, looking out of it, feels unsettled. These are small conventions, but a film that breaks them without reason tells the audience, subliminally, that something is off. Which is sometimes exactly what the director wants.
The moving camera

A static shot is a painting; a moving shot is a sentence. A pan turns on a vertical axis. A tilt on a horizontal. A dolly moves the camera bodily through space. A tracking shot follows alongside a subject. A crane lifts. A Steadicam — the Garrett Brown invention of 1975 that put a camera on a spring-loaded harness — floats. Paul Thomas Anderson's long opening tracking shots, Alfonso Cuarón's apparent single-take sequences in Children of Men, Martin Scorsese's Copacabana tracking shot in Goodfellas: the moving camera is now as expressive as any cut.
Why coverage matters

On a professional set, a scene is typically shot from three or four angles — master wide, over-shoulder one way, over-shoulder the other, and close-ups of each actor — regardless of what the director thinks they will use. This is called coverage, and it is insurance. Editing rooms are full of scenes saved by a single unplanned cutaway. A director who understands shot types understands, in advance, exactly how little coverage they can get away with and still have a cuttable scene. Hitchcock famously pre-visualized his films so completely that he shot no extra footage. Most mortals shoot more.

The 180-degree rule: once you establish two characters facing each other, the camera must stay on one side of an imaginary line between them. Cross it and the characters appear to have switched places. The rule is broken with purpose occasionally — Kubrick does it in The Shining to make a hallway disorienting — but it is always a decision.

dek: Wide, medium, close — and the grammar a director borrows every time a camera rolls.
name: Shot Types
sections: Angle, framing, and the space around the subject

body.text: In 1977, an editor named Marcia Lucas sat in a Los Angeles cutting room with three hundred thousand feet of film and a movie that did not work. Her husband George had turned in a two-hour space opera with interminable action and no narrative pulse. Over the next two months, she and two other editors cut out whole subplots, rebuilt the final space battle entirely, and handed back the film that the world would see as Star Wars. The movie exists as anyone remembers it because of the editing. That is not an unusual story; it is the ordinary story of filmmaking.
Why editing is the heart of cinema

Directors point at the shots; editors decide the movie. Writing happens on paper; direction happens on the set; but the film the audience watches is built in an edit suite over many months, from many more hours of footage than will ever make it to screen. Thelma Schoonmaker, who has cut every Martin Scorsese film since Raging Bull, has said that editing is the only place in filmmaking where the final form of the movie is decided. Every other craft makes raw material. The editor makes the film.
Continuity and the Kuleshov effect

In 1917, the Soviet filmmaker Lev Kuleshov ran an experiment. He intercut the same blank-faced shot of an actor with three different images: a bowl of soup, a dead woman in a coffin, a little girl playing. Audiences, shown the sequences, reported that the actor was hungry, grieving, tender — though his expression had not changed. The Kuleshov effect is the founding observation of film editing: meaning is generated between shots, in the audience's mind, not inside any single shot. Every edit exploits this. The editor's real medium is not pictures. It is what the audience assembles from them.
Rhythm, the editor's music

A scene has a rhythm, and the rhythm is the editor's. Cut too early and the audience feels jerked; cut too late and they get bored. Walter Murch, in his short book In the Blink of an Eye, argues that the correct cut is often exactly where an audience member would blink, because an eye-blink is a small mental break — a natural cut point in human perception. The best editors watch the film dozens of times, listen to their own attention, and cut where the mind wants the cut. Rhythm is as much of editing as any other craft.
Cut, dissolve, and the uncommon transitions

The straight cut is the default and, in the mature craft, nearly always the right answer. Dissolves soften a transition and suggest time passing; fade to black marks a chapter. Wipe transitions are now the province of Star Wars sequels and low-budget wedding videos — the language of a different era. A good editor uses the fancy transitions sparingly because they draw attention to themselves. The audience should feel the movie, not the editing. That is what invisibility means.
The editor as writer

Editors rewrite movies. They reorder scenes, cut characters entirely, combine footage from different takes into a single performance, and invent endings the script did not have. Dede Allen on Bonnie and Clyde, Anne V. Coates on Lawrence of Arabia, Verna Fields on Jaws — each of them substantially shaped the film they cut. A director who treats the editor as a collaborator, not a technician, makes better movies. This is why many of the best directors in the world started as editors, and why the relationship between a director and their editor often lasts longer than any marriage in the business.
The screenplay is the first draft of a film. The shoot is the second. The edit is the last, and the one the audience will see.

dek: The invisible art — a hundred small decisions that shape rhythm, continuity, and what an audience thinks is happening.
name: Editing
sections: Why editing is the heart of cinema
Cut, dissolve, and the uncommon transitions

body.text: A household kept its first written budget thousands of years before it kept written poetry. The clay tablets of Sumerian temple economies — barley in, barley out — are among the earliest pieces of writing humans produced. The point has not changed: knowing where the money goes is the precondition of everything else you might want it to do.
Knowing where it goes

Almost everyone underestimates two categories of spending: small recurring charges, and food bought outside the house. The first is invisible because it is automated; the second because it is social. Before you change anything, write down a single honest month. The exercise is uncomfortable — that is the point — and it is also the only step in personal finance that has been shown to work for nearly everyone, regardless of income.
A few systems that work

The most durable budgeting systems are the ones simple enough to keep going when life gets busy. The 50/30/20 rule, popularized by Senator Elizabeth Warren in her 2005 book with her daughter, allocates roughly half of after-tax income to needs, thirty percent to wants, twenty percent to savings and debt repayment. Zero-based budgeting, the YNAB approach, gives every dollar a job before the month begins. The envelope method — physical cash divided by category — is the oldest of all and still the most concrete.
The fixed-and-flex split

A useful refinement is to separate fixed costs (rent, insurance, the cell phone, the gym) from flexible ones (groceries, transit, going out). Fixed costs are decisions you make once a year; flexible costs are decisions you make every day. Most people who feel out of control financially are actually out of control on the fixed side — they have committed to a level of obligation that leaves the flexible side starving. Pruning a single recurring charge is worth more than refusing a hundred coffees.
Why it works

Budgeting is not really about restraint. It is about attention. The act of writing down what you spend changes what you spend, even if you make no rules — a finding so consistent across studies that behavioral economists have a name for it: the measurement effect. The number on the page is a quiet, repeated question: was that worth it? Most people, asked the question carefully, change their answer.
A budget is not a spreadsheet; it is a conversation with your future self. The spreadsheet is just where you write down what you decided.

dek: The household ledger is older than money — and still the bedrock of every financial life.
name: Budgeting

body.text: In 1974, a Vanguard founder named Jack Bogle ran the numbers and concluded that the stock-picking industry, in aggregate, would underperform the market it was picking from — by exactly the cost of its own fees. He launched the first index fund the next year. Wall Street called it Bogle's Folly. The numbers since have been brutal in his favor.
Compound interest

Albert Einstein probably did not call compound interest the eighth wonder of the world — that quotation is apocryphal — but the point survives the misattribution. A dollar invested at seven percent doubles in roughly ten years. Doubles again in ten more. The doubling is what people miss. A young person who invests a small amount and forgets about it will, by retirement, have more than someone twice their age who invested ten times as much and started late.
The case for index funds

A broad, low-cost index fund — the total US market, say, or the total world market — buys a tiny piece of every public company in the index. You pay essentially nothing in fees. You do not have to know which companies will win. You will own them all, in proportion. Decades of academic work, capped by Eugene Fama's Nobel for the efficient-market hypothesis, suggest that for almost all individual investors this is the rational choice. The exceptions, like Warren Buffett, agree publicly that they are exceptions.
Asset allocation

The single decision that matters most is the split between stocks and bonds. Stocks rise more over decades and fall harder in bad years; bonds do the reverse. A common rule of thumb is to hold a bond percentage roughly equal to your age, though that is conservative for most modern lives. The actual rule: hold enough bonds that you will not panic-sell stocks in a 2008 or a 2020. Whatever number lets you sleep is the right number for you.
The behavioral problem

Most investors lose money not from picking bad investments but from selling at the wrong time. The market drops thirty percent; they sell. It recovers in three years; they buy back in. Repeated quietly across a decade, this trims several points off annual returns. Automating contributions, ignoring the news, and never checking the balance more than once a quarter are not minor optimizations — they are the whole game.
The stock market is a device for transferring money from the impatient to the patient.

dek: Most of investing is doing very little, very consistently, for a very long time.
name: Investing

body.text: The modern American income tax was born in 1913, the year the Sixteenth Amendment was ratified. The first form was four pages long, including the instructions. The current Form 1040 packet runs over a hundred pages. The tax has grown because the country has — but the underlying machine is still simple, and one Saturday a year is enough to understand your own corner of it.
What you actually pay

In the United States your paycheck is reduced by federal income tax, state and sometimes city income tax, and FICA — the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes. The income tax is progressive: the next dollar you earn is taxed at a higher rate than the first dollar. FICA is flat up to a wage cap. Self-employed people pay both halves of FICA, which is why a freelance gig that pays the same hourly rate as a salaried job actually pays less. Most other countries operate similar machines under different names.
Brackets and the marginal mistake

A common confusion: people think a raise can push them into a higher bracket and leave them with less money. It cannot. Brackets work on the marginal dollar. If you cross from the 22% bracket into the 24% bracket, only the dollars above the line are taxed at 24%. Everything below is still taxed at the lower rates. Understanding this single fact resolves a startling fraction of all bad tax decisions.
Deductions and credits

A deduction reduces the income on which tax is computed. A credit reduces the tax itself. A thousand-dollar credit is worth a thousand dollars; a thousand-dollar deduction is worth your marginal rate times a thousand — for most people, two or three hundred. Most filers take the standard deduction, which the 2017 reform roughly doubled and which now beats itemizing for the great majority of households. Tax-advantaged accounts — 401(k), IRA, HSA, 529 — each shelter income in a different way and reward people who learn the small differences.
Why doing it yourself is fine

For salaried workers with no rental property, no business, and no foreign income, the IRS Free File program — and now the Direct File pilot in many states — handles a return in under an hour. The major paid software is fine, but its core feature is that it makes you feel safer, not that it finds money the free options miss. If your situation is genuinely complicated, hire a CPA. If it is not, the form rewards your time directly.
Filing late is far worse than paying late. The failure-to-file penalty is ten times the failure-to-pay penalty. File on time even if you cannot pay; ask for an installment plan after.

dek: The annual chore that funds the country — and rewards anyone willing to spend a Saturday understanding it.
name: Taxes
sections: Why doing it yourself is fine

body.text: In Seattle in the early 1970s, the cardiologist Leonard Cobb decided to teach ordinary citizens how to perform CPR. Within a few years, the city had the highest survival rate from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of any major city in the world. The intervention was not a new drug or a new device. It was teaching the bystanders nearest the body to do something useful in the four minutes before the ambulance arrived.

Reading this lesson is not training. Take a Red Cross or American Heart Association CPR course in person; the muscle memory of pressing two inches deep, a hundred times a minute, is what saves lives. This page is background, not certification.
What cardiac arrest actually is

Cardiac arrest — distinct from a heart attack — is the heart suddenly losing its ability to pump blood. The person collapses, stops breathing normally, and within minutes the brain begins to die from lack of oxygen. Survival drops by roughly seven to ten percent for every minute that passes without CPR. After ten minutes, with no intervention, almost no one survives. The point of CPR is not to restart the heart — that almost always requires a defibrillator — but to keep enough blood moving to the brain that defibrillation, when it arrives, has someone to bring back.
Hands-only CPR

For an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally, the American Heart Association recommends hands-only CPR for untrained bystanders: call 911, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about two inches deep, at the rhythm of the Bee Gees song "Stayin' Alive" (about 110 beats per minute). Do not stop until trained help arrives or the person starts breathing. Trained rescuers add rescue breaths in a 30:2 ratio. Hands-only is simpler, more memorable, and just as effective for the first several minutes of an adult arrest.
The AED

An automated external defibrillator is a small box found in airports, gyms, schools, and most public buildings. Open the lid and a recorded voice walks you through the entire procedure — where to place the pads, when to stand clear, when to deliver the shock. The machine analyzes the heart rhythm and only delivers a shock if a shock will help. Using one wrong is essentially impossible; not using one is what kills people.
A real course is not optional

A two-hour CPR class is the highest-leverage health investment most adults will ever make. The Red Cross, the American Heart Association, and the YMCA all offer them; many workplaces will pay for them. Take one once, then refresh every two years. The skill atrophies quickly and the moment you need it will be the worst day of someone's life.

dek: Two minutes of trained chest compressions can double or triple a stranger's chance of surviving cardiac arrest.
name: CPR & AED
sections: A real course is not optional

body.text: A healthy adult body holds about five liters of blood. Losing one liter brings on shock; losing two is usually fatal. The good news is that almost every survivable hemorrhage can be controlled by a bystander with their bare hands and a piece of cloth — provided they know to keep pressing, and to keep pressing for longer than feels reasonable.

This lesson is background, not training. The civilian Stop the Bleed program runs free hour-long courses in most US cities; take one. The skills with a tourniquet and a wound-packing gauze are physical and need real practice.
The triage of a bleed

Not every bleed is an emergency. A scrape, even a long one, will usually clot on its own. The bleeds that kill are the ones that do not slow down: blood spurting in time with the heartbeat (an arterial bleed), or a steady dark flow that soaks through cloth in seconds (a heavy venous bleed). The first decision is the simplest: call 911 if the bleeding is more than you can control, or if the wound is to the head, neck, chest, or abdomen.
Pressure, then more pressure

Place a clean cloth — a folded T-shirt works — over the wound and press down hard with the heel of your hand. Then do not let go. If blood soaks through, do not lift the cloth; add another cloth on top and keep pressing. The most common mistake bystanders make is checking too soon, which dislodges the clot that was beginning to form. Hold pressure for at least ten minutes by the clock. If you can elevate the wound above the heart, do it.
Tourniquets — when and how

A tourniquet is for a limb wound that direct pressure cannot control. Modern combat-style tourniquets — the CAT-7 is the standard — saved enough lives in Iraq and Afghanistan that the medical consensus on civilian use reversed completely. Apply two to three inches above the wound, never on a joint, and tighten until the bleeding stops. It will hurt. Note the time on the tourniquet and on the patient's forehead. Do not loosen it; let the hospital do that.
Wound care after the bleeding stops

Once the bleeding is controlled, irrigate with clean water if available, cover with a clean dressing, and get the person to medical care for stitches and a tetanus check if the wound is deep, dirty, or in a high-tension area. A wound left open more than six to eight hours generally cannot be closed primarily — it heals by what doctors call secondary intention, which leaves a wider scar.

dek: Direct pressure stops nearly every survivable bleed — and most people do not press hard enough or long enough.
name: Bleeding & Wounds
sections: Wound care after the bleeding stops

body.text: In 1972 a Cincinnati surgeon named Henry Heimlich, frustrated that thousands of Americans were choking to death every year, designed and demonstrated the abdominal-thrust maneuver that would carry his name. The American Red Cross now teaches a slightly modified sequence — five back blows first, then thrusts — but the core insight is his: a sharp expulsion of air from below the obstruction can launch it out of the airway like a champagne cork.

A real first-aid course teaches you the feel of these maneuvers on a mannequin, which a written description cannot. Take one. In an actual emergency, call 911 first if anyone else is present, then act.
Recognizing it

A choking person who can cough, speak, or breathe noisily has a partial obstruction. Encourage them to keep coughing — the cough is more effective than anything you can do. Do not slap their back; you may dislodge the object further down the airway. A complete obstruction looks different: silence, panic, hands at the throat, lips going blue. That is when you act.
Back blows and abdominal thrusts

For an adult or child over one year old, the current sequence is five sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, followed by five abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich maneuver): stand behind the person, make a fist just above their navel, grasp it with your other hand, and pull sharply upward and inward. Alternate the cycles until the object comes out or the person becomes unconscious. If they go down, lower them gently to the floor and begin CPR — chest compressions can themselves dislodge an obstruction.
Infants are different

For a baby under one year, do not use abdominal thrusts — their organs are too fragile. The infant sequence is five back blows with the baby face down on your forearm, head lower than torso, then five chest thrusts with the baby flipped face up, two fingers in the center of the chest. Repeat until the airway clears or the baby is unresponsive. Choking deaths in infants are usually preventable by cutting grapes lengthwise, avoiding whole nuts under four, and watching small children with small toys.
Aftercare

Anyone who has received abdominal thrusts that worked should still see a doctor — the maneuver can occasionally bruise an organ. Anyone who lost consciousness during a choking event should be evaluated even if they recover quickly, because foreign material may have entered the lungs and seeded a pneumonia that shows up days later.

dek: Five back blows, five abdominal thrusts, repeat — until either the airway clears or the person becomes unconscious.
name: Choking

body.text: Every failure on a fishing line begins at a knot. When the eight-pound rainbow throws its head at the edge of the pool and the leader goes slack, the tippet almost never broke in the middle; it gave at the hook eye, where the angler tied a careless clinch and did not wet the line before pulling tight. A fisherman's whole hardware is a rod, a reel, a length of monofilament, and a lure; three of those are bought and one is tied, and the tied one decides the afternoon.
The clinch, improved

The improved clinch knot — five turns around the standing line, pass the tag through the loop at the hook eye, then back through the big loop just formed — is the North American default for attaching a hook, swivel, or lure to monofilament or fluorocarbon up to about fifteen-pound test. Trout anglers have used it for a century; bass anglers, mostly, too. Tied wet and pulled slowly, it tests at about 95 percent of line strength. Tied dry and jerked tight, it cuts itself at the turns and breaks at 60. The improvement over the plain clinch is the final tag-through-the-loop pass, which prevents slippage on thinner line.
The Palomar, the lazy one

For anyone with imperfect eyesight or cold hands, the Palomar knot is easier and nearly as strong. Double over six inches of line, pass the loop through the eye, tie a loose overhand, pass the hook through the loop, and pull. Three steps. It tests at 95 percent on braided line and is the braid angler's standard. Fly fishermen use it less — they are tying to small tippet eyes and prefer the clinch — but for spin fishing it is the workhorse that forgives fatigue.
Joining two lines: blood and uni

The blood knot joins two lines of similar diameter — building a leader that steps down from thick butt to thin tippet — with a symmetrical five-turn-on-each-side arrangement that pulls flat and clean. The double uni knot does the same job with unequal diameters (mono to braid, for instance) and is simpler to tie, which is why saltwater anglers mostly use it now. A good fly leader in 2026 is typically mono blood-knotted to mono, down through four or five steps; a good bass or salmon leader is just a mono shock tippet uni-knotted to a braided main line.

Wet every knot with saliva or water before pulling tight. Monofilament heats as the turns seat, and dry-tied knots lose up to a third of their strength. The half-second of spit is the difference between a landed fish and a story about one.
The loop that matters

For streamers, saltwater flies, and any lure whose action you want to preserve, a loop knot — most commonly the non-slip mono loop (Kreh loop), four turns, taught by Lefty Kreh in his casting clinics for forty years — lets the fly swim freely instead of riveted stiffly to the tippet. It is the last knot most fly fishermen learn. It is also the one that most changes what a fly does in the water.
Practice on the couch

Animated Knots by Grog — a free website, also an app — shows each knot as a step-by-step animation with the tag end highlighted in color. Ten minutes a night on dry line, from a couch, turns the three knots above into muscle memory by the weekend. A fisherman who has to look at a diagram on the riverbank has lost the bite; one whose hands know the turns ties without thinking, and is already casting again.

body.text: In Norman Maclean's 1976 novella A River Runs Through It, the narrator's father — a Presbyterian minister in Missoula, Montana — teaches his two sons to fish by a metronome, four counts back and four counts forward, so that the rod stops at ten o'clock and at two o'clock and the line rolls out in a straight line on the Blackfoot. "To him," Maclean writes, "all good things — trout as well as eternal salvation — come by grace and grace comes by art and art does not come easy." No sport in English has been written about more lovingly, or more honestly about its own difficulty.

body.alt: A fly fisherman casting on a river
body.caption: Fly fishing — the line, not the lure, carries the weight.

body.text: A line you cast, not a lure you throw

Every other kind of fishing casts by throwing a weighted lure and letting the line follow. Fly fishing reverses the physics: the weight is in the line itself, a tapered length of plastic-coated braid, and the angler propels it with the rod by loading the line in a back-cast and releasing it in a forward stroke. The fly at the end, which imitates a mayfly or caddis or emerger, is virtually weightless — often a hook dressed in hackle and thread, no heavier than a dime. Everything about the equipment follows from this inversion. The rod is long and flexible; the line is heavy for its thickness; the leader steps down in diameter from a thick butt to a hair-thin tippet so that the energy of the cast rolls smoothly to the fly and lays it on the water without a splash.
The cast

Lefty Kreh, the Baltimore casting clinician who taught half the country's fly fishermen before his death in 2018, reduced the cast to five principles: the rod tip must travel in a straight line; longer strokes for longer casts; the stroke must accelerate to a stop; the back-cast and forward-cast must be 180 degrees apart; the line must be tight at the start of the stroke. Everything past those five is ornament. A beginner who understands them becomes competent in a summer; most fly fishermen never do understand them and cast for forty years anyway.
The drift

The whole point of the cast is to deliver a fly so that it drifts on the current at the same speed as the natural flies the trout is eating. Drag — any bow or tension in the line that pulls the fly unnaturally across the current — is the single most common reason a fisherman catches nothing. Mending, a sideways flip of the line to match the water's differential speed, is the technique that prevents drag. An angler who can read the seam where fast and slow water meet, and mend her line to float a fly naturally down that seam, will outfish better casters who cannot.
Matching the hatch

Wild trout in a good river eat, in a given week, a predictable sequence of aquatic insects — the hatch. Match the size, silhouette, and color of the bug on the water, and the trout treats your imitation as food. Miss any of those three by much, and she treats it as a piece of fluff. The working fly fisherman carries a dozen core patterns (Parachute Adams, Elk Hair Caddis, Pheasant Tail, Hare's Ear, Woolly Bugger) in three sizes each. That is enough to cover most North American rivers most of the year. The rest is pattern proliferation for its own sake — though the lifetime project of tying your own flies is one of the old pleasures of the sport, and no dollar in your vest produces more satisfaction than the one you catch a fish on with a fly you tied.

Barbless hooks, crushed with pliers or bought that way, release cleanly and hurt the fish less. Keep a wild trout wet while unhooking; hold it in the current until it swims from your fingers. The fish you let go today is the one someone teaches a child to catch in three years.
The lineage of books

The fly-fishing library is older and better than the hobby deserves. Walton's Compleat Angler (1653) is the founding text; Dame Juliana Berners' Treatyse of Fysshynge with an Angle (1496) is older. In English prose of the last century, John Gierach's Sex, Death, and Fly-Fishing (1990) is the companion volume for anyone who will read anything well written; Roderick Haig-Brown's A River Never Sleeps (1946) is the Pacific Northwest answer to Walton. David James Duncan's The River Why (1983) is the great American coming-of-age novel about the subject. Maclean remains the only American who turned fishing into literature.
The fish and the watershed

Wild trout are a litmus test for clean cold water. Where they still swim, the watershed is roughly in working order; where they have vanished, something is wrong a hundred miles upstream. Trout Unlimited, the American conservation organization, has spent fifty years restoring streams with volunteer labor — 539 miles reconnected and 830,000 acres protected by 2026. To fish a wild-trout river seriously is to take on some responsibility for it. Most anglers do.

dek: The cast and the drift — where angling ceases to be catching and becomes reading the water.
name: Fly Fishing
sections: A line you cast, not a lure you throw

body.text: Under the linoleum of a 1940s kitchen in Brooklyn, a renovator will almost always find a hardwood floor — narrow strips of white oak or southern yellow pine, tongue-and-grooved, face-nailed through the tongue, laid down by a crew that finished the job in a week and expected it to last the life of the building. They were right. Eighty years later, you sand it twice, stain it once, and walk on it for the rest of your life.
What a hardwood floor actually is

A hardwood floor is a stack of precisely milled boards, each with a small protruding tongue along one long edge and a matching groove along the other. Laid side by side, they interlock. The boards are fastened through the tongue at a forty-five-degree angle with a flooring nailer, which hides the fastener inside the joint — every board is held by its neighbor, and the weight of the whole field bears evenly on the subfloor below. A floor installed this way will survive a hundred years of heels, dog claws, and furniture, and still have enough thickness left for a fresh sanding.
Solid versus engineered

Solid hardwood is a single plank sawn from a log — three quarters of an inch thick, usually, able to be sanded and refinished six or eight times. Engineered hardwood is a thin layer of true hardwood bonded to a plywood substrate; more dimensionally stable, cheaper, installable over concrete or radiant heat where solid wood would cup and split, but limited to one or two refinishings before the veneer is gone. Both are real wood. Both have their place. Neither is laminate, which is a photograph of wood printed on paper and sealed under plastic — the industry calls it "wood-look" for a reason.
Racking the floor

Before the nailer ever comes out, a careful installer racks the floor: opens every bundle and arranges the boards dry across the room, matching color, shuffling short pieces among long, staggering end joints at least six inches between adjacent rows. This is an aesthetic choice that pays back every time the floor is seen. Acclimation comes first — the wood sits in the room for at least forty-eight hours, ideally a week, so its moisture content equilibrates with the space. Skip the acclimation and you get gaps in February and buckling in August.
Sanding and the finish

A newly installed solid floor is rough, slightly uneven where boards meet, and full of the footprints of whoever laid it. Three passes with a drum sander — 36 grit, 60, 100 — level it. An edger handles the perimeter. A final buff with a screen smooths the transitions. Dust off. Then the finish: two or three coats of oil-modified polyurethane, waterborne poly, or penetrating oil. Each coat is lightly abraded before the next. A professional finish costs the builder three days and looks like glass for twenty years.
Moisture is the enemy

Every failure mode a hardwood floor has — cupping, crowning, gapping, buckling, mold — starts with moisture. Solid wood expands across the grain when it absorbs water and shrinks when it loses it, and the movement is measurable in any board wider than three inches. The National Wood Flooring Association's installation guidelines specify moisture-content differentials of two to four percent between floor and subfloor before installation, measured with a pin-type meter. A floor installed over a concrete slab with no vapor barrier, or during a humid week before the heat comes on, is a floor that will move. The craft is as much weather forecasting as it is carpentry.

The tool that defines the trade is the pneumatic flooring nailer — a heavy steel hammer-driven tool that drives a barbed cleat through the board's tongue at precisely the right angle. A good installer sets one board every four or five seconds.
How to think about it

Wood breathes with the weather. Installation is a weather-forecasting job as much as a carpentry one. Every board grows and shrinks across its grain with humidity; the room expands and contracts with temperature; the subfloor moves with season. The installer's task is to give all of them room to move in predictable ways — expansion gaps at the walls, staggered joints, the field floating on a subfloor it is nailed to but not glued to. Skip the steps that give the wood room, and the wood will take the room it needs anyway, usually by buckling into your hallway in July.
Work through one

An installer is given 300 square feet of 3/4"×4" unfinished white oak to lay in a second-floor bedroom over a plywood subfloor. The wood arrives on a Monday; she stacks it in the room loose, in small piles so air circulates. Wednesday (48-hour minimum acclimation) she measures moisture content: subfloor 10%, boards 9.5%. Good — within the 2% NWFA spec. She lays tar paper or felt over the subfloor as a moisture retarder, snaps a chalk line parallel to the longest wall (1/2" off the wall for expansion), pulls the first board tongue-out. Face-nails through the groove side (the first row cannot tongue-nail), then switches to the pneumatic nailer for every board after, a cleat every 8 inches through the tongue. Stagger end joints at least 6 inches between adjacent rows. Last row: rip to fit with a quarter-inch expansion gap, face-nail, cover with baseboard. One day's installation for 300 square feet, with a helper.
Try these

First: measure the moisture content of a piece of lumber at your local hardware store with a pin-type meter (they often have one at the service desk). Compare kiln-dried framing lumber (around 12–15%) to hardwood flooring (typically 7–9%). The difference is why flooring is never installed straight off a truck. Second: rack a small area of actual hardwood boards dry. Shuffle short and long, dark and light grain, staggered end joints. The pattern is pleasing when it is truly random; look for the stripes of repetition and rearrange. Third: hammer a few cleats through a board tongue by hand. The angle — 45 degrees, head buried just below the tongue surface — is the hardest part of the job and the reason the pneumatic nailer exists.
When it goes wrong

Cupping (boards higher at edges than in the middle) means the bottom of the floor is wetter than the top — a vapor-barrier failure, a plumbing leak underneath, or a basement below without proper ventilation. Fix the moisture source; the wood may flatten over months or may need to be replaced. Crowning (opposite) means the top was wetter — a spill that sat too long, or the room was mopped wet. Gapping in winter means the house was too dry during installation; a humidifier helps. Buckling (boards lifting off the subfloor) means severe moisture; a catastrophic failure requiring refloor. Squeaks are almost always loose nails rubbing against a joist or a gap between subfloor and floor; trim-screws through the face into the joist fix them, countersunk and filled.
What to try next

Past straight nail-down installs, the next rungs are engineered flooring on glue-down or float installations (over concrete), herringbone and chevron patterns (which require cutting every board at 45 degrees), and stain-and-finish work (where the final look depends on how the wood is prepared as much as on what is put on it). Past that: historic floor restoration (pulling old square-nailed pine, salvaging and reusing), wide-plank custom installs, parquet and inlay work. Don Bollinger's book and the NWFA's technical library are the complete professional curriculum.

dek: Tongue, groove, nail, sand — a craft that borrows the tools of carpentry and leaves you walking on the result.
name: Hardwood
sections: What a hardwood floor actually is

body.text: At Chogha Zanbil, in what is now Iran, archaeologists dug out a thirteenth-century-BC ziggurat faced with glazed bricks. The glaze still shines. The Persians, the Romans, the Ottomans, and the Moors all treated tile as a structural material and a language. Walking through the Alhambra in Granada, you are looking at the same craft a modern tilesetter does in a Brooklyn bathroom — smaller tiles, softer grout, and the same ruthless attention to a flat substrate.
A four-thousand-year-old building block

Ceramic tile is clay, fired to hardness, sometimes glazed. Porcelain tile is fired hotter and denser, nearly waterproof on its own. Natural stone — marble, travertine, slate — is cut into tile-shaped pieces and shares the craft. What all of them have in common is that they are thin, hard, brittle, and need to be set on a surface flat enough, still enough, and waterproof enough to let them survive decades of foot traffic or weekly hot showers. Get the substrate right and the tile will outlast your mortgage. Get it wrong and you will be regrouting in three years.
Substrate is the job

The difference between a good tile job and a lifetime headache is what lies under the tile. Plywood flexes under foot traffic and cracks grout lines; you do not tile directly on plywood. The honest substrates are cementitious backer board screwed over the plywood, an uncoupling membrane like Schluter-Ditra that lets the tile move independently of the structure, or a proper mud-set mortar bed — the old-school method, still the gold standard for showers. The TCNA Handbook from the Tile Council of North America specifies, in engineering-grade detail, which assembly is appropriate for which application. Good shops keep a copy on the truck.
Thinset, notches, and back-buttering

Thinset is a modified cement mortar mixed on the job to the consistency of smooth peanut butter. A notched trowel, held at a steep angle, combs it into parallel ridges that collapse uniformly when each tile is pressed and twisted into place. For larger tiles the setter also spreads thinset on the back of the tile itself — "back-buttering" — to eliminate voids. The goal is full coverage: at least eighty percent of the back of a tile bonded to the substrate on a floor, ninety-five percent in a wet area. Voids are where cracked tiles and loose tiles begin.
Grout, caulk, and the last ten percent

After the thinset cures for a day, the joints are filled with grout — a fine-sand cement for wide joints, an unsanded version for joints under an eighth of an inch. Grout is packed into every joint with a rubber float, worked diagonally, then washed off the tile surface before it sets hard. The only joints that get caulk rather than grout are the changes of plane: inside corners, the line where tile meets the tub, the transition between floor and wall. Every caulk joint flexes; every grout joint stays put. Confusing them is the single most common source of cracked tile and water damage.
Layout: where the cut tile lives

The professional difference is in layout. A novice starts at one wall and works across; the last row of tile against the far wall ends up as a narrow sliver. A professional measures the full room, finds the center, and plans the layout so that cut tiles are balanced — the same sliver on both walls, rather than a whole tile on one side and nothing on the other. On a tiled wall, layout plans where the horizontal band of cut tile will sit: below the eye line, above the tub, tucked under a trim piece. A good layout is invisible. A bad layout is the one thing guests notice.

The tool that defines the trade is the notched trowel. A quarter-inch V-notch, a half-inch square-notch, a three-sixteenths U-notch — each one lays down a different volume of thinset. The wrong notch is the wrong job. A professional tilesetter owns half a dozen.
How to think about it

Tile is only as good as what it sits on. The substrate is the whole game. Every failure you will ever see in tile — cracked grout lines, loose tiles, leaking showers, lippage where adjacent tiles are out of plane — originates in the substrate. Before a single tile is laid, the mortar bed, the backer board, the membrane, and the slope-to-drain must all be right. Fix the substrate first, and tile becomes a careful but forgiving craft. Skip the substrate, and no amount of thinset or grout care rescues the job.
Work through one

A tilesetter is given a 60 sq ft bathroom to tile with 12×12 porcelain. She starts with the subfloor — a 3/4" tongue-and-groove plywood, adequate. Over it she screws down 1/4" cementitious backer board (HardieBacker) in thinset-bedded sheets, seams taped with alkali-resistant mesh tape. The backer-board layer is what makes this a tilable floor. Next she dry-lays the field without thinset to plan the layout: measuring diagonally from corner to corner to find the true center, adjusting the grid so cut pieces at opposite walls are equal. She snaps perpendicular chalk lines as reference. Then: mix thinset to peanut-butter consistency, comb with a 1/4" × 3/8" U-notch trowel in parallel ridges, back-butter each 12×12 tile (they are too big for trowel-comb only), press into place with a slight twist, verify lippage with a straightedge. Grout 24 hours later with unsanded grout for 1/8" joints, wash diagonally with a damp sponge, let haze for 30 minutes, buff with a dry cloth. Caulk every change-of-plane joint instead of grouting. Two days of work for a tight professional floor.
Try these

First: examine a tile floor in your home or a public building. Find a caulk joint (usually at a baseboard or where floor meets wall) versus a grout joint (between tiles in the field). The caulk is slightly softer, sometimes visibly different color, and always at a change of plane. Second: mix a small batch of thinset to the right consistency. Start with the powder in a bucket, add water a little at a time, mix with a paddle, let "slake" (rest) for 5–10 minutes, then remix. The final mix holds ridges when combed and does not sag off a vertical surface. Too thin: it sags and fails to hold tile. Too thick: it does not bond. Third: dry-lay a small area of 12×12 tiles on the floor. Measure the room, find center, plan the cuts at opposite walls to be equal. This exercise is the whole difference between amateur and professional work.
When it goes wrong

Cracked grout lines in a straight run almost always indicate substrate movement — the subfloor is flexing, the backer board was not bedded in thinset, or a structural joint was grouted instead of caulked. The fix is uncoupling: add a Ditra membrane on future work, or replace the failed section. Loose tiles are void coverage failures — insufficient thinset on the back, poor trowel angle, or thinset that skinned over before the tile was set. Efflorescence (white haze on grout) is mineral deposits from water migration; seal and re-grout. Shower leaks past the tile find the weakest waterproofing point; the solution is a full tear-out and a proper waterproof substrate like Schluter Kerdi. Lippage — adjacent tiles out of plane — is prevented at install with a leveling system, not corrected after.
What to try next

Past simple field tiles, the next rungs are shower construction (waterproofing, curbs, benches, niches), large-format tile (requires flatter substrate, back-buttering, leveling systems), natural stone (no sealers and no acidic cleaners, different fastener grades), mosaics and decorative inlays, and mud-set work (the classical method with a thick mortar bed, still the gold standard for showers). The CTEF Certified Tile Installer credential is the industry gateway; Michael Byrne's Setting Tile is the book the certification curriculum is mostly drawn from.

dek: Thinset and tolerances — the patient trade that turns a floor or a wall into weatherproof geometry.
name: Tile Setting
sections: Grout, caulk, and the last ten percent
Layout: where the cut tile lives

body.text: In July 2023, a woman in country Victoria, Australia, served a beef Wellington made with what she told police were foraged mushrooms. Three of her four guests were dead within a week; the fourth spent nearly two months in hospital. The fungus was the death cap, Amanita phalloides, which contains amatoxins that destroy the liver silently for a day before the symptoms return. No foraging subject can begin anywhere else. The rule of the harvest is absolute certainty, or you leave it.
The rule of absolute certainty

Sam Thayer, the Wisconsin forager who has spent forty years in the field and written three of the best books in English on the subject, states the rule in one line: identify the plant by every one of its features, consistent with published keys, using at least two independent sources, or do not eat it. Eighty percent sure is zero percent. "Looks like" is not identification. A smartphone photo-matching app is a way to generate hypotheses, never a verdict. The error rate that matters is not the app's; it is yours in the moment you want the answer to be yes.
What a careful forager looks like

She learns one plant a season — spring ramps in the Catskills one year, summer lamb's-quarters in the community-garden edges the next. She reads two references before tasting any new species, then a third. She takes tiny first portions and waits a day. She never harvests anything lookalike-rich (morels, chanterelles, milkweed shoots) from the first patch she finds; she confirms the ID from a known patch before she trusts her own eye. She writes down the dates and places in a notebook, because a forager's memory is worse than she thinks.
Ethics: take a tenth

Wild populations do not exist to feed you. Dig one ramp in ten, or none. Never strip a patch. Do not post the coordinates of rare stands on social media — an online ramp post can wipe out a forty-year colony in a weekend. The old New England woodcraft motto, take what you need and leave more than you take, predates any modern ethic and still governs the field. The Forest Service sets formal quotas on many species on federal land; most states require a commercial permit past a household threshold. Match those rules or tighten them.

If you cannot identify the plant at every stage of its life cycle — flower, leaf, root, seed head — you are not ready to eat it. A safe forager knows what the plant looks like in October and in March, not only on the afternoon it tempts her.
The law and the land

Public-land rules vary. National parks almost universally prohibit consumptive foraging; national forests permit it in small amounts; state and local rules are a patchwork. New York City park regulations forbid removing any plant matter — yes, even dandelions — and NYPD Parks Enforcement does in fact write tickets. On private land you need the landowner's permission, in writing if you are planning to return. There is no forager's exemption in the trespass statute, and a good relationship with a landowner is worth more than any patch.
Start with the unmistakable

Samuel Thayer's recommended beginner list — dandelion, wild strawberry, nettle, cattail, wood sorrel, and maybe black walnut if you live east of the Mississippi — is what he calls the "forager's first year." None of them has a dangerous lookalike. Each teaches one habit: the root dig, the seasonal stalking, the blanch, the crack-and-pick. A year spent on six plants is better than a week spent on sixty, and it is how every serious forager any of us knows actually began.

dek: The rule of absolute certainty, the habit of leaving more than you take, and why one plant a season is enough.
name: Safety & Ethics
sections: What a careful forager looks like
The ethics of the wild harvest
The law, which is not optional

body.text: On a damp October morning in 1881, the French mycologist Lucien Quélet was walking a beech wood in the Jura when he noticed a yellow-orange mushroom with forked ridges running down its stem. He named it Cantharellus cibarius, the chanterelle, and added it to the catalog of safely edible European fungi. A century and a half later, that catalog is longer but not by as much as people think. Of an estimated 2.2 to 3.8 million fungal species on Earth, humans eat fewer than a hundred reliably, and roughly a dozen can kill you from a single bite.

body.alt: Golden chanterelle, Cantharellus cibarius
body.caption: A golden chanterelle — one of the "foolproof four" beginner mushrooms, with forked ridges running down its stem rather than true gills.
body.credit: Björn S. · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0

body.text: The kingdom below the soil

A mushroom is the fruiting body of a fungus — a small, briefly visible organ attached to a vastly larger organism, the mycelium, which is a branching network of white threads threaded through soil or wood. Most fungi are invisible most of the time. Merlin Sheldrake's 2020 book Entangled Life is the best popular introduction to the kingdom in a generation, and makes clear why a forager who thinks of mushrooms as individual objects misses the point. She is harvesting a single week's seasonal bloom from a perennial organism that may be older than she is.
The foolproof four

Traditional mycological clubs in North America teach a starter list — chanterelle, morel, chicken-of-the-woods, and giant puffball — as the "foolproof four." The phrase is a slight overstatement: chanterelles have a toxic lookalike in the jack-o'-lantern, morels have the poisonous verpa and the false-morel gyromitra, chicken-of-the-woods on eastern red cedar or eucalyptus can cause gastric upset, and puffballs must be sliced open to confirm the flesh is pure white and featureless (if it is not, it might be a young Amanita). But with those cautions taught carefully, the four will carry a beginner through a first season without a hospital visit.
The four that will kill you

Amanita phalloides — the death cap — is responsible for the majority of fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide. It looks benign: pale cap, white gills, smooth stalk, a ring, a cup at the base half-buried in the leaf litter. Its toxins destroy the liver over two to five days after the gastric symptoms have already passed. Amanita virosa, the destroying angel, is its pure-white cousin. Amanita ocreata is the western version. Galerina marginata, a small brown mushroom on rotting wood, contains the same amatoxins and has been mistaken for psilocybin species with predictable outcomes. None of the four has a useful field test. The only reliable defense is not eating any small brown mushroom, any white-gilled mushroom with a ring and cup, or any unknown Amanita, ever.

There is no home test for amatoxins. Boiling does not destroy them. There is no reliable folk-taste test — "edible" and "deadly" mushrooms taste similar. The rule: one species a season, confirmed with a club member or professional. Nothing else is safe.
Spore prints and keys

A spore print — cap laid gills-down on paper overnight — gives the color of the spores, a character that distinguishes whole families the eye cannot. Brown-spored Galerina from white-spored Pholiota, white-spored Amanita from pink-spored Pluteus, black-spored Coprinus from everything else. Michael Kuo's MushroomExpert.com is the best free resource in English; its keys walk the reader through spore color, cap texture, gill attachment, and habitat in the order a working mycologist asks the questions. David Arora's Mushrooms Demystified is the print counterpart — 959 pages, the standard for the Pacific coast but broadly useful.
Clubs, not solitudes

The North American Mycological Association keeps a list of affiliated clubs in most metropolitan areas; their guided forays are free or nearly so. Go to a foray before you eat. An experienced member will walk the floor of the woods with you, and a two-hour walk in her company will teach more than a month of books. This is the one subject where apprenticeship, not autodidacticism, is the professional habit. If you skip it, you are gambling with a loaded die.

dek: High reward, high risk — the kingdom of fungi, and why no serious forager picks a mushroom alone in the first year.
name: Mushrooms
sections: The four that will kill you

body.text: If a game is running smoothly at sixty frames per second, it is doing the same set of things every 16.67 milliseconds: reading the controller, moving characters, resolving collisions, playing sounds, and drawing a fresh picture on the screen. The loop that does this has been the skeleton of real-time games since Pong in 1972. Everything interesting in a game engine — physics, animation, networking, AI — hangs off it.

body.alt: The original Pong upright arcade cabinet.
body.caption: The original Pong cabinet. The game loop inside it ran at 60 Hz, on hardware that predates the microprocessor. Fifty-four years later, the loop you will write does the same three things in the same order.

body.text: A real-time program is a fixed budget

Film runs at 24 frames per second, television at 30, modern games at 60 or 120. At 60 Hz, the whole loop has to finish in under 17 ms — or the screen skips a frame, and the player feels it as a stutter. Most of game programming is a budget exercise: what can be done in that time, what must be skipped, and what can be amortized across frames. Unlike a web server, which can queue work, a game cannot apologize and serve the next player later. The clock does not wait.

The most expensive common operation is drawing. Modern GPUs can push tens of millions of triangles per frame, but only if you organize the work so they can pipeline it — batch similar draw calls, upload geometry once, avoid state changes. The art is in the organization, not the raw capability. John Carmack used to say that id Software's secret was that the team understood exactly where each frame's 16 ms went. Everything else followed.
The three phases of the loop

Input: poll the keyboard, mouse, gamepad, touchscreen for what changed since the last frame. Update: advance the simulation — move entities, run AI, tick timers, resolve physics and collisions. Render: build a list of draw calls and hand it to the GPU. Every modern engine, from Unreal to Unity to Godot, has these three phases under some name. Robert Nystrom's Game Programming Patterns, which is free online, devotes a whole chapter to the loop and why you should not write your own from scratch if an engine's will do.

body.caption: Pong, running. The 1972 game loop that invented the genre — and the pattern every modern engine still follows.

body.text: Fixed timesteps and the Glenn Fiedler problem

The simple loop updates the world by however much real time has passed. The trouble is that variable time produces non-reproducible, non-deterministic physics — a fast machine and a slow machine get different results from the same inputs. Glenn Fiedler's 2004 article Fix Your Timestep!, still the most-linked post in game programming, lays out the standard answer: run the physics on a fixed timestep (say, 120 Hz), regardless of frame rate, and interpolate the rendering. That separation — simulation at a fixed rate, rendering at the display's rate — is quietly what makes every serious game feel solid.
Decouple simulation from rendering. Run the simulation on a fixed timestep. Interpolate the visuals. If you take one thing from the subject, take that.
What the engines actually buy you

You can write a game loop in fifty lines of C and some platform calls — Handmade Hero, Casey Muratori's long-running livestream, does exactly that. Most developers use Unity, Unreal, or Godot because writing the loop, the renderer, the audio mixer, the physics, the scripting, and the asset pipeline is a second full-time job. An engine is mostly other people's solutions to problems you will otherwise hit in month three.

The calculation in 2026 looks something like this: if you are shipping a commercial game in under two years, use an engine. If you are learning, writing a tiny 2D game, or doing something the engines do badly (a rhythm game with strict timing, an unusual input device, a port to obscure hardware), write your own. Almost nobody should write their own on the first project.
The rendering pipeline

Under the render phase lives another pipeline entirely. Vertex shader, rasterization, fragment shader, blending — a story with its own decades of literature. The modern state of the art, as of 2026, is Vulkan, Metal, and Direct3D 12, with WebGPU joining as the cross-platform web story. All of them expose the same rough model — you upload data, describe what you want drawn, let the GPU work. The old fixed-function pipeline (OpenGL 1.x, DirectX 9) has been gone long enough that a new programmer may never encounter it, and should not.

body.label: Why 60 Hz
body.text: Sixty frames per second is not arbitrary. It matches the 60 Hz refresh rate of North American CRTs, which was chosen because the US electrical grid is 60 Hz, which was chosen by Westinghouse in 1893 after a long argument with Edison. The entire visual language of games inherits from a choice made for generators, not eyeballs.
Where to start if you're starting

Download Godot, which is free and honest about what it is. Follow the three-hour "Your First 2D Game" tutorial. Ship the tutorial result, verbatim, to itch.io. Then change one thing and ship it again. The loop you will build inside the engine will be boring and five lines long. That is the right amount of boring. The rest of the game is where your design decisions go.

dek: The heartbeat of every real-time game — a cycle that reads input, updates the world, and draws it, sixty times a second.
name: The Game Loop

body.text: In 1980, a twenty-two-year-old at Atari named Ed Logg watched a tester hand the controller back after a few minutes of his half-finished game and say, quite politely, that he had to get back to work. Logg went back and cut two-thirds of the features, added a scoring ramp, and shipped Centipede. It became one of the best-selling arcade games of the decade. Game design is the part of making games that no engine will do for you, and the history is full of moments like that one — where a designer threw away most of what they had built because the player, who saw none of it, was not having fun.
Rules are not the point; the experience is

In 2004, Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc, and Robert Zubek published a short paper called MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design, which has become the field's default vocabulary. Mechanics are the rules a designer writes. Dynamics are the behaviour that emerges when players run the rules. Aesthetics are the feelings the dynamics produce — fantasy, challenge, fellowship, discovery. A designer composes mechanics, but a player experiences aesthetics; the path from one to the other is never short and often surprising.

body.caption: Mark Brown, "Designing a Game around ONE Mechanic" — Portal, Downwell, Baba Is You, case studies in what happens when one idea is squeezed.

body.text: Feel is engineering, not magic

Steve Swink's Game Feel (2008) is the best book in the field on why two shooters can have identical mechanics and feel completely different. The difference lives in the hundred tiny things under the rules: how quickly a jump responds, how long a hit-flash lasts, how much the camera shakes on impact, how the sound cuts. These are choices a programmer and a designer make together, and they are what separates a game that feels sharp from one that feels mushy.

Jan Willem Nijman of Vlambeer — the designer behind Nuclear Throne and Super Crate Box — gave a GDC talk in 2013 called "The Art of Screenshake" that became required viewing in the field. He listed roughly thirty specific tweaks that give a game impact: muzzle flash, knockback, sleep frames, particles, camera shake, sound layering. Any one of them adds nothing. All of them together are why Vlambeer's games feel like no one else's.
Loops within loops

A well-designed game is a set of nested feedback loops: the second-to-second loop (moving, shooting, jumping) inside a minute-to-minute loop (clearing a room, winning a match) inside a session loop (advancing a campaign) inside a meta loop (unlocks, progression). Each layer needs its own pacing and reward. Raph Koster, in A Theory of Fun (2004), argues that fun is mostly the brain noticing it has learned a new pattern — and a good game is a sequence of patterns, served at the rate a human can eat them.

The single cheapest improvement to a game in its first playable week: speed up the time from input to feedback. Shorter menus, fewer splash screens, instant respawns. Players will forgive many things but not a lag on the thing they pressed.
Playtesting is the only truth

Every designer, asked how they know a mechanic works, will eventually give the same answer: they watched someone play. Jesse Schell's The Art of Game Design organizes its hundred "lenses" — diagnostic questions a designer can ask about a game in progress — around this loop. You can argue in a meeting for a week about whether a level is too hard. Sit a stranger at the controller and you will know in three minutes.

The practical discipline is to watch silently. Do not explain the controls. Do not hint. Do not defend. Note every place the player hesitates, every place they do the wrong thing, every place they laugh. At the end, ask one question: what did you think was going to happen? The gap between what they expected and what happened is the design work for the next week.

body.label: The tutorial problem
body.text: A surprising amount of design time — sometimes half the budget of the first playable — goes into teaching the player how to play. Portal (2007) is the canonical example of teaching-by-level-design: every new mechanic is introduced in a room that is impossible to fail. The result is the rarest thing in games — a tutorial that is also the best level.
A short reading list for the unconvinced

If you do not think design is a real discipline, read the Nijman talk, then Schell's book, then Swink's book, then subscribe to Mark Brown's Game Maker's Toolkit. By the third case study you will be arguing about camera shake like a professional. By the tenth you will want to make something. Making something, and watching a stranger play it, is the only education that closes the loop.

body.cite: Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun
body.text: Fun from games arises out of mastery. It arises out of comprehension. It is the act of solving puzzles that makes games fun.

dek: The craft of arranging rules and feedback so that a player wants to play one more time.
