Modern climbing manuals are explicit about which knots to use with which ropes.
Inspect before you trust

The discipline that distinguishes climbers and sailors from casual rope users is the habit of inspection. Tie the knot, dress it (smooth out the curves so each strand sits where it should), set it (tighten by pulling on each strand separately), then look at it. A climber's tie-in is checked by their partner before every climb. A sailor's docking line is glanced at after every adjustment. The inspection takes seconds and prevents nearly every rope failure that does not involve the rope itself breaking. The habit is more important than knowing one more knot.

Better to know a knot and not need it, than need a knot and not know it. The motto belongs to Animated Knots — and to every working sailor, climber, and arborist who has ever done something useful with a rope.

dek: Every knot has a job; matching knot to job is most of what working people with rope actually do.
name: When to Use What

body.text: Every time someone buys coffee, takes a job, clicks "I agree," or rents an apartment, a contract is formed. Most are never read, most are never disputed, and most are, from the law's point of view, entirely valid. Contract law is the quiet machinery that allows strangers to cooperate at scale — and most of the time you only notice it when it is broken.

body.caption: The Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE), now in the Louvre. Among its 282 laws are the earliest surviving rules for sales, rentals, and deposits — contract law, in the original.
body.credit: Mbzt, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: The four elements

A legally binding contract, in the common-law tradition, requires four things: an offer; an acceptance; consideration (something of value exchanged by each side); and, in most places, legal capacity. A bargain to paint my house for a thousand dollars has all four. A gift promise does not, because only one side is giving anything, and contract law will not enforce it.

Offer and acceptance seem simple until a lawyer draws them. A billboard advertising a car is not an offer; it is an invitation to treat. The email reply that says "agreed, except let's push closing to Friday" is not an acceptance; it is a counter-offer, which destroys the original offer. First-year law students spend weeks on these small distinctions because millions of dollars turn on them in commercial disputes.
Consideration, the odd requirement

The consideration doctrine is the most distinctive feature of common-law contract. Continental civil-law systems (France, Germany, Japan) do not require it; a serious promise intentionally made can be binding on that basis alone. The American rule — that a contract needs bargained-for exchange — is still debated, and courts have invented workarounds like promissory estoppel for the obvious cases it gets wrong. If your employer promises you a bonus and you turn down another job on the strength of the promise, the consideration doctrine technically says you have no contract. Promissory estoppel says you might still win.
When it is not a contract

Some agreements are not enforceable no matter how carefully they are drafted. A contract for an illegal purpose (to commit a crime), a contract signed under duress, a contract with a minor, a contract whose performance is impossible from the start, a contract that violates public policy (a covenant not to compete drafted too broadly, an exculpatory clause for gross negligence) — each is void or voidable. The list is shorter than a layperson imagines; the system is biased toward enforcement, and for good reasons.
Remedies for breach

When a party breaches, the default remedy in common law is damages — a money payment designed to put the non-breaching party where they would have been if the contract had been performed. Courts are reluctant to order specific performance (making the breaching party actually do the thing they promised); they prefer letting money settle it, except for unique goods like land and art. The "efficient breach" doctrine, championed by law-and-economics scholars like Richard Posner, even argues that breach is sometimes good: if the breaching party gains more than the non-breaching party loses, damages put things right and society is better off.
The Uniform Commercial Code

American commercial contract law runs on the Uniform Commercial Code, drafted by Karl Llewellyn in the 1940s and 1950s and adopted (with minor variations) by every U.S. state. Article 2 of the UCC governs sales of goods; its default rules fill in the gaps every time a purchase order is silent on a detail. Even people who have never heard of Llewellyn rely on him every time they buy something on the internet.

The UCC is a remarkable intellectual achievement. Llewellyn, a legal realist at Columbia, wanted the Code to reflect how merchants actually behaved, not an idealized theory. Whole passages of Article 2 reflect trade-usage realities — "course of dealing," "usage of trade," good-faith obligations — that older common-law doctrine had under-specified. The international counterpart is the CISG (Contracts for the International Sale of Goods), adopted by most major trading nations except the United Kingdom and India.

A contract does not have to be in writing. In most U.S. states, a verbal agreement to paint a house is just as enforceable as a written one — provided the price is below the Statute of Frauds threshold (typically $500 for goods under Article 2) and both sides can prove what was said.
Learn it: the IRAC method

Every first-year law student learns the IRAC framework — Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. It is how a lawyer breaks down any legal problem. Practice it here. Facts: On Monday, Alice emails Bob: "I'll sell you my 2018 Honda for $9,000. Let me know by Friday." On Wednesday, Bob replies: "I'll take it for $8,500." On Thursday, Alice sells the car to Carol for $9,500. Is Alice liable to Bob?

Issue: Did Alice and Bob form a binding contract? Rule: A contract requires offer, acceptance, and consideration. A counter-offer (different price) is not an acceptance; it is a new offer that terminates the original. Application: Alice's Monday email is an offer. Bob's Wednesday reply proposes a different price; that is a counter-offer, which destroys Alice's original offer. Alice had no outstanding offer to Bob when she sold to Carol. Conclusion: No contract formed between Alice and Bob. Alice is not liable. This is what IRAC does — it forces the lawyer to name the issue, state the governing rule, apply it carefully, and reach a defensible conclusion. Every case brief you will ever read follows this structure.
Worked example: the Peerless ships

Raffles v. Wichelhaus (1864) is the canonical law-school case on mutual mistake. Two English merchants contracted for cotton to be shipped from Bombay on a ship named "Peerless." There were two ships called Peerless in Bombay harbor that year. The seller meant the December Peerless; the buyer meant the October Peerless. When the cotton arrived on the December ship, the buyer refused delivery. The court held there was no contract — the parties had never in fact agreed on the same subject matter. Read this case cold and you will never forget that a "meeting of the minds" means the minds actually have to meet. The practical lesson: if a contract term is ambiguous and both parties understood different things, and neither is more reasonable than the other, there is no enforceable bargain.
Practice problems

Problem 1. A bakery owner tells a neighbor over coffee: "I'll give you 500 dollars to paint the fence." The neighbor says nothing but goes home, buys paint, and paints the fence the next day. Is there a contract? Which elements are or are not met?

Answer: Offer: yes. Acceptance: contested — silence is ordinarily not acceptance, but *performance* can be acceptance of a unilateral offer. Consideration: yes (painting for money, each party giving up something). Under modern American common law, the bakery owner is likely bound because the neighbor's full performance accepts the offer. The restoration doctrine would reinforce this. If the neighbor had just *started* painting, the question gets trickier — Restatement § 45 protects the offeree against revocation once performance begins.

Problem 2. A drafting clause says: "Time is of the essence." A different clause says: "Minor delays shall not constitute material breach." A party delivers three days late. Is the delay a breach? How do you read the contract?

Answer: The two clauses conflict. Courts use several interpretive canons: specific provisions control general ones; handwritten and typed terms beat printed form language; ambiguity is construed against the drafter (contra proferentem). The honest answer is that a court will look to the parties' course of dealing, trade usage, and drafting history to decide which clause dominates. This is why contract drafting matters: every such ambiguity costs somebody money in litigation.

Problem 3. A homeowner hires a contractor to build a pool for $50,000. Halfway through, the homeowner loses their job and can no longer pay. They tell the contractor to stop. The contractor has already spent $30,000 on materials and labor. What is the contractor entitled to recover?

Answer: The contractor has a claim for expectation damages — the position they would have been in had the contract been performed. That is typically the contract price ($50,000) minus the cost to complete, or equivalently, the cost incurred plus the lost profit. If the contractor's expected profit was $10,000 on a $50,000 project with $40,000 of costs, and they have incurred $30,000 so far, they should be made whole at $30,000 + their remaining $10,000 profit = $40,000. The homeowner's financial hardship is not a legal defense; changes in a party's ability to pay are not grounds to rescind. This is harsh, and it is the rule.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What are the four elements of a common-law contract? (2) What is consideration, and why does civil law not require it? (3) What is promissory estoppel? (4) Name three things that make a contract voidable. (5) What is the Uniform Commercial Code, and which article governs sales of goods? (6) Distinguish expectation, reliance, and restitution damages. (7) What is a "meeting of the minds," and what case is the classic illustration?
The learning progression

Brand new? Read the Cornell LII contract entry and watch three LawShelf contract videos. Try reading a real contract you've signed (a lease, a terms of service) and locate the offer, acceptance, consideration, damages clauses, and severability. Once you've got the basics? Read Fried's Contract as Promise cover to cover and do a first-year contracts casebook's first chapter (Kessler and Fine, or Farnsworth). Work the IRAC method on ten classic cases. To go further? Take contract law in an LLM or JD program, or read the Restatement (Second) of Contracts cover to cover. The next level is commercial: UCC Article 2, CISG, and the international-arbitration literature (Gary Born, Redfern and Hunter).

body.text: In English, the phrase "guilty act" sounds tautological. In Latin — actus reus — it is a term of art, and its counterpart mens rea, the "guilty mind," makes the whole difference. A surgeon who performs a fatal operation has committed a guilty act (the killing) without a guilty mind (intent). The law has been drawing that line since at least the twelfth century, and a first-year criminal-law class spends a semester on where, exactly, to put it.

body.caption: Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr. (1841–1935), associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court for nearly thirty years. His 1881 book The Common Law set out the actus reus / mens rea framework in plain English.
body.credit: Harris & Ewing, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: The two elements

Almost every crime at common law has the same structure: the act (actus reus) plus the mental state (mens rea). The Model Penal Code, drafted by the American Law Institute in 1962 and adopted in some form by most U.S. states, formalized four levels of mens rea — purposely, knowingly, recklessly, and negligently — and a criminal-law exam will still ask you to distinguish them. Purposely: the defendant wanted the result. Knowingly: the defendant knew the result was virtually certain. Recklessly: the defendant disregarded a substantial and unjustifiable risk. Negligently: the defendant should have been aware of such a risk.
Justifications and excuses

A defense is a reason the state's case should fail even if both elements are proved. Some are justifications (self-defense, defense of others, necessity, defense of property): the act was not wrongful in the circumstances. Others are excuses (insanity, duress, infancy, involuntary intoxication): the act was wrongful, but blaming this particular defendant would not be just. The distinction is subtle; it matters a great deal in practice, because a justification legalizes the act (others may not interfere with it) while an excuse only exempts this defendant from blame.
Why punish at all

Philosophers and criminologists have offered five justifications for punishment: retribution (the offender deserves it), deterrence (others will be discouraged), incapacitation (the offender can't do it again from prison), rehabilitation (the offender can be changed), and restoration (the victim, community, and offender can be reconciled). Every sentencing scheme is a weighted mix of these; none of them dominates alone. The argument over the weights is the political debate about criminal justice in miniature.

Retributive theory, as articulated by Kant, says wrongdoers must be punished because they deserve to be — regardless of consequences. Consequentialist theory, from Bentham onward, says we punish to reduce future crime, full stop. Most working systems are hybrids: they set sentencing ranges by the retributive gravity of the offense, then adjust within the range for consequentialist reasons (first offense, cooperation, treatment availability).
The procedural backstop

In most legal systems today, the state must prove criminal guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; the defendant is presumed innocent; the defendant is entitled to counsel; and a person cannot be tried twice for the same offense. These are not accidents. The package was assembled over centuries in response to actual abuses, and any serious conversation about reform has to specify which of these protections one is willing to weaken, and by how much.
The American peculiarity

The United States holds about 5% of the world's population and about 20% of the world's prisoners. The incarceration rate has roughly quadrupled since the 1970s; it peaked around 2008 and has declined modestly since. A vast literature — Michelle Alexander's The New Jim Crow (2010), Bruce Western's Punishment and Inequality (2006), John Pfaff's Locked In (2017), and Elizabeth Hinton's From the War on Poverty to the War on Crime (2016) — argues about why. The immediate causes (longer sentences, more prosecutions, aggressive drug laws, plea bargaining) are easier to agree on than the deeper ones (racial politics, deindustrialization, federalism).

The reform argument is now broadly bipartisan but stalls on specifics. Bail reform, cash bail abolition, sentencing reductions for nonviolent drug offenses, Ban the Box, and prosecutorial reform have all made partial progress at the state and local level. What has not been tried at scale, anywhere, is a serious reduction in sentences for violent offenses — which is where most of the incarcerated population actually is.

body.cite: William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765)
body.text: It is better that ten guilty persons escape than that one innocent suffer.

The presumption of innocence is not a direct command of the U.S. Constitution. It was read into the Due Process Clause by the Supreme Court in Coffin v. United States (1895), drawing on Roman and English law going back two millennia. The Court called it "axiomatic and elementary." Its practical force depends entirely on how seriously a given courtroom takes it.
Learn it: reading a criminal statute

Pick up any state criminal code and read the homicide section. You will find the same nested structure everywhere. First-degree murder usually requires killing + specific intent + premeditation. Second-degree murder drops premeditation. Voluntary manslaughter drops specific intent (heat of passion). Involuntary manslaughter drops even intent (recklessness or gross negligence). Each rung down the ladder removes one mental-state element; each rung changes the sentence range, often by decades. A defense lawyer's job is often not to contest the killing but to argue about which rung of the ladder the facts actually reach. This is why mens rea is called the "guilty mind" in the singular — there are four flavors in the Model Penal Code (purposely, knowingly, recklessly, negligently), and every element of every crime carries its own required flavor. Reading a criminal statute is an act of decomposition.
Worked example: the self-defense analysis

Facts: A man is followed home at night by someone he does not recognize. The follower pulls out what turns out to be a wallet. The man, fearing a weapon, shoots and kills the follower. Is this self-defense? Walk through the elements. (1) Imminence — was the threat immediate, not speculative? Yes, the follower is present. (2) Reasonableness — would an ordinary person in that situation have believed they were in danger of great bodily harm? Probably — unknown stranger following at night, reaching into a jacket. (3) Proportionality — was deadly force necessary to meet the threat? Harder — the man had no prior knowledge it was a weapon. (4) Retreat — many but not all jurisdictions require retreat if safely possible before using deadly force. "Stand your ground" states remove this requirement. The same facts can produce acquittal in Florida (no duty to retreat) and conviction in Massachusetts (duty to retreat). Self-defense is not one doctrine; it is a state-by-state patchwork.
Practice problems

Problem 1. A hunter, aiming at what he believes is a deer in dim light, shoots and kills another hunter. Is this murder, voluntary manslaughter, involuntary manslaughter, or no crime? Which mens rea applies?

Answer: Almost certainly involuntary manslaughter — killing by gross negligence or recklessness. The hunter did not intend to kill a person (no purpose), did not know with certainty it was a person (no knowledge), but a reasonable hunter should have identified the target before firing. Some jurisdictions would prosecute as "criminally negligent homicide" instead. In a few states with no negligent-homicide statute, the conduct might result in no criminal charge at all and only civil liability. The same conduct, the same death, three different legal classifications across American jurisdictions.

Problem 2. A defendant confesses to a crime after being interrogated for eight hours without being told of her right to remain silent. At trial, the prosecution wants to introduce the confession. What is the governing Supreme Court case? What must the prosecution show to admit the confession? What is the constitutional basis?

Answer: Miranda v. Arizona (1966). Before custodial interrogation, police must warn the suspect of the right to remain silent, that anything said can be used against them, the right to counsel, and the right to appointed counsel if indigent. Without the warnings, statements are inadmissible in the prosecution's case-in-chief. Constitutional basis: Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination, as incorporated against the states by the Fourteenth. Exceptions exist (public-safety exception, routine booking, spontaneous statements).

Problem 3. A defendant is clearly mentally ill but is capable of distinguishing right from wrong. Under the M'Naghten rule, is the defendant eligible for an insanity defense? Under the Model Penal Code test? What policy trade-off do the two tests reflect?

Answer: Under M'Naghten (1843), the defendant must not know what he was doing or not know it was wrong — a narrow cognitive test. So a defendant who knows right from wrong fails the test. Under the MPC (1962), the defendant is insane if, due to mental disease, he lacks substantial capacity either to appreciate the criminality of his conduct *or* to conform his conduct to the law — a broader test that includes "volitional" incapacity. The MPC approach acknowledges that severely mentally ill defendants may know right from wrong but be unable to resist acting. After the 1982 Hinckley verdict, several states narrowed the test back toward M'Naghten. The policy trade-off: broader insanity tests acquit defendants who are not morally blameworthy; narrower tests avoid "abuse" of the defense and protect public confidence.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What are the two elements of most crimes? (2) Name the four Model Penal Code mens rea levels in order of severity. (3) Distinguish a justification from an excuse. (4) State the four classic purposes of punishment. (5) Under what circumstances are Miranda warnings required? (6) What is the reasonable-doubt standard, and how does it differ from "preponderance" and "clear and convincing"? (7) Name two recent reforms of American criminal-justice practice and one effect each has had.
The learning progression

Brand new? Read Blackstone's Commentaries Book IV Introduction. Watch five LawShelf criminal-law videos. Read one Supreme Court opinion (Gideon is short and accessible). When you can walk through an arrest-to-appeal flowchart from memory, you have the skeleton. Once you've got the basics? Read Stevenson's Just Mercy and Alexander's The New Jim Crow, and work the first chapter of a 1L criminal-law casebook (Kadish, Schulhofer, and Steiker). To go further? Take criminal law and criminal procedure in a JD or LLM program. Read Packer's "Two Models of the Criminal Process" (1964) and Herbert Packer's Limits of the Criminal Sanction. Then dive into contemporary policy literature: Pfaff's Locked In, Gottschalk's Caught, and the Marshall Project's ongoing reporting.

body.text: On February 24, 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall handed down an opinion that was, on its face, a procedural defeat for the plaintiff. William Marbury did not get his commission. But the reason he did not get it — that the statute under which he sued was unconstitutional — gave the Supreme Court the power it has exercised ever since: to strike down an act of Congress. Nothing in the Constitution says the Court may do this. Marshall simply said it could, and every subsequent justice has agreed.

body.caption: The U.S. Supreme Court building in Washington, completed in 1935. Before that, the Court sat for 146 years in rooms borrowed from Congress. "Equal Justice Under Law" is carved above the west entrance.
body.credit: dbking, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: The doctrine of judicial review

Marbury v. Madison is the most consequential case in American constitutional law, and the one that is most arguably made up from whole cloth. Marshall's reasoning — that the Constitution is law, that courts interpret law, and therefore that courts must decide what the Constitution means when it conflicts with a statute — is plausible but not inevitable. Most other constitutional democracies have since adopted some version of judicial review, but some (the United Kingdom, New Zealand, the Nordic countries) have deliberately stopped short of giving courts the power to strike down legislation.
Individual rights

Much of modern constitutional law is about the rights of individuals against the state: freedom of speech, freedom of religion, due process, equal protection, the protection against unreasonable searches. In the U.S., most of these were written in the first ten amendments in 1791; the Fourteenth Amendment in 1868 extended most of them to restrain state governments, not just the federal one. The application to each new technology and circumstance — wiretapping, abortion, same-sex marriage, thermal imaging of houses, GPS tracking, cell-tower data — is the running project of the field.

Incorporation — the doctrine that the Bill of Rights applies against state governments through the Fourteenth Amendment — was a slow twentieth-century project. Not every clause has been incorporated; the Seventh Amendment's civil-jury right, the Grand Jury Clause, and the Third Amendment's anti-quartering clause have not. The doctrinal history of "selective incorporation" is essentially the history of the Supreme Court between 1897 and 2010.
How judges decide

Constitutional interpretation is fought along several lines at once. Originalists (Scalia, Thomas, Barrett) argue that the meaning of a clause is fixed at the time of ratification. Living-constitutionalists (Brennan, Ginsburg, Breyer) argue that the document's broad language adapts to changing circumstance. Textualists focus on the words; purposivists on the intent; structuralists on the whole architecture. Any serious constitutional-law course spends at least as much time on method as on outcomes, because the method is usually doing the real work.
The great cases

Certain cases are load-bearing for the American constitutional architecture. McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) established broad implied federal powers. Brown v. Board (1954) desegregated public schools. Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) guaranteed counsel to indigent defendants. New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) protected the press. Roe v. Wade (1973), and its 2022 reversal in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health, shaped the abortion right and its withdrawal. Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) recognized same-sex marriage. Reading any one of these with the majority, concurrence, and dissent together is more useful than reading any single textbook chapter.
Looking outward

The German Federal Constitutional Court, the Indian Supreme Court, the South African Constitutional Court, and the European Court of Human Rights all do comparable work on different documents. A comparative glance is humbling: some systems handle rights-protection, federalism, and judicial legitimacy better than the U.S. in some respects, worse in others. The German court's proportionality analysis, for example, is a more structured way of weighing rights against state interests than the American "tiers of scrutiny" — and much of the world has adopted it.
The current moment

American constitutional law is in a period of unusual visible contestation. The Supreme Court's current majority has overturned Roe, Chevron (administrative deference), and Loper Bright (administrative deference again); has substantially expanded the scope of Second Amendment protection; and has narrowed the Voting Rights Act. Whether this represents a durable constitutional realignment or an eventually reversed moment is one of the open questions of the decade. A reader trying to understand the field in 2026 needs to be comfortable reading fresh 5-4 and 6-3 opinions, not just canonical cases.

The Supreme Court hears about 70 cases per year out of roughly 7,000 petitions. The Justices vote on cert in private conference; four votes are required to grant review (the "rule of four"). Most constitutional law in practice is made by the lower federal courts, whose opinions are final unless the Supreme Court intervenes.
Learn it: the tiers of scrutiny

American constitutional law runs on three "tiers" of judicial scrutiny. Learn them and you have a large fraction of Equal Protection and Due Process doctrine in your head. Rational basis (the lowest tier): the law is valid if it is rationally related to a legitimate government interest. Almost any law survives this; the government usually wins. Intermediate scrutiny: the law must be substantially related to an important government interest. Used for sex-based classifications and some First Amendment cases. Strict scrutiny (the highest): the law must be narrowly tailored to a compelling government interest. Used for race-based classifications, fundamental rights, and content-based speech restrictions. Strict scrutiny is, in practice, usually fatal to the law in question, which is why the Court's *choice of tier* often determines the outcome before any facts are weighed.
Worked example: reading Brown v. Board

Brown v. Board of Education (1954) is the most important American judicial decision of the twentieth century, and it is short — about nine pages. Read it with three questions. (1) What precedent was overruled? (Plessy v. Ferguson, 1896, which had held "separate but equal" constitutional.) (2) On what ground? (Not on original intent — the Fourteenth Amendment's drafters ratified segregated schools. Instead, Chief Justice Warren relies on the *social reality* of education's role and the demonstrated psychological harm of segregation.) (3) What does this tell you about originalism vs. living constitutionalism? (Brown is hard to justify on purely originalist grounds. Justice Scalia, a committed originalist, eventually argued Brown was correct on a "faithless" reading of the Fourteenth — showing that originalism and result can diverge.) Brown is the case that makes the interpretive debate real.
Practice problems

Problem 1. A city passes an ordinance requiring all licensed taxi drivers to be at least 21 years old. A 19-year-old with a commercial driver's license sues, arguing the rule violates Equal Protection. Which tier of scrutiny applies, and who is likely to win?

Answer: Age is not a suspect classification under current doctrine; rational-basis review applies. The city need only show the age rule is rationally related to a legitimate interest (public safety, insurance risk). It will almost certainly win. A very different result would follow if the ordinance targeted race, national origin, or alienage.

Problem 2. A state enacts a law forbidding abortion after six weeks. Before Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health (2022), which Supreme Court case controlled? What standard did it impose? After Dobbs, what standard applies?

Answer: Before Dobbs, Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992) controlled, applying an "undue burden" standard — laws placing a substantial obstacle in the path of a pre-viability abortion were unconstitutional. Dobbs overturned Roe and Casey; abortion regulation now receives rational-basis review. States may largely restrict or permit abortion as they choose, subject only to the very weak constraint that the regulation be rationally related to a legitimate state interest. Within 18 months of Dobbs, 14 states had enacted near-total bans; others expanded protections. This is the clearest recent example of how a shift in doctrine transfers questions from courts to politics — as living-constitutionalists feared and originalists intended.

Problem 3. A public university's admissions policy gives explicit numerical weight to race in order to increase diversity. What is the governing case? What tier applies? What arguments do both sides make?

Answer: SFFA v. Harvard (2023) is the governing case. Race-based classifications trigger strict scrutiny. The university must show a compelling interest (diversity was accepted in Grutter) and narrow tailoring. In SFFA, the Court held that Harvard's and UNC's race-conscious admissions failed narrow tailoring and effectively ended race-conscious admissions in American higher education. The university argues diversity benefits pedagogy and democracy; opponents argue race-based classifications are unconstitutional on their face. Both frames have textual, historical, and prudential support. The answer in any given term depends on who is on the Court.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What did Marbury v. Madison establish and on what reasoning? (2) Name the three tiers of scrutiny and when each applies. (3) What is incorporation, and what Amendment does it work through? (4) Distinguish originalism, textualism, and living constitutionalism. (5) Name three landmark cases that shaped twentieth-century individual-rights doctrine. (6) What is the "political question" doctrine, and why does it exist? (7) How does the German Basic Law's proportionality framework differ from American tiers of scrutiny?
The learning progression

Brand new? Read the U.S. Constitution front to back. Read Marbury v. Madison and Brown v. Board. Watch one National Constitution Center "We the People" debate. Once you've got the basics? Read Amar's America's Constitution: A Biography and Scalia-Gutmann's A Matter of Interpretation back to back. Watch five Supreme Court oral arguments on Oyez. To go further? Take constitutional law in JD or LLM. Read Tribe's American Constitutional Law (3 volumes — not cover to cover) as a reference. Read Dworkin's Freedom's Law and Whittington's Constitutional Interpretation. For comparative depth, read David Landau and Rosalind Dixon on abusive constitutionalism — the current scholarly frontier.
