When water rushes down a stack, it pulls air behind it. Without a vent, that air is pulled from nearby traps, siphoning them dry. The vent admits atmospheric air into the drain system so the water can flow without creating a vacuum. Every trap needs a vent within a fixture-specific distance (typically 5–8 feet for 1½" arms). The vent either ties back into the main stack above the flood rim of the highest fixture, or rises independently through the roof.
Trap arm distance

A 1½" trap arm can run 6 feet horizontally before it must reach a vent. 2" arm, 8 feet. 3" arm, 10 feet. 4" arm, 12 feet. These are code minimums — the UPC and IPC tables are on every plumber's phone.
Wet venting

In a typical bathroom group, the lavatory's drain can serve as the vent for the toilet and tub below it — provided the geometry and size meet the code. This is called wet venting. It eliminates one roof penetration and a lot of pipe. Read Code Check Plumbing before you try it; the rules are specific.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: Venting a second-floor lavatory: the drain runs 5 feet to the main stack. A 1½" vent rises from the top of the trap arm (just above the trap weir) and ties into the stack above the flood rim of the highest fixture on that stack (the tub). One vent, no roof penetration.
Sizing the drain

Every fixture has a "drainage fixture unit" (DFU) value — a kitchen sink is 2, a bathroom group is 6, a toilet is 3, and so on. The main stack and the building drain are sized to carry the total DFU load. The Code Check flipchart has the table; a 3" stack handles most single-family houses, a 4" stack handles a commercial multi-bathroom layout.
Troubleshooting

The sink drains slowly. Partial clog — snake it from the cleanout. A distant trap smells. Siphoning from a long-run or blocked vent. Trace the drain; look for a capped vent or a bird's nest in the stack cap. Gurgling when a toilet flushes. Inadequate vent — the drain is pulling air through other traps. Add a vent or an air admittance valve. A basement floor drain smells. Trap has dried out; pour in water.
Going deeper

After you can size a standard bathroom group, the next topic is cast-iron drain assembly (for sound-damping in commercial), commercial grease traps, and graywater systems. The Uniform Plumbing Code and the International Plumbing Code diverge at chapter 9 (venting) — if you work near a jurisdiction boundary, know both.

body.label: Practice this week
body.text: Draw the DWV for a typical bathroom group — toilet, sink, tub — on paper. Size every pipe. Show the vent path. Check against Code Check Plumbing. You will see why plumbing is called a "system" and not a "pipe."

body.label: Self-check
body.text: Why does a drain need a vent? (So water can flow without pulling traps dry.) What is the typical slope of a residential 2" drain? (1/4" per foot.) What is the maximum trap arm for a 1½" drain? (6 feet.) If any stumps you, read Code Check Plumbing chapter 9.

First project: install a P-trap and trap arm for a new bathroom lavatory, including a 1½" vent tying back into the stack. A single Saturday. Under $30. You will meet slope, trap, and vent together on one fixture.

dek: Gravity takes the water down; the vents keep the gas out of the house.
name: Drain-Waste-Vent

body.text: The plumbing in a finished house is mostly invisible. What the client sees and uses is the fixture — the faucet that turns, the sink that drains, the toilet that flushes, the shower head that drips or does not. A fixture is where the hidden labor of rough plumbing meets daily life, and where a careless installation shows itself within weeks. The difference between a fixture installed correctly and one installed quickly is often a quarter of an inch nobody is looking at.

body.caption: A modern toilet on a 12-inch rough-in.

body.text: The whole idea

Every fixture is a final consumer of the plumbing system with one supply side, one drain side, and a trap. The installer's job is to marry those three to a specific fixture with the right mounting, the right gasket, and the right hardware — and to leave the result level, plumb, and leak-free.
Before you start
Tools

Channel-lock pliers, a basin wrench (the awkward tool for faucet nuts under a sink), a level, a wax ring or neoprene seal, Teflon tape, a tube of plumber's putty, a slip-joint pliers, shims, a pencil. A flashlight with a magnetic tail is the plumber's most-used gadget after channel-locks.
Safety

Shut off water at the local angle stop before disconnecting anything. Have a bucket and rags. Never put your face under a stop valve you are opening — the gasket may give. Porcelain is heavy; a toilet tipping onto your foot is the most common non-slip injury in residential plumbing.
Words to know

Rough-in — the distance from the finished wall to the center of the fixture drain (12" for a standard toilet). Flange — the ring that seals the toilet to the drain. Wax ring — the seal between toilet and flange. Angle stop — the small shutoff under a sink or toilet. Supply riser — the flexible line between angle stop and fixture. Escutcheon — the decorative cover over a pipe penetration. Cartridge — the replaceable valve inside a modern faucet.
Rough-in dimensions — the hidden geometry

The rough plumber sets stub-outs at exact distances from the finished wall and floor. 12 inches from the finished wall to the center of the toilet flange. 8 inches on-center for a kitchen faucet. 21 inches from the finished floor to the center of a bathroom sink supply. A rough-in off by half an inch forces the finisher to cut the drywall or tile — expensive on a finished wall.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: Standard bathroom rough-ins: toilet flange 12" from back wall, 15" minimum from side wall, center 30" from any other fixture. Lavatory: supply stubs at 21" and 22" above finished floor (21 for cold, 22 for hot is a common convention), drain at 18" above floor, 4" off-center left or right depending on pedestal. Keep these on a laminated cheat sheet.
Setting a toilet

A toilet bolts to a closet flange set into the floor. A wax ring crushes between the flange and the bowl, sealing porcelain to drain. The bowl is shimmed level from underneath; the tank is bolted to the bowl with a rubber gasket; the supply line flexes from the angle stop up into the tank.
The install sequence

Confirm the flange is at finished-floor height or slightly above (not below — or the wax ring will not seal). Set the bowl on the flange dry-fit; mark around it with a pencil. Remove. Place the wax ring on the flange (or on the bowl, your choice). Set the bowl onto the wax ring, rocking slightly so the ring compresses. Shim to level in all four directions. Tighten the closet bolts in small steps, alternating sides. Tank: place the rubber gasket under the flush valve nut, bolt the tank to the bowl. Supply line: slip-joint to angle stop, thumb-tight, then quarter-turn with pliers.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Overtightening the closet bolts. Porcelain is brittle; too much force cracks the bowl at the base, and the crack will leak six months later. Snug plus a quarter-turn, maximum.
Installing a faucet

Modern single-handle faucets are mostly tool-free once you have the basin wrench. Drop the faucet through the sink deck from above, reach underneath, thread on the mounting nuts, snug with a basin wrench. Connect supply risers from the angle stops to the faucet inlets. Turn water on with the faucet open so air escapes; check for leaks at every joint.
Choosing supply risers

Braided stainless-steel supply risers are the modern standard — flexible, durable, and rated for hot water. The cheap plastic risers that come in big-box store kits are fine for bathroom use but break down under kitchen conditions. Spend the extra three dollars on stainless.
Sinks, tubs, showers

A drop-in sink sets on a bead of silicone in the countertop cutout; an undermount sink is clipped from below. A tub spout pushes onto a stub-out or threads on a 1/2" nipple. A shower valve is roughed into the wall before tile goes on — the valve must be plumb and its center must be at the manufacturer's specified depth from the finished tile face, or the trim will not seat.
Troubleshooting

The toilet rocks. Not shimmed; rock will crack wax ring seal within days. The toilet weeps at the base. Wax ring failed — pull, reset with a new ring. The faucet drips. Cartridge worn or sediment in the seat. Disassemble and replace. The sink drain leaks. Slip-joint nuts not square, or the trap is not aligned. Loosen and reassemble.
Going deeper

After basic fixture installation, the next skills are tile-set shower installations (pan liners, pre-slope, curb construction), tankless water heaters, and whole-house water filtration. Every fixture manufacturer publishes install manuals free on their site — read them before the first job on a new brand.

body.label: Practice this week
body.text: Replace a bathroom faucet. Shut off angle stops, disconnect supplies, unscrew the mounting nuts from below with a basin wrench, lift the old faucet, drop in the new one, reverse. One hour, under $100 in a quality faucet. You will meet every faucet install you ever do again.

body.label: Self-check
body.text: Why shim a toilet level? (An unshimmed toilet rocks; rocking breaks the wax-ring seal.) Why use braided supply risers in the kitchen? (Hot water breaks down the cheap plastic.) What is the standard toilet rough-in? (12 inches.) If any stumps you, watch Roger Wakefield "How to install a toilet."
First project: replace an angle stop and supply riser under a sink. Thirty minutes, $10 in parts. You will never again be afraid of the turn-off valve under a fixture.

dek: The visible plumbing — sinks, toilets, faucets — and the inches of installation that decide the feel of a room.
name: Fixtures

body.text: Around 350 BCE, in a grove outside Athens, Aristotle gave his students a handout. There were six kinds of government, he said, and they came in pairs: rule by one, by a few, or by many, each in a healthy and a corrupted form. Monarchy and tyranny, aristocracy and oligarchy, polity and democracy. The scheme was not complete, and Aristotle knew it was not. It is still, two millennia later, the place any course on comparative politics begins.

body.caption: A Roman copy of a Greek bronze bust of Aristotle (384–322 BCE), Palazzo Altemps, Rome. His Politics catalogued 158 Greek constitutions and classified them by who ruled.
body.credit: Jastrow, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: The modern democratic family

Most of what we call democracy today is representative rather than direct. Citizens elect officials who legislate on their behalf, and the institutions that constrain those officials — courts, free press, independent bureaucracies, civil society — do more of the work than the ballot. Within this family there are substantial differences. A parliamentary system, like the United Kingdom's, fuses the executive and the legislature. A presidential system, like the United States', separates them. A semi-presidential system, like France's Fifth Republic, does some of both. Each has characteristic strengths and pathologies.

Juan Linz's 1990 essay "The Perils of Presidentialism" argued that presidential systems are more prone to breakdown than parliamentary ones, because an elected president and an elected legislature can both claim democratic legitimacy when they disagree. The empirical record — Latin America through the twentieth century, parts of Africa after 1990 — has been kind to his argument. The American case, where the system has held for 235 years, is the interesting outlier.
Autocracy, old and new

An autocracy concentrates political power in one person or one small group. Pre-modern monarchies relied on dynastic legitimacy; modern authoritarian regimes lean on some mix of nationalism, economic performance, repression, and managed elections. Political scientists — Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way, among others — now classify many twenty-first-century regimes as "competitive authoritarian": elections happen, but the playing field is so unequal that the outcome is rarely in doubt. Russia under Putin, Hungary under Orbán, Turkey under Erdoğan, and Venezuela under Chávez and Maduro have all been assigned to this category at some point in the last two decades.
The hybrid middle

Pure democracies and pure autocracies are the extremes of a spectrum; most governments live somewhere between. Theocracies mix religious and political authority (Iran); constitutional monarchies keep a royal head of state while devolving power to an elected parliament (Japan, Sweden, Spain, the United Kingdom); one-party states combine meritocratic bureaucracy with tight political control (China, Vietnam, Singapore); military juntas hold power with a civilian face (several in West Africa in the 2020s). The classification schemes — Freedom House, Polity, V-Dem, the Economist Intelligence Unit — each draw the lines differently and argue with each other about where specific countries sit.
Federalism, confederation, unitary

Cutting across the democracy/autocracy axis is a separate question: how is power divided vertically? A federal system (the United States, Germany, India, Australia) constitutionally reserves powers for subnational units. A unitary system (France, Japan, most African states) concentrates them in the center, even where it devolves administratively. A confederation (the historical United States under the Articles of Confederation, or the modern European Union on some readings) gives more power to the parts than to the whole. Which a country has shapes everything from tax policy to how quickly a pandemic response can be mounted.
Why the form matters

Amartya Sen observed in 1999 that no functioning democracy has ever suffered a serious famine. The claim oversimplifies, but it points at something real: the form of government shapes which information reaches decision-makers, which decisions are reversible, and whose interests get protected in a crunch. A regime is not an ornament. It is the software on which everything else runs.

The late-twentieth-century story was that democracy was slowly winning. Larry Diamond, Samuel Huntington, and others called it "the third wave." The 2010s and 2020s have complicated the story. V-Dem's annual Democracy Report records a decade-long decline in the average level of liberal democracy worldwide. Whether this is a durable reversal or a temporary pause is one of the live questions of contemporary political science.

body.cite: Winston Churchill, House of Commons, 11 November 1947
body.text: Democracy is the worst form of government, except for all those other forms that have been tried from time to time.

The United Nations has 193 member states. Freedom House rates about 83 of them "free" in its 2024 report, 56 "partly free," and 54 "not free." The share of the world's population living in "free" countries has fallen below 20% for the first time in the survey's half-century.
Learn it: diagnosing a real regime

Pick an unfamiliar country — Senegal, say, or Moldova. Work through Levitsky and Way's four diagnostic questions in order. (1) Are national elections free and fair in the sense that the outcome is not a foregone conclusion? (2) Do opposition parties have meaningful access to media, to state resources, and to public spaces? (3) Is the judiciary independent enough to strike down executive overreach when it occurs? (4) Can civil society — journalists, unions, NGOs — operate without fear of state retaliation? Four yeses means liberal democracy. Four noes means consolidated authoritarianism. Any mixed pattern puts the regime in the "hybrid" middle, where most of the world's population now lives.

Run the exercise on the United States in 1855 (answer: electoral democracy for white men, authoritarian in the South for Black residents; hybrid). Run it on Singapore today (dominant party, reasonably free elections, limited press freedom, independent judiciary in commercial matters). Run it on China (single-party state, no national contested elections, but substantial local experimentation and meritocratic bureaucracy). The point of the four questions is not to produce a label but to notice which features of a regime are present and which are not — so that any subsequent conversation is about specific mechanisms, not about slogans.
Worked example: reading Federalist 10

Madison's Federalist 10 (1787) is the single most important 3,000 words in American political thought. The argument has four steps, and you can reconstruct them cold. Step 1: the greatest threat to popular government is "faction" — a group united by interest adverse to the common good. Step 2: faction has two cures — remove its causes (impossible without destroying liberty) or control its effects. Step 3: control of effects works better in a large republic than a small one, because a large territory contains more competing factions and no single one can dominate. Step 4: representation ("filter") purifies the popular will through elected representatives. Every criticism and defense of the American system since has been an argument with one of those four steps.

Now practice the method: pick another Federalist (51 on checks and balances, 78 on the judiciary) and try to state its argument in four steps without looking. When you can do that for all three, you have read the constitutional founding.
Practice problems

Problem 1. Country X has a parliamentary system with proportional representation, a ceremonial monarch, and a single-chamber legislature. Country Y has a presidential system with first-past-the-post districts, a written constitution with an entrenched bill of rights, and a bicameral legislature. Which system is more likely to produce gridlock between the executive and the legislature, and why? Which is more likely to produce frequent changes of government?

Answer: Y (presidential, separate elections for executive and legislature) is more likely to produce gridlock, because both branches can claim a democratic mandate and neither can force the other to act. X (parliamentary) is more likely to produce changes of government, because the prime minister falls whenever the coalition breaks. Linz (1990) is the classic argument; the empirical pattern holds.

Problem 2. Use the Freedom House 2024 map. Pick two countries with similar GDP per capita but very different Freedom House scores (e.g., Singapore and Costa Rica, or Saudi Arabia and Chile). What does this pairing tell you about the relationship between wealth and democracy? What is the name of the thesis — Seymour Martin Lipset's — that predicts wealth causes democracy, and what are the main empirical challenges to it?

Answer: Lipset's "modernization thesis" (1959) argued that economic development leads to democratization. Cases like Singapore and Saudi Arabia show rich autocracies persist; cases like India and Costa Rica show poor democracies work. The current empirical view (Przeworski and others) is that wealth helps *sustain* existing democracies but does not reliably *cause* transitions. It is useful for any political conversation to know both what Lipset claimed and what the revised view says.

Problem 3. A hybrid regime holds national elections that the incumbent party always wins with 55–65% of the vote. Independent observers report no fraud on election day, but state media gives the opposition little coverage, the judiciary declines to hear opposition complaints, and large public-sector employers circulate "guidance" about voting. Using Levitsky and Way's term, what is this regime? What is the single most important variable for predicting whether it will liberalize or consolidate into authoritarianism?

Answer: Competitive authoritarianism. Levitsky and Way's 2010 book argues the single most important variable is "linkage" to Western democracies (trade, education, diaspora, institutional ties). High-linkage regimes tend to liberalize; low-linkage ones tend to consolidate. Hungary and Serbia are high-linkage cases (both inside the EU's orbit); Belarus and Zimbabwe are low-linkage. The predicted outcomes have largely held since 2010.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What are Aristotle's six regime types? (2) Why did Juan Linz argue presidential systems break down more often? (3) Name three non-electoral features a liberal democracy requires. (4) What is "competitive authoritarianism," and name two current examples. (5) Draw the Levitsky-Ziblatt "democratic guardrails" — mutual toleration and institutional forbearance — and give a recent American example of each eroding. (6) What does Sen's famine claim assume, and what is one serious counter-example?
The learning progression

Brand new? Watch Smith's first six Yale PLSC 114 lectures and read Federalist 10, 51, and 78. Then pick a country not your own and write a one-page diagnosis of its regime using Freedom House's checklist. When you can do that in an hour, you have the working vocabulary. Once you've got the basics? Read How Democracies Die and Why Nations Fail, and follow Francis Fukuyama's Substack for one month — you will see the live arguments as they are made. To go further? Take a graduate comparative-politics field course (Shapiro, Mainwaring, Levitsky all teach public-accessible versions). The serious readers then read Tocqueville in French, Weber's Politics as a Vocation, and Huntington's Political Order in Changing Societies in order.

dek: The same problem solved in a dozen different ways, from Athenian assembly to modern parliamentary democracy.
name: Forms of Government

body.text: In the summer of 1787, fifty-five men met in a sweltering room in Philadelphia with the windows nailed shut against eavesdroppers. They had come to fix the Articles of Confederation; by September they had written something else. The Constitution of the United States is four pages long, it is the oldest still in use, and it was the product of a bad-tempered compromise between people who disagreed almost as much as they agreed.

body.caption: Howard Chandler Christy's 1940 painting Scene at the Signing of the Constitution of the United States, hanging in the U.S. Capitol. Thirty-nine of the fifty-five Philadelphia delegates signed on 17 September 1787.
body.credit: Howard Chandler Christy, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: What a constitution is for

A constitution does two jobs. It organizes the government — who does what, how power is shared, how officials are chosen — and it constrains the government, by putting some things off-limits even to a majority. The second job is harder. A bill of rights that can be suspended by a simple vote is not much of a constraint. Most modern constitutions make amendment deliberately difficult for this reason.

John Rawls, in A Theory of Justice (1971), argued that a well-designed constitution should be the kind of thing rational people would agree to behind a "veil of ignorance" about their own place in the resulting society. Whether you like his answer or not, the question he asked — what would fair rules look like if you did not know who you were going to be? — is the right one to hold in mind while reading any constitution.
Written, unwritten, and mixed

The United States, India, Germany, and Japan have written constitutions in a single document. The United Kingdom, Israel, New Zealand, and San Marino have no single document and rely on a collection of statutes, court decisions, and unwritten conventions. A third group (Canada, South Africa) has a central written text plus a tradition of unwritten constitutional conventions alongside it. The interesting comparative question is not whether a constitution is written but whether it is actually followed: written paper tigers exist, and so do unwritten but durable restraints.
Judicial review and its discontents

In 1803, in Marbury v. Madison, the U.S. Supreme Court claimed the power to strike down federal laws as unconstitutional. Nothing in the document itself says it may. Chief Justice John Marshall's reasoning was that the Constitution is law, that courts interpret law, and therefore courts must decide what the Constitution means when it conflicts with a statute. The argument is plausible but not inevitable; most other constitutional democracies have adopted some version of judicial review, but several (the United Kingdom, New Zealand, the Nordic countries in various ways) have deliberately stopped short of giving courts the power to strike down legislation.

The critique from the left of judicial review is that unelected judges overturn democratic majorities; the critique from the right is the same critique about different cases. Both are right more often than either wants to admit. Jeremy Waldron's 2006 article "The Core of the Case Against Judicial Review" is the cleanest statement of the democratic worry. Its defenders — including the German and South African constitutional courts in practice — argue that precisely the point of a constitution is to constrain majorities. The argument has no final answer and is not supposed to.
Amendment

A constitution's amendment rule is, in some ways, its most important article. The United States has amended its constitution 27 times since 1789, 15 of those before 1870. The difficulty of amendment — two-thirds of both houses of Congress plus three-quarters of the states — is famously high. The Indian constitution, by contrast, has been amended over 100 times; the German Basic Law 60-plus times; some parts of the Australian constitution require a national referendum and have rarely passed. Comparative constitutional law asks whether an easier or a harder amendment rule is better, and the honest answer is "it depends on everything else."
When constitutions fail

A constitution is a coordination device: it works only if the powerful people in a society agree to keep playing by it when the stakes are high. The 1936 Stalin Constitution of the USSR was a model of liberal protections on paper; it protected no one. Weimar Germany had one of the most carefully drafted constitutions of its day and collapsed in a decade. The lesson is that constitutional text is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. What finally holds a constitution in place is a political culture of acceptance — and that culture, once lost, is very hard to rebuild.

The United States Constitution, at about 7,600 words, is among the shortest national constitutions in active use. The Indian Constitution, with over 146,000 words, is the longest. Neither length predicts durability or democratic quality.
Learn it: the three-step anatomy of any written constitution

Pick up any national constitution and answer three questions in order. (A) How is power organized? Find the articles on the executive, legislature, and judiciary; note how each is selected, how long it serves, and who can dismiss it. (B) What is entrenched against majority change? Find the amendment clause; find the bill of rights (or its absence); find any unamendable clauses ("eternity clauses" like Germany's Article 79(3) on human dignity). (C) Who resolves disputes about the document itself? Find the judicial-review mechanism, its personnel, and its selection. Do this for the U.S. Constitution, then for Germany's Basic Law, then for South Africa's 1996 constitution, and you will have the comparative-law toolkit in an afternoon.
Worked example: Marbury, the move

Read Marshall's opinion in Marbury v. Madison (1803) with three questions in hand. First: what is the actual legal holding? (Answer: §13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 is unconstitutional; the Court cannot issue the writ Marbury asked for.) Second: what does Marshall have to establish to reach that holding? (Answer: that the Constitution is law, that courts say what the law is, and therefore that courts can refuse to apply statutes that conflict with the Constitution.) Third: what does Marshall *not* say that a less-clever opinion might have? (Answer: he does not say the Court can order the president to do anything. The procedural defeat for Marbury is the price of the institutional victory for the Court.) This is the single most artfully constructed opinion in American legal history. Read it slowly.
Practice problems

Problem 1. Country A's constitution can be amended by a simple parliamentary majority. Country B requires two-thirds of the legislature plus three-quarters of the sub-national units. Which constitution is more likely to function as an actual constraint on the government? What are the likely failure modes of each?

Answer: B is the stronger constraint — an amendment rule too easy to use makes the constitution effectively just a statute. But B can also ossify (the U.S. has not passed a substantive amendment since 1971, arguably 1791). Very-hard-to-amend constitutions can produce "judicial amendment" as courts reinterpret to cope with changed circumstances. Neither extreme is clearly better; the design question is context-dependent.

Problem 2. A president signs an executive order that clearly contradicts a statute passed by Congress. A district court rules the order unlawful. The president ignores the court's injunction and continues to enforce the order. What is the constitutional crisis, and what institutions are supposed to resolve it?

Answer: This is the classic "who will enforce the court's order" problem, famously raised by Andrew Jackson ("John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it"). The formal answer is Congress (impeachment) and ultimately the electorate. The deeper answer, from Levitsky and Ziblatt, is that constitutional democracy runs on norms of compliance that no document can self-enforce. This is why the question is a recurring one.

Problem 3. Germany's Basic Law has an "eternity clause" (Article 79(3)) protecting human dignity and the federal structure from any amendment. The U.S. Constitution has only one entrenched clause — the guarantee of equal Senate representation per state. Which approach do you think handles the tension between democracy and constitutionalism better, and why?

Answer: There is no settled answer — this is one of the live debates in comparative constitutional law. The German approach says some values are so foundational that even a supermajority should not be able to amend them. The American approach trusts the political process more and the text less. Your answer should identify the trade-off, not just pick a side. Reading Bruce Ackerman's We the People and Dieter Grimm's Constitutionalism: Past, Present, and Future together is the best way to see both.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What two jobs does every constitution do? (2) What is judicial review, and where does it come from in the U.S. text? (3) Name three countries with no single-document constitution. (4) What does "incorporation" mean in U.S. constitutional law? (5) Contrast originalism and living constitutionalism in one sentence each. (6) Name the three Federalist essays most often cited, and what each claims.
The learning progression

Brand new? Read the U.S. Constitution front to back (it is about 45 minutes) with the Cornell LII annotations open. Then read Federalist 10, 51, and 78. Then watch Smith's Yale lectures on the constitutional founding. Once you've got the basics? Read Akhil Amar's America's Constitution: A Biography and take the National Constitution Center's free online course with Jeffrey Rosen. To go further? Pick one comparative constitution (Germany's Basic Law, the 1996 South African Constitution, India's 1950 Constitution) and read it with its contemporary scholarly commentary; then compare it to the American document clause by clause. Serious readers take Ackerman's Yale seminar or its recorded equivalents, and read Dworkin's Taking Rights Seriously alongside Scalia's A Matter of Interpretation.

dek: The rulebook — the document or practice that constrains the people who run the government.
name: Constitutions

body.text: Around 400 BCE, an Athenian general named Thucydides wrote the history of a war he had fought in and lost, and in a short aside he offered a theory. The Peloponnesian War, he said, had one cause that mattered: "the rise of Athens and the fear that this inspired in Sparta." Twenty-five centuries of international relations scholarship is, in one sense, a footnote to that sentence.

body.caption: A Roman copy of a Greek bust of Thucydides (c. 460 – c. 400 BCE). His History of the Peloponnesian War remains the founding text of international relations as a realist discipline.
body.credit: Shakko, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: The three schools, briefly

Modern IR organizes itself around a small number of traditions. Realism (Morgenthau, Waltz, Mearsheimer) sees states pursuing power in a self-help world. Liberalism (Keohane, Nye) argues that institutions, trade, and democratic peace soften anarchy. Constructivism (Wendt, Finnemore) treats interests and identities as socially constructed, not fixed. Marxism and post-colonial scholarship add a class and a power-over-the-global-South lens. A careful reader listens for which tradition an argument is drawing on.
Anarchy, and what it implies

The key structural feature of international politics, for most theorists, is anarchy — not chaos, but the absence of a global government above sovereign states. There is no international police to call when a neighbor invades. This simple fact, realists argue, forces even peaceful states to worry about their own security, arm themselves, and watch their rivals. The result is the security dilemma: one state's defensive preparations are another state's offensive threat. Liberals respond that institutions like the UN, the WTO, and the EU partially substitute for a world government. Both claims contain truth; which matters more varies by issue.
Deterrence, alliances, and the nuclear question

In 1945, the United States ended a war by incinerating two cities. The weapons have not been used in anger since. Deterrence theory — most of it worked out by Thomas Schelling in the 1950s and 1960s — is the uncomfortable body of knowledge about why. Schelling's The Strategy of Conflict (1960) and Arms and Influence (1966) remain in print; the current reappearance of nuclear threats around the Ukraine war has brought both books back into university reading lists they had briefly left.

Nine countries currently possess nuclear weapons. The nonproliferation regime built around the 1968 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty has had mixed success: it has not prevented India, Pakistan, Israel, or North Korea from acquiring weapons, but it has slowed the spread from the 15 to 20 states that once seemed likely to go nuclear to the 9 we actually have. The regime's central argument — nuclear-armed states will reduce arsenals if non-nuclear states forgo acquisition — is under visible strain as of 2026.
Non-state actors, now more than ever

Twentieth-century IR was largely about states. Twenty-first-century IR is also about transnational corporations, non-governmental organizations, terrorist networks, and — more recently — a small number of very large technology companies with the effective reach of middle powers. No single theory has absorbed this shift cleanly. The field is in an interesting moment.
Climate and other commons

Climate change is the hardest case IR currently faces: a problem that cannot be solved unilaterally, in a system with no enforceable global authority. The Paris Agreement (2015) is a voluntary regime of nationally determined commitments; Elinor Ostrom's earlier work on polycentric governance is increasingly cited as the theoretical scaffold. Whether this approach can actually produce outcomes adequate to the physical problem is one of the defining open questions of the century.

The emerging subfields — cyber conflict, pandemic preparedness, AI governance, space policy — are each, in effect, new tests of the same structural question: can sovereign states coordinate in the absence of a sovereign above them? The history of international relations is the answer, still being written.

The "democratic peace" is one of the most-discussed empirical regularities in international relations: established liberal democracies almost never fight each other. Michael Doyle formalized the observation in 1983; it has held up reasonably well to challenge. Whether the pattern reflects democracy itself, or something else correlated with democracy, is the live argument.
Learn it: reading an international crisis in four theories

Take Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Write one paragraph explaining why it happened in the voice of each theoretical tradition. A *realist* (Mearsheimer) says NATO expansion created a security dilemma Russia could not tolerate; structure produced the war. A *liberal* (Ikenberry) says the war shows the fragility of the rules-based order when a revisionist great power no longer accepts it; institutions matter but can be broken. A *constructivist* (Wendt) says the Russian elite's identity and its narratives about Ukraine — not material interests alone — are doing the work; you cannot predict the war from capabilities alone. A *Marxist* (David Harvey) says the invasion is the latest round in the contest for energy resources and pipeline routes; accumulation logic remains central. Each paragraph catches something real. No paragraph is the whole story. Getting fluent means being able to write all four.
Worked example: the Cuban Missile Crisis as game theory

In October 1962, the United States discovered Soviet missiles in Cuba. Kennedy's advisers proposed three options: (A) diplomatic negotiation, (B) naval quarantine (blockade), (C) air strike. Each choice affected the Soviet reaction. Schelling's framework — reciprocal fear of surprise attack — predicted that both sides would look for moves that demonstrated resolve without forcing the other side to escalate. The quarantine was exactly that: visible enough to commit the U.S. publicly, slow enough to give Khrushchev time to back down. The secret deal (U.S. missiles in Turkey traded for Soviet missiles in Cuba) preserved both leaders' face. Read Allison's Essence of Decision (1971) for three different theoretical lenses on the same thirteen days; it is the single best case study in the IR teaching canon.
Practice problems

Problem 1. Two states share a border and a history of conflict. State A builds up its military "for defense." State B, unable to distinguish defensive from offensive preparations, builds up in response. Both end up more vulnerable and more paranoid than before. What is this phenomenon called? What is the standard realist remedy, and what is a liberal alternative?

Answer: The security dilemma (Herz, 1951). Realist remedies: balance of power, clear alliance structures, deterrence. Liberal alternatives: arms-control treaties with verification, economic interdependence, confidence-building measures. The U.S.-Soviet strategic-arms treaties (SALT, START) are the canonical example of successful liberal mitigation of a severe security dilemma.

Problem 2. A rising power's GDP growth outpaces the incumbent hegemon's for two decades. Graham Allison surveyed 16 historical cases of a rising power challenging an incumbent over 500 years. In how many did war follow? What variables best predicted when it didn't?

Answer: 12 of 16 resulted in war; 4 did not. The non-war cases (Portugal-Spain in the late 15th century, UK-US handoff 1894–1918, USSR-US cold war, UK-France 20th century) share common features: cultural/institutional similarity, presence of a shared threat, or nuclear deterrence. Allison's argument for US-China is that the pattern is alarming but not destiny; careful statecraft has mattered in the 4 successful cases.

Problem 3. A small state cannot credibly threaten a large state militarily. What non-military levers of power are available to it? Name three real-world examples of small states exerting disproportionate global influence.

Answer: Soft power (Nye) — attraction via culture, values, legitimacy. Smart power — combining hard and soft levers. Niche specialization — Switzerland in banking and mediation; Ireland in corporate taxation; Qatar in media (Al Jazeera) and aviation; Singapore in finance and shipping; the Vatican in moral authority. The lesson: power in the international system is multi-dimensional, and states that play to their structural position outperform those that chase great-power symbols.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) State the central claim of realism in one sentence. (2) What is the security dilemma, and why is it harder than an arms race? (3) What did Thucydides mean by "the real cause" of the Peloponnesian War? (4) Name three international institutions and what problem each solves. (5) What does soft power rely on that hard power does not? (6) What is the "nuclear taboo," and why might AI and cyber be eroding it?
The learning progression

Brand new? Read the Melian Dialogue (Thucydides, Book V.84–116), then watch Graham Allison's TED talk and one LSE lecture by Mearsheimer. Write a one-page comparison of realist and liberal explanations of a current event. Once you've got the basics? Read Waltz's Theory of International Politics (chapters 5–6) and Keohane's After Hegemony (first two chapters). Follow Foreign Affairs for three months and notice which authors come from which tradition. To go further? Take a graduate IR seminar or read Jervis, Schelling, and Wendt back to back. For the current moment, read the weekly War on the Rocks essays and Tom Friedman with equal skepticism; notice the prose conventions.

dek: The study of what happens between states — and of why a world of many rulers has never quite settled down.
name: International Relations

body.text: In 1890 a Harvard professor named William James, then 48 and the brother of the novelist Henry, published a two-volume work called The Principles of Psychology. He had been writing it for twelve years; he hated it by the end; he warned his publisher that it was "a loathsome, distended, tumefied, bloated, dropsical mass." It is also one of the most readable books ever written in English about the mind, and it remains in print today. James opened the modern study of cognition by describing the obvious: that consciousness is a continuous stream, not a chain of discrete links; that attention is selective; that a habit is memory that has sunk below awareness; that emotion is, at least in part, the feeling of the body's response to a situation. He was trained as a physician; he thought of the mind as something that happens in a body.
Attention, the bottleneck

The central surprise of attention research is how little we see at once. Classic change-blindness demonstrations — Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris's "invisible gorilla" study is the famous example — show that an observer focused on one task (counting basketball passes between players in white shirts) will miss a person in a gorilla suit walking across the middle of the frame, stopping to thump its chest, and walking off. About half of observers fail to see the gorilla. Attention is a spotlight, and the darkness around it is larger than the lit circle. The practical consequence is that we do not see most of what is in front of us; we see what we have already decided is worth looking at.
Working memory's famous seven

In 1956 George Miller, then at Harvard, published a paper for the Psychological Review called "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information." He began by complaining that he had been persecuted by an integer for seven years — the same number kept appearing in absolute-judgment studies he had done and read about. His claim: the capacity of short-term memory is about seven items. Later work has revised the figure down — more like four, if you are careful about chunking — but the underlying claim has held up. The mind's scratchpad is surprisingly small. Most of what feels like thinking is the clever deployment of that small space: chunking letters into words, words into phrases, phrases into gists.
System 1 and System 2

Daniel Kahneman's 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow gathered thirty years of his work with Amos Tversky — Tversky died in 1996, and Kahneman won the Nobel in Economics in 2002 largely for their joint work — into a single accessible frame: the mind runs two systems, loosely. System 1 is fast, automatic, intuitive, usually right, and hard to turn off. System 2 is slow, effortful, analytic, and in principle capable of catching System 1 when it is wrong, though in practice it is lazy and expensive to run. Most of the famous cognitive biases — anchoring, availability, loss aversion, the conjunction fallacy — are described as System 1 defaults that System 2 fails to correct. Kahneman himself was careful to note that the two-system language is a deliberate fiction, a useful metaphor rather than a claim about neural architecture.
The replication decade

Psychology in the 2010s went through a careful public self-examination about which of its famous findings actually held up under replication. The Reproducibility Project: Psychology tried to reproduce 100 published findings and reported, in Science in 2015, that only about 36 percent replicated with full statistical significance. Kahneman-Tversky work on heuristics and biases largely survived. Ego depletion — the claim that willpower is a finite resource used up by earlier self-control — did not replicate. Social priming as originally reported has largely failed. Preregistration of hypotheses, open data, and registered reports are now standard at the better journals, and the field's evidentiary threshold has substantially risen. A serious student of cognition today reads the original papers alongside the published replications, and treats any single surprising finding with a measure of patience.
What cognition is for

The deeper question, still unsettled, is what cognition is built to do. One tradition treats the mind as a general-purpose computer that happens to run in wet hardware. Another — the evolutionary-psychology tradition that descends from Cosmides and Tooby in the 1990s — treats it as a bundle of relatively specialized problem solvers, each tuned by selection to handle a recurring ancestral problem (finding mates, avoiding predators, navigating kin relationships). A third, predictive-processing tradition, treats the brain as a prediction machine that generates a model of the world and updates it against incoming sensory error. These frames are not mutually exclusive, and the research that matters increasingly tries to put them in the same sentence.

body.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890)
body.text: Consciousness, then, does not appear to itself chopped up in bits... It is nothing jointed; it flows. A "river" or a "stream" are the metaphors by which it is most naturally described.

dek: Attention, memory, and thought — the software of the mind, studied with stopwatches and surprisingly clever experiments.
name: Cognition

body.text: In the 1920s a young Swiss biologist named Jean Piaget, working at Alfred Binet's intelligence-testing laboratory in Paris, noticed something more interesting than whether children got test questions right: the particular wrong answers they gave, at the particular ages they gave them. Four-year-olds, he found, had consistent confusions that seven-year-olds had moved past. Asked whether a tall thin glass held more water than a short wide one with the same volume poured into it, four-year-olds almost always said the tall one had more; seven-year-olds had learned to conserve. Development was not just accumulation of facts; it was a series of stages, each with its own logic, each built on the one before.
Piaget and his four stages

Piaget argued that cognitive development proceeds through four stages. Sensorimotor (birth to about two) — the infant learns about the world through action, and figures out that objects continue to exist when out of sight. Preoperational (two to seven) — symbols and language arrive, but logical manipulation of them is still shaky; conservation fails. Concrete operational (seven to eleven) — children can reason logically about physical objects but struggle with abstractions. Formal operational (eleven onward) — hypothetical and systematic reasoning, the kind that lets a teenager think about what would happen if gravity were reversed. Modern research has softened the stage boundaries and pushed several of the abilities Piaget dated as late down into infancy, but the basic framework still appears in most developmental-psychology textbooks.
Vygotsky, the social child

The Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky, writing in the 1920s and early 1930s and mostly ignored in the West until his work was translated in 1956 (he died of tuberculosis in 1934, at 37), argued that development is fundamentally social. Children learn by doing things with more skilled partners, not by exploring alone. The gap between what a child can do independently and what she can do with help is what he called the zone of proximal development. Teaching, on Vygotsky's view, is the careful scaffolding of help into that zone and the gradual withdrawal of it as competence consolidates. A child is first extra-mental — her thinking lives in dialogue with a more skilled other — and only later internalizes the dialogue as private thought.
What infants actually know

The last thirty years of infant research have pushed the field toward richer pictures of early cognition. Alison Gopnik at Berkeley and Elizabeth Spelke at Harvard, using looking-time and habituation methods — infants look longer at events that violate their expectations — have shown that babies as young as three or four months track objects as they pass behind screens, expect solid objects to remain solid, distinguish agents (things that move on their own) from objects, and make rough probability judgments about how unlikely a given event was. Gopnik and colleagues have argued that infants are, essentially, scientists — making models, running experiments, updating on evidence. The newborn is not a blank slate; she is a small researcher running experiments on the world with almost no hands.
Attachment, and what it does

Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation procedure, published in 1969, became the standard tool for classifying infant-caregiver attachment. A twelve-month-old is briefly separated from her mother and then reunited; her behavior in the reunion episode reveals a relatively stable style — secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-ambivalent, and (added later) disorganized. Attachment classifications at one year predict outcomes measurable decades later: peer relationships, academic engagement, romantic patterns. The mechanism is not fate; it is the way early experience with responsive or unresponsive caregiving shapes the child's working model of relationships. Much of the field's current policy work, through organizations like the Harvard Center on the Developing Child, turns on this fact.
Across the whole life

Erik Erikson's eight-stage model of psychosocial development, published in 1950 in Childhood and Society, extended the developmental question across a whole life — from the infant's trust-versus-mistrust through the elder's integrity-versus-despair, with a late-adolescent identity-versus-role-confusion in the middle that has become, for a good reason, the stage most every first-year psychology student remembers. Modern life-span psychology retains the spirit: late adolescence, early adulthood, midlife, and old age each have characteristic developmental tasks and characteristic ways to fall short of them. "Emerging adulthood," a stage added by Jeffrey Arnett in 2000, tries to capture the extended period in modern industrial societies between leaving adolescence and taking on full adult roles.

The Harvard Center on the Developing Child estimates that more than a million new neural connections are formed every second in the first few years of life. Early experience is not nostalgia; it is neurodevelopment.

dek: How a mind grows — from a newborn who cannot yet focus her eyes to an adult still adjusting to her own parents.
name: Developmental Psychology

body.text: In 1883 a German psychiatrist named Emil Kraepelin, then 27 and newly appointed to the University of Dorpat, published the first edition of a textbook that classified mental illnesses by the course they took over time. He argued that two large groups — what we now call schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (then dementia praecox and manic-depressive illness) — could be distinguished by whether they resolved or progressed. His method was patient: he kept detailed records of thousands of patients over decades and tracked their trajectories. Kraepelin's approach of careful long-term observation, rather than Freud's narrative interpretation — the two men worked at the same time and largely ignored each other — is the one modern clinical psychology has inherited.
The DSM, and why it keeps changing

The American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders — now in its fifth edition, revised in 2022, 991 pages long, describing about 300 disorders — is the field's operating system. It defines each disorder by symptom clusters, minimum duration, and functional impairment. The categories are practical rather than fundamental: they are useful for insurance coding, for clinical communication, and for research, but they are revised every decade or two and every revision is argued over vigorously. The DSM-III in 1980 threw out the psychoanalytic framework of earlier editions; the DSM-5 in 2013 added binge-eating disorder and merged Asperger's into autism spectrum; each change reshapes which patients get which label, and which diagnoses are reimbursable.
Evidence-based treatment

The cleanest results in clinical psychology come from cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for anxiety disorders and unipolar depression — its effect sizes in randomized trials are modest but consistent, and it works about as well as antidepressants for most cases of moderate depression, better in combination. Specific medications have real effects: SSRIs for depression and anxiety, mood stabilizers (lithium, valproate) for bipolar illness, second-generation antipsychotics for schizophrenia. Psychodynamic approaches retain a clinical tradition but a smaller evidence base, though brief psychodynamic therapy does have randomized trials supporting it for some indications. EMDR, exposure therapy, and interpersonal therapy each work for specific problems. The field's honest position is that we know some things work, we know some things do not, and we are still unsure about a good deal in the middle. Aaron Beck, who founded cognitive therapy in the 1960s after noticing that depressed patients had systematic thinking biases, lived to see CBT become the most empirically validated talk therapy in the world.
Memoir as evidence

Some of the clearest writing about mental illness comes from clinicians who have had it themselves. Kay Redfield Jamison, a psychologist at Johns Hopkins and one of the world's authorities on bipolar disorder, has written extensively about her own experience of the illness — including the lithium that eventually stabilized her. Elyn Saks, a law professor at USC, has written about her schizophrenia. These first-person accounts are not a substitute for clinical training or for the research literature, but they are a corrective to the textbook temptation to reduce a life to a category. A clinician who has read Jamison or Saks or Andrew Solomon's Noonday Demon alongside the DSM treats patients differently.
The scale problem

The global burden of mental disorder, measured in disability-adjusted life-years, is on the order of a trillion dollars a year. About one in eight people worldwide lives with some form of mental disorder. The supply of trained clinicians is a tiny fraction of what the need would imply — most low- and middle-income countries have fewer than one mental-health professional per hundred thousand people. Self-directed CBT workbooks, short-term group therapy, stepped-care models, and trained non-specialists work for milder presentations and scale better than traditional practice; they do not replace specialist care for severe illness, but they can extend reach dramatically. Every serious clinical-psychology program now includes training in how to triage, how to refer, and when to back away.

Nothing on this page is clinical advice. If you or someone you know is struggling, the place to start is a conversation with a qualified clinician. In the U.S., the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is reachable by call or text 24/7.

dek: The study and treatment of the disordered mind — a field with a long history of wrong answers and a short history of cautiously better ones.
name: Clinical Psychology

body.text: Social psychology as an experimental discipline was largely founded by Jewish émigrés from Germany in the 1930s — Kurt Lewin at Iowa and MIT, Solomon Asch at Swarthmore, Leon Festinger at Stanford. They came to the United States with a specific question, sharpened by what they had just watched happen in Europe: how do ordinary people come to do extraordinary things in groups? How does an unremarkable bureaucrat sign a deportation order? How does a neighbor inform on his neighbor? The field's most famous experiments and its most durable ideas both trace to that generation and that question. Asch's line-length study, Milgram's shock generator, Festinger's cult infiltration — they were, first of all, attempts to understand fascism.
The classic studies, handled with care

Asch's 1950s conformity experiments — subjects called an obviously shorter line "longer" when a group of confederates did — have replicated reliably and hold up under modern scrutiny. About a third of trials produced conformity to the wrong answer, and three-quarters of subjects conformed at least once. Festinger's cognitive-dissonance theory, the idea that inconsistency between belief and action is uncomfortable and motivates change, has held up in hundreds of studies across many paradigms. Stanley Milgram's 1960s obedience studies have a more complicated record: the headline finding — that about two-thirds of subjects continued to administer "shocks" to an unseen learner when urged to by an experimenter — replicates, but recent reanalyses of the archived audio recordings by Gina Perry and others have shown the experimenters pressing subjects much harder than Milgram's original reports acknowledged. Zimbardo's 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment, once a staple of introductory textbooks, has been substantially discredited as it was originally presented; archival tapes show Zimbardo and his team coaching guards to behave more harshly.
The replication decade

The 2010s were a public reckoning for social psychology. The Open Science Collaboration, a volunteer consortium of 270 researchers, in 2015 published a Science paper reporting they had tried to reproduce 100 prominent published findings and succeeded at about a third; effect sizes, on average, were about half of those originally reported. Social priming — the claim that subliminal cues (reading words about old age, holding a warm coffee) can dramatically change subsequent behavior — fared especially poorly. Ego depletion — the claim that willpower is a finite resource — failed to replicate in a large multi-lab study. Power posing did not reliably change hormones. Preregistration of hypotheses, open data, and registered reports are now standard at the better journals; the older literature is now read with an eye to which findings have been independently reproduced under modern methodological standards.
What has held up

The robust residue is still a substantial field. Kahneman-Tversky work on judgment under uncertainty. Bystander intervention research (with nuance — Latané and Darley's specific numbers and the Kitty Genovese back-story have been revised, but the core effect is real). The fundamental attribution error — our tendency to attribute others' behavior to character and our own to circumstance. Minimal-group effects, in which even arbitrary group assignments produce in-group favoritism. Self-affirmation effects on academic performance. Moral foundations research, though contested. The basic finding that context shapes behavior more than people expect, and that people underestimate that effect in themselves, has held up as one of the field's durable contributions.
Where the field is useful

Public-health messaging, voter turnout, tax compliance, energy conservation, hiring bias, classroom climate, organ donation rates — all turn out to be, in substantial part, problems about what the relevant reference group is doing and how people construe it. Making the "default" the behavior you want dramatically changes uptake. Letting people know that most of their neighbors conserve energy reduces their use; telling them they are above or below average has effects in both directions. The field has become quieter and more careful; it has also become more practically useful. Cass Sunstein and Richard Thaler's Nudge draws on this literature; so does a generation of applied behavioral-science work inside governments, from the UK Behavioural Insights Team to the White House's own Social and Behavioral Sciences Team.

The Stanford Prison Experiment (1971) is frequently cited as evidence that "ordinary people become brutal in a prison-guard role." Archival recordings released since have shown Zimbardo and his team actively coaching guards. Treat the study as a cautionary tale about research design rather than a finding about human nature.

dek: Why people in groups act oddly — and why some of the twentieth century's most famous experiments on that question have not replicated.
name: Social Psychology

body.text: In 1858 a long-shot Senate candidate named Abraham Lincoln stood up at the Illinois Republican convention and announced, in his second sentence, that "a house divided against itself cannot stand." His advisors had begged him to cut the line. He left it in. Fifteen minutes later he had built the rest of the speech around that single image, and the speech — and the image — went on to do most of the work of winning him the presidency. The structure of a memorable talk has not changed since: name the idea, build the supports, leave the listener something they can repeat by Tuesday.
One idea, named early

A talk is not a paper. The audience cannot reread paragraphs they missed; they cannot flip back to clarify a definition. They can hold one idea, with maybe three supporting points, and one resonant ending. Most bad talks fail at the first step — they have four ideas, or no idea, and the audience never quite locks on. Before you outline anything, write the central claim of the talk in one sentence. If you cannot, the talk is not ready.
The three-body shape

The classical structure inherited from rhetoric — exordium, narration, division, proof, refutation, peroration — collapses, for most modern talks, into a clean three-act shape: tell them what you are going to tell them, tell them, tell them what you told them. Inside that, the standard pattern is one idea, three supports, one closing image. Twenty minutes for the whole thing if it is a TED-style talk; forty-five if it is a lecture. Anything longer needs to be broken up with questions, exercises, or two clearly separate halves.
The opening you cannot wing

The first thirty seconds of a talk decide whether the audience leans in or starts checking their phones. The two openings that almost never work: a long throat-clear about how grateful you are to be there, and a definition. The two that almost always do: a concrete moment ("It is 1858, and a long-shot candidate is about to give the most reckless speech of his career") and a real question that the talk will answer. Whatever you choose, write it out word for word and rehearse it until it is muscle memory. The middle of the talk you can improvise; the open you cannot.
The close that lasts

The Heath brothers, in Made to Stick, argue that a memorable idea has six properties — simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, story. A good closing has at least four of them: a single sentence that names the central claim, dressed in a concrete image, ending on an emotional beat. "I have a dream" is the model. The summary close — "in conclusion, we have learned that…" — is its opposite, and is the surest way to leak energy in the last seconds you control.
The shortest possible test of a talk: tell a friend the one sentence the audience should leave with. If you cannot say it in one sentence, the audience will not be able to either.

dek: A talk that lands has a sturdy spine — one big idea, three or four supports, an opening that hooks, a close that sticks.
name: Talk Structure

body.text: In 1980 the rhetorician Albert Mehrabian's thirty-year-old research was misquoted into a slogan: communication is 7% words, 38% tone, 55% body language. Mehrabian himself spent the rest of his life correcting the misuse. The original finding applied only to the narrow case of inconsistent emotional messages. But like many half-remembered statistics, the slogan survives because it points at a real thing: when a speaker's words and body disagree, the audience believes the body.
The voice

A talk delivered in a monotone at a steady pace — the default mode of an inexperienced speaker — flattens into background noise within two minutes. The four levers that control this are pitch, pace, volume, and pause. The pause is by far the most underused. A two-second silence after a key sentence does more work than three more sentences explaining it. Pace varies by section, slowing at moments of weight and speeding up through narrative. Pitch should rise on a question and fall on a statement; up-talk — rising at the end of every sentence — drains authority faster than almost any other habit.
The body

Stand with your weight even on both feet, hands at your sides or visible above the waist. Move when you have a reason to: a step forward to emphasize a point, a step back to mark a transition. Do not rock; do not pace. Eye contact should land on individuals long enough to feel like a conversation — three or four seconds each — never sweep over the room like a sprinkler. In a large room, pick four or five faces in the four corners and the middle, and rotate among them. They will feel addressed; everyone around them will feel addressed too.
Nerves and what to do with them

The Harvard psychologist Alison Wood Brooks ran a series of experiments showing that people who reframed pre-talk anxiety as excitement — not "I am nervous," but "I am excited" — performed measurably better. The body produces the same chemicals for both states; only the label differs. The cardiovascular machinery of nerves is also useful information: the racing heart and the dry mouth are giving you energy. Use it. Speakers who work to feel calm before a talk often look flat. Speakers who work to feel ready often crackle.
Slides as a service to the talk

Slides should support the speaker, not replace the speaker. If your audience can read your slide, they will, and they will stop listening. Garr Reynolds and Edward Tufte have spent careers arguing for the same thing: large images, six words or fewer per slide, no bullet lists. The model is a cinema title card, not a textbook page. If you find yourself with twelve bullets and a small font, what you actually need is a handout, and your slides should be cut.
Record yourself once with the camera on. Watch it on mute. The number of nervous habits — fidgets, weight shifts, hand flutters — that disappear forever after a single watch is genuinely surprising.

dek: Pace, pause, eye contact — the body of the speaker is half the message, and almost none of it is the words.
name: Delivery
sections: Nerves and what to do with them
Slides as a service to the talk

body.text: On a hilltop in what is now the West Bank, sometime in the second millennium BCE, a man named Abram — later Abraham — is said to have heard a voice promising him land, descendants, and a covenant. Whatever the historical kernel, the story became foundational for three traditions: Judaism, which holds that the covenant is with the Jewish people; Christianity, which holds that it was extended through Jesus to all humanity; and Islam, which holds that Muhammad restored and completed the same original faith. Between them, these three traditions shape the lives of more than half the planet.
Shared inheritance

The three traditions share a story — monotheism, prophetic revelation, the patriarchs, a final judgment — and differ sharply on what happened along the way and what it means. All three revere Abraham. Jews and Christians share the Hebrew scriptures (which Christians call the Old Testament). Christians and Muslims both believe Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary, a miracle worker, and a messenger of God; they disagree on whether he was divine and whether he died on the cross. Muslims hold Jesus to be a prophet and Muhammad, in the seventh century, to be the seal of the prophets. The disagreements have been consequential. The overlap is still the deepest ecumenical ground available.
Judaism

Judaism is the oldest of the three, with roots in the Bronze Age and continuous religious practice for more than three thousand years. Its foundational text is the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh — Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim). Rabbinic Judaism, the form inherited by almost all modern Jewish communities, crystallized in the centuries after the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE, and its core texts are the Mishnah (c. 200 CE) and the Talmud (c. 500 CE), massive compilations of legal and ethical discussion. Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, and Reconstructionist movements all descend from nineteenth- and twentieth-century attempts to live rabbinic Judaism in modernity.
Christianity

Christianity began as a Jewish messianic movement in Roman Palestine in the first century CE and became, within three centuries, the official religion of the Roman Empire. Its central claim is that Jesus of Nazareth, crucified under Pontius Pilate around 30 CE, was the long-promised Messiah, the incarnate Son of God, and rose from the dead. The tradition split into Orthodox (the Eastern Roman Empire) and Catholic (Rome) in 1054, and Catholicism split again at the Reformation in 1517 into Catholic and Protestant branches. Contemporary Christianity, with about 2.4 billion adherents, is the largest religion in the world.
Islam

Islam began in 610 CE when, according to the tradition, the Prophet Muhammad received the first revelations of the Qur'an in a cave outside Mecca. The Qur'an is, for Muslims, the literal word of God in Arabic — an uncreated text that Muhammad memorized and dictated over twenty-three years. The core practices are the Five Pillars: the declaration of faith (shahada), prayer five times a day (salat), almsgiving (zakat), fasting during Ramadan (sawm), and the pilgrimage to Mecca once in a lifetime (hajj). The community split shortly after Muhammad's death into Sunni (about 85–90% of Muslims today) and Shia (most of the rest), over the question of rightful succession. Islam now has about 1.9 billion adherents.
Living together

The three traditions have rarely been at peace with each other and have occasionally lived remarkably well together. Medieval Islamic Spain — al-Andalus — produced three centuries of serious mutual scholarship: Maimonides wrote in Arabic, Averroes's commentaries on Aristotle reached Aquinas by way of Latin translators in Toledo. The founding documents of each tradition, read across, are more often complementary than opposed. A serious student of any one of them tends, over time, to read the other two.
Baha'i, Druze, and Samaritan communities also count as Abrahamic; each deserves its own study. The three-tradition summary above is a rough sketch, not a complete map.

dek: Three traditions — Judaism, Christianity, Islam — that trace their origin to a single covenant and now count more than half the world's believers.
name: Abrahamic Religions

body.text: In a forest ashram in northern India, sometime in the sixth century BCE, four teachers worked out the central vocabulary of Indian religion: dharma — the moral order and the duty each being has within it — and karma — the lawful consequence of action, binding beings across lifetimes. The elaborations of those ideas over the next twenty-five centuries produced four distinct religions — Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism — that share a family resemblance and count, together, around 1.3 billion adherents.
Hinduism as a family of traditions

Hinduism is the oldest of the four, with scriptural layers stretching from the Vedic hymns (c. 1500 BCE) through the philosophical Upanishads (c. 700 BCE) to the great epic poems the Mahabharata and the Ramayana (c. 200 BCE–200 CE). It is less a single religion than a family of traditions sharing a vocabulary: karma, dharma, moksha (liberation), the cycle of rebirth (samsara), and a pantheon that resolves, for most thoughtful Hindus, into the worship of Brahman — the ultimate reality — through one or another of its many faces. The Bhagavad Gita, an 18-chapter dialogue embedded in the Mahabharata, is probably the single most-read Hindu text worldwide.
The Buddha's analysis

Siddhartha Gautama — the Buddha — was born a prince in what is now Nepal around the sixth century BCE. His insight, after six years of ascetic practice, was that the root of suffering is craving and that craving can be unlearned. The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path are the shorthand. Buddhism split into Theravada (the "teaching of the elders," dominant in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia), Mahayana (the "great vehicle," dominant in East Asia, with its bodhisattva ideal), and Vajrayana (Tibetan, ritualized, deeply scholastic). Buddhism has about 500 million adherents today.
Jainism and the ethics of non-harm

Mahavira, a contemporary of the Buddha, taught a tradition even more rigorous in its asceticism and more radical in its non-violence (ahimsa) — extending the principle not just to humans and animals but, as far as possible, to every living being. Jain monks wear face masks so they do not inhale insects. The tradition is smaller today — around four to five million — but has had an influence far out of proportion to its numbers, including on Gandhi, who took ahimsa as the central principle of his political method.
Sikhism: the most recent synthesis

Guru Nanak, born in 1469 in the Punjab, founded Sikhism as a synthesis of Hindu bhakti devotion and Islamic monotheism. The tradition has ten human Gurus, culminating in Guru Gobind Singh, who at his death in 1708 declared that the scripture itself — the Guru Granth Sahib — would be the perpetual living Guru for the community. Its central teachings are the oneness of God, the equality of all human beings (Sikhism rejects caste), honest work, sharing with others, and constant meditation on the divine name. Around 25 to 30 million Sikhs live today, most in Punjab but now distributed worldwide.
The common grammar

The four traditions disagree on almost every metaphysical claim — whether the self exists, whether there is a creator God, whether liberation is personal or impersonal — and share a grammar that Western philosophy lacks. Karma is not divine reward but causal lawfulness. Dharma is not commandment but the right way of being, given what one is. Rebirth is not theological consolation but a technical premise about why practice matters. To read any of the four Indian traditions carefully is to learn a second way of talking about ethics and existence.

dek: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism — the great Indian religions, four paths through a single vocabulary of karma and liberation.
name: Dharmic Traditions

body.text: Before the Greeks called it philosophy, before the Chinese called it history, before the Hebrews called it law, every civilization we know of was telling stories: how the world came to be, why the stars move, where the dead go, how the first humans were shaped from clay or wood or maize. These stories are not bad science or early theology. They are a third thing — myths — doing work that no other kind of discourse does as well.
What myth is for

Myths do several things at once. They explain: why thunder happens, why women give birth in pain. They sanction: the king rules because of a covenant, the priest speaks because of an ancestor. They console: the dead are not gone, they are in the West, or in the sky, or waiting. And they teach: by giving the difficult emotions — rage, grief, love, temptation — figures large enough to carry them. A myth is, at its best, a compressed curriculum in how to be a person in a specific world.
Four traditions, quickly

Greek myth — the gods of Olympus, Heracles, Odysseus, Oedipus — was elaborated by Homer, Hesiod, and the Athenian tragedians, and preserved through Ovid's Latin retelling. Norse myth — Odin, Thor, Loki, Ragnarok — survives mainly in the thirteenth-century Icelandic Eddas of Snorri Sturluson, who wrote them down when the tradition was already fading. Mesopotamian myth — the Epic of Gilgamesh, the Enuma Elish creation epic — is the oldest we have textual access to, and is the direct ancestor of several biblical narratives (the flood, most notably). African, Indigenous American, Polynesian, and Aboriginal Australian mythologies — living traditions, not mere relics — are equally deep but less often translated into the languages in which this page is written.
Patterns without universality

Joseph Campbell's The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) argued that many myths share a single underlying structure — the hero's journey of departure, initiation, return. The idea inspired the screenplay of Star Wars and has been enormously productive commercially; it has also been criticized, fairly, for flattening genuine cultural differences. A more careful current view is that certain patterns (creation ex nihilo or from a cosmic egg; trickster figures; flood stories) recur often enough to be suggestive without being universal, and that the differences between traditions are usually more interesting than the similarities.
Reading myth well

A modern reader approaching myth has two traps. One is to treat the stories as charming nonsense — decorative, infantile, superseded. The other is to treat them as hidden truth — psychological archetypes, coded wisdom, a universal key. The more honest posture is closer to the one a literary reader takes toward Shakespeare: these stories were made to do real work for real people, they are still unusually efficient at doing it, and the most rewarding way to read them is slowly, in good translation, and on their own terms.
Myths are public dreams; dreams are private myths.

dek: The stories humans have told each other about gods, heroes, and the origins of everything — ancient, universal, and alive.
name: World Mythology

body.text: Strip away the software, and a robot is a machine for turning electrical signals into mechanical motion — and, in the other direction, for turning physical quantities (angles, distances, temperatures, images) into electrical signals. Every robot ever built, from the 1961 Unimate arm at a General Motors plant in New Jersey to a 2026 humanoid walking around a warehouse, is fundamentally a transducer sandwich with computation in the middle.
