body.alt: The Unimate industrial robot pouring coffee for a woman at the Biltmore Hotel, 1967.
body.caption: Unimate, pouring coffee at the Biltmore Hotel in 1967. The first industrial robot; six years old in this photo, and already being rented out for press events.

body.text: The short catalogue of common sensors

A working roboticist spends most of her time with a small set: encoders (how far has this motor turned), inertial measurement units (accelerations and angular rates in three axes), force-torque sensors (how hard is the tip pressing), ultrasonic and time-of-flight range finders (how far is that), cameras (a grid of photon counts), lidar (millions of ranges per second). Each measures one thing, imperfectly, in its own coordinate frame, at its own rate. The entire intellectual content of perception is about reconciling those measurements into something a controller can use.

The modern drop in cost has been dramatic. A 9-axis IMU that would have cost $2,000 in 2005 is $3 in 2026. A lidar that was $70,000 is under $500. A depth camera indistinguishable from a research-grade 2010 stereo rig is $150. Almost everything interesting a contemporary robot does would have been financially impossible fifteen years ago, independent of the algorithms.
Actuators: the world fights back

The other half of the sandwich is actuation. Brushless DC motors dominate — in drones, wheels, and quadrupedal legs — because they are efficient, controllable, and have become cheap. Stepper motors turn in fixed increments and are useful when you know exactly where you want to be (3D printers, CNC machines). Pneumatic and hydraulic actuators produce enormous forces per unit weight, at the cost of hoses, compressors, and mess — which is why industrial arms are largely electric now. Between an actuator and the world sits the gearbox, and most real-world robot failures live there.

body.caption: Computerphile on the sensor stack in self-driving cars — lidar, radar, cameras, and how their measurements are combined.

body.text: Sensor fusion and the Kalman filter

No sensor is trustworthy on its own. A GPS drifts, an IMU integrates error, a camera misidentifies, a lidar is noisy. Rudolf Kalman's 1960 paper on recursive filtering gave the field its first principled way to combine noisy measurements into a single best estimate, and the Kalman filter and its descendants — extended, unscented, particle — remain the backbone of every serious state estimator. If a modern robot is not falling down, it is because sensor fusion is quietly running, dozens of times a second.

The ROS (Robot Operating System) ecosystem is not strictly an operating system — it is a set of libraries and tools for publishing and subscribing to sensor and actuator messages. Since its 2007 release, it has become the lingua franca of academic and much of commercial robotics.
The mechanical and electrical are not optional

A recurring lesson, painful for software people: a robot that cannot move, cannot. The mechanical design, the electrical bus, the power budget, the EMI on the motor wires — any of these can make the most elegant code useless. The working roboticist has to know enough of each discipline to recognize whose problem an anomaly belongs to before the debugging session ends at dawn.

Rod Brooks — the MIT professor who founded iRobot and Rethink Robotics — has been saying for three decades that the hard problems in robotics are on the hardware side, not the software side. He has mostly been right, and nothing about modern AI has changed that. A learned policy that handles every lighting condition still cannot, on its own, make a gripper close at the right torque.
The 2020s sensor revolution

The combination of a new generation of low-cost lidars (solid-state, MEMS), dense depth cameras (Intel RealSense, Luxonis OAK), low-drift IMUs, and GPU-accelerated perception has changed what a serious hobbyist robot can do. Autonomous indoor mapping, once a research project, is a weekend kit in 2026. The gap between research and practice has narrowed. The interesting open problems have moved up the stack — into planning, manipulation, and the long tail of the physical world.

body.label: Moravec's paradox
body.text: Hans Moravec observed in 1988 that the easy problems for humans — reaching for a cup, climbing a stair, recognizing a friend — are the hard problems for robots. Forty years on, that paradox is intact: a machine can beat a grandmaster at Go and still cannot reliably load a dishwasher.

dek: The transducers that turn the world into numbers — and the motors that turn numbers back into motion.
name: Sensors & Actuators

body.text: In 1788, James Watt patented a centrifugal governor — a pair of weighted balls spinning on an axis that rose as the engine ran faster and closed a valve to let in less steam. It was the first machine that corrected itself: a physical implementation of negative feedback, a century before anyone had a theory of it. Every control system built since, from the thermostat on a wall to the flight computer on a drone to the stabilization code on a rocket, is a descendant of that pair of spinning balls.

body.alt: Boulton and Watt centrifugal governor, 1788.
body.caption: A Boulton and Watt governor from 1788 — the first widely-deployed feedback controller. The faster the engine turned, the higher the balls flew, the more the steam valve closed.

body.text: The error-correcting loop

A controller has a reference (the setpoint — a temperature, an angle, a velocity), a sensor reading (the actual value), and a control signal (what we send to the motor or valve). The core idea is to drive the error — reference minus actual — to zero, using feedback. Norbert Wiener, in Cybernetics (1948), gave the field its name and its place in intellectual history; Hendrik Bode and Harry Nyquist at Bell Labs had already worked out most of the mathematics for stable feedback amplifiers in the 1930s.
PID: the 1922 idea that will not die

The Russian-American engineer Nicolas Minorsky published the PID algorithm in 1922 while trying to steer US Navy ships automatically. Almost every controller you meet in industry is still PID. P: correct proportionally to the current error. I: correct for accumulated past error (to cancel drift). D: correct for the rate of change of error (to avoid overshoot). Tuning the three gains — by Ziegler–Nichols, by auto-tuning, or by hand — is the trade skill control engineers build in their first year. The Wikipedia article on PID is unusually good on the intuition.

body.caption: Steve Brunton, Control Bootcamp: Overview — the opening lecture of the best free control theory series on the internet.

body.text: State-space, linear, and nonlinear

Classical control assumes a single input and a single output. Modern control — developed around Kalman's work in the 1960s — treats a system as a vector of states evolving by linear differential equations. A lot of the real world is not linear, but linear theory carries you further than you would guess, because many systems look linear near the operating point you care about. Linear Quadratic Regulators (LQR) and Model Predictive Control (MPC) are the two tools a working roboticist is likeliest to reach for once PID stops being enough.

"When in doubt, use brute force — or a PID controller." — Ken Thompson (adapted). The joke is half true: most problems worth solving in industry are still solved with PID, and you will be a better engineer for knowing why.
Underactuation and the interesting half of the field

A walking biped has more degrees of freedom than motors; a quadcopter has four rotors controlling six dimensions of motion; a skater has a foot, not a wheel. These are underactuated systems, and the clever part of the subject is about controlling things that cannot be directly told what to do. Russ Tedrake's free MIT textbook, Underactuated Robotics, is the best modern treatment — and the reason most of Boston Dynamics' early engineering lineage traces back to his lab.

The aesthetic of the field is oddly musical. A well-tuned controller looks like a good jazz soloist: it does not fight the instrument, it does not over-commit, it corrects when the instrument corrects. Watch a high-quality quadcopter recover from a kick, or an Atlas humanoid catch itself after a stumble, and you are watching nonlinear control at a level that was a research frontier five years ago.
Control, meet learning

The most active frontier in 2026 is the marriage of classical control with reinforcement learning — training neural-network policies in simulation and transferring them to hardware. It works, dramatically, for tasks (quadruped locomotion, dexterous manipulation) where writing an analytical controller is brutal. It fails, also dramatically, when the simulator is not honest about what the real world will do. The working attitude: learn what you cannot easily derive; derive what you want to trust.

body.label: Sim-to-real
body.text: A whole subfield has grown up around making a policy trained in simulation work when transferred to a real robot. The techniques — domain randomization, system identification, online adaptation — are still art more than science. Boston Dynamics, ETH Zurich, and a dozen startups have spent the 2020s quietly solving sub-problems that, a decade ago, would have been whole PhD theses.
A practical path through the subject

For a working engineer in 2026: Steve Brunton's Control Bootcamp playlist on YouTube gets you intuition for classical and modern control, end to end, for free. Åström and Murray's Feedback Systems is the clean textbook companion. Tune a PID on a 3D-printer extruder, then on an inverted pendulum in simulation, then on a small quadruped. At each step you will learn more than a semester of lectures could teach. The subject rewards practice.
A controller that works on paper and not on hardware has, in the end, taught you only what is wrong with your paper.

dek: How to make a physical system do what you want, in the presence of noise, delay, and its own bad habits.

Why linear theory takes you far
A practical path through the subject

body.text: Roof shingles are one of the oldest ideas in construction: overlap small flat units from the bottom up so that water runs down the finished face and never reaches the substrate. Cedar shakes at Plimoth Plantation. Slate on the Pantheon. Clay tile on every nineteenth-century Italian villa. Asphalt on three-quarters of American roofs for the last hundred years. The material changes; the logic does not.

body.caption: An asphalt-shingled roof in course.

body.text: The whole idea

Water sheds by gravity. Overlap small flat units so every drop runs down the visible face and off the edge. Add underlayment beneath for the drops that inevitably get through. Flash every penetration and every plane change. The whole discipline of roofing is built on that four-sentence rule.
Before you start
Tools

A roofing hammer or pneumatic coil nailer. Roofing nails (galvanized, 1¼" for typical architectural shingles). A utility knife with hook blades. A chalk line. A flat bar. A tape measure. Harness and lanyard for fall protection. Soft-soled boots. Tear-off shovel (if stripping an old roof).
Safety

OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M requires fall protection above six feet, including on residential roofs. A proper anchor, harness, and lanyard are not optional — roofing is the most lethal trade per worker in American construction. More people die off ordinary two-story houses than off ten-story commercial buildings, because commercial crews take fall protection seriously.
Words to know

Pitch — roof slope, expressed as rise-over-run (6/12 means 6" of rise per 12" of run). Underlayment — the water-resistive layer under the shingles (felt paper or synthetic). Ice-and-water shield — a self-adhered rubberized membrane at eaves and valleys. Starter strip — the first course that the second course bonds to. Exposure — the visible part of each shingle (5⅝" typical for 3-tab). Ridge cap — the shingles at the peak. Drip edge — the L-shaped metal at the eaves.
Underlayment

The first layer over the sheathing. Traditionally 15 or 30-lb felt paper; modern practice is synthetic underlayment (lighter, stronger, less UV-sensitive). In the first three to six feet from the eaves — the ice-dam zone — a self-adhered ice-and-water shield is code-required in most cold climates. In valleys, a full-width ice-and-water shield runs the length of the valley, then the field underlayment laps over it.
Starter course

Before the first course of regular shingles, a starter strip runs along the eaves. You can buy purpose-made starter strips, or cut them from the top of 3-tab shingles (removing the tabs, leaving the bonding strip). The starter is installed with its adhesive strip along the bottom edge, so the first full course bonds to it. Without a starter strip, the first course has no bond and lifts in the first windstorm.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: Installing on a 40-foot eave: snap a chalk line 1/2" below the eave (so the starter overhangs into the gutter). Lay the first starter strip aligned with the gable end. Lay subsequent pieces end-to-end, overlapping by 1/4". Nail 1" above the adhesive strip. First course of architectural shingles then sits on top, offset by a half-tab.
Field courses

Each course starts at the gable end and runs across. Architectural shingles (laminated) require an offset of 6 inches per course; the manufacturer specifies the pattern on the package. Nails go in the designated nail zone (a strip indicated on the shingle itself, usually with a line or color band), four per shingle for most installs, six in high-wind zones. Nails below the line void the warranty; nails above the line fail to hold the shingle.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Overdriving the nails. The gun set too hot punches the nail through the shingle; the shingle then has nothing to hold it. Set the nail gun so the nail seats flush but does not sink below the shingle surface.
Hips and ridges

The peak of the roof and every hip get a ridge cap — specialized shingles (or cut-down 3-tabs) bent over the peak and installed from the far end of the ridge toward the prevailing wind. Each cap covers the nail of the one before it. On an open-hip or ridge-vent installation, the cap shingles are nailed to each side of the ridge-vent material, leaving a slot below for warm air to escape the attic.
Ventilation — the forgotten step

A roof without adequate ventilation fails prematurely — shingles cook from below, ice dams form in winter, and the attic becomes uninhabitable. Code requires a minimum 1:150 ratio of net free vent area to attic floor area, split roughly 50/50 between intake (soffit vents at the eaves) and exhaust (ridge vent at the peak). Adding insulation without improving venting is a common retrofit error.
Troubleshooting

Shingles lift in wind. Nails driven too high, or no starter strip. Granules in the gutter. Normal for the first few years (construction debris), problematic for older roofs (end of life). Leak at a valley. Valley underlayment laid incorrectly, or nails within 6" of the valley centerline. Leak at a penetration (vent pipe). Flashing failed; see the Flashing topic. Attic condensation. Inadequate ventilation; add soffit vents.
Going deeper

After basic asphalt, the next materials are standing-seam metal (crimped or snap-lock panels), slate (carpenter's craft with 80-to-400-year life), clay tile (fire resistance, thermal mass), and synthetic shingles (composites mimicking slate or cedar). NRCA's Steep-Slope Roof Systems Manual is the trade's own reference; Mike Guertin's "Roofing with Asphalt Shingles" is the working-roofer's book.

body.label: Practice this week
body.text: Install shingles on a dog house or small shed. All the operations of a full roof — underlayment, starter, courses, hips — at a scale that fits in the driveway. One hour, $20 in materials. You will know whether you enjoy the work before committing to an actual roof.

body.label: Self-check
body.text: What is the minimum roof pitch for standard asphalt shingles? (4/12.) What is the purpose of the starter strip? (Gives the first course something to bond to.) Why does ventilation matter? (Prevents ice dams, cools shingles from below, keeps attic dry.) If any stumps you, watch Essential Craftsman's roofing series.

First project: re-shingle a shed or outbuilding. Permit usually not required for outbuildings under 120 sq ft. Two afternoons. Under $100 in materials. Every technique from a full roof, at a safe scale.

dek: Asphalt, slate, metal, tile — the overlap, the course, and the weather above it.
name: Shingles

body.text: Almost every roof failure is a flashing failure. The field of shingles, if installed correctly, holds water out for thirty years; but at every chimney, every dormer, every vent pipe, every wall-to-roof junction, there is a seam the shingle cannot close on its own. Flashing is the thin metal — lead, copper, aluminum, stainless, sometimes rubber or self-adhered membrane — that bridges those seams and sends the water back onto the shingles where it belongs.

body.caption: Step flashing at a wall-to-roof junction.

body.text: The whole idea

Every flashing does the same thing: overlap the adjacent material in the direction of water flow, so water runs down the face of the flashing and onto the shingles below. If you can see at a glance which direction water travels across a detail, you know whether the flashing is right-side-up or upside-down. Almost every leak is flashing that was installed inverted.
Before you start
Tools

Tin snips. A hand brake or seamer for bending metal. A chalk line. Roofing nails and screws. A flat bar. Caulk gun with polyurethane or butyl sealant. Flashing material: aluminum is cheap and the residential default; copper outlasts the shingles (and costs five times as much); lead for complex chimney work; self-adhered membrane for belt-and-suspenders backup.
Safety
Fall protection, as always. Cuts from metal edges — gloves. Sheet-metal dust from cutting — safety glasses. Never drive fasteners where water will flow; every penetration is a potential leak.
Words to know

Step flashing — L-bent pieces stepped up a wall-to-roof junction, one per shingle course. Counterflashing — the piece that covers the top edge of the step flashing, often let into a masonry reglet. Valley flashing — wide metal or membrane running the length of a roof valley. Pipe boot — flashing for a vent pipe penetration. Kickout — the short flashing at the bottom of a wall-to-roof junction that directs water into the gutter. Cricket — a small roof built on the uphill side of a chimney to divert water around it. Reglet — the groove cut into masonry to receive counterflashing.
Step flashing

The canonical roof-to-wall junction. At every shingle course, a rectangular piece of metal — typically 5" x 7", bent along the long axis into an L — is laid so the horizontal leg goes under the shingle above and the vertical leg sits against the wall. The next course of shingles covers the bottom of the vertical leg. Counterflashing covers the top of the wall leg. The weatherproofing is the result of the two overlaps in the correct direction.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: Flashing where a roof meets a side wall: at each course of shingles, slide a step flashing under the shingle. The vertical leg extends 4" up the wall. The horizontal leg is 4-5" wide, covering most of the shingle's width. The next course of shingles covers the horizontal leg of the flashing below. Repeat up the wall. Finally, wall siding or counterflashing covers the vertical legs from above.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Using one long strip of flashing instead of step-by-step pieces. Water running down the wall then hits the single long piece and is diverted sideways at the wall-roof junction, often finding its way behind the siding. Step flashing, one piece per course, is the only way that works.
Valleys — open or closed

Open valley: a wide strip of metal (aluminum, copper, or 24-gauge galvanized) runs the length of the valley, exposed; shingles on both sides are trimmed back to show a 4-6 inch strip of metal in the valley center. Closed valley: shingles are interwoven across the valley or laid through it; the valley is underlaid with ice-and-water shield or metal but not visible. Open valleys shed water faster and last longer; closed valleys are cheaper and more common. Both work if underlayment is correct.
Chimneys — the hardest flashing

A chimney has four sides, each needing a different flashing. Front (downslope): a one-piece apron flashing covers the intersection and extends up the chimney 4-6". Sides: step flashing, one per shingle course, with counterflashing cut into the mortar joint. Back (upslope): a saddle or cricket — a small roof that splits water around the chimney, flashed to the main roof. Every flashing is overlapped by the next higher one; every counterflashing covers the top of the next lower flashing. A mis-flashed chimney is the most common serious roof leak.
Penetrations

Plumbing vents, chimneys, bath fans, skylights — each requires a flashing designed for that penetration. A typical plumbing vent gets a pipe boot: a flange with a rubber collar sized to the pipe. The flange sits under the shingles upslope of the pipe and over the shingles downslope. Skylights come with manufacturer-supplied flashing kits; use them.
Kickout flashings

Where a sloped roof meets a wall at an angle — e.g., where a roof runs past the corner of a house — the water flowing down the wall/roof junction must be diverted into the gutter. A kickout flashing is a small bent piece at the bottom of the run that catches water and redirects it out. Skip the kickout and water runs behind the siding; the sheathing rots within five years. Matt Risinger has built his reputation on harping about this one detail.
Troubleshooting

Leak appears near a chimney. Flashing at the back (upslope) is missing the saddle. Install a cricket. Water stain on drywall ten feet from the roof edge. Wicking — could be coming from far upstream. Inspect all flashings on the path from roof to stain. Gutters overflow at one point only. Kickout flashing missing. Leak at a pipe penetration. Pipe boot collar cracked from UV; replace.
Going deeper

After basic residential flashing, the next territories are architectural metal (custom copper detailing on high-end residential), low-slope membrane terminations (TPO, EPDM), historic restoration (lead flashing on copper, or copper over slate), and commercial roof details. NRCA's Architectural Metal Flashing Manual is the trade's reference; the FGI Field Guide is the installer's pocket version.

body.label: Practice this week
body.text: Bend a piece of flashing by hand on a bench vise and a block of wood. Make a simple step flashing (5" x 7", bent on the long axis at 90°). Do ten. You will learn to read sheet metal: which way it wants to go, how much force to apply, how to correct a bent piece without kinking it.

body.label: Self-check
body.text: Which way does step flashing overlap? (Each upper piece overlaps the one below, shingle-fashion.) What is a kickout flashing for? (To direct water from a roof-wall junction into the gutter.) Why install a cricket on the upslope side of a chimney? (To split water flow around the chimney.) If any stumps you, watch Matt Risinger's kickout-flashing video.

First project: install a pipe-boot flashing around a plumbing vent stack on a small shed. Cut the shingles away, slip the boot under the upslope shingle, lap the next course over the flange, seal with a small bead of roof cement. Thirty minutes. You will understand how every penetration is flashed.

dek: Where two planes meet, water tries to get in — and flashing is how the roofer says no.
name: Flashing

body.text: In 2011, an American ultrarunner named Scott Jurek finished a 46-mile traverse of Madeira in six hours and change. An exercise physiologist at a research lab clocked him at a cadence of 185 steps per minute across the run, barely drifting, mile after mile on broken terrain. The cadence was no accident. Jurek had reshaped his stride through years of deliberate work. His form was not beautiful for its own sake. It was economical — every foot landing did less damage, every stride wasted less energy, and that compound savings was what let him cover fifty miles and wake up the next morning able to do it again. Form is not about looking like a runner. It is about being one for a long time.
The quiet premise of running form

Humans are endurance runners. The hunting-gathering ancestors of modern humans evolved the long-distance-running body — the sprung arches, the long Achilles tendons, the sweat glands that outperform any other mammal at shedding heat. The form of an efficient runner, in any culture, is broadly the same. Upright posture, relaxed shoulders, arms swinging from the shoulder joint, short ground contact, high cadence, mid-foot or fore-foot landing under the center of mass. Bad form — overstriding, heel-slamming, collapsed posture, stiff arms — costs the body every stride. A decade of it produces knee problems, plantar fasciitis, and a runner who has quit running by forty. Good form, thirty thousand foot strikes at a time, compounds the other way.
Cadence, the one number that matters

If you change one thing about your running, change cadence. Elite distance runners turn over around 180 to 190 steps per minute across almost any pace. Beginners typically run around 150 to 170. A low cadence forces a longer stride, which forces the foot to land in front of the body, which produces a braking force every step that stresses the knees and hips. Raising cadence by five to ten percent — often as simple as running to a metronome or a playlist at 175 bpm — shortens the stride automatically, moves the landing under the body, and reduces impact forces by a measurable percentage per step. It is the single highest-return adjustment a runner can make.
Foot landing and the shoe debate

The heel-versus-forefoot-landing debate of the 2000s is largely settled. The answer is: it depends. The foot should land under the hip, not far in front of it, and the body's weight should pass quickly over the foot without lingering. Which part of the foot first touches the ground matters less than where the foot is when it touches. At race pace most fast runners land on the mid-foot or forefoot because it is biomechanically efficient at speed. At slow recovery pace many elites heel-strike, because overstriding is less dangerous when the forces are low. The "barefoot running" movement of the 2010s turned out to be partly right and partly oversold; shoes matter, but running form matters more.
Posture, and the single word "tall"

The single most useful form cue any coach gives is "run tall." Imagine a string pulling up from the crown of the head; feel the rib cage stack over the pelvis; let the arms hang from relaxed shoulders. A runner who runs tall has their center of gravity where it belongs and their whole body aligned for efficient propulsion. A runner who hunches, collapsing the chest and tucking the pelvis, is running against their own skeleton. Running tall is not about chest-puffing or military posture. It is about allowing the spine to stack without slumping. One cue. Repeated every mile. Changes a career.
How form is actually changed

Form drills — A-skips, B-skips, high knees, butt kicks, strides — exaggerate the movements of good running and let the body learn them in isolation. Two or three times a week, a set of four drills for fifteen minutes, for a few months, rewires the running stride more reliably than any amount of "try to run better" self-talk. Jay Johnson's runners do them. Shalane Flanagan's runners do them. They do not look glamorous in the park. They work. The other reliable form-builder is strides — four to six relaxed twenty-second sprints at the end of an easy run, once or twice a week, focusing on posture and cadence. Runners who do strides consistently look and feel different within a month.

First month: run four days a week. Two miles the first two weeks, three miles the second two. Use a metronome app set to 175 bpm and try to land with the beat. At the end of every easy run, do four twenty-second strides on a flat stretch of grass, focusing on running tall. No speed work. No hills. Go easy enough that you could hold a conversation the whole way. After thirty days, the body has the foundation it needs to start actually training.

dek: Posture, cadence, landing — the small mechanical habits that let a body run for a lifetime without breaking.
name: Form
sections: The quiet premise of running form
Cadence, the one number that matters

body.text: Arthur Lydiard, a New Zealand milk-truck driver who coached himself to a 2:54 marathon and then took a generation of Kiwi runners to Olympic medals in the 1960s, preached one idea: most running should be easy, and only a small fraction should be hard. A half-century later the idea has been confirmed in exercise physiology labs, rebadged as "polarized training," and adopted by nearly every serious distance runner. Eighty percent of Eliud Kipchoge's mileage is easy. Eighty percent of the mileage of every top marathoner is easy. A runner who trains hard all the time does not improve faster. They just break down faster.
The simple idea behind every plan

A running plan is a schedule of runs that progresses mileage, introduces quality gradually, and arrives at a goal race in peak form. The underlying logic is simple. Easy aerobic running builds the cardiovascular base that lets the body use oxygen efficiently and clears out fatigue. Harder workouts — tempo runs, intervals — improve the body's ability to run at higher effort without blowing up. Long runs build the specific durability to hold pace for race distance. A plan combines all three in the right proportions. A bad plan does too much quality, not enough base, or too little recovery. Almost every running injury of a healthy person comes from one of those three errors.
The three kinds of run

Easy runs should be slow. The cardiovascular system adapts best to long, low-intensity stress, and easy runs should actually feel easy — a conversational pace where a full sentence can be spoken without gasping. Tempo runs, sometimes called threshold runs, are sustained efforts at "comfortably hard" pace — about what you could hold for an hour of racing — usually twenty to forty minutes after a warmup. They train the lactate-threshold system. Interval workouts alternate hard efforts with recovery — 6×800m at 5K pace with 400m jog, for instance — and train the VO2max and neuromuscular systems. Most plans use all three, in something like a 4:1 ratio of easy to hard mileage.
Mileage builds slowly

The ten-percent rule — increase weekly mileage by no more than ten percent per week — is approximate and widely cited. A more careful approach is to build for three weeks and recover for one, repeating the cycle. Twenty miles a week becomes 22 becomes 24 becomes 20 (cutback) becomes 26 becomes 28 and so on. This block-and-cutback pattern lets the body adapt without the cumulative stress that causes running injuries. A runner who tries to double mileage in two months will fracture a foot. A runner who builds patiently over a year will arrive at race day fit, intact, and under-trained enough to still have something to give.
The taper

The final two or three weeks before a goal race are the taper — mileage drops by thirty to fifty percent while the intensity of key workouts is preserved. The body needs time to absorb the training. A runner who does full mileage the week before a marathon runs the race exhausted; a runner who tapers arrives rested, rebuilt, and carrying the full fitness the training produced. Tapers feel strange — the runner usually feels sluggish, anxious, and convinced they are losing fitness. They are not. Trust the taper. The race proves it.
Race day

Start too slow. The most common race-day mistake is going out at an adrenaline-fueled pace the body cannot sustain. A 5K runs ten to twenty seconds per mile slower in the first mile than the second. A marathon runs thirty seconds per mile slower in the first three miles than the second three. A runner who follows this rule and keeps their first miles unambitious will be passing people for the last half of every race they ever run. A runner who goes out hard will get passed for the last half of every race they ever run. The pattern is so reliable it reads like a law of nature. It is, in practice, a law of racing.

First plan: Hal Higdon Novice 1 or the NHS Couch-to-5K. Twelve to twenty weeks. Three to four runs a week. One long run on Saturday. One "quality" session midweek if you are ready. No heroics. Finish the plan. Run the race. Repeat, at the next distance up, six months later.
Train slow to race fast.

dek: Easy, tempo, long — three kinds of run in varying proportions over a careful buildup.
name: Training Plans
sections: The simple idea behind every plan

body.text: The Phoenicians sailed the Mediterranean three thousand years ago in vessels that could only go where the wind pushed them. The lateen sail of the medieval Arab dhow, and the fore-and-aft rigs that came after it in northern Europe, transformed the relationship between wind and water — for the first time a boat could sail across the wind, and even, by zigzagging, against it. Every modern sailor learning to read the wind around their boat is learning the geometry that took two thousand years to discover.
The wind's clock

A modern sailor names the boat's direction not by compass, but by the angle between the boat's heading and the wind. Imagine the wind as the twelve o'clock position on a clock; the points of sail are the angles the boat can sit relative to it. Close-hauled is sailing as close to the wind as the boat will go — about 45 degrees off, on either side. Beam reach is sailing perpendicular to the wind. Broad reach is sailing well off the wind. Run is sailing directly downwind. Each point requires a different set and trim of the sails, and each carries the boat through the water in a different way.
The no-go zone

The wedge of about 90 degrees — 45 degrees on either side of dead upwind — is the no-go zone, the directions a typical sailboat cannot sail. To get to a point upwind of where you are, you must zigzag — sail close-hauled on one side of the wind, then come about and sail close-hauled on the other. The journey is a series of long diagonals, each called a tack. Total distance sailed is greater than the rhumb line, but the boat does, eventually, reach upwind. Modern racing boats can hold tighter angles; modest cruisers cannot do better than about 45 degrees.
Reaches and runs

A beam reach — wind across the side of the boat — is the fastest and easiest point of sail for most modern sloops and the one most sailors prefer. The boat heels to leeward, the sails are eased to about 45 degrees off the centerline, and the apparent wind feels strong. A broad reach is faster still in moderate winds. A run, dead downwind, sounds easy but is the most dangerous point — the boom can swing across without warning (an accidental jibe) hard enough to break the rig or knock a crewmember overboard. Most experienced sailors broad-reach in zigzags downwind rather than run square.
The forces, briefly

A sail upwind works like an aircraft wing held vertical: the curved leeward surface accelerates the air across it, creating lower pressure that pulls the boat forward. The keel below resists sideways motion, converting the pull into forward speed. Downwind, the sail is acting more like a parachute, simply caught by the wind. The fact that a sailboat can sail toward the wind that is pushing it baffled mariners for two thousand years and was understood properly only with the development of fluid dynamics in the early twentieth century.

Tell a beginner sailor "the wind is your dance partner, not your enemy" and they think you are speaking poetically. After a few seasons they realize you were being literal — every adjustment is a response to what the wind has just done.

dek: Where the wind comes from, relative to the boat, names every direction a sailboat can go — and decides what the sailor must do.
name: Points of Sail

body.text: When the boat changes direction so that the wind, which had been blowing from one side, now blows from the other, the maneuver has a name. Through the wind it is a tack; away from the wind, downwind, it is a jibe. The first is gentle and forgiving; the second can be violent and dangerous if mishandled. Knowing the difference, and the small choreography that goes with each, is the moment a passenger becomes a crew.
Tacking through the wind

When close-hauled, the bow is pointed about 45 degrees off the wind. To tack, the helm is pushed down (the tiller toward the sail) so the bow swings up through the eye of the wind and falls off on the other side. The sails luff briefly as the bow crosses dead upwind, then fill on the new side as the boat completes the turn. The crew releases the windward jib sheet as it crosses, and pulls in the new leeward sheet hand over hand. A clean tack takes a few seconds; a sloppy one stalls the boat in irons, the bow stuck head to wind, requiring a bit of reverse-rudder to recover.
Jibing — the careful one

A jibe is the same maneuver but downwind: the stern crosses the wind instead of the bow. The catch is that on a run the boom is far out over the leeward rail, and during the maneuver it must swing across the boat — across the heads of any inattentive crew — and then snap into position on the other side. An uncontrolled jibe in any wind worth sailing in can break the boom, tear the sail, snap a stay, or knock a crew member overboard. The controlled version: ease the mainsheet, rotate the boat so the wind comes from a beam, watch the boom carefully as it crosses, and ease the new sheet out smoothly.
The choreography of the cockpit

A boat sailed by two or more people works best when each crew member knows in advance who does what during a maneuver. The standard call: the helmsman announces "ready about" (the crew prepares the new sheet, the off-side crew unwinds the active sheet); the crew responds "ready" when set; the helmsman calls "helm's a-lee" or "tacking" and turns. A jibe gets its own warning — "stand by to jibe" — because a head meeting an unannounced boom can end a season. Practiced, the maneuver is one of the more elegant pieces of choreography in any sport.
Beating to windward

Sailing toward an upwind destination requires repeated tacks — long zigzags called beats. The strategy is part geometry (the longer leg first, ideally), part tactics (use shifts in wind direction to gain ground), and part respect for tide and current, which can erase or amplify each tack's gain. A good beat is the most satisfying point of sail to do well. A poor one can keep a boat working hard for an afternoon and end up with no progress made. The competitive racer's sense of the wind — knowing twenty seconds before the cruising sailor that a header is coming — is a skill built only by hours on the water.
In all but light air, sailors call out "boom!" before a jibe. Crew duck. The boom does not. The single most common cause of head injury on small sailboats is an unexpected jibe.

dek: Two ways of changing tack — through the wind, or away from it — with very different consequences if you get them wrong.
name: Tacking & Jibing

body.text: The computer password was invented by Fernando Corbató at MIT in 1961, when he split the shared IBM 7094 into private user accounts on what became the Compatible Time-Sharing System. The following year, a grad student named Allan Scherr printed the password file and used other people's time-shares to exceed his quota. The first password breach happened within months of the first password. Sixty-five years later, the particulars change and the basic lesson does not.

body.alt: An Enigma machine on display.
body.caption: Before passwords there were passphrases, code books, and cipher machines. The Enigma, above, was broken in 1940. A modern password defeated by the same kind of effort would be broken in seconds.

body.text: Length and entropy, not asterisks

For a long time, websites demanded mixed cases, numbers, and symbols — rules that pushed everyone to write P@ssw0rd1 on a sticky note. NIST dropped those rules from its 2017 Digital Identity Guidelines and most serious security teams have followed. The current guidance is simpler: favor length over composition, ban known-breached passwords, and never force arbitrary rotation. A long passphrase of common words, chosen randomly, is harder to crack than a nine-character mix of gibberish and far easier to type. The XKCD strip about correct-horse-battery-staple was right; NIST eventually agreed.

Underneath, the measure is entropy — roughly, the log of the number of possible passwords you could have chosen. A ten-character password chosen from printable ASCII has about 66 bits of entropy; a four-word passphrase from a 7,776-word dictionary has about 51. The second is slightly weaker mathematically but enormously harder to mistype, remember, or lock yourself out of. The UX wins.
The three factors, and why two is the floor

Authentication uses some mixture of three things: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone, a hardware key), and something you are (a fingerprint, a face). Any one of them, used alone, is a single point of failure. Two-factor authentication — a password plus a second factor — is the largest reduction in practical risk most users can make in an evening. Among the second factors, a FIDO2 hardware key (YubiKey, Titan) is the strongest; a phone authenticator app is a clear second; SMS codes are a distant third, because phone numbers can be stolen through SIM-swap attacks that are now routine.

body.caption: Mike Pound, "How NOT to Store Passwords!" on Computerphile — plaintext, hashing, salting, bcrypt.

body.text: Password managers, the boring answer that works

No one can remember a unique random twenty-character password for every site. The only honest answer is a password manager. A good manager generates long random passwords, fills them in automatically, and syncs across devices behind one strong master passphrase (and, ideally, a hardware-key second factor). The tradeoff — a single vault that is catastrophic if breached — is a good one for almost everyone, because the alternative is reuse and reuse is how most real compromises start.

The LastPass breach of 2022 — in which an attacker eventually got copies of customers' encrypted vaults — is the canonical cautionary tale. The important takeaway is not that managers are unsafe (the vaults whose masters were strong have held up; the vaults whose masters were weak have been cracked) but that your master passphrase deserves the same care as a cryptographic key. Twenty characters, random, and a hardware-key second factor.
The best password in the world is still catastrophic if you reuse it and one of the sites where you used it gets breached. A password manager turns reuse from a temptation into an inconvenience.
Passkeys, the grown-up replacement

The next step is not a better password; it is no password. Passkeys, standardized by the FIDO Alliance and built on the WebAuthn protocol, replace a shared secret with a public-private key pair stored on your device. The server never sees anything that can be stolen and replayed. Apple, Google, and Microsoft have shipped passkey support across their operating systems through 2023–2025, and major sites are rolling out support. The transition will take years, but for new accounts in 2026 a passkey is the right default.

The experience of using a passkey, once you are over the unfamiliarity, is much better than a password. You touch a fingerprint sensor or Face-ID; the operating system finds the right key; you are in. There is no sharing, no typing, no breach exposure. The only serious hesitation — what happens if you lose all your devices at once — is answered by the cloud-sync providers (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password) offering passkey recovery. The UX has finally grown up.

body.label: The math behind a passkey
body.text: A passkey is a public-key keypair. When you register with a site, your device generates a new private key and sends only the public key to the server. When you log in, the server sends a challenge; your device signs it with the private key; the server verifies the signature with the public key it already has. Nothing shared, nothing reusable, nothing phishable. The same cryptography behind TLS now protects your login.
What to do this weekend

Install a password manager. Let it generate a strong passphrase for your email. Use the manager to generate long random passwords for the ten accounts you use most. Turn on two-factor authentication on your email, bank, and any account that holds real money — hardware key if possible, authenticator app if not. Check Have I Been Pwned for addresses you use. If any account offers a passkey, set one up. You will have reduced your risk by more than any other forty-minute task in computing will.

dek: The oldest authentication mechanism in computing — and the one most often done badly.
name: Passwords & 2FA
sections: Password managers, the boring answer that works

body.text: Every year, Verizon publishes a Data Breach Investigations Report — the most widely-cited empirical survey of how real organizations actually get compromised. The 2025 edition, like every edition before it, puts the same two culprits at the top of the list: humans tricked into giving up credentials, and long-unpatched software. The spectacular zero-day exploits in the press are a small share of the total. The mundane categories are where the damage lives.
Attackers are patient, not magical

The mental image of hacking is a hooded person typing quickly. The real pattern is far less dramatic: reconnaissance, phishing, a foothold on one laptop, lateral movement, escalation, and eventually ransomware or data theft. Lockheed Martin called this the "kill chain" in 2011, and the MITRE ATT&CK framework has since catalogued every documented step at every stage. Reading ATT&CK is the closest thing a new practitioner has to an encyclopedia of what is actually being done.
Phishing is a design problem

Most breaches still begin with an email. A message arrives that looks like the right sender, with a link that looks like the right domain, leading to a page that looks like the right login. The user types their password. Defences are layered: DMARC on the mail server, URL rewriting at the gateway, a second factor at the login, user training for the gap. Hardware-key second factors are the only countermeasure that meaningfully defeats a well-crafted phishing site, because the key signs only the real domain and refuses the lookalike.

body.caption: IBM Technology on modern phishing — spear, whaling, smishing, quishing.

body.text: Malware, and the economy behind it

Modern malware is not a lone teenager's project. Ransomware-as-a-service lets criminal affiliates rent the tooling and take a cut of the payout; initial-access brokers sell footholds; cryptocurrency makes the final payment plausible. Kim Zetter's Countdown to Zero Day (2014) remains the best long-form account of the escalation — the Stuxnet attack on Iran's centrifuges marked the moment nation-state malware became public knowledge. The lesson for a working developer is not to write antivirus code, but to assume the host is compromised and design accordingly.
Ransomware as a business

From roughly 2017 onward, ransomware has been the single most impactful category of cybercrime by dollar volume. Colonial Pipeline in 2021 shut down the US eastern seaboard's gasoline supply for days. The UK NHS WannaCry outbreak in 2017 postponed surgeries. Chainalysis estimates global ransomware payments topped $1 billion in 2024. The crime works because the payoff is large, the risk of prosecution is small (the operators are typically in jurisdictions that will not extradite), and most victims have not tested their backups recently enough to know if they can refuse.

The defensive lessons are old and dull: maintained offline backups, tested restores, least-privilege network segmentation, endpoint monitoring, a retainer with a DFIR firm before you need one. None of them scale the way everyone wishes they did. All of them work.
A 2025 rule of thumb: if your system relies on users noticing a suspicious email, you have a system that will fail. Build as if a motivated attacker has already reached the login page.
Threat modeling is the habit that catches the rest

The most durable security skill is the question: what are we protecting, from whom, under what assumptions? Adam Shostack's four questions — what are we working on, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, did we do a good job — organize a practice that does not need a specialist. Threat models are cheapest at the whiteboard stage of a design and most expensive at the post-mortem stage of an incident. Make them a habit at the first.

body.label: STRIDE
body.text: Microsoft's STRIDE framework — spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege — is the oldest and still most-used threat-model taxonomy. Walk through each of the six for any new feature. Most of the real threats will show up in one of the first three.
What actually works

The security controls that pay off disproportionately: hardware-key 2FA on every identity, a password manager, automatic operating-system updates, browser-based isolation for high-risk work, backups you have actually restored once, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework as a scaffolding for the first year of any serious program. Everything else — the acronyms, the vendors, the annual RSA keynotes — is a detail. Most organizations that get compromised do so because they skipped one of the first three.

dek: The short list of attacks that account for most of what actually goes wrong — and the threat-modeling habit that catches them.
name: Common Threats

body.text: Every small engine at the back of a garage — the chainsaw, the weed trimmer, the Briggs & Stratton in the old rotary mower — has, at its heart, a carburetor the size of a small orange, held together with four screws and a gasket. It is the last place in modern small-engine work where the problem is almost always mechanical and almost always fixable by hand. Fuel injection has crept into larger lawn tractors and the occasional snowblower, but the carburetor is still how most of these engines meet their fuel, and it is still the first place a small-engine mechanic looks when the machine will not start.
A plain idea, elegantly solved

A carburetor uses the Bernoulli principle. Air rushes through a narrow throat; the pressure in the throat drops; fuel, held at atmospheric pressure in a small bowl below, is pushed up through a calibrated jet into the airstream, atomizing as it goes. The result is a combustible mist that the engine sucks into the cylinder. The whole device is passive — no electronics, no sensors, no electricity. Lay one on a bench next to a 2026 fuel injector and it looks ancient. It works anyway.
Anatomy of a simple carburetor

The float bowl at the bottom holds a small reservoir of fuel, kept at a constant level by a pivoting float and a needle valve — the same principle as the toilet tank. A main jet, a small brass fitting with a calibrated hole, meters fuel into the throat at running speed. A pilot jet handles idle. A throttle plate above regulates airflow; a choke plate above that enriches the mixture for cold starts. Most small-engine carburetors add a small accelerator pump to squirt extra fuel when the throttle opens suddenly, because the airflow moves faster than the fuel can follow. Ten or twelve parts total. Any working mechanic can have one apart in five minutes.
Why it fails, always in winter

Carburetors die from varnish. Modern gasoline, especially the ethanol-blended kind sold in most American pumps, begins to evaporate and gum within about thirty days in a fuel tank. By spring, every small passage in the carburetor is partly or fully blocked by brown varnish that looks like old maple syrup. The engine cranks and coughs and will not quite start. The mechanic pulls the bowl, soaks the metal body in a can of carb cleaner overnight, and runs a fine wire through each jet. Nine out of ten won't-start calls on a spring Saturday end with a clean carburetor and fresh fuel.
Rebuild, clean, or replace

A carburetor rebuild kit — gaskets, seals, a fresh needle-and-seat, sometimes a new float — costs ten dollars. A complete replacement carburetor, often Chinese-made, costs twenty. There is a live debate among small-engine technicians about when to rebuild and when to replace; purists insist that the original metal body is always better, pragmatists point out that a cheap replacement lasts eight years in normal homeowner use. Most working shops do a bit of both. Either way, the ritual is the same: drain the old fuel, pull the carburetor, clean or replace, reinstall with fresh fuel stabilized for winter, and watch the machine come back to life.
Two-stroke carburetors are different

The chainsaw's carburetor is a Walbro or a Zama — a diaphragm carburetor, not a float bowl. Because a chainsaw is used at any angle, including upside down, it cannot rely on gravity holding fuel in a bowl. Instead, pulses of crankcase pressure from the engine's two-stroke cycle work a flexible diaphragm that pumps fuel through a metering lever. Mixture is set by two brass screws labelled "L" for low speed and "H" for high speed, adjusted by a splined tool that the homeowner never owns. A well-tuned Stihl saw runs like a sewing machine. A badly tuned one seizes on the first hot day.

The tool that defines the trade is the Stihl carburetor adjustment tool — a tiny splined screwdriver, the size of a matchstick, that fits the mixture screws on sealed small-engine carburetors. Without it you cannot tune a chainsaw. With it, any two-stroke can be set to run right in about a minute.
How to think about it

A carburetor is a perfume atomizer that happens to feed an engine. The same Bernoulli principle that draws perfume into moving air draws fuel into the intake charge. The cleverness of the design is in the calibration — different jets, different throats, different accelerator systems — each tuned to a specific engine's demand. But the underlying physics is simple enough to grasp in a minute, which is why a carburetor rarely baffles a curious owner for long. Fuel injection is more accurate, more adaptive, and more efficient. The carburetor is more honest: a narrow throat, a calibrated hole, and moving air. That is the whole story.
Work through one

A rotary mower will not start in April after sitting all winter. The technician's workflow: drain the tank into a jar — brown varnished fuel smells like shellac, confirming old gas. Remove the fuel line from the carburetor inlet. Remove the air filter housing and the carburetor mounting screws. Pull the carburetor off; note the linkages and the gasket orientation for reassembly. Remove the float bowl (one bolt). Pump out the old fuel; the bottom is coated in varnish. Remove the float, the needle, the seat. Blow out every passage with carb cleaner; run a fine wire (guitar string works) through the main jet and the pilot jet; repeat carb cleaner. Install a rebuild kit — new gaskets, fresh needle — reassemble. Reinstall on the engine. Fill tank with fresh gasoline plus stabilizer. First pull: pops. Third pull: runs. Tune idle screw to smooth. Total time: forty-five minutes. Cost: ten dollars of gaskets and two gallons of gas.
Try these

First: identify a carburetor on any small engine in your world — a mower, a generator, a chainsaw, a snowblower. Find the bowl at the bottom (float-style) or the diaphragm cover (two-stroke). Find the choke lever, the throttle lever. The linkages are all visible; follow them. Second: with the engine off and the cap removed, sniff the fuel. Fresh gasoline smells sharp and slightly sweet; old gasoline smells sour and slightly fishy. If it smells wrong, the carburetor probably needs cleaning even if the engine starts. Third: buy a carburetor rebuild kit for a specific engine (search the model number plus "carb kit"). Sit at a kitchen table and disassemble, study, and reassemble the carburetor once without running the engine. The whole machine is visible and mechanical.
When it goes wrong

A carburetor that seems clean but still runs rich means the float is waterlogged or out of adjustment — sinks too far, unseats the needle, floods the bowl. A brass float can be re-soldered; plastic floats are always replaced. A carburetor that runs lean means a jet is partially blocked or an air leak exists between carburetor and engine — spray carb cleaner on the gasket surfaces with the engine running; RPM change = leak. A chainsaw that cuts out at full throttle usually has the "H" screw set too lean, and the saw is about to seize; richen (turn counter-clockwise) a quarter turn and retest. Flooding at startup means the choke was used too long or the needle-and-seat is leaking — inspect.
What to try next

Past basic bowl carburetors, the next rungs are diaphragm carburetors on two-stroke equipment (Walbro and Zama), complex multi-barrel carburetors on larger lawn tractors, electronic fuel injection on newer equipment, and ultrasonic-cleaning professional rebuilds. Paul Dempsey's book is the classroom text for the trade; donyboy73 and Steve's Small Engine Saloon are the best free video resources. A career path exists in professional equipment-equipment-repair shops, mower dealers, and rural service operations.

dek: A needle, a jet, a float, and a draft of moving air — the small machine that fed every engine for a century.
name: Carburetors
sections: Why it fails, always in winter

body.text: On the first warm Saturday in April, in any American suburb, a particular sound drifts over the backyard fences: a pull-cord rope, yanked and yanked again by a man who is hoping this is the year his mower starts on the first try. It rarely is. The cure is not a new mower. It is a two-hour sitting-on-the-driveway tune-up — the same one grandfathers did for sixty years, with the same three components the engine needs and nothing more mysterious than a spark plug wrench.
Three things an engine needs

A small four-stroke engine needs spark, fuel, and air. A spark plug fires at the right moment. Clean fuel reaches the carburetor. Clean air reaches the intake. If all three are present, the engine runs. If even one is missing or wrong, nothing happens. The whole of small-engine troubleshooting is figuring out, in a sensible order, which leg of the stool has gone bad. A spring tune-up restores all three preemptively, which is why it works.
The spring ritual

Pull the spark plug, read it, and replace it — a new one costs two dollars, and a black or oily old plug tells you something the new plug will also reveal next year. Drain the old fuel from the tank into a jar; if it smells like varnish, it is varnish. Fill with fresh gasoline stabilized for storage. Pop the air-filter housing and either blow out a foam element or replace a paper one. Drain the oil from the sump, refill to the mark on the dipstick with fresh SAE 30 or 10W-30. Check the blade. Start the engine. Listen for a clean idle. The whole job takes an hour and a half on a push mower, longer on a riding tractor, and it prevents almost every common failure the homeowner-repair forums complain about.
Sharpening the blade, which counts as maintenance

A dull mower blade does not cut grass; it tears grass. The tear leaves the torn tip brown and the lawn looking yellow from the street. A sharp blade leaves a clean green cut. Blades are sharpened once a season with a bench grinder and a file, or swapped for a new one for twelve dollars at a hardware store. This is the one maintenance item even careful owners forget, and the one that makes the most visible difference in the lawn itself. Chainsaws have the same problem on a shorter timescale: a fresh chain makes a chainsaw feel like a new tool.
Why the Stihl survives a decade of abuse

The Stihl chainsaw, the Honda lawn-and-garden engine, the Kohler Command on a riding mower — these are the machines in the folklore of every suburb, famous for starting on the third pull after a decade sitting in a shed. The secret is not just good manufacturing; it is that their owners tend to know about fuel stabilizer, about running the carburetor dry at the end of the season, about storing with fresh oil. The machines are worthy of the attention. A neglected Stihl dies as fast as any other small engine. A tuned one lasts a working life.
Reading a spark plug

The spark plug is an engine's diary. A healthy plug comes out with a light tan deposit on the electrode — the color of milk-coffee — indicating clean, complete combustion. A plug crusted with black, dry carbon indicates a rich mixture or a stuck choke. An oily black plug indicates oil is getting into the combustion chamber, either past worn rings or past bad valve seals. A white or chalky plug indicates a lean mixture or an air leak, sometimes a cooling problem. A plug with the electrode burned round indicates detonation, usually from the wrong heat range or bad fuel. Ten seconds looking at an old plug will tell a careful mechanic most of what there is to know about the engine below it.

Ethanol is the great enemy of small engines. Ten percent ethanol gasoline — the standard pump blend in the United States — absorbs water and corrodes carburetor bodies over a storage winter. Real-gas stations or canned ethanol-free fuel are worth the surcharge for any engine that sits for more than a month.
If it starts on the first pull in April, you did the tune-up right in October.
How to think about it

A tune-up is giving the engine clean examples of each of the three things it wants: clean air, clean fuel, and strong spark. Each one has a consumable part that represents it — air filter, fuel in the tank, spark plug. Replace or refresh the consumables and the engine has no excuse for running poorly. This is why the spring tune-up is a ritual rather than a diagnosis: you are restoring the engine's inputs to known-good, which eliminates three out of four possible failure modes in a single morning. If the engine still misbehaves afterward, the fault is not in the inputs; it is in the engine itself, and that is a different afternoon.
Work through one

A typical push-mower spring tune-up, thirty minutes of actual work. Step one: warm the engine by running it briefly, then shut off and drain the oil while warm — pulled plug, tipped mower onto its side (carburetor up, always), oil flows into a pan. Step two: refill with fresh SAE 30 to the full mark on the dipstick. Step three: remove the air filter — foam gets soap-washed and re-oiled, paper gets thrown away and replaced. Step four: pull the spark plug with a socket; inspect the color; gap a new plug to 0.030" (or manufacturer spec) and install. Step five: drain the old fuel (don't forget the carburetor bowl) and refill with fresh gasoline plus STA-BIL. Step six: sharpen or replace the blade. Step seven: pull the starter cord; the engine should start in one or two pulls. Tune the idle screw if needed. Total: thirty minutes; the mower is now good for the season.
Try these

First: remove the spark plug from a small engine in your life. Read it against the standard color chart (easily findable on NGK or Autolite's sites). What did the engine tell you about how it has been running? Second: perform a compression test on the same engine — a thirty-dollar gauge, screwed into the plug hole, reads the cylinder's pressure at full crank. A healthy four-stroke small engine reads 90–120 psi; below 60 means worn rings or valves. Third: time yourself doing a full spring tune-up on a cooperative small engine. First time: an hour. Third time: under thirty minutes, with fewer tools needed each round.
When it goes wrong

An engine that will not start after a tune-up has had something broken, not fixed. The most common mistake is the fuel cut-off — many mowers have a valve between tank and carburetor that a tune-up can leave closed. Second is the spark plug not torqued firmly (loose plug = no compression in that cylinder). Third is the air filter installed upside-down or incorrectly seated, starving the engine of air. Fourth is over-filling the oil — above the dipstick max foams the oil and the engine cannot lubricate. Fifth is fuel stale before you got to it; drain and refill with truly fresh gas. If none of those: test spark (remove plug, ground to block, crank, look for spark), test fuel delivery (prime or choke, observe), test compression. One of the three will be failing.
What to try next

Past the spring tune-up, the next rungs are full service on four-stroke engines (valve clearance adjustment, governor adjustment, carburetor rebuild), chainsaw service (chain maintenance, clutch and bearing wear, two-stroke carb tuning), riding mower service (deck leveling, belt replacement, hydro transmission fluid), and winter storage protocols (proper shutdown, stabilizer dosage, plug preservation). Paul Dempsey's book is the full curriculum. EETC certification is the professional path.

body.text: Every morning in Lower Manhattan, a room full of strangers meets before a judge, follows rules almost none of them have read, and accepts an outcome they did not choose. None of it is biology. A wedding, a mortgage, a traffic stop, a visa interview, a Thanksgiving dinner — each one is an institution, running on nothing but the shared agreement that it is a thing. Sociology, as a discipline, is largely the study of how that agreement gets and stays made.

body.caption: Émile Durkheim (1858–1917), the French sociologist whose 1895 Rules of Sociological Method first argued that societies have their own facts, studyable on their own terms.

body.text: Durkheim's strange discovery

Émile Durkheim, writing in France in the 1890s, argued that societies had their own facts — patterns that existed outside any particular person and pressed on individuals the way the weather does. His book Suicide (1897), still taught in every introductory course, showed that suicide rates varied systematically by country, by religion, by marital status. Protestants died by suicide more often than Catholics; unmarried men more than married ones; the pattern held across decades and languages. No individual psychology, Durkheim argued, could explain that regularity. Something above the person was doing the work.

The discipline of sociology was born the moment someone took that observation seriously. Institutions, in Durkheim's term, are "social facts" — patterned, exterior, constraining. You did not invent marriage; you found it in the world and it shaped what you did. The same goes for money, school, language, military service, the idea of a weekend.
The canonical list

Every introductory textbook teaches a short list of core institutions: family, education, religion, economy, polity, and (more recently) media. Each solves a recurring problem — reproduction, socialization, meaning, allocation, coercion, information — and each has its own internal specialists, its own rituals, its own distinctive way of failing. A good sociologist's first question about any practice is not "is it useful?" but "what institution is it part of, and what does that institution ask of the people in it?"
Formal and informal, written and unwritten

Douglass North, who won the 1993 Nobel in economics for taking institutions seriously, distinguished formal institutions (written rules — constitutions, contracts, statutes) from informal ones (custom, reputation, trust). The interesting cases are mixed. The United States Congress has standing rules, but it also has norms — the filibuster, senatorial courtesy, the hold, the blue slip — that carry almost as much weight and leave no paper trail. When an institution comes apart quickly, it is usually the unwritten rules that went first.

Elinor Ostrom, the only woman to win the economics Nobel (in 2009), spent her career showing that communities routinely invented local institutions to manage common-pool resources — grazing lands, fisheries, irrigation systems — without any central state. Her design principles (clear boundaries, monitoring by users, graduated sanctions, nested governance) are now standard reading for anyone who thinks real-world rules must always come top-down.
Why institutions last

Institutions are sticky. A constitution written in 1787 still shapes American politics; a code of Roman law from the sixth century still shapes European private law; a liturgical calendar written in the fourth century still tells most of the world when to put up a tree. This inertia is a feature, not a bug. Institutions trade responsiveness for predictability, and predictability is most of what makes cooperation between strangers possible. The cost, as Max Weber warned, is an iron cage — the rationalized, rule-bound order of modern life that frees us from tradition and then traps us in its own logic.
Why they fail

An institution is, ultimately, a coordination device: it works only if the powerful people in a society agree to keep playing by it when the stakes are high. The Stalin Constitution of 1936 was a model of liberal protections on paper; it protected no one. Robert Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000) tracked the slow hollowing of American civic life — the Elks, the PTA, the bowling leagues, the local paper — and argued that what went with them was a capacity for collective action. Institutions are cheaper to tear down than to build; once the habit of acceptance is lost, it takes a generation to rebuild.
How they change

Institutions change in two modes. The slow mode is drift: old rules stay on the books while practice quietly moves underneath them. The fast mode is a shock — a war, a depression, a plague, a scandal — that makes the old arrangement visibly untenable and opens a window for redesign. The American New Deal, the British National Health Service, the European Union, the Voting Rights Act, the internet: each was rushed into existence in a moment of crisis or possibility and then settled into the slow institutional time afterward. A sociologically literate reader learns to spot which mode a given society is in.

Max Weber used the phrase "the iron cage" (stahlhartes Gehäuse) to describe the rationalized, rule-bound order of modern life — an order that frees us from tradition and then traps us in its own logic. Parsons's 1930 translation fixed the phrase in English; the original is closer to "shell as hard as steel."

body.cite: Émile Durkheim, The Rules of Sociological Method (1895)
body.text: Every society has a structure which is independent of the wills of its individual members.
Learn it: disassemble an institution

Pick an institution you participate in daily — a job, a school, a congregation, a grocery store, a DMV. Answer seven questions in order. (1) What recurring problem does it solve? (2) What are its formal rules — written, enforced by official sanctions? (3) What are its informal norms — unwritten, enforced by social disapproval? (4) Who are its specialists, and what do they know that laypeople don't? (5) What is the entry ritual (how does someone become a member)? (6) What is the exit ritual (how does someone leave)? (7) What would cause the institution to fail, and how would you see the failure in advance? An hour spent writing out these seven answers for "a Thursday 8 a.m. staff meeting" will teach you more about workplace institutions than a week of HR training. Do it for "marriage," "jury duty," or "the New York subway." The method travels.
Worked example: why tipping is sticky

Tipping in American restaurants is an informal institution with surprisingly durable features. Formal rules: there are none — a diner is not legally obligated to tip. Informal norms: 15–20% of the pre-tax bill is the expected range; servers actively depend on tips because U.S. federal law allows a "tipped minimum wage" as low as $2.13 per hour. Specialists: waiters develop tacit knowledge of which tables will tip well and how to pace service accordingly. Entry ritual: a server is hired, trained, and introduced to the tip-out structure (bartenders, bussers, hosts). Exit: leaving is easy; changing the system is not. Why does this institution persist even though most economists consider it inefficient? Because every individual actor has weak incentives to defect: diners worry about being seen as cheap, restaurants worry about losing servers, states worry about wage-law politics. The institution is stuck at a suboptimal equilibrium — classic coordination failure. Several European countries have successfully moved to no-tip systems; the U.S. has not. Comparative institutional analysis makes the stickiness legible.
Practice problems

Problem 1. A new app forms a neighborhood "buy nothing" group where neighbors give unused items to each other for free. Within a year it has 3,000 members. Describe it as an institution using Ostrom's design principles. Which principles does it satisfy, and which might it struggle with?

Answer: Clear boundaries (member vs. non-member, geographic scope): satisfied. Monitoring by users (admin volunteers, members flagging bad behavior): satisfied. Graduated sanctions (warning → removal): usually satisfied. Collective-choice arrangements (members can propose rules): partial; informal. Nested governance: weak; tied to the app company's policies. Recognition by higher authorities: weak. The group is a modern, light-weight common-pool resource institution; its fragility comes from dependence on a private platform. Read the principles in chapter 3 of Governing the Commons and match them to your local group; the fit will be striking.

Problem 2. A long-standing informal norm in a workplace — "no one emails after 6 p.m." — suddenly breaks down when a new senior hire emails at 9 p.m. every night. Predict what happens in the next six months, and describe which mechanisms of informal sanction would (or would not) be activated.

Answer: Most likely outcome: the norm erodes quickly, because hierarchical asymmetry blocks informal sanction. Peers can grimace at a 9 p.m. email from another peer; they cannot easily sanction a senior. Over six months, the unspoken expectation will shift toward "you should at least read after hours," even if most don't reply. If the new hire leaves, the norm may partially snap back. This is how a relatively stable institutional norm (working hours) can be quickly destabilized by a single high-status actor. Formal policy would have to catch up with the shift, often reactively.

Problem 3. A constitutional democracy's political parties stop conceding elections, begin labeling the other party as illegitimate, and start using parliamentary procedures as weapons rather than coordination devices. What are Levitsky and Ziblatt's "soft guardrails," and what happens when they erode?

Answer: The two soft guardrails, per How Democracies Die, are mutual toleration (accepting that the other party is a legitimate competitor) and institutional forbearance (not exercising every legal power available). Without these, normal constitutional machinery can be weaponized: court-packing, impeachment-as-policy, filibuster abuse, refusal to confirm nominees. The formal rules remain in place; the democracy erodes anyway. The empirical sequence from Hungary, Poland, and Venezuela is instructive. The U.S. has exhibited stress on both guardrails since roughly 2016; Levitsky and Ziblatt consider this the slow-burn pattern, not a sudden coup.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What is a "social fact"? Give one example that couldn't be explained by individual psychology alone. (2) What do Douglass North and Elinor Ostrom contribute to institutional analysis that Durkheim and Weber did not? (3) Distinguish formal and informal institutions; give one example of each. (4) What is "path dependence"? (5) Name three of Ostrom's eight design principles. (6) What does Weber mean by "the iron cage"? (7) Why is institutional inertia a feature, not a bug?
The learning progression

Brand new? Watch Crash Course Sociology episodes 1–4 and 27. Read Durkheim's The Rules of Sociological Method, chapter 1. Spend an hour writing out the seven questions above for one institution you know well. Once you've got the basics? Read Weber's Protestant Ethic and North's Institutions, Institutional Change and Economic Performance. Take Szelényi's Yale course. To go further? Take graduate-level social theory. Read Giddens' Central Problems in Social Theory, and Searle's The Construction of Social Reality for the philosophy of institutions. The current frontier: institutional economics of development (Acemoglu and Robinson), computational institutional design (mechanism design), and the sociology of the administrative state.

dek: The invisible scaffolding — families, courts, schools, markets — that makes a society possible.

body.text: In the reading room of the British Museum, between 1850 and 1867, a thickly bearded German refugee named Karl Marx wrote the book that gave the study of class its vocabulary. He was an exile, nearly broke, kept afloat by a textile heir in Manchester. The paradox is not incidental. The most influential critique of capitalism was subsidized by its profits.

body.caption: Karl Marx in 1875, age 57. Two volumes of Capital would be published after his death; the last manuscripts were edited by Friedrich Engels.
body.credit: John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: Marx: class as a relation to the means of production

For Marx, a class is not an income bracket. It is defined by its relation to the means of production: you either own them (the bourgeoisie) or you sell your labor to those who do (the proletariat). Everything else — politics, culture, law — follows from that economic base. The analysis is reductive by design; its power is that it makes predictions.

Marx's predictions did not all come true. The working class of the advanced industrial countries did not, on the whole, become revolutionary. The proletarianization of society was partly reversed by the rise of a large professional and managerial middle class. But the framework — that the work you do for pay, and for whom, structures almost everything else about your life — has proved remarkably durable. Modern labor economists using individual wage data and modern sociologists using life-history interviews mostly rediscover Marx in technical drag.
Weber: three dimensions, not one

Max Weber, writing a generation later, thought Marx had collapsed too many things into one. Weber split stratification into three: class (economic position), status (social honor), and party (political power). A rich drug dealer and a broke duke occupy different boxes on each axis. Most modern sociology runs on Weber's scheme, not Marx's — the measurement is easier, and it catches the prestige dimension (professors, nurses, teachers) that a pure wage-based account misses.
Bourdieu and the hidden capitals

Pierre Bourdieu, in postwar France, added a twist neither had named.
