Alongside economic capital, he argued, there is cultural capital (the right vocabulary, the right reference, the right fork) and social capital (the right address book). These hidden assets are handed down as carefully as money, and they explain why schools reproduce class rather than breaking it. A child who arrives at university already knowing how to talk to a professor has an advantage worth more than a full tuition scholarship to a student who does not.

Bourdieu's 1979 book Distinction mapped the taste preferences of the French middle class — the music they listened to, the food they ate, the furniture they bought — and showed that these choices, which felt like expressions of free individuality, tracked class position with uncanny precision. Every subsequent study of gentrification, of educational inequality, of the "college experience" is in conversation with Distinction whether or not it cites the book.
What the numbers now show

Inequality, measured by the share of national income held by the top one percent, collapsed in the mid-twentieth century in most Western democracies and has climbed steadily since about 1980. Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014), drawing on two hundred years of tax records, showed the U-shape clearly and argued that it reflects a deep property of capitalism rather than an accident of policy. His prediction — that the return on capital r tends to exceed the growth rate g, so wealth concentrates — is disputed by economists but has become part of the common vocabulary of the field.

Measurement matters. The Gini coefficient compresses inequality into a single number between zero and one. The Lorenz curve visualizes it. The Palma ratio (top 10%/bottom 40%) is a less-known alternative that better tracks political consequence. Any writer talking about inequality without naming a measure is leaving themselves a rhetorical loophole; a careful reader insists on one.
Mobility, which is not the same question

High inequality is compatible with high or low mobility between the income levels. The United States, often described as the land of opportunity, has relatively low intergenerational mobility — a child born in the bottom quintile has about a 7% chance of reaching the top quintile. The Scandinavian countries, with lower inequality, have roughly double the rate. Raj Chetty and the Opportunity Insights team at Harvard have built the best data we have on this, by neighborhood, for the whole United States. The maps they produced are genuinely shocking when you zoom in on your own zip code.
Intersectionality

Kimberlé Crenshaw's 1989 legal article coined the term intersectionality to describe the observation that experiencing class inequality is inflected by experiencing racial and gender inequality at the same time, and that the combination produces something different from the sum. A working-class Black woman in Memphis does not experience her life as 33% class plus 33% race plus 33% gender. The framework has expanded far beyond law; it is now the default language of contemporary American sociology. Critics warn against using it to shut down class analysis altogether; supporters argue that the three axes are inseparable in practice.

body.cite: Karl Marx & Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto (1848)
body.text: The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.

The United States spent about 4% of its GDP on welfare and social-insurance payments in 1960. It spends about 19% today. Inequality, meanwhile, has grown. Both facts are true; reconciling them is most of the argument in contemporary American social policy.
Learn it: compute a Gini coefficient by hand

Imagine five households in a village, with annual incomes $10, $20, $30, $40, and $100. Sort them in ascending order (already done). Compute the cumulative share of total income as you add each household: $10/$200 = 5%; $30/$200 = 15%; $60/$200 = 30%; $100/$200 = 50%; $200/$200 = 100%. Plot those values against cumulative share of population (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 100%) — that is the Lorenz curve. The Gini coefficient is the area between the Lorenz curve and the 45-degree "perfect equality" line, divided by the area of the triangle below the 45-degree line. For this tiny example, the Gini comes out to about 0.40. For reference: Scandinavian countries run around 0.25; the U.S. is around 0.40; South Africa is around 0.63. Doing it by hand for a small example makes the number concrete in a way the textbook cannot.
Worked example: why the U.S. Gini rose after 1980

The U.S. Gini coefficient was about 0.35 in 1980 and is about 0.41 today. Piketty, Saez, and the World Inequality Lab have decomposed the rise. Contributing factors in approximate order of size: (1) Top-income pull: the top 1% captured an increasing share of pre-tax income, driven by executive pay, capital income, and the reduction of top marginal tax rates from the 1980s. (2) Wage stagnation at the median: real wages for non-college workers have barely grown since 1980. (3) Declining unionization: from about 25% of the workforce in 1980 to about 10% today. (4) Educational polarization: college-wage premium roughly doubled. (5) Tax policy: capital gains taxed at preferential rates, payroll taxes regressive. All of these are live policy debates; the sociological vocabulary (class, power, status) maps onto each, though in different ways. You do not need to memorize the magnitudes — you need to recognize that inequality is a composite of several independently moving parts, each traceable to identifiable institutional choices.
Practice problems

Problem 1. Two siblings — one a neurosurgeon earning $500,000, one a high-school teacher earning $55,000 — grew up in the same house. Marx would call them the same class; Weber would split them. Who is right? How would Bourdieu analyze the pair?

Answer: Both partial. Marx would focus on the underlying structural position — both sell their labor, though at vastly different rates, and neither owns the means of production (the hospital, the school). Weber would split them along at least two axes: economic class (very different income and wealth trajectories) and status (doctors carry more social prestige than teachers in modern America). Bourdieu would add that they share substantial cultural capital and social capital from their shared upbringing — shared vocabulary, shared networks, shared comfort in middle-class settings — but that their economic capital differs. The full picture requires all three frames. This is why the Weberian scheme is the practical workhorse: it catches what Marx misses without throwing his structural insights away.

Problem 2. A city has a median household income of $60,000 but a mean of $95,000. What does this gap tell you? Which number should a journalist use to describe "the typical household," and which to describe the overall size of the economy?

Answer: The gap means the income distribution is right-skewed — a small number of very high incomes pull the mean above the median. The median is the better "typical household" number; the mean is more accurate for aggregate purposes like tax revenue projections. A careful journalist reports both. The U.S. and most advanced economies show mean/median income gaps of roughly 1.4–1.6; the bigger the gap, the more unequal the distribution.

Problem 3. A child born to parents in the bottom quintile of the U.S. income distribution has about a 7.5% chance of reaching the top quintile as an adult. In Denmark, the same figure is about 14%. Why is U.S. mobility lower than Denmark's, and what are the three most-cited structural explanations?

Answer: Raj Chetty's Opportunity Insights work has identified five key factors: (1) residential segregation (U.S. neighborhoods concentrate by income to a greater degree); (2) school quality differences (U.S. school funding ties to local property taxes); (3) family structure (U.S. has higher rates of single parenthood, which correlates with worse mobility); (4) social capital and community connectedness (measured by cross-class friendships in Facebook data); (5) labor-market institutions (U.S. has less collective bargaining and weaker job protections). Causality is complicated — these factors correlate heavily with each other — but each is associated with mobility independently in Chetty's data.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) What does Marx mean by class? (2) What three dimensions did Weber add? (3) What is cultural capital? Economic capital? Social capital? (4) State the Gini coefficient's definition in plain English. (5) How did Piketty argue r > g matters for long-run inequality? (6) Distinguish inequality from mobility. (7) What does "intersectionality" mean, and who coined the term?
The learning progression

Brand new? Watch Wilkinson's TED talk and Piketty's. Read Chapter 1 of The Communist Manifesto. Compute the Gini on a toy example by hand. Once you've got the basics? Read The Spirit Level and Our World in Data's inequality explainer cover to cover. Take Szelényi's Yale course. To go further? Work through Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century. Take Chetty's Harvard course on opportunity. Read Bourdieu's Distinction (slowly). The serious frontier is empirical: the World Inequality Database maintained by the Paris School of Economics, and the replication literature on intergenerational mobility estimates.

dek: The oldest argument in sociology — who has what, and why — and the one that never quite finishes.
name: Class & Inequality
sections: Class, race, gender, and the intersectional turn

body.text: In a cold concrete courtyard in Bali in April 1958, Clifford Geertz and his wife were watching an illegal cockfight when the police raided it. They ran with everyone else. That afternoon of shared flight earned Geertz the village's trust, and the essay it produced — "Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight" — reshaped how sociologists, anthropologists, and historians think about culture.

body.caption: Max Weber (1864–1920). His 1905 Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism argued that a religious attitude had produced a particular kind of economic culture — an argument still disputed in every decade since.

body.text: Culture, as a working definition

In everyday speech, culture means opera and museums. In sociology it means something wider and quieter: the shared web of meanings, habits, norms, and signals that lets members of a group understand each other without being told. A handshake, a table manner, a pop song everyone knows, the protocol for getting into an elevator — each is a piece of culture in this sense. An American visitor who has never been told the rule knows, at a restaurant in Tokyo, that something is off when she tips the waiter; the embarrassment is the culture, made visible by its violation.

Raymond Williams's Keywords (1976) traced the English word "culture" through two centuries of shifting use — from "tillage" in the eighteenth century, to "individual refinement" in the nineteenth, to the anthropological "whole way of life" in the twentieth. The word carries all three meanings at once, and the slippage between them is the source of most bad arguments about the subject. A careful writer specifies which sense is in play.
Thick description

Geertz's most useful idea was borrowed from the philosopher Gilbert Ryle: a wink is not a twitch, and to tell them apart you have to know the context. "Thick description" is the ethnographer's attempt to write culture down in a way that catches the meaning, not just the movement. It is why reading a good ethnography feels like being let in on a joke. A "thin" description of the cockfight would record the time, the two birds, the bets, the outcome. A thick one explains why a man would mortgage his house over a fight; why the fighters are called "bapak" (father) of their birds; what it means when a high-status man loses to a low-status one. The movement is not the event.
Subcultures, always

No society has a single culture. The Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (1964–2002), led by Stuart Hall, studied how working-class British teenagers built mod, punk, rude-boy, and skinhead scenes that were both products of and arguments with the dominant culture around them. Dick Hebdige's Subculture: The Meaning of Style (1979) read punks' clothes the way a literary critic reads a poem and is still the place to meet the idea.

Every subsequent scene — hip-hop in the South Bronx, evangelical Christianity in the suburbs, the hacker milieu around Berkeley, the drill scene in Chicago, furries, ballroom — is legible through the same frame: small groups assembling their own meaning systems inside (and sometimes against) a larger one. Cultural sociology is the branch of the field that pays serious attention to them.
Values, norms, and the hard case

A value is a deep preference ("individual freedom matters"); a norm is a rule that implements it ("do not stand so close to a stranger on the subway"); a sanction is what happens if you break the norm (a glare, a move, in some places a fight). A culture is the bundled-together values, norms, and sanctions of a group. The hard case is when groups disagree about their values and find themselves in the same institutions: a liberal democracy with a religious minority, a company merging two national offices, a city with new immigrants and long-term residents. Most of what gets called the "culture wars" is a fight at this seam.
Why culture keeps changing

Culture is not a possession; it is a running argument. Technology, migration, generational turnover, and contact between groups are always reshaping what "we" means for any given we. In 1995, calling a cousin in another country required a calling card and planning; in 2025 it is a daily habit. The shape of family life, the speed of news, the vocabulary of the young — every serious student of culture learns that static descriptions go out of date fast. The sociologist's job is to stay close enough to notice the shift without flattening it into a single headline.

Marshall McLuhan's "the medium is the message" — a slogan from Understanding Media (1964) — is one of the most-quoted and least-understood claims in the field. McLuhan meant that the form in which information is delivered shapes thought more than the content does: a culture of print thinks differently from a culture of television, regardless of what is printed or broadcast. Apply the idea to smartphones and the last twenty years stop being mysterious.
Learn it: a five-step thick description

Sit in a setting you know well and do the following. (1) Write a thin description of a single event (e.g., "a man held the door for a woman"). Thirty seconds. (2) Write everything a stranger would need to know to understand what happened — who these people are to each other, what register of behavior this is ("polite but not flirtatious"), what kinds of meanings the gesture carries ("chivalrous? condescending? automatic?"). (3) Describe the wider norms of the setting — is this an office, a café, a street? Does this gesture mean something different at work? (4) What would a breach look like? If he had failed to hold the door, what would happen? If he held it for every woman but no man, what would that signal? (5) What does the whole package reveal about the culture — small-town Midwestern, corporate New York, LGBT Berlin? The same 30-second event produces very different thick descriptions in different places. This is Geertz's method in miniature.
Worked example: the hip-hop subculture as Hebdige reads it

Dick Hebdige's Subculture: The Meaning of Style (1979) analyzed British punks. Apply his method to early 1980s hip-hop in the Bronx. (1) Visible style: baggy pants, kangol hats, Adidas shell-toes, breakdancing stance, graffiti tags. (2) What ordinary meanings were these items stealing and repurposing? (Graffiti took public space; sneakers moved from athletic gear to street identity; the DJ turntable turned a consumer product into a musical instrument.) (3) What social position was being negotiated? (A post-industrial South Bronx with limited economic futures; Black and Latino youth carving cultural space.) (4) How did the dominant culture respond? (First as nuisance, then as commodity — by 1985, breakdancing was in Pepsi commercials; by 1995, hip-hop was the best-selling American music genre.) (5) What does the trajectory tell us? (The co-option that Hebdige predicted — subcultures get commodified and defanged — but also the durable reshaping of the dominant culture itself.) You can run this analysis on any subculture: skater, furry, ballroom, gamer, crypto bro.
Practice problems

Problem 1. A newcomer to a workplace is told "we don't really do formal performance reviews here — we just have a vibe." What is the newcomer likely missing, and what kind of cultural knowledge do they need to acquire?

Answer: The newcomer is likely missing an implicit evaluation system that exists in social cues (being invited to lunches, being looped into email threads, being asked for opinions in meetings) rather than in paperwork. This is cultural capital in Bourdieu's sense — knowing how to read the signals is part of competence. Workplaces with "no formal review" typically have stricter informal evaluation than those with explicit systems; the newcomer needs a mentor or close observer who can translate the tacit norms into explicit advice.

Problem 2. An American and a Japanese colleague exchange business cards. The Japanese colleague receives the card with two hands, reads it carefully, and places it on the table in front of her. The American glances at it and puts it in his back pocket. Neither intended rudeness. What is going on?

Answer: Two cultures with different card-exchange norms meeting at an interaction. In Japan, meishi exchange is a formalized ritual — the card is a representation of the person, handled with care. Putting it in a back pocket (literally sitting on it) is seen as disrespectful. The American's informal handling is not rude in his culture; the Japanese formal treatment is not sycophantic in hers. Cultural-competence training in multinational companies largely exists to surface these micro-norm mismatches. Hofstede's dimensions of cultural variation (power distance, individualism vs collectivism, etc.) formalize the patterns.

Problem 3. A group of teenagers in a small American town has adopted a slang vocabulary borrowed from global hip-hop and internet culture. Local elders complain they are "losing the culture." Using the sociological definition of culture, who is right?

Answer: Neither fully. The teenagers are not "losing" culture — they are constructing a new one, which is what every youth cohort does. The elders are right that local culture is changing, but this is a universal, not a decline. The sociological move is to describe the dynamics (what is being borrowed, what resists borrowing, what functions the new vocabulary serves for identity and belonging) without prejudging the change as loss or gain. Culture is always a running negotiation between generations; the argument between elders and teenagers is itself a cultural institution.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) State the sociological (not everyday) definition of culture. (2) What is thick description, and what philosopher's concept did Geertz borrow it from? (3) Distinguish values, norms, and sanctions. (4) What is a subculture, and how does Hebdige read one? (5) What did McLuhan mean by "the medium is the message"? (6) Distinguish cultural relativism from ethnocentrism. (7) Give one example of a cultural practice being commodified by the mainstream.
The learning progression

Brand new? Watch Wade Davis's TED talk and two Crash Course Sociology episodes on culture. Read Geertz's "Deep Play" essay. Take one walk in a neighborhood not your own with a notebook and do the five-step thick description exercise. Once you've got the basics? Read Raymond Williams's Keywords and a few chapters of Bourdieu's Distinction. Watch any episode of Planet Earth or a good ethnographic film. To go further? Take a cultural-sociology course. Read the Writing Culture volume and Clifford Geertz's Works and Lives. Read Stuart Hall's essays on encoding/decoding. For the modern frontier, read Michèle Lamont's work on boundaries, and Gary Alan Fine's sociology of small groups.

dek: Not high art versus low — the shared patterns of meaning that a group of people barely notice they share.
name: Culture
sections: Values, norms, and the hard case

body.text: In 1895, Émile Durkheim made a claim so counterintuitive it still startles first-year sociology students: crime is normal. A society entirely without deviance, he wrote, would not be a better society — it would be a society that had stopped changing. Every redrawing of the moral line begins with somebody crossing one. The Jesus who overturned the tables in the temple was, in his time, deviant. So was the abolitionist, the suffragette, the gay-rights marcher, the whistleblower. Yesterday's deviant is often tomorrow's reformer, and the mechanism by which the label switches is one of the central problems of the field.

body.caption: Michel Foucault in Brazil, 1974. His Discipline and Punish (1975) reshaped the sociology of deviance by reframing punishment as a technology of power.
body.credit: Rogério Assis, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: Deviance, defined sideways

A deviant act is one that violates a norm — a rule, written or not, whose breach draws a social reaction. The reaction can be a raised eyebrow, a bar fight, a prison sentence. Sociologists pay close attention to the range because it tells them what kind of norm was broken and how much work the group is doing to hold it in place. A breach that produces a shrug was barely a norm; a breach that produces a riot was load-bearing.
Becker and the labelers

Howard Becker's 1963 book Outsiders argued that deviance is not a property of the act but of the reaction to it. Smoking marijuana and playing jazz after midnight were deviant in Chicago in 1950 because of who was watching, not because of what was in the pipe. The move from behavior to label reframed an entire subfield. If deviance is what we call deviance, then the interesting question is: who does the calling, and for whom, and why?

Labeling theory has an uncomfortable corollary. Once a person is labeled — the suspended student, the ex-convict, the addict — the label itself shapes the subsequent life, often locking the person into the deviant role. Primary deviance (the first act) is ordinary; secondary deviance (the act after one has been caught) is shaped by the reaction. Most American research on recidivism still runs in this track.
Goffman's ordinary policing

Most social control is not done by police. Erving Goffman showed, in a string of slim books in the 1960s (Asylums, Stigma, Interaction Ritual, Behavior in Public Places), how much of it happens in the subway, the elevator, the dinner table — tiny corrections (a glance, a silence, a raised voice) that hold the unwritten rules in place. A great deal of what ordinary citizens call "manners" is social control in mild disguise; a great deal of what governments call "law enforcement" is social control in loud clothing.
The major theoretical schools

Four schools compete to explain deviance. Strain theory (Robert Merton, 1938) says deviance emerges when a society offers shared goals (wealth) but unequal means to reach them; the people locked out innovate, retreat, rebel, or ritualize. Control theory (Travis Hirschi, 1969) reverses the question: why does anyone conform? The answer is social bonds — attachment, commitment, involvement, belief — and deviance rises when the bonds weaken. Labeling theory, covered above, is the third. Conflict theory (descending from Marx) argues that what counts as deviance reflects the interests of the powerful. Modern research almost always picks up two or three of these at once.
Moral panics

Stanley Cohen's Folk Devils and Moral Panics (1972) studied a mid-1960s British panic over mods and rockers and gave the field a durable concept: a moral panic is an episode in which a social group is suddenly defined as a threat to societal values, amplified by media, and sanctioned out of proportion to the threat. Subsequent panics — satanic daycare, crack mothers, mugging, the war on drugs, "youth crime" — have followed the pattern closely. Not every public concern is a moral panic, but enough of them are that the concept is a permanent part of the sociological toolkit.
Why the line keeps moving

Same-sex marriage, smoking indoors, corporal punishment of children, swearing on television, interracial relationships, marijuana use, unwed motherhood — the deviant line has moved on each of these within one American lifetime, and in several cases has reversed. Sociologists study the mechanisms of moral change without prejudging it. The student who asks "But aren't some things really wrong?" has asked the right question. The honest answer is: sociology studies how the line gets drawn; ethics asks where it ought to go. The two disciplines need each other and are not the same.
Deviance is not a quality of the act the person commits, but rather a consequence of the application by others of rules and sanctions to an "offender."
Learn it: analyze a deviant act four ways

Take a specific deviant act — say, shoplifting a bottle of wine from a supermarket. Four theoretical lenses each tell a different story. (1) Strain theory (Merton): if the culture says everyone should be prosperous but blocks legitimate paths for some, those people "innovate" into crime. Apply: the shoplifter is experiencing strain between the goal of consumption and limited legitimate means. (2) Control theory (Hirschi): deviance is what happens when social bonds weaken. Apply: is the shoplifter attached to family, committed to a job, involved in institutions, believing in laws? (3) Labeling theory (Becker): the meaning of the act depends on who notices and reacts. Apply: the same shoplifter with a clean record may be let off with a warning; a prior conviction changes the career trajectory. (4) Conflict theory (descended from Marx): laws serve the interests of the powerful. Apply: note how shoplifting is heavily policed in small amounts while wage theft by employers — quantitatively larger — is barely prosecuted. No one theory catches the whole picture. A working sociologist uses two or three at once.
Worked example: the moral panic

Stanley Cohen's 1972 framework identifies five stages of a moral panic. Apply them to the 1980s American "satanic daycare" panic. (1) Something is defined as a threat to social values (reports of ritual abuse of children in preschools). (2) The media amplifies the threat with dramatic imagery (Geraldo specials, 20/20 investigations). (3) The condition produces moral outrage (legislative action, task forces, prosecutions — the McMartin trial, the Kern County cases). (4) Experts emerge with authoritative explanations (the "satanic ritual abuse" therapy industry, some of which produced false memories). (5) The panic recedes, either because the threat is neutralized or because it runs out of fuel, often leaving institutional damage. By the mid-1990s, most of the prosecutions had been overturned or discredited; many of the accused had served years in prison. The satanic-daycare panic is now the paradigm case in sociology of panics; the same five-stage model maps onto the Red Scare, the crack-mothers panic of the 1980s, the 2000s sex-trafficking panic, and several more recent episodes. Knowing the pattern doesn't make individual cases easy to judge; it does make you skeptical of the genre.
Practice problems

Problem 1. A small-town district passes a rule banning visible tattoos for teachers. A teacher with a discreet tattoo on her forearm is reprimanded. Is this a case of primary or secondary deviance? How would labeling theory interpret what happens next?

Answer: Primary deviance (the act itself — having a tattoo — is minor and contextually norm-violating). Secondary deviance would be the subsequent behavior shaped by the label: the teacher now identified as "the teacher with the tattoo" might begin to embrace the label, seek out colleagues with similar stances, or leave for a more permissive school. The label reshapes identity. Becker's point is not that tattoos cause problems; it is that the *reaction* to them produces new social trajectories. Whether this is good or bad depends on the case.

Problem 2. A sociologist wants to study an "underground" community (say, illegal street racers, or people who hold raves in abandoned buildings). Design a method that respects Becker's insight about labeling without producing harm.

Answer: Challenges: (a) access requires trust, which takes time and social capital; (b) research protections (IRB approval) must balance informed consent against the community's reasonable fear of exposure; (c) the researcher's presence can itself alter behavior (Hawthorne effect); (d) publication can bring unwanted attention. Standard mitigations: pseudonyms, composite characters, delayed publication, member-checking (letting community members review drafts), participation as a member rather than a distant observer (Venkatesh's Gang Leader for a Day is a model, and a cautionary tale). Ethical fieldwork on deviance is always a negotiation; there is no one right protocol.

Problem 3. The U.S. decriminalized marijuana in many states between 2012 and 2024. Strain, control, labeling, and conflict theorists might each say something different about the sociological consequences. What would each emphasize?

Answer: Strain: the strain between legitimate goals and prohibited means is reduced; one deviance-producing condition is removed. Control: legalization may weaken some informal social bonds (the community of underground users dissolves) and strengthen others (family health norms around usage). Labeling: the prior "criminal" label is removed for new users; old convictions still carry weight unless expunged. Conflict: legalization exposed how racially unequal enforcement had been — marijuana prosecutions had disproportionately targeted Black men; legalization has not retroactively corrected most of the damage. Each theory captures something the others miss. The empirical evidence, accumulated over a decade, is consistent with each in different ways.
Self-check

Check yourself. (1) Why did Durkheim call crime "normal"? (2) Distinguish primary and secondary deviance. (3) State strain theory in one sentence. (4) What are Hirschi's four social bonds? (5) What is a moral panic? Name one historical example. (6) What is a "total institution," per Goffman? (7) Why does labeling theory make the reaction, not the act, the analytic center of deviance?
The learning progression

Brand new? Watch Crash Course Sociology episodes 18–20 and Bryan Stevenson's TED talk. Read Durkheim's chapter 3 of The Rules of Sociological Method. Once you've got the basics? Read Becker's Outsiders cover to cover. Work through Goffman's Asylums. Take Szelényi's Yale course on classical social theory. To go further? Take a graduate course in the sociology of deviance or criminology. Read Foucault's Discipline and Punish slowly. Read the primary literature on mass incarceration (Wacquant's Punishing the Poor, Gottschalk's Caught, Alexander's New Jim Crow). For current empirical work, read Bruce Western, Devah Pager, and Matthew Desmond.

dek: Every rule implies a rule-breaker; sociologists study the rule and the breaker together.
name: Deviance & Norms

body.text: In 1964, a twenty-seven-year-old stand-up named Woody Allen was writing material in a small office above a Manhattan deli when he came up with a joke he would tell on stage for years: "I took a speed-reading course and read War and Peace in twenty minutes. It involves Russia." The joke is ten seconds long. It has two parts. The first part is the premise and setup, establishing a specific speed-reading claim; the second is the punch, collapsing the premise with the absurd reduction of a nine-hundred-page novel to two words. The structure is not unique to Allen. It is the basic shape of almost every joke a stand-up has ever told.
The basic shape

Most jokes are two-part: a setup that leads the audience in one direction, and a punch line that reveals the setup meant something else. Comedy writer and teacher Greg Dean built his whole pedagogy around this — the "target assumption" is what the setup invites the audience to think; the "reinterpretation" is what the punch reveals to be true instead. The gap between the two is where the laugh lives. A setup that is too long loses the audience; a punch line that is too predictable gets nothing. Professional comics spend their careers tightening both halves and testing the gap onstage.
Misdirection in a sentence

A great setup does two jobs simultaneously: it plants an assumption the audience expects to be true, and it does so in the fewest words possible. Mitch Hedberg, the late American stand-up who specialized in one-liners, was a surgeon of setups. "I used to do drugs. I still do, but I used to, too." The setup — "I used to do drugs" — invites the audience to expect a reflection. The punch swaps that for a blunt present-tense reveal, then appends a grammatically absurd rider. The whole joke is fifteen words. Every one of them is working.
The tag

After the punch line, a well-built joke sometimes carries a tag — a second, smaller punch that rides on the first laugh. Tags let a comic mine a premise for more material without returning to the setup. Seinfeld's bits often have three or four tags running off a single setup; Hannah Gadsby's Nanette is structured around a shift that happens when she refuses the tag the audience expects and delivers something else instead. The tag is optional. The craft is knowing when to let the punch land alone.
Callbacks

A callback returns to a joke from earlier in the set, usually in an unexpected context. Done well, a callback makes the audience feel smart — they get it because they remember — and creates a structure above the individual jokes. A good set has two or three callbacks; a great one has a callback that lands in the last thirty seconds and reframes the whole hour. Mike Birbiglia's long-form sets are almost always callback-driven. The skill is harder than the one-liner. It requires holding the entire architecture in the comic's head at once.
Why the premise is everything

Under every joke is a premise — an observation or opinion the joke is built on. "Airline food is bad" is a premise (now exhausted). "My mother is impossible to please" is a premise. "I have a complicated relationship with my body" is a premise. The joke is the craft of shaping the premise into setup and punch. A weak premise cannot be saved by great punch lines. A strong premise gives the comic material for an entire set, possibly a special. The first skill a new comic learns is how to generate honest, specific premises — because everything else is construction on top of that foundation.

Most new comedians write too many jokes and too few premises. The experienced move is the opposite: find ten strong premises you have something real to say about and write twenty jokes on each. A premise list is worth more than a joke list, every time.

dek: Setup, punch, turn — the two-part architecture of every laugh.
name: Joke Structure

body.text: A stand-up who has found their voice is instantly recognizable — close your eyes and you can tell whether you are listening to Pryor, to Rivers, to Seinfeld, to Gadsby, to Bargatze, to Wanda Sykes. The voice is not an accent or a speech pattern. It is the composite of what they choose to talk about, how they see the world, what they find funny, what they refuse to laugh at. A new comic writes jokes that work. A comic with a voice writes jokes that could only have come from them. The difference is not a matter of jokes. It is a matter of self.
What voice means in stand-up

Voice is point of view. A stand-up's voice is the consistent, recognizable angle from which they look at the world — what they notice, what they dismiss, what they take personally. George Carlin's voice was a linguistic irritation with power and hypocrisy. Joan Rivers's voice was cruel, specific, defensive glamour. Mitch Hedberg's voice was a drifting, surreal logic that ran perpendicular to ordinary perception. The jokes themselves differ wildly from comic to comic, but each comic's jokes share a point of view so consistent it functions as a signature.
Honesty specific enough to sound like you

Writing teachers say to write what you know; stand-up coaches say to write what you feel. A comic looking for their voice works on premises drawn from their actual life — their family, their body, their anxieties, their neighborhood, their politics — rather than generic premises they have heard work on television. This is risky: specificity means the audience might not relate. It is also the only way to sound like yourself. A joke about airline food is indistinguishable from every other comic's joke about airline food. A joke about the specific things your mother said to you at Thanksgiving in 2019 is yours forever.
Finding it in the first hundred sets

The common estimate is that a new comic needs a hundred or two hundred stage sets before a voice begins to emerge. Before that, the comic is experimenting — trying observational, trying confessional, trying one-liners, trying stories. Somewhere in the third or fourth month, one angle starts working more consistently than the others, and the audience starts recognizing the comic. This is the voice, revealing itself. A working comic then spends the next five years tending it. A comic who tries to choose their voice intellectually, without the stage time, gets it wrong.
The fight with the room

A new comic's voice sometimes does not match what the room wants. A careful, observational comic bombs at a drunk basement club. A rowdy club comic bombs at an early-evening arts-festival theater. The easy answer is to change the voice to match the room, and for a year it works. The long answer is the opposite: find the rooms that want the voice you actually have, work them, and let the voice get stronger there. A comic who survives this fight becomes themselves. A comic who doesn't becomes a working journeyman with no distinguishable signature.
Keeping it once you have it

The last problem is keeping the voice once you find it. Fame changes a comic's life; the voice that made them has to survive the change. Chris Rock has said that every comic's best material is written in the club, not in the hotel after the special. A comic who stops hanging out in clubs stops writing in the voice that made them. This is why the great ones — Seinfeld, Rock, Chappelle, Tig Notaro — keep dropping in at the tiny rooms on MacDougal and Melrose and in Montreal. The voice is a muscle. Stop using it and it atrophies.
The comic's voice is the sum of every decision they make on stage — what they talk about, how they phrase it, what they leave out. You cannot write it. You have to find it.

dek: Point of view is the whole instrument — without it, the best jokes land on no one in particular.
name: Finding Your Voice
sections: Honesty specific enough to sound like you
Finding it in the first hundred sets
Keeping it once you have it

body.text: In 1972, a small Cessna carrying a Uruguayan rugby team crashed in the high Andes. Sixteen of the forty-five passengers and crew were alive seventy-two days later when two of them, having walked out of the mountains, brought help to the rest. The survivors had everything they needed to die — and they would have, except they prioritized correctly. Their first day was about shelter from cold. Their first weeks were about water from snow. The decision to make food from the bodies of the dead came after the more immediate problems were addressed. Survival, the field instructors at NOLS like to say, is not a problem to solve. It is a sequence to follow.
The clock that decides everything

The Rule of Threes is a useful clinical estimate of how long a healthy adult can go without each of survival's four essentials. Three minutes without breathable air — for example, lost in smoke, or trapped under water. Three hours without shelter from severe weather — exposure to cold rain, hard wind, or extreme heat will kill before dehydration. Three days without water. Three weeks without food. The numbers are approximate and conditions vary, but the order of priority is correct: respond to the smallest number first. Most people who die in survival situations do so because they reverse the order — they spend their first hours hunting for food while shelter and water remain unaddressed.
Stop, think, observe, plan

When you realize you are lost or in trouble, do nothing for a few minutes. The acronym taught at almost every survival school is STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. The instinct to keep moving in any direction is dangerous; the instinct to react to the panic is worse. Sit. Inventory what you have. Look at what is around you. Make a plan that uses the daylight you have left. The single best predictor of survival in wilderness emergencies is not skill or fitness. It is the ability to remain calm enough to choose the next action.
Shelter before fire

In any cold, wet, or windy condition, shelter is the first task. Hypothermia can kill in hours; the wet hiker who decides to gather firewood before getting under cover often does not live to light the fire. The minimum useful shelter is anything that breaks the wind and gets you off the ground. A space blanket, a fallen tree, a rock overhang, a hasty lean-to of branches — these are not luxuries. They are the difference between a body that maintains 98 degrees and one that does not. Build the shelter before darkness; build it where you are, not where you would prefer to be.
When to stay put

For most lost hikers, the right answer is to stay where you are. Your route was probably known to someone; search and rescue starts there. A moving target is much harder to find than a stationary one, and the stationary one can spend its energy on shelter and signal rather than navigation. The exceptions are narrow: if the location is genuinely unsafe, if rescue is unlikely (no one knew where you were going), or if you are within a confident half-day's walk of certain help. Most survival emergencies are best solved by sitting still and being noisy — bright signal mirror, loud whistle, a fire that smokes.

Always tell a trusted person where you are going and when you will be back. Carry a map and compass and know how to use them. A satellite messenger like a Garmin inReach has saved more wilderness travelers in the past decade than any other piece of equipment. Survival is mostly prevention.

dek: Three minutes without air, three hours without shelter, three days without water, three weeks without food — the survivalist's clock.
name: The Rule of Threes

body.text: Some of the oldest hearths in the human archaeological record — at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, dated to about a million years ago — predate Homo sapiens by hundreds of thousands of years. Our ancestors were tending fire before they had the brains to write about it. The skill that defined our species, more than any tool, is the ability to make and keep a fire going on demand. The good news is that almost anyone can learn it. The bad news is that almost no one has practiced it lately, and the night you need to is a poor time to start.
The fire triangle

A fire requires three things in the right proportions: heat, fuel, and oxygen. Remove any of the three and the fire dies. Almost every failure to start a fire is a failure on one of these axes — wet fuel that never reaches ignition temperature, a smothered structure that cannot breathe, an ignition source that cools too fast. The simple model is enough to diagnose almost every problem with a struggling fire and to fix it: more air for a smoldering fire, drier and finer fuel for a fire that will not catch, a bigger ignition source for a fire that keeps going out.
Tinder, kindling, fuel

Every fire is built in three classes of material. Tinder catches a spark or holds a flame: the dry inner bark of birch or cedar, fluff from cattail heads, fine dry grass, dryer lint, char cloth, the cotton ball with petroleum jelly that lives in every prepared kit. Kindling carries the flame upward: pencil-thin dry twigs, split fatwood, slivers of resinous pine. Fuel keeps the fire alive: progressively larger wrist-thick branches, then split logs as the bed of coals develops. The mistake beginners make is to skip a class — to put kindling on tinder before the tinder is established, or to put fuel on kindling that has not built a real bed of glowing wood.
A good lay

The teepee is the classic shape — tinder in the center, kindling stacked around it like a small wigwam, fuel added once the structure is burning. The lean-to lays a long support stick over a windbreak, with kindling leaning against it; useful in wind. The log-cabin is built like a child's log cabin around a tinder core; useful in wet conditions because it is more stable as it burns down. Choose your shape for the conditions, but build it carefully — most fires that fail have been built sloppily, with too much smothering material at the base.
Methods, in order of difficulty

The right answer is to carry a Bic lighter — the most reliable, cheapest, lightest piece of survival equipment available. A waterproof match case is the second redundant layer. A ferrocerium rod (a "ferro rod" or "fire steel") throws bright sparks into prepared tinder and works wet and at high altitude where lighters can fail. The bow drill, the hand drill, the fire piston, the fire plough — primitive friction methods all — work but require an order of magnitude more skill, dry conditions, and the right woods. They are worth learning; they are not worth depending on. Carry the lighter.

Build the fire small. Most beginners build fires twice as big as they need; the bigger fire wastes fuel, scorches whoever is sitting near it, and makes a poor cooking fire. A small steady fire is more useful than a roaring one and far easier to maintain.

dek: A controlled fire is warmth, light, water-purification, signal, and morale — and the difference between knowing how to start one and not is small until it isn't.
name: Fire

body.text: In 1898, at the Moscow Art Theatre, a forty-year-old amateur named Konstantin Stanislavski walked into rehearsals for Chekhov's The Seagull and began asking his actors questions no Russian director had asked before. Why does your character enter this room? What happened to him before he walked in? What does he want from the person he is about to meet? By the time the curtain rose, Stanislavski had invented the way modern actors work, and the method — the System, as his students called it — has governed American and European acting ever since. Everything currently taught in a conservatory is an argument with, or a refinement of, Stanislavski.
The Russian invention

Before Stanislavski, stage acting was declamatory — gesture-based, outward, indicated. Actors studied poses in books and chose "the jealous pose" or "the terrified pose" from a menu. Stanislavski asked, instead, what a real human being in the character's circumstances would actually do, and trained his actors to recreate the inner life that produced the behavior. His system was codified in three books — An Actor Prepares, Building a Character, Creating a Role — and passed through his students to America via the Group Theatre in New York in the 1930s. The line from Stanislavski through Lee Strasberg, Stella Adler, and Sanford Meisner is the backbone of modern American acting.
Given circumstances

The actor's first job is to understand what the playwright has given. Who is this person? Where are they? What time of day, what season, what century? What has just happened to them? What relationships do they have with the other people in the scene? These are the "given circumstances" — the factual conditions the actor will play into. A Chekhov actor who has not thought carefully about whether the samovar has been lit is not ready for the scene. A Mamet actor who has not counted every real-estate deal in the text is similarly unprepared. The text is the floor. The circumstances are the walls.
Objective and action

An objective is what the character wants. An action is what they do to get it. Stanislavski required actors to state both in transitive-verb form: not "to be angry" (a feeling, not an action) but "to make him apologize" (a doable thing). Every beat of every scene has its objective and its action, and a well-prepared actor knows both. The late Uta Hagen, in her book Respect for Acting, spelled the discipline out in nine questions every actor must answer before walking on stage. Asked what she taught students, Hagen said: "I teach them how to read a script."
Breath, body, voice

Acting is a physical craft. An actor who cannot be heard in the back of the room is an actor who is not yet working. Cicely Berry, the Royal Shakespeare Company's voice director for nearly fifty years, trained Judi Dench, Ben Kingsley, and a generation of British stage actors in a voice practice built around breath, rib cage, resonance, and attention to every vowel and consonant in a Shakespearean line. Tadashi Suzuki, working from Japanese Noh tradition, trained the body with a footwork practice that now bears his name. No serious acting school skips the physical training. The body is the instrument. The script is the score.
The American branches

The Group Theatre split in the 1930s, and its students founded three distinct schools. Lee Strasberg's Method, at the Actors Studio, emphasizes emotional memory — the actor drawing on private life to fuel the moment. Stella Adler, who had worked directly with Stanislavski in Paris, rejected emotional memory and emphasized imagination and given circumstances. Sanford Meisner at the Neighborhood Playhouse stripped the work down to the famous repetition exercise and a single principle: acting is living truthfully under imagined circumstances. Al Pacino studied with Strasberg. Robert De Niro studied with Adler. Diane Keaton studied with Meisner. All three are Stanislavski, branched.
Acting is living truthfully under imagined circumstances.

dek: Given circumstances, objectives, and actions — a century-old Russian grammar for behaving truthfully in front of a thousand people.
name: Acting

body.text: Before 1874, theaters had stage managers. After 1874, they had directors. That year the Duke of Saxe-Meiningen brought his ensemble to Berlin with a production of Julius Caesar in which every crowd member had a distinct character, every costume had been researched from paintings, and every piece of stage business had been rehearsed with the same care as the verse. The production was a sensation; the idea — that a single imagination should shape every element of a production — became the modern theater. The director is not an ancient role. It is a recent invention, and still a contested one.
The director invented late

The great actor-managers of the English nineteenth century — Garrick, Kean, Irving — ran their own companies and performed the leading roles, and that was the model until the Meiningen Ensemble toured Europe. By 1905 Konstantin Stanislavski in Moscow and Max Reinhardt in Berlin were working as full-time directors. By 1920 the role was established. By 1950 every serious production had one. The director's job, as it settled, was to unify everything — casting, set, lighting, music, performance — around a single interpretation of the text. Elia Kazan called it "the controlling intelligence of the production." Peter Brook called it "holding the empty space."
Reading the play

A director's first job is to read the play until they know what it is about. Not the plot — the meaning. Kazan, before rehearsing A Streetcar Named Desire, wrote long notes on what the play was "really" about: "the destruction of the last chivalrous civilization by the new barbarism." Every choice in rehearsal then served that spine. A director who begins rehearsal without that clarity ends up arbitrating performances instead of shaping one. Tablework — the first days of rehearsal spent sitting around a table reading the play aloud — is where that clarity is tested, among actors, out loud, in dialogue.
Casting and the tablework

Casting is the largest single directorial decision. Elia Kazan liked to say that casting was eighty percent of directing; Harold Prince said ninety. The right actor for a role brings half the performance already. Around the table, the director reads the play with the cast, asks questions, challenges assumptions, listens. This is not a rehearsal; it is a parliament. A director who rushes tablework and gets into blocking on day two is a director who will relitigate the play in tech week. A director who lingers at the table risks boring the cast. The line between "enough" and "too much" is a professional instinct earned by doing it wrong twice.
Blocking — the director's handwriting

Blocking is where actors stand and how they move through the space. Good blocking serves the story; bad blocking serves nothing. A character who crosses to the window when they decide to leave has made a visual argument. A character who stands still when they should have moved has drained the scene of a choice. Directors block intuitively (Mike Nichols famously said he blocked whole productions in thirty minutes and spent the rest of the time refining) or systematically (Peter Hall mapped the entire play on graph paper before day one). Both approaches work. What does not work is blocking on the fly, without thought, and hoping the actors will cover.
The room and the show

The thing a great director protects is the room — the rehearsal atmosphere. Actors are asked to be vulnerable in public, in front of strangers, for weeks, on someone else's words. A director who mocks, humiliates, or picks favorites destroys the room, and the performance is flat on opening night. A director who holds the room — safe, focused, playful — gets performances no one knew they had in them. Elia Kazan, who was not a gentle man, nevertheless wrote that the director's most important quality was the ability to make an actor feel seen. The show the audience watches on opening night was built in that room, months before.
I can take any empty space and call it a bare stage. A man walks across this empty space whilst someone else is watching him, and this is all that is needed for an act of theatre to be engaged.

dek: Shaping the whole — casting, rehearsing, staging, and holding every choice to the same spine of meaning.
name: Directing

body.text: In a 1954 speech at the Northwestern University centennial, President Dwight Eisenhower attributed to a "former college president" a distinction that would outlive its source: "I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent." The original speaker is lost; the line is now in every productivity book ever written. The reason it survives is that almost everyone, on close inspection, spends most of their day doing the urgent and almost none of it doing the important.
The Eisenhower distinction

Stephen Covey turned the line into a four-quadrant matrix in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People: urgent and important (crises), important but not urgent (long-term work), urgent but not important (interruptions), and neither (waste). His central observation, repeated in nearly every modern productivity framework, is that highly effective people do most of their work in the second quadrant — the things that are important and not yet on fire. Most people do most of their work in the first and third, where the day forces their hand.
The to-do list as a half-solution

A flat to-do list is the productivity tool everyone tries first and almost everyone abandons within a month. The reason is that lists do not distinguish a thirty-second task from a three-month project, and they do not distinguish urgent from important. The fix is layered: a long capture list of everything you might do, a much shorter weekly list of three to five things that actually move important work forward, and a daily list of one or two specific blocks that get the next concrete step done. The discipline is in pruning, not collecting.
Capture, then decide

David Allen's Getting Things Done, the dominant productivity system since 2001, makes one move that almost every other framework borrows: separate the act of capturing what is on your plate from the act of deciding what to do about it. Anything you might do goes into a single trusted inbox. Once a week, you process the inbox into projects, next actions, and someday-maybe items. The cost of switching back and forth between capturing and deciding is the source of most productivity friction; the discipline of separating them is most of the value Allen offers.
Saying no on purpose

The other half of priority management is the part most people will not do: declining things. Greg McKeown's Essentialism makes the case that disciplined no's are what create the conditions for important work. The Stanford computer scientist Donald Knuth famously stopped using email in 1990, on the grounds that being on top of things and getting to the bottom of things require very different cognitive postures. Most people cannot do what Knuth did; everyone can decline a few of the meetings on their calendar this week.

A surprisingly useful question, asked once a week: of everything I did the past seven days, which two or three things will still matter in a year? Almost everyone is shocked by how short the answer is.

dek: Distinguishing what is urgent from what is important is the oldest move in productivity — and the one most often inverted.
name: Priorities
sections: The to-do list as a half-solution

body.text: In 1988, the mathematician Paul Erdős, by then in his seventies, was still doing about twelve hours of mathematics a day. He had no fixed home, no children, almost no possessions; he traveled between universities with a suitcase and worked, with whoever was available, on the next problem. He died in 1996, the most prolific mathematician in history by a wide margin. Erdős is an extreme case of what the Georgetown computer scientist Cal Newport calls deep work — and his career is also the case for why you might want some of it in yours.
Newport's claim

Newport's 2016 book Deep Work argues that the ability to do cognitively demanding work for long, undistracted stretches is becoming both more valuable and more rare. More valuable because the economy increasingly rewards the work that machines and short-attention humans cannot do; more rare because the dominant tools of the modern workplace — email, Slack, the open office — are designed in ways that make sustained focus structurally difficult. The argument is not new; the synthesis is, and the case has held up.
The cost of switching

The psychologist Sophie Leroy coined the term attention residue in 2009 to describe what happens when you switch from one task to another: a fraction of your attention stays behind on the first task for as much as fifteen or twenty minutes. A morning of "just checking email" between tasks is a morning in which no task ever gets the speaker's full mind. Newport's prescription is mostly to refuse the switch — long blocks, single tasks, no inboxes open — but his more practical contribution is the diagnostic: most modern knowledge work is shallow not because it is unimportant but because it has been chopped into pieces too small for anyone's attention to land.
Building the practice

Almost everyone who does deep work for a living protects time the same way: by ritual. Tchaikovsky composed every morning from nine to noon. Maya Angelou rented a hotel room for the day and wrote on a yellow pad. Knuth declined email. The specific ritual matters less than the fact that it exists, recurs, and is defended against the easy interruptions of the day. For most people the right starting move is more modest: a single ninety-minute block in the morning, before the inbox is opened, with the phone in another room. Done daily for six weeks, this single change tends to produce more visible work than any other productivity intervention.
A note on shallow work

Shallow work — email, scheduling, status updates, meetings about meetings — is not in itself a moral failing. It is part of nearly every job. The trouble is that shallow work expands to fill any time available, and most people give it the morning, which is the cognitive prime. The simple inversion — shallow work in the afternoon, deep work in the morning — is most of what Newport recommends. The remaining ten percent is having the conversations with your colleagues required to make that calendar possible.

body.cite: Cal Newport, Deep Work (citing Winifred Gallagher)
body.text: I'll live the focused life, because it's the best kind there is.

dek: Sustained, undistracted focus is the rarest professional capacity left — and the one most worth protecting.
name: Deep Work

body.text: In 1948, the Linde Division of Union Carbide introduced a welding process that fed a continuous wire electrode through a torch while shielding the arc with inert gas. It was meant for aluminum; steel, it turned out, loved it too. Within a decade, the American auto industry had adopted what became known as Gas Metal Arc Welding, or MIG. The process did not require the skill of stick welding or the patience of TIG. It was fast, forgiving, and could be learned in a long weekend. Every car built in Detroit from the 1960s on was held together, in part, by MIG welds.

body.caption: A MIG weld in progress.

body.text: The whole idea

Hold a gun, pull a trigger, wire feeds out, an arc melts a puddle, you drag the puddle along the joint. The machine keeps every parameter constant so the welder can focus on travel speed and puddle size. Learn the sound of a good MIG arc — a crisp, continuous bacon-frying sizzle — and you have 90% of the skill.
Before you start
Tools

A 120-volt or 240-volt MIG machine (Hobart, Lincoln, Miller all make good entry machines at under $700). A bottle of 75/25 argon-CO₂ shielding gas. 0.030 or 0.035 ER70S-6 wire. An auto-darkening welding helmet. Leather gloves. A grinder with a cut-off wheel. Vise-Grip locking clamps. Fire-resistant jacket or apron. Cheap safety glasses to wear under the hood.
Safety

UV from the arc will sunburn exposed skin in thirty seconds and damage eyes in less. An auto-darkening helmet is not optional. Fumes from galvanized steel cause zinc fume fever — use a respirator on coated metal. Ventilate. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.252 is the standard. AWS Safety in Welding is the trade's own guidance.
Words to know

GMAW — Gas Metal Arc Welding (the formal name for MIG). Shielding gas — the inert gas flowing around the arc. Wire feed speed — how fast the wire leaves the gun, in inches per minute. Voltage — sets the arc length and heat. Short-circuit transfer — the low-voltage mode where the wire touches the puddle and shorts briefly; good for thin metal. Spray transfer — high-voltage mode where metal sprays across the arc; faster, for thicker steel. Stickout — how far the wire extends from the tip (typically 3/8").
The machine

Every MIG machine has a wire-feed speed knob and a voltage knob, plus a gas flow meter on the regulator. Inside the door of every quality machine is a settings chart for the wire diameter you are using: find your metal thickness, note the starting voltage and wire speed. That is the starting point; fine-tune by ear and eye.
Running a bead

Hold the gun at about 15° from vertical, pushing or pulling the torch along the joint. Keep 3/8" of wire out of the tip. Pull the trigger: the wire feeds, the arc strikes, a puddle forms. Move at a steady pace — a good bead looks like a stack of dimes or a smooth ripple pattern. The arc should sound like bacon frying. If it pops and spits, turn down the voltage. If it sputters and the wire bunches, turn up the wire speed.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: A flat-position butt weld on 1/8" mild steel: 0.030 wire, 75/25 gas at 25 CFH, voltage around 18, wire speed around 270 IPM. Stickout 3/8". Travel speed about 12 IPM. A clean bead is about 5/16" wide. Adjust voltage for the sound, wire speed for the puddle size. Practice on scrap until the bead is consistent.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Moving too fast. A beginner instinctively hurries; the bead thins, the puddle does not wet into the base metal, and cold laps form (metal piled on top without fusion). Slow down until the puddle clearly flows out to both edges of the joint.
Joints

Five fundamental joints: butt (two pieces edge-to-edge), lap (one over the other), tee (perpendicular), corner (two edges forming an L), edge (two pieces standing upright). Every structure made of steel reduces to combinations of these. Practice each on scrap until the bead reads clean.
Settings, in practice

For mild steel: 0.030 wire and 75/25 argon-CO₂ for anything under 1/4" thick. Pure CO₂ is cheaper but spits more; the 75/25 blend is the working-shop default. On anything over 1/4", move to 0.035 wire and consider spray transfer. On galvanized, expect extra fume and porosity — grind the zinc off the weld zone first.
Troubleshooting

The bead is piled up, not flat. Travel speed too slow, or voltage too low. Spatter everywhere. Voltage too high for wire speed; turn voltage down. Weld is porous. Shielding gas blew away (draft or wind), or the metal was dirty/galvanized. Wire crashes into the plate and bunches. Wire speed too high, voltage too low. The arc is erratic. Bad ground clamp connection; clean the metal where the clamp lands.
Going deeper

After a weekend of mild-steel butts and lap joints, the next steps are out-of-position welding (vertical and overhead), flux-cored wire (for outdoor work where shielding gas blows away), and aluminum MIG (which requires a spool gun or push-pull torch). Jeffus's "Welding: Principles and Applications" is the classroom text; AWS SENSE certification is the national credential.

body.label: Practice this week
body.text: Weld twenty flat-position butt joints on 1/8" mild steel scrap. Cut each in half with a grinder; look at the weld cross-section. The weld bead should wet into both pieces of base metal, with no cold lap. By the twentieth weld, most beginners get a consistent, good joint.

body.label: Self-check
body.text: What sound does a good MIG arc make? (Bacon frying.) What is the typical stickout? (3/8".) Why does galvanized steel cause porosity? (Zinc vaporizes in the arc.) If any stumps you, watch Essential Craftsman "Introduction to Welding."
First project: weld a simple steel frame — four pieces of 1"x1" angle iron mitered at 45° and MIG-welded at the corners. One hour of shop time. You will meet every basic MIG operation in one project.

dek: Wire-feed welding — the process that built modern American manufacturing, and the easiest way in.
name: MIG Welding

body.text: In 1941, engineers at Northrop Aircraft developed a welding process that used a non-consumable tungsten electrode and helium shielding gas, originally to weld magnesium airframes. Seventy-five years later, the same process — now usually run with argon and called Gas Tungsten Arc Welding, or TIG — is the standard for any weld that must be strong, precise, and photographed.

body.caption: TIG and MIG side by side.

body.text: The whole idea

Hold a torch with a sharpened tungsten electrode in one hand. Dip filler rod into the puddle with the other. Control the amperage with a foot pedal. Unlike MIG, nothing is automatic — you are adjusting heat, speed, and filler by hand at the same time. The craft is closest in feel to playing a wind instrument.
Before you start
Tools

An AC/DC TIG machine (Lincoln Precision TIG, Miller Syncrowave, or an inverter like Everlast at budget). A bottle of pure argon shielding gas. Tungsten electrodes (2% lanthanated for most work, pure tungsten for aluminum on older AC machines). Cerium or thoriated tungsten for some applications. Filler rod (ER70S-2 for steel, 4043 or 5356 for aluminum, 308L for stainless). A foot pedal. Same PPE as MIG.
Safety

Same as MIG, plus: tungsten electrodes can break off in the puddle and fly. Grind tungsten with the wheel running along the tip, not across — a cross-grind produces airborne particles. If you use thoriated tungsten, grind only in a well-ventilated area with a dust collector.
Words to know

GTAW — Gas Tungsten Arc Welding. Tungsten — the non-consumable electrode. Filler rod — the hand-fed rod melted into the puddle. Foot pedal — controls the arc current. AC balance — the ratio of positive to negative half-cycles in AC (for aluminum). Back purge — argon behind the weld to prevent oxidation (stainless, titanium). Gas lens — a nozzle insert that produces smoother, more concentrated shielding.
The torch

A TIG torch holds the tungsten electrode in a collet and directs shielding gas around it through a ceramic or glass cup. The tungsten is sharpened to a point for DC (steel and stainless) or balled at the tip for older AC machines (aluminum). Modern inverters run square-wave AC and use a sharpened tip on aluminum too.
Three hands, one puddle

Left hand moves the torch at a steady pace. Right hand dips the filler rod into the puddle and withdraws it, rhythmically, just as the puddle reaches its hottest point. Right foot modulates the pedal — down for more heat, up for less. All three coordinate through the hood at a viewing distance of about eight inches. Beginners try to do everything at once and dip the tungsten immediately, contaminating it. Masters pace their hands and feet like a drummer.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: A carbon-steel butt weld on 1/8" mild steel: DC electrode negative (DCEN), 2% lanthanated tungsten sharpened to a point, pure argon at 15 CFH, pedal amps maxed at about 100. Strike the arc on the starter plate. Walk the arc to the start of the joint. Puddle forms; dip filler. Move forward an eighth-inch; puddle forms again; dip. Repeat. The bead should look like a stack of dimes.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Dipping the tungsten into the puddle. The molten steel contaminates the tungsten; the arc wanders; the weld is ruined. Stop, grind the tungsten clean, restart. Everyone does this their first hundred welds.
Steel

Steel TIG runs on DCEN (electrode negative). Pure argon. ER70S-2 filler. A sharpened tungsten. Amperage sized to metal thickness: roughly 1 amp per 0.001" of thickness (so 1/8" = 0.125" = 125 A max). Pedal-modulate to avoid burn-through.
Aluminum — the hardest common metal

Aluminum runs on AC. The alternating current cleans the oxide layer (half the cycle) and melts the metal (the other half). AC balance — the ratio — is adjustable on modern machines; more cleaning for dirty metal, more penetration for thick. 4043 filler for most work, 5356 for high-strength or anodized applications. Pre-heat thick aluminum; it sucks heat away from the puddle like a sponge.
Stainless — the surface matters

Stainless runs on DCEN like steel, with ER308L or ER316L filler. The challenge is heat: stainless warps easily and discolors at moderate heat. Low amperage, fast travel, back-purge on pipe welds to prevent internal oxidation (the dreaded "sugar"). The finished weld, done right, is the silver color of the base metal, not rainbow-heat-tinted.
Troubleshooting

Tungsten contaminated. Stop, break off the contaminated tip, regrind. Weld is black/crystalline. Not enough shielding gas or too much pressure (gas blowing away from the puddle). Turn CFH down and check cup integrity. Bead is humped. Travel speed too fast — puddle not wetting out. Aluminum won't form a puddle. Metal too thick for amperage, or AC balance too far toward cleaning.
Going deeper

After carbon steel and aluminum, the next domains are stainless pipe with back-purging, titanium (requires elaborate gas shielding), and pulse TIG (current alternates between high and low to control penetration on thin metal). Jody Collier's entire channel is a graduate school on the subject.

body.label: Practice this week
body.text: On a scrap plate of 1/8" mild steel, practice laying down a puddle without filler. Just drag the arc and let the steel flow in place. When you can produce a clean, shiny puddle trail for 6 inches without dipping the tungsten, add filler. Build the hands before you build the bead.

body.label: Self-check
body.text: What current does TIG use on aluminum? (AC.) What does DCEN stand for? (Direct Current Electrode Negative.) What prevents internal oxidation on stainless pipe welds? (Back purge with argon inside the pipe.) If any stumps you, watch Jody Collier "TIG Welding for Beginners."

First project: a small picture frame in mild steel 1/8" flat bar, TIG-welded at the miters. One morning. You will meet pedal control, tungsten handling, and filler timing in a project that is genuinely yours.

dek: The slowest, cleanest welding process — and the one that reveals the welder.
name: TIG Welding

body.text: A stick welder on a windy hillside, welding pipe two hundred miles from the nearest air compressor, is running a process that has not fundamentally changed since 1927. Shielded Metal Arc Welding — SMAW, or stick — uses a consumable electrode coated in flux. The electrode melts to form the filler; the flux melts to form a shielding slag. You need no shielding gas, no wire feeder, no clean workpiece. You need a transformer, a ground clamp, and a stick.

body.caption: The SMAW process: coated rod, arc, slag, weld metal.

body.text: The whole idea

Strike an arc between a coated steel rod and a grounded workpiece. The rod melts into the puddle; the flux coating vaporizes into a shielding gas and forms slag on the cooled weld. You move at a steady pace, maintaining a consistent arc length roughly equal to the rod diameter. That is the entire process. Everything else is variation by rod type and position.
Before you start
Tools

A stick welder (AC or AC/DC; the Lincoln Tombstone AC225 has been in production since the 1960s). Rods — start with E6013 at 1/8" diameter for general work. Leather gloves and jacket. Auto-darkening helmet. Chipping hammer and wire brush. A ground clamp. Lots of scrap plate.
Safety

Same UV and fume concerns as MIG. Additionally: hot slag flies off the weld as it cools — wear long sleeves and keep the collar buttoned. The flux coating of some rods (low-hydrogen 7018s) must be kept dry; moisture in the coating causes hydrogen cracks in the weld. Store rods in a rod oven or hermetic tube.
Words to know

SMAW — Shielded Metal Arc Welding. Electrode — the coated rod, also called stick. Flux — the coating that vaporizes into shielding gas and forms slag. Slag — the glassy coating on the finished bead. Arc length — distance from the rod tip to the workpiece, usually equal to rod diameter. Polarity — DCEP (reverse polarity, electrode positive) for most applications; DCEN or AC for specific rod types. E-number — the rod classification; E6010 is a 60 ksi all-position rod with a cellulose coating.
Electrodes — the whole kit is in the coating

Stick rods are classified by a four-digit AWS number. E6010: cellulose coating, all positions, deep penetration, for pipeline root passes on dirty steel. E6011: AC-friendly version of 6010. E6013: general-purpose, easy to strike, mild steel. E7018: low-hydrogen rod, smooth bead, high tensile strength, required on most structural work. Learn 6013 first (easy), then 7018 (harder but more common in the trade).

body.label: Worked example
body.text: A beginner running a 1/8" E6013 on 1/4" mild steel, flat position: amperage around 110-130, DCEP or AC. Strike by scratching like a match, lift to establish the arc, then lower to 1/8" above the work. Travel at a pace that makes the bead 3x the rod diameter wide (about 3/8" on a 1/8" rod). The bead should be uniform and slightly crowned.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Arc length too long. The bead becomes wide and splattered; the flux cannot shield the puddle adequately. Keep the arc about one rod diameter long. If you hear the arc sputter and hiss, you are too far; if it sticks and goes dark, too close.
Striking the arc

Two methods. The scratch start: drag the electrode across the workpiece like striking a match. The tap start: tap the rod straight down, then lift. Both establish the arc; scratch is easier for beginners. If the rod sticks to the work, bend the electrode holder sharply to break it free.
Running a bead

Hold the rod at 15-30° off perpendicular, leaning in the direction of travel. Maintain arc length. Drag for E6013 and E7018 (most common stick rods); push for cellulose rods like E6010. Travel at the speed that produces a uniform bead — beginners tend to move too fast. Listen: a steady bacon-frying crackle means a clean arc. Pops and spatter mean arc too long.
Reading the slag

After the bead cools, chip the slag with a hammer. A clean weld has slag that chips off in sheets, revealing a uniform bead with regular ripples. Uneven slag coverage or pockets mean travel speed was wrong. Cracks in the slag can indicate cracks in the weld beneath. After slag removal, wire-brush the bead.
Positions

Flat (1G): easiest. Horizontal (2G): moderate; gravity pulls the puddle down, so the bead tends to sag. Vertical (3G): harder; either run uphill (most common) or downhill (faster but shallow penetration). Overhead (4G): hardest; gravity tries to drop the puddle onto the welder. Structural welders must pass qualification tests in at least 2G, 3G, and 4G.
Troubleshooting

Rod sticks to work. Arc went too short; break free and restart with more arc length. Bead is porous. Wet rod (7018 especially) — bake or replace. Slag gets trapped in the weld. Travel too fast; slow down or reduce rod angle. Weld is undercut at the edge. Arc too long or travel too fast. The weld cracks. Wrong rod for the metal, or quench-cooled from high heat.
Going deeper

After flat-position mild steel, the progression is vertical (3G), overhead (4G), structural certification (AWS D1.1), and pipe welding (uphill 6010 root, 7018 fill). Hoobasar Rampaul's "Pipe Welding Procedures" is the bible of the pipeline trade; Bob Moffatt's videos show the technique.

body.label: Practice this week
body.text: Lay twenty flat-position E6013 stringer beads on scrap plate. Chip each, inspect, and note what was different between the clean ones and the sloppy ones. By the twentieth, your bead starts to stabilize.

body.label: Self-check
body.text: What is the typical arc length? (One rod diameter.) Why must 7018 rods be kept dry? (Moisture causes hydrogen cracking.) Which rod is common for pipeline root passes? (E6010.) If any stumps you, watch Essential Craftsman "Stick Welding Tips for Beginners."

First project: weld two pieces of 1/4" flat bar together in a lap joint with E6013 on a cheap stick welder. Chip the slag, inspect, and cut through the joint with a grinder to see the penetration. One hour. Cost under $10 in rods.

dek: Shielded metal arc welding — rugged, portable, and still the process that holds pipelines and pressure vessels together.
name: Stick Welding

body.text: On a limestone hillside in the Côte d'Or, eighty miles southeast of Paris, a single species of grape has been planted and replanted for a thousand years.
